reverse_caption: Keep the height and the outer frame style the same, but stretch the picture horizontally by placing six side-by-side copies of the original interior area inside one enlarged frame. In each copy, every non-background object keeps its exact shape and position within its tile, while its color advances one step through a fixed six-color cycle; the first tile is the original, and the next five tiles are successive recolorings. The background and border colors do not change.

The input is split into several equal-height scenes by solid horizontal divider rows. Across these scenes, a left-hand scaffold stays the same while the pattern in the remaining columns may change; the output removes the divider rows, keeps the first scene intact, and then places the later scenes to its right using only the columns that are not part of the shared left scaffold. In other words, repeated common columns are shown once, and each subsequent scene contributes only its new/right-side content in order; if a later scene adds nothing new, nothing extra appears.

The input contains four same-colored cells marking the corners of a rectangle. The output keeps the same height but triples the width, placing two copies of that corner-marked rectangle: one flush on the left side and one flush on the right side. In the middle gap, it adds a diamond of the same color whose top and bottom vertices lie on the original top and bottom rows and whose left and right vertices lie on the rectangle’s vertical midpoint row; only the key corner/vertex cells are shown, not filled shapes.

Treat each connected non-background figure as a separate object, keeping its shape and any embedded accent-colored cells unchanged. Rebuild the scene by placing these objects side by side with exactly one blank column between their bounding boxes, ordered by vertical position: the object whose top starts lowest in the original grid goes leftmost, and the highest-starting object goes rightmost. Their row placements are preserved, so the change is mainly a horizontal repacking that removes the wide empty gaps.

The grid contains one isolated central anchor cell and some colored marker cells placed only in the corners. In the output, each non-background corner marker is moved next to the anchor while keeping its color: upper-left corner goes above the anchor, upper-right goes to its right, lower-left goes below it, and lower-right goes to its left. The anchor itself stays in place, and the original corner positions are erased so everything else becomes background.

The original grid is kept, including the regular lattice of isolated marker cells on a plain background. A new accent-color pattern is then added across the bottom using the last two marker rows: each motif is a 3x3 block centered on the upper of those two rows, with a wider 3x9 bar directly below it centered the same way. This motif repeats horizontally at a fixed spacing across every fourth marker-column, and if the pattern runs past the right edge, only the in-bounds portion is shown.

The input is made of several same-sized 10×10 copies of one picture placed side by side. These copies are mostly identical, except that some cells in different copies are replaced by a special marker/highlight color.

The output collapses the repeated copies into a single 10×10 grid by superimposing them: keep the common underlying color wherever all copies match, and place the marker/highlight color wherever any copy shows it at that position. In effect, the result is the shared base picture with all highlighted differences from the separate copies combined together.

The input contains up to four same-sized solid blocks placed in the four cardinal slots of a larger square layout: top-center, middle-left, middle-right, and bottom-center. The output keeps the original as the first section, then stacks three more sections underneath it, each the same size as the input and showing the whole block arrangement rotated one more quarter-turn clockwise around the empty center. The canvas width stays the same while the height becomes four times the input height, and each colored block keeps its size and color while moving to its rotated slot.

The small accent-colored pattern in the upper band is erased: its cells are replaced by the surrounding upper-band color, and if that accent pattern dips into the middle band, those dipped cells also become upper-band color. In the middle band, the dark cutout shape is almost complete; the output adds exactly one missing cutout cell at its exposed side to make that lower figure more balanced/symmetric. All other cells, including the bottom border row, stay unchanged.

Each input has a thin vertical marker in one non-background color and a separate irregular shape in another non-background color, between a solid top band and a solid bottom band. The output converts the marker to the irregular shape’s color, then finds the shape’s strongest vertical stem (the column of that shape with the most cells) and extends that stem straight up and down in the same color, filling it continuously from the second row of the grid to the row just above the bottom band. The rest of the irregular shape is preserved.

Each input row is built from several solid horizontal blocks separated by single-column background gaps, and the same pattern is repeated on every row. The blocks use one main fill color followed by a trailing run of another color, with each successive block getting larger than the previous one. The output keeps only the largest/rightmost block and discards the background separators and all smaller earlier blocks.

The grids contain a multicolored motif whose rows are built around a central vertical color, plus some short two-cell marker versions of that motif. In the output, every occupied row of such a motif is extended one cell to the left using the local frame color, so single-center rows become a two-cell pair, three- and four-cell rows gain a new leftmost cell, and the short marker pair is normalized into that same left-extended form. The color used for the new left edge comes from the enclosing region: the upper panel’s solid fill above the divider, or the divider/border color for motifs in the lower panel.

The input is a long horizontal strip made of several equal-sized 5-row panels, separated by full-height divider columns of a distinct empty color. The transformation removes those divider columns, cuts the strip into its 5x11 panels, and stacks the panels vertically in the same left-to-right order. Each panel’s internal pattern is preserved exactly, including any small marker cell in the upper interior row.

The output is made by placing 8 copies of the entire input side by side, forming a horizontal filmstrip. In each panel, all non-blue objects stay fixed, but the blue shape(s) are shifted horizontally through an oscillation: original position, one step right, two steps right, one step right, original, one step left, two steps left, one step left. When the blue shape moves, it can cover whatever is in its new location, and the parts of its original position that are no longer occupied are repainted with the outer background color.

The grid keeps the same height but is stretched horizontally into a longer strip made of repeated equal-width sections separated by full-height one-cell vertical divider lines in the foreground color. If the input already has such a divider, its position sets the section width; if not, the whole input acts as one section, and new divider lines are inserted between repeated sections. Any other foreground shape to the right of the original divider is not copied in full: it is reduced to a single foreground marker placed in the middle repeated section at roughly the same relative row/offset.

The input contains two identical solid horizontal bands, one in the upper half and one in the lower half, separated by a blank horizontal gap and surrounded by the same blank side borders. The output keeps the same height but concatenates several copies of this whole pattern side by side: first the original, then versions where the two bands are progressively shaved by 1 more row from their inward-facing edges (bottom of the top band and top of the bottom band), until they disappear completely. A final unmodified copy of the original pattern is placed at the far right.

The foreground pattern is spread across four equal-width horizontal sections of the input, with each section containing a translated fragment of the same overall design. The output is made by folding those four sections on top of each other into a single section-width canvas and taking the union: any cell that is filled in any section becomes filled in the output at the same within-section position. This preserves the row positions, shrinks the width to one repeat block, and combines all repeated fragments into one overlaid composite.

The output is made by placing five same-sized panels side by side, using the input scene as a template. The first and last panels are full copies of the input, the second and fourth panels keep only the horizontal bar, and the middle panel keeps only the large lower mound/triangle. Inside that middle large shape, the small upper triangle from the input is reproduced upside down at the top of the large shape and recolored with a new highlight color, while all other removed cells become background.

The input is a horizontal strip of equal-sized frames, and the output compresses it back to one frame by overlaying the different versions of the same shapes. Parts of a shape that stay fixed across the shown states remain in the original foreground color, while parts that are present in only some frames (added/removed/extensions of the shape) are recolored with a new highlight color. Fully unchanged objects stay entirely in the original color; changing objects become two-color composites showing their combined footprint.

The input is divided into several equal-width subgrids stacked vertically, with each subgrid separated by a blank horizontal row. Each subgrid has the same header row and a solid bottom stripe, while the inner cells contain that panel’s own pattern. The transformation removes the blank separator rows and reassembles the stacked subgrids side-by-side from left to right, preserving every panel’s contents exactly. The bottom solid stripe from each panel joins into one continuous bottom row in the output.

The input is ignored except for its 4-row canvas size: the output is always expanded horizontally into a 4×16 grid and the original colored cells disappear. A fixed foreground pattern is drawn on the background, with the top row containing one solid block on the right, and each lower row splitting that block into smaller repeated blocks whose widths halve each time. This creates a stepped, self-similar triangular/fractal-like arrangement of foreground cells across the four rows.

The lone non-marker source cell acts as a starting point, and every marker cell is treated as a destination. The output is a horizontal strip of same-sized frames: in each frame the marker pattern is copied unchanged, while the source color has advanced one more step along the discrete straight-line path from the source toward every marker, keeping all previously drawn path cells. So the strip shows the simultaneous construction over time of all source-to-marker connections, concatenated from left to right.

The input contains a hollow-looking frame made of one non-background color surrounding a solid rectangle of another color. In the output, only the frame color matters: each frame cell is expanded by one step in the four cardinal directions, and the union of those expansions becomes the new shape, while the inner rectangle color disappears. This creates a larger rounded-diamond/octagon-like region centered on the same object, sometimes leaving a tiny background gap where opposite expansions do not meet.

The output is made by taking the entire input grid exactly as it is and repeating it horizontally in a row. Eight identical copies are concatenated side by side, so every object, diagonal line, central divider row, and color pattern stays unchanged within each copy. Nothing is recolored, moved, or mirrored; only the canvas width increases by tiling the original scene 8 times.

Take the single large object made of a body color plus embedded marker cells, and regularize it into a solid right-pointing block: fill its whole overall span, removing all internal gaps, so the middle rows become a full rectangle while only the top and bottom rows remain shortened from the original tip column to the right edge. Then place five vertically separated copies of this normalized shape, recolored in a fixed sequence that starts with the original body color and ends with the marker color. The marker cells are preserved by checkerboard parity: markers on one parity appear in copies 1 and 3, markers on the opposite parity appear in copies 2 and 4, and in the final copy the whole shape is the marker color so those markers are absorbed.

The grid is widened by adding a new block on the right while keeping the height unchanged. The added block is an exact copy of the left half of the original image, copied row-by-row and appended to the far right of the existing grid. Nothing inside the original area is modified; only this repeated left-side pattern is added.

The grid contains several horizontal bands of repeated diamond-like symbols placed at fixed center positions, with blank rows separating the bands. In the output, the first two symbols from the left in every band are forced to be the larger diamond version, while every symbol from the third position onward is forced to be the smaller inner-diamond version. The background, spacing, and overall grid size stay unchanged; only the size/template of each repeated symbol is standardized according to its left-to-right index.

The output is formed by cropping the input down to the smallest rectangular region that contains all cells different from the uniform outer background color. Everything outside that bounding box is discarded, while the pattern inside is copied exactly as-is. If the cropped pattern contains holes or interior cells of the same color as the outer background, those interior cells are preserved rather than removed.

A single large patterned shape near the left is preserved, and an identical copy of that shape is added to its right. The position of the new copy is determined by the small marker object on the right: the copy is placed halfway between the original shape and that marker, keeping the same row alignment and exact pattern. The right-side marker and vertical reference line stay unchanged; only the duplicated shape is newly painted into the empty background.

Find the cross-shaped figure whose four arms extend from an empty center, with a different color on each arm. The output makes four side-by-side copies of this same cross on a canvas four times wider, keeping each copy’s shape, arm lengths, and row positions unchanged. In the first copy the arm colors stay as in the input, and in the next three copies the colors are reassigned as if the color arrangement around the center were rotated clockwise by 90°, 180°, and 270°.

The input contains a centered, upward-pointing triangular stack made of one foreground color on a uniform background. In the output, the triangle keeps exactly the same position and row lengths, but its rows are recolored by height: the top single cell stays in the original foreground color, and each lower horizontal layer gets a different color in a fixed top-to-bottom sequence. The background is unchanged, and only the triangle’s internal row colors change.

The input is split into equal vertical panels, each containing the same main emblem: a large filled block with a small hole, plus a small 2x2 marker at the panel’s lower-right. Exactly one panel is different because it has extra small attachment cells around the emblem; the output keeps only that panel and discards the others. Within the kept panel, the main emblem, background, and 2x2 corner marker stay the same, while the attachment cells are recolored: most of them become one highlight color, but the attachment cells in the row directly beneath the emblem’s footprint become a second highlight color, forming a short base.

The output places four copies of the entire square input side by side: the original, then a 90° counterclockwise rotation, then a 180° rotation, then a 90° clockwise rotation. In each copy, one cell of the main foreground region is changed to a new highlight color: specifically, the region’s extreme outward tip in the original picture (the rightmost cell on the middle row), with that same tip moving to the top, left, and bottom in the rotated versions. All other cells, including the background and the second foreground region, are preserved by the corresponding rotation.

The output is made by stacking two copies of the input vertically. The top half is unchanged, while in the bottom half the dark/black connected pattern is redrawn upside-down within its own bounding box: its row structure is vertically mirrored, and cells it leaves behind revert to the plain background unless another object already occupies them. In this mirrored copy, the new top row of the dark pattern is drawn as one continuous horizontal bar from its leftmost dark cell to its rightmost dark cell, which closes any small gap there.

The grid contains a fixed structure: a vertical spine crossing a horizontal bar near the top, with a few accent cells attached immediately to the spine’s right side. The spine, top bar, and background stay unchanged; only those right-side accent cells are edited. Any accent that is a lone single cell stays where it is, while any vertical stack of two or more adjacent accent cells is removed and replaced by one single accent cell at the bottom of that same right-adjacent column.

The input grid is made of three identical vertical sections placed side by side, with the same background and the same small foreground pattern repeated across the width. The output keeps only one of these repeated sections, effectively cropping the grid to the leftmost third while preserving all rows unchanged. In other words, remove the duplicated copies and retain a single original tile.

The input contains the same horizontal scene repeated several times down the grid: a small marker block near the left and one or more larger foreground shape pieces, with full-background spacer rows between copies. The transformation keeps the full width and extracts a single repeat unit from the topmost copy, removing the extra top margin and all duplicate lower copies. Any blank row that belongs inside the repeated unit is preserved, but separator-only rows between units are not.

The input consists of several identical picture panels repeated side by side, separated by single blank columns. The output collapses these repeats into one panel: keep the shared panel pattern exactly once, using the leftmost panel’s size and appearance. Any isolated marker pixels that appear outside the repeated pattern are transferred into this single panel according to their row and their within-panel column position, and they are recolored to a new highlight color; if multiple markers land on the same spot, they simply coincide.

The input contains several foreground diamonds of different sizes on a uniform background. The rule is to identify the largest diamond and treat it as the template, ignoring the smaller diamonds. The output keeps the same height as that largest template and builds a new wide image by repeating that diamond horizontally five times, flush next to each other on the same background.

The grid has a repeating column pattern: full-height separator columns of one color appear at a fixed interval, and the other non-background color appears as a partial motif made of a horizontal bar on one row plus some incomplete vertical columns. The output completes this motif across the whole repeating structure by extending every column containing the motif color to full height and by copying the horizontal bar left and right with the same period. Separator-color cells are preserved as blockers on that row, so the replicated bar passes through all other cells but does not overwrite separator cells unless that separator was already absent there.

Each scattered marker dot is turned into a downward zigzag trail: the original dot disappears, then on each lower row the trail alternates between the dot’s column and the column just to its right, starting with the down-right cell. These trails continue through empty background until they hit the edge or an existing non-background structure, and all trails are overlaid together. The cross-like object, the horizontal bar above the bottom, and the solid bottom row remain unchanged.

The output keeps the same height as the input but expands the width by repeating the entire input pattern horizontally four times. Equivalently, each row is copied side-by-side four times in the same order, so every foreground block and background gap reappears unchanged in each repeated section. No recoloring, rotation, or vertical duplication occurs.

First simplify the picture: each cross-shaped object is reduced to just its central cell, while lone single cells disappear; the long horizontal bar at the bottom is kept unchanged. Then take this simplified grid and repeat it as three identical copies stacked vertically, so the output has the same width as the input but triple the height.

The output keeps every cell pattern exactly the same, but extends the grid by placing a second identical copy of the entire input directly underneath the first. In other words, the full input image is duplicated vertically, preserving all colors, holes, and small markings in the same column positions. Nothing is recolored or rearranged inside the original pattern; only a full-height vertical repeat is added.

The picture contains three independent structures: a small set of guide dots in the upper left, one horizontal bar, and a central marker with one or more matching satellite markers. The horizontal bar is extended by exactly one cell on its right end. Around the central marker, take one existing satellite’s offset and rotate that offset 90° counterclockwise to place an additional satellite; the original markers stay in place. The upper-left guide dots are kept as they are, except that a dot may be added in the position corresponding to this newly introduced direction if it is missing.

The input consists of two identical pictures placed side by side, with a single vertical separator column in a distinct marker color between them. The transformation removes that separator and discards one duplicate copy, leaving just one of the repeated halves. All colors and internal patterns within the kept half stay unchanged.

The input is a wide strip made from several adjacent square panels placed side by side; the panel width matches the grid height. The output keeps only the leftmost square panel exactly as it is and removes all panels to its right by turning those cells into background. In other words, the transformation crops out the first repeated tile while preserving the original overall canvas size.

The picture is made of four 5×5 symbols separated by single blank columns, and the output keeps those symbols in the same order while extending the strip to the right with two more 5×5 symbols. The two diagonal/K-like symbols are copied unchanged, but the symbol shaped like an upward-opening wedge loses its bottom horizontal bar, and the symbol shaped like a downward-opening wedge is reduced to just its top horizontal bar. After the original four-symbol strip, two fixed extra symbols are appended: first a small sparse slanted fragment, then a symbol consisting only of a top horizontal line.

The brown cells form a large symmetric hollow frame, and the output redraws that same frame one cell inward on every side, creating a smaller inset version of it. The blue cells are the interior pattern carried into this shrunken frame: their arrangement is compressed/redistributed to fit the reduced space while keeping the same general structure and symmetry, and stray blue cells outside the main framed region disappear. Everything else remains background.

View the input as a coarse array of same-sized colored rectangles, separated by background gaps. The output is made by placing several copies of this whole array side by side; in each copy, a single wraparound descending diagonal (top-left to bottom-right in the copied layout corresponds to moving one row down and one column left among the tile positions, with wraparound/shift) is erased to background, while all other tiles stay unchanged. Across the successive copies, this erased diagonal is cyclically shifted so that all possible placements of that diagonal mask are shown.

The only changed area is the patterned strip near the top. In that strip, every cell of the repeating zigzag/alternating color is recolored to the same color as the scattered marker cells already present below it, while the alternating gap cells inside the strip are turned into a new highlight color; separator cells stay unchanged. That highlight color is also added one row above the strip’s top row and one row below its bottom row, but only in the columns where the zigzag-color cells were converted, while the lower rectangular blocks and all other cells remain unchanged.

The input grid is divided into two equal horizontal halves. The output is made by overlaying the top half onto the bottom half row by row, so the result has the same width but only half the height. For each paired cell position, any non-background mark from either half is kept in the output, preserving its color, while cells stay background only if both halves are background there.

The input is a vertical stack of repeated hollow outline shapes, each containing a short horizontal marker bar on one row inside the shape. The transformation makes the canvas twice as wide and places a second identical copy of that whole stacked arrangement directly to the right of the original, preserving the spacing, outlines, and marker bars while leaving the background unchanged.

The input contains a slanted container or frame made of one dominant border color, surrounded by empty background. The output removes the outside background, then rectifies this trapezoid-like shape into a straight rectangular panel whose width matches the container’s bottom edge and whose height matches its full vertical extent. Each row inside the frame is horizontally expanded to that full width, preserving the left-to-right order of the interior motif colors, so the slanted sides become vertical borders and the inner colored marks appear stretched across the row.

Treat the picture as a horizontal strip of square panels, each panel being as wide as the grid is tall. These panels are consecutive frames of a 4-step cycle: a small 2x2 marker moves from panel to panel by a displacement that turns 90 degrees counterclockwise each time, and the surrounding two-color motif advances in the same frame sequence. The output keeps the given panels unchanged and appends the missing next panel(s) on the right until the strip contains four panels total.

The output places three horizontal copies of the scene side by side: the original pattern on the left, a derived version in the middle, and the original again on the right. In the middle copy, every non-background cell is merged into a single new color, and the picture is split by its central empty horizontal row: cells above that row are shifted one step upward, while cells below it are shifted one step downward, widening the central gap. The topmost and bottommost rows are thus lost from this middle copy, and any vacated space becomes background.

The input is a tiled pattern of identical vertical panels separated by background lines, where each panel contains the same fixed top-to-bottom stack of colors repeated in horizontal bands. The output is a horizontal strip of many copies of the whole grid, one copy for each input column. In each copy, everything stays the same except possibly one panel: if the scanned column is the first filled column of a panel, that panel’s color stack is shifted up by one cell; if it is the second filled column, that panel’s stack is shifted down by one cell; otherwise the copy is unchanged.

Each puzzle starts with one or more thin vertical rails made of a dominant line color, with a few cells on those rails replaced by a second accent color. The output keeps those original rail cells, then expands them into wider patterns by drawing short horizontal bars and diagonal connectors in the empty space around and between neighboring rails. Where rails agree, the dominant color forms the connecting shape; where the accent-color positions create offsets, that accent color is propagated along the corresponding diagonal/zigzag parts of the connector.

The input contains multiple copies of the same small motif: a short horizontal bar with one distinguished cell in it, plus two markers above it. Elsewhere, isolated cells of another color appear below some copies, each aligned to one particular column of that motif’s bar. The output compresses everything into a 2-row strip whose width is the motif bar’s length, and places a single isolated cell in the leftmost bar position that is never used by any of those aligned cells; all other output cells are background.

The solid rectangular block of the third color is the anchor: it keeps the same size and stays in the same place in the output. Ignore that block by treating its cells like empty space, then shift the entire remaining pattern (the filled region and the holes/cutouts) one cell down and one cell right with wraparound at the grid edges. Finally, place the unchanged inner rectangle back on top in its original position.

The input consists of several equal-sized panels arranged side by side and separated by full-height divider columns. Each panel has the same left small block and right small block, but the larger middle block changes color from panel to panel. The output removes the divider columns and collapses the repeated panels into one panel-sized grid that keeps only the cells common to every panel, so the invariant side blocks remain and the varying middle region becomes background.

The grid is expanded horizontally into three equal-width panels. The left and right panels are exact copies of the original input, while the center panel is a left-right mirror of the input, so each row appears as original, reversed, original. Any solid horizontal divider line is simply continued straight across the full new width, and background cells remain background.

The input is a tall stack made from repeated copies of the same smaller horizontal scene, with blank rows separating the internal subparts. The transformation keeps the width the same but crops away the redundant lower repetitions, outputting just one full repeating unit: the topmost complete copy of the pattern. All objects, colors, and their positions inside that kept unit stay unchanged.

The output is a horizontal strip of successive snapshots of the same picture. Starting from the original grid, the colored shape(s) are shifted left by one cell at each step while keeping their rows unchanged; anything that moves past the left border is clipped away, and the background stays empty. These snapshots are then placed side by side, so the result is a wide image showing the object sliding left across repeated frames.

Each input has a uniform background, a full-width horizontal band near the top, a small solid rectangular patch of a different color, and several isolated marker pixels scattered elsewhere below. The output keeps the background, the top band, and the rectangle unchanged, removes all of the scattered marker pixels, and places a single marker pixel inside the rectangle at a fixed spot: one cell down and one cell right from the rectangle’s top-left corner.

Treat the wide input as several equal square panels placed side by side, where each panel has the same height as the whole grid. Collapse these panels into one square output by stacking them on top of each other cell-for-cell, using the background as transparent. When more than one colored pixel lands on the same cell, a fixed color priority is used: the side/outer color wins over the broad filler color, which wins over the accent/highest-priority-looking central color.

Each input has one foreground shape on an otherwise empty grid; that shape is treated as a partial trace/shadow of a larger solid square region. In the output, the implied square is completed and filled uniformly, expanding mainly upward and sideways from the given trace, while any original foreground cells that stick out below the completed square are kept as they are. So the sparse stepped outline becomes a dense filled block of the same foreground color.

The output overlays a fixed pixel-art stencil onto the noisy grid, using the single rare marker color already present in the input. This stencil is centered in the board and consists of three separate horizontal bands, each 5 cells tall, with one blank row between bands; the top and bottom bands are narrower, while the middle band is the widest, and the same internal on/off pattern is reused in every example. Any cell covered by this stencil is repainted to the marker color, overwriting whatever was there, while all cells outside the stencil stay unchanged.

The grid is split into equal-width vertical panels by the repeated fixed motif in the bottom rows; that lower motif stays unchanged and serves as a divider/template. In the upper part, each panel contains a small pattern made from the two non-background colors, and the sequence of these panel-patterns contains one pair of identical neighboring panels. The output cyclically reorders the upper panel-patterns so that the second panel of that identical pair becomes the first panel, with the remaining panels following in the same wraparound order, while all fixed background/template cells remain as they were.

The input is made of several equal-width copies of the same picture placed side by side, forming horizontal panels. The output collapses these repeated panels into a single panel of the original tile width. When corresponding cells differ between copies, the result keeps the value that is repeated/consistent across the copies, so stray mismatching cells are corrected while the main shape and background stay the same.

The picture is split by color into four separate layers. Build an output canvas with double the input height and double the input width, then place each non-background color alone in its own quadrant, keeping every cell in the same relative position it had in the original grid: the outer frame-like color goes to the upper-left, the alternating companion frame color to the upper-right, the inner stroke color to the lower-left, and the innermost accent color to the lower-right. All other cells in each quadrant become background.

The large solid-colored region is split into vertical compartments by one-cell-wide divider columns. Find the one compartment that contains no special colored shapes or markers inside it; that compartment is the only "plain" section. In the output, that compartment is shifted down by one row relative to the outer background: its cells on the top edge are replaced by the surrounding background color, and the same-width strip is added on the bottom edge directly below it in the region’s base color.

The input contains several separated copies of the same outlined shape, all built from the same border/frame color and aligned in the same way. Each copy carries different extra markings inside the frame or along one row/edge; the output removes the duplicates and keeps just one copy-sized crop, using the shared frame as a template. Onto that single template, the distinctive non-frame markings from all copies are superimposed in their corresponding positions, so the result is one composite version of the repeated shape.

The grid is turned into a vertical stack of four same-width copies, so the output is 4 times taller while the dominant fill and the empty right-edge strip stay unchanged. The only changing object is the short accent-colored vertical segment next to that empty strip: copy 1 is unchanged, copy 2 moves one interior cell of the segment one step inward into the main field, copy 3 moves the segment’s bottom cell one row downward, and copy 4 places the whole segment one row lower than in the original.

The non-background cells are treated as fragments of a fixed centered template: three nested hollow square frames inside the grid, with the very outer border of the grid left unchanged as background. In the output, those square perimeters are completed at their proper offsets, so the sparse input pieces become full ring outlines. Any fragment keeps its color and location on its ring, and that color is extended along the corresponding perimeter segment; if only one color is present, all three frames are completed in that color, while multiple colors divide the completed frame segments between them.

The output keeps the grid’s full height but reduces its width to exactly one third of the input width. It does this by cropping out the leftmost third of the columns and discarding the remaining columns on the right. All colors and row structures inside that retained left section stay unchanged.

The output widens the canvas and places two transformed copies of the same large symmetric figure side by side, with a single blank separator column between them. First, the special marker that sits at the middle of the figure’s right outer edge is moved horizontally inward onto the figure’s central vertical spine, staying on the same row. Then the left copy is a left-right mirror of this adjusted figure, while the right copy is a top-bottom mirror of it.

The grid has a repeating four-color diagonal background, plus one large solid rectangular block in a different color and some marker cells that stay fixed. The output stacks four full copies of the input vertically; in the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th copy, that block-shaped region is repainted with each of the four background colors in cycle order. Where the examples show an overlapped placement cue, the recolored block is used in that same offset relationship (leaving any uncovered strip of the original block visible), while the rest of the scene remains unchanged.

The input is made of repeated 3-row horizontal color bands, with blank separator rows between them. Each new 3-row block overlaps the previous one by its last two rows, so together the blocks encode one longer ordered sequence of solid-color rows. The output removes all separator rows and merges the overlapping blocks into that single continuous list, keeping the first block and then appending only the new final row from each subsequent block.

The input is a noisy or incomplete representation of one or more alternating two-color checkerboard layers, where different layers use different square sizes. The task is to identify the checker sizes present in the input, then rebuild each one as a clean full grid of the original width and height, preserving the alternating phase seen in the example. These reconstructed checkerboards are then stacked vertically in layer order, going from the outer/smaller-scale pattern toward the inner/larger-scale pattern and back symmetrically when the input has symmetric nested layers.

The input contains a single isolated marker cell in one color and a separate set of cells in another color arranged as a diagonal line slanting down-left. The transformation deletes the entire diagonal object while leaving the lone marker untouched in its original position. Nothing else is added, moved, or recolored; the background simply fills the removed diagonal cells.

The grid is mostly preserved: the large hollow frame on the left, the long vertical divider, and all other scattered shapes stay where they are. The only change is that each highlighted cell sitting on the vertical divider is expanded into a small 3-column patch of the same highlight color centered on that divider, so an isolated seed becomes a side/full/side motif across three rows, while adjacent seeds merge into a taller merged patch. The divider’s original color remains visible in the center column wherever that cell was not itself a highlighted seed.

The full-width bar and any matching full-height bars act as dividers, splitting the input into equal subpanels. The output keeps only one panel’s width, removes the vertical divider columns, and overlays the repeated outline-colored fragments from all panels in aligned coordinates so they combine into a single more complete shape. Any small non-background, non-outline marks are preserved only from the leftmost panel, while corresponding marks from the other panels are discarded; the horizontal divider row remains across the output.

The grid is divided into vertical panels by narrow separator columns, and each panel contains the same small multicolored figure near the bottom on a uniform background. In the input, some cells inside each figure’s local 3×3 footprint are still separator-colored/empty, even though they are enclosed by the figure. The output changes those internal empty cells to the surrounding background color, effectively solidifying/cleaning each small figure, while the true separator columns and all other parts of the grid stay unchanged.

The input is a tall grid made by vertically repeating the same two-color pattern, but one of the repeated copies is corrupted by an inserted strip of a third, standout color. The transformation discards the repeated stack and keeps just one intact instance of the pattern: the clean top block above the corrupted/marked section. The width and cell arrangement of that surviving block stay unchanged.

Split the wide input into four equal square panels laid side by side; the output has the same height and the width of one panel. The two busy colors that fill most of the input act as noise, while the true picture is the sparse pattern made from the background color plus the small accent/center marks, repeated across the panels with partial corruption. Reconstruct a single clean square by taking the non-noise marks from the repeated panels at their matching coordinates and placing them on a uniform background-color field.

The two matching cells near the top act as starting points for two mirrored diagonal traces of that same color. These traces go downward while moving inward toward each other; once they meet in the middle, they continue downward while moving outward again, forming a symmetric hourglass/diamond pattern clipped by the grid edges. The single special cell near the bottom center changes to a different highlight color, while the other lower marker cells remain as they are unless the new diagonal pattern passes over them.

The input consists of four equal-width copies of a row-patterned scene placed side by side, so the output keeps the same height but shrinks the width to one quarter. To make the output, align those four vertical panels and merge them into one: for each position, keep the panel’s ordinary row background color unless any panel places a foreground mark there, in which case that mark appears in the merged cell. In effect, the repeated panels are overlaid into a single composite panel, so scattered or partial shapes from different copies combine into one complete shape.

The grid is cut vertically into its natural repeating slices, as indicated by the repeated narrow column-patterns in the large middle band and the matching sparse marker columns above and below. A trailing right-hand suffix that does not belong to the reusable left pattern is removed, and the remaining left portion is copied unchanged a second time immediately to its right. No colors are remapped; the transformation is purely a horizontal crop-then-duplicate of the repeating structure.

The output is formed by rotating each row of the grid one cell to the right. In every row, the item at the far right edge wraps around to become the new far-left cell, while all other cells—including background and the repeated colored pattern pieces—shift right by one position. The grid size and all colors stay the same; only this horizontal cyclic shift occurs.

The input is divided into five equal-width vertical color stripes. In the output, these stripe colors are reorganized into a new layout whose band thickness equals one stripe width: the leftmost input stripe becomes a full-width top band, the middle input stripe becomes a full-width bottom band, the fourth stripe becomes a left block in the middle section, and the second stripe becomes a right block in the middle section. The remaining fifth stripe fills the entire central area between those two side blocks, spanning the full height of the middle section.

The upper 5-row strip is a fixed binary template made of several small glyphs separated by blank columns, and the lower strip is a recolored, partially drawn continuation derived from that template. In the output, the top template is left unchanged, while the lower colored pattern is completed to the right in the same 4-column-by-4-column progression, forming a descending staircase/snake with any missing horizontal runs or two-row transition pieces filled in. In short, the bottom shape is an incomplete copy/trace of the top code, and the task is to finish that trace.

The grid contains a full-width horizontal bar in one color, some shorter horizontal bars of that same color, and a separate blob-like figure in another color. In the output, each shorter bar of the line color is slid horizontally to the right until its right end is flush with the grid’s right border, while keeping its row and length unchanged. Bars that already touch the right edge stay where they are, and the other-colored blob and the full-width bar are unchanged.

The input is made of two identical copies of the same picture placed side by side horizontally. The transformation removes the redundant duplicate and keeps just one copy, producing a grid with the same height but half the width. All internal objects, colors, and their positions within that single remaining panel stay unchanged.

The output keeps the original grid unchanged on the left, but extends the canvas to twice the original width. The new right half is a copy of the left half shifted one cell to the right inside its own section: a background column is inserted at the start of that half, and the rightmost column of the copied section is dropped. As a result, the vertical non-background bars appear again in the right half, offset by one cell and separated from the original pattern by background space.

The input is split into four equal vertical panels, each showing the same large stepped mound/triangle on a uniform background. The output keeps only one panel-width and reconstructs the shared prototype of that repeated figure by comparing the four copies: preserve the common stepped foreground shape in its main color, but remove the small isolated marker pixels above it and correct any odd-colored defect pixels embedded in some copies back to the figure/background pattern.

The input is a wide strip made of several repeated horizontal blocks on a uniform background; each block contains a left shape outlined in one accent color with a second accent embedded in it, followed by a right shape built around a filled core. The output keeps only the rightmost such two-shape block, cropping away all other repeated copies. Inside that kept block, the highlighted cells in the left shape are regularized into one clean continuous stroke that fits the figure (removing any extra bit sticking above it, or extending the stroke by one missing step), while the right shape stays unchanged.

The output is a horizontal filmstrip made by placing several same-sized copies of the input scene side by side, each copy showing the next stage of a rightward motion. The key moving part is the uniquely colored cell/column inside the 3-row rectangular block: at each frame it advances one step to the right, and any cells it leaves behind turn into background, so the block may first appear to slide right and then open a gap behind the moving marker. The separate right-side guide structures (the horizontal bar and any vertical barrier) stay fixed in the same local position in every frame, and the number of frames is exactly the number of rightward steps shown.

The non-background cells form a roughly symmetric hollow figure with an outer boundary already indicated by side posts and one or more horizontal bars. In the output, the enclosed central area of that figure is made solid: every background cell inside the span between the left and right sides and between the upper and lower bars is filled with the figure’s color. The exterior background and the figure’s outer outline remain unchanged.

The non-background cells form a horizontal sequence of small motifs, each with its own main color and the same small accent structure. The output keeps the original picture on the left, then extends the canvas to the right by reflecting the sequence across a vertical axis through the rightmost motif: that rightmost motif stays in place as the center, and all motifs to its left reappear on the right in reverse order with identical shapes and spacing. Only the mirrored copies are added; nothing else changes.

Each non-background shape is given a one-step southeast "shadow" in the special marker color. Concretely, every occupied cell generates marker-color copies immediately to its right, immediately below, and diagonally down-right, while the original cell itself keeps its original color if it belongs to some other object. Cells already in the marker color therefore just expand into thicker 2x2-based blobs, and when these shadows overlap they merge.

Treat the input as consecutive 4-row blocks, each containing one cell on the right, one in the middle, one on the left, and another in the middle. For every such block, make four 2-cell excerpts in this fixed order: (top cell + bottom cell), (third-row cell + bottom cell), (second-row cell + third-row cell), and (top cell + second-row cell), keeping each copied cell in its original column. Stack all excerpts from all blocks vertically in those four batches, and insert an empty row between every output row, so the width stays the same while the height is expanded.

The scattered foreground blobs are isolated, each blob being a centered diamond/pyramid-like shape on the plain background. The output turns the whole strip into equal square panels, adds a new border color around the outside and between panels, and places one blob in each panel on the original background, centered within the panel (cropping only if a blob is larger than the panel interior). The blobs are reordered by size so that the smallest ones go at the two ends and sizes increase toward the middle, with the largest blob in the center, creating a left-right symmetric sequence.

The input is made of several narrow panels placed side by side, usually separated by blank columns; each panel shows the same basic figure but some copies are shifted, partially altered, or contain stray extra colored marks. The output compresses these repeated panels into a single panel by keeping the consensus version of the main structure at each corresponding position, preserving the shared vertical stem and middle motif while removing outlier shifts and incidental noise colors. In short, it extracts one cleaned prototype from multiple noisy horizontal repeats.

The output is made by stacking four blank copies of the original canvas vertically, creating four same-width panels of the input’s height. In each panel, only one extracted/normalized foreground shape is kept: cells of the original object pattern are preserved in the same color while the rest becomes background, and the kept parts are shifted into a compact standardized placement within that panel. Different inputs can yield four different extracted shapes, or the same extracted shape repeated in all four panels.

The input contains several non-background fragments, but the only part kept is the large rightmost cluster: a broad region of the dominant non-background color that may contain a few cells of a second accent color inside it. The output is formed by cropping away everything to the left of the last full empty vertical separator, so the frame starts at that separator’s right side and extends to the original right edge while keeping the full original height. The kept region’s internal pattern and colors are unchanged; only the left-side fragments are discarded.

Each input has a mostly uniform background, one full-width guide row in a different color, a compact rectangular target block near the right side, and several unrelated horizontal segments in a third color. The output keeps the same width but is vertically cropped down to the short horizontal band centered on the target block, preserving the rows between that block and the nearby guide row (including the guide row when it lies inside the retained band). The scattered horizontal segments of the third color are not carried over unless they share a kept row with the target area.

The tall input is made of several repeated horizontal bands, each with the same arrangement: a solid 4-by-3 block on the left, a short vertical 3-cell strip nearby, and a fixed small motif on the right. The output crops the grid down to just the first such band from the top, keeping the same width and the band’s full vertical span. Within that retained band, the left rectangular block is recolored to a single new uniform color, the nearby vertical strip is recolored to match the main color used in the right motif, and the background plus the right motif stay unchanged.

The input consists of two identical copies of the same pattern placed side by side in the left and right halves of the canvas. The transformation removes the duplicated right half and outputs only the left half of the grid, preserving all cells there exactly. In other words, the result is a vertical crop to one repeated panel.

The output is made by placing four transformed copies of the entire input side by side, so the height stays the same and the width becomes four times larger. The four panels are the original picture, the picture rotated a quarter-turn counterclockwise, the picture rotated half-turn, and the picture rotated a quarter-turn clockwise. When a rotation would swap height and width, it is centered into the original frame size, with excess cropped or empty space padded by background.

Each input has a solid vertical bar in one color, plus a single marker cell of another color attached immediately to its left on one specific row. The output keeps the bar and marker in place but widens the grid to the right; on the marker’s row, it draws a horizontal stripe starting just to the right of the bar that alternates marker-color, background, marker-color, background all the way to the new right edge. All other rows remain unchanged except for the added background space.

The input is divided into several equal-width candidate panels separated by a vertical divider color. In each panel, the same two motifs appear on the same background structure: a small upper symbol and a larger lower stair-step symbol, but the larger symbol is placed at different offsets from panel to panel. The output is exactly the one panel where the lower symbol is in the closest valid position relative to the upper symbol—effectively the best-aligned/just-about-touching arrangement—while all other panels and the divider columns are discarded.

The output is made by stacking four same-width copies of the scene vertically, so the final grid is four times as tall as the input. In the first block the objects stay unchanged; in the next three blocks, each non-background connected object is rotated in place within its own tight bounding box by 90° counterclockwise, 180°, and 90° clockwise, while keeping the bounding box’s top-left position fixed. The background stays empty, and all objects are transformed independently before being combined back into each stacked section.

The non-background drawing is made of several colored motifs in separate horizontal zones, plus special zero-colored bars and a final bottom row containing zeros followed by a terminal strip. The output crops away the unused far-right background and rebuilds the scene on a taller blank canvas by extracting these motif-zones as intact pixel patterns and restacking them into separate horizontal bands/snapshots, so that some bands show only a subset of the original left-to-right motifs while preserving their internal shapes and relative ordering. The zero regions are also pulled out into their own horizontal bands, and only a small remnant of the bottom terminal strip is kept near the upper right.

Each non-background object is extracted and shifted so that its own bounding box is aligned to the same top-left anchor position. The shifted shapes are then superimposed on one another on an otherwise empty background, so overlapping or nested patterns merge into a single composite figure. In the output, every kept cell is shown in one common foreground color, and all original separate objects elsewhere in the grid disappear.

Identify the single compact multicolored block and separate it from the rest of the grid, which is mostly background plus scattered single-cell marker dots. The output is a vertical stack of copies of the original grid with that compact block erased to background; the number of stacked copies matches the block’s width. Across those copies, the scattered marker dots stay fixed, while a few extra marker dots are added in each copy to encode one vertical slice (one column) of the removed block.

The input is a horizontal strip of identical framed panels, each with the same border and mostly uniform interior, but with a small accent-color pattern embedded in the lower part. The output keeps all existing panels unchanged and appends one more panel of the same size on the right. This new panel is formed by continuing the left/right cyclic horizontal progression of the lower accent pattern seen from panel to panel in the input, with the motif wrapping around when it reaches a side.

The transformation deletes every object made of the same recurring highlight color—the one appearing as small horizontal pairs, 2×2 blocks, and short vertical/horizontal fragments in the upper scene. Those cells are turned into background, while all other colored structures, including the multicolored motifs and the lower checkerboard region, stay exactly unchanged.

The grid contains a dominant background, one or two meaningful colored shapes, and a third color that acts like an unwanted overlay or marker. The transformation removes every cell of that marker color and replaces it with the background, while leaving all other colored shapes exactly unchanged in position and form. This includes isolated marker cells, diagonal runs, and even full horizontal marker bands.

The input contains several identical foreground motifs stacked vertically, separated by empty background rows and surrounded by empty background columns. The transformation first crops one motif to its tight bounding box, removing all blank border space, and then builds the output by stacking that cropped motif vertically with no gaps. The number of stacked copies in the output is one more than the number of motif copies visible in the input.

Each non-background color is treated as a fragment of a larger canonical shape and is completed in place. The two block-like colors are expanded to solid rectangles covering the full span suggested by their outermost cells, the corner/frame-like color is completed into a larger filled square with a single hole at its center, and the small accent-colored fragment is expanded into a 3x3 patch near its original position. When these completed shapes overlap, the accent patch overrides its neighboring rectangle, and the square-with-center-hole overrides the adjacent rectangle on its right.

The input contains a hollow rectangular frame in one solid color and, elsewhere, a separate one-row multicolored strip. Read the strip from left to right and take its first segment whose length matches the inner width of the hollow frame. In the output, that segment is copied as a new 2-row rectangle by repeating the same sequence on two consecutive rows, placed in empty space down and to the right of the frame, while the original frame and original strip stay unchanged.

The grid is extended only in height: the right-hand solid background rectangle is repeated unchanged, while the patterned left section is turned into four stacked blocks of the original height. Those four blocks are the same diagonal/checker wedge shown in the input, then its corresponding versions for the other directions (as if the wedge were reflected/rotated around the implied square corner structure). When the left pattern is symmetric, these stacked variants can look identical; otherwise each block shows a different orientation of the same staircase-like motif.

Identify the smallest square region centered on the non-background figure, keeping both the figure and the alternating horizontal stripe pattern inside that square. Make four full-grid panels: in each one, paste that square back into the same place after rotating it by 0°, 90°, 180°, and 270° respectively, while leaving the rest of the striped background unchanged. Then concatenate the four panels from left to right.

The input is a vertical stack of identical small framed panels separated by blank background rows, where the panel’s three inner rows are repeated and later panels show incremental edits to the interior sequence. The transformation treats these stacked panels as a progression over time: it keeps only the lowest (latest) panel state and removes all earlier copies. The output is a shortened grid containing that final framed panel in the top panel position, with all remaining space left as plain background.

The colored shapes are treated as separate motifs ordered from top to bottom in the input, while preserving each motif’s exact color and internal geometry. The output keeps one copy of the original arrangement, then adds new copies where those same motifs are rearranged into an evenly spaced horizontal lineup in the original order, a vertically reordered stack in reverse order, and another horizontal lineup in reverse order. In every added arrangement, only the positions change; the motifs themselves are unchanged.

The output turns the single scene into a 4-panel horizontal strip: the whole input grid is copied side by side four times, preserving the background, the left stair-like trace, the small solid rectangle, and the vertical guide line near the right edge. Across these panels, the small paired-marker object near the rectangle is animated along a diagonal/stair-step path suggested by the trace; as it passes the rectangle, it can overwrite some of that rectangle’s cells before continuing into lower rows. In short, the rule is “repeat the scene four times as successive frames, with only the paired moving object changing position from frame to frame.”}

The wide input is made of several side-by-side repetitions of the same design, mixed with incomplete copies of it on alternating blocks. The transformation keeps exactly one complete repeated block and discards the other horizontal repetitions, preserving the block’s internal background margins and foreground shape exactly. In effect, the output is a single tile of the repeated pattern rather than the whole repeated strip.

The input consists of four equal mini-grids placed side by side, all showing the same basic framed shape but in different main colors, with some extra pixels added as noise. Use the repetition to find the stable pattern: keep the parts of the leftmost mini-grid that match the shared structure, and also keep any accent pixels that appear in the same relative position in all four copies. Any pixel that appears only in some copies is treated as a stray intrusion and removed, so the output is a cleaned version of the first panel only.

The grid is divided into equal-height horizontal panels, where each panel’s height matches the grid width, so the input is a vertical stack of square subgrids. The output keeps the full original stack unchanged, then appends a vertically mirrored continuation made from the earlier panels in reverse order, excluding the last panel. As a result, the panel sequence becomes a palindrome from top to bottom, while every panel’s internal pattern and colors stay exactly the same.

The two main non-background trail colors are transformed together: every cell of the first trail color moves one square left and becomes the second trail color, while every cell of the second trail color also moves one square left and becomes the first trail color. The small auxiliary marker colors do not swap; they are shifted one square diagonally up-left instead. If a moved marker lands where the shifted/swapped trail already goes, the trail color occupies that cell and the marker is effectively hidden.

The scattered clusters in the outline color are treated as incomplete silhouettes: each cluster is completed into a solid filled shape, turning the sparse edge-like pattern into a dense inward-facing blob/trapezoid. A separate full-height vertical strip exactly three cells wide is then drawn through the middle of the grid in a new color. The marker-color cells are preserved when they stay outside those filled shapes, but any marker cells that lie in or interact with the middle strip remain as marker-colored patches inside that otherwise newly colored strip.

The tall input is divided into equal square panels stacked vertically. Each panel shows the same motif—made of a large central shape plus smaller accent cells—rotated 90 degrees from one panel to the next. The output keeps only one panel: it is the next rotation in that sequence, i.e. the first panel rotated by 90 degrees once for each stacked panel (wrapping around every four turns).

The input consists of several equal-height horizontal panels stacked vertically, each panel repeating the same overall layout of small marker shapes while the main larger filled shape may use a different color. The transformation crops away all lower panels and keeps only the topmost panel exactly as it appears, preserving all of its objects and background unchanged.

The input consists of three equal-width panels placed side by side, each with the same small base pattern on the lower active row(s) and a different shifted fragment above it. The output collapses these three panels into a single panel by aligning them and taking the union of the upper fragment cells. The shared lower motif is kept as it is, while all cells belonging to the overlaid upper fragments are recolored into one single highlight color.

The large grid is divided into equal framed panels, each containing a smaller multicolored motif in its inner blank area. Panels are compared by the structure of that inner motif, ignoring the specific palette and allowing rotated versions to count as the same; later repeated motif-types are discarded while the first occurrence is kept. The output is then rebuilt from the remaining full panels, including their frame/background, packed together in reading order as a smaller composite image.

The input contains a small, centered diamond-like marker: an outer ring in one non-background color surrounding a darker inner cross, with a single background cell at the exact center. In the output, that outer color is expanded symmetrically into the largest possible filled diamond centered at the same point, reaching the grid borders at the middle of each side. The darker inner cells disappear, and every cell inside the large diamond becomes the outer color except for the one central background cell, which stays unchanged.

The input is a hollow square frame with one border color on the top and bottom edges, a different border color on the left and right edges, and an empty interior. The output repeats this whole square four times side by side: 1st and 3rd copies stay in the original orientation, while 2nd and 4th copies are rotated by 90 degrees, which swaps which border color appears horizontally versus vertically. The inside cells remain unchanged in every copy.

The grid is divided into several same-sized horizontal panels by full blank separator rows. The output keeps all existing panels unchanged, then adds one more blank separator row and appends an exact copy of the first (top) panel at the bottom. Each copied panel preserves all internal objects and their positions exactly.

The input is a stack of similar panels separated by a full divider row; the output keeps only the top panel above the divider. In that kept panel, focus on the small shape at the left: overlay it with the corresponding left-hand shape from the first panel below the divider, so the shape becomes the union of both footprints. Cells belonging to the lower panel’s version are recolored to a new highlight color, while any cells that belong only to the top panel’s original shape keep their original color; the rest of the panel stays unchanged.

The entire input grid is copied vertically three times to make an output that is three times as tall but the same width. The top and bottom copies stay exactly the same as the original, while the middle copy keeps the same object shapes and positions but changes every foreground mark from the original object color to a different highlight color. The background remains unchanged in all three sections.

The output keeps the grid the same size and preserves the exact pixel pattern, but swaps the roles of the two colors everywhere. Every cell of the foreground color becomes background, and every background cell becomes the foreground color. No objects move, resize, or change shape; it is a full color inversion of the entire binary image.

The background stays unchanged, while each foreground object is regularized according to its shape. Any isolated horizontal bar is extended two cells further to the right. Any corner-shaped object made of a top horizontal arm and a left vertical arm is completed into a hollow rectangle by adding the matching right side and the matching bottom side, keeping the original top and left edges in place.

The non-background pattern is mostly preserved, but any solid horizontal bar is rotated into a vertical bar of the same color and same length. The new vertical bar is centered on the original bar’s midpoint and placed within the corresponding row band, while existing diagonals and existing vertical lines remain unchanged. The output keeps the same height and adds a large blank background extension to the right.

The grid is mostly unchanged, but a second full-width horizontal bar is added using the same color as the existing full-width bar near the bottom. This new bar is drawn on an otherwise empty background row somewhere above the small colored shapes, so that the collection of shapes becomes bracketed between two identical horizontal separators. All other bands and small objects keep their original colors and positions.

The small two-color foreground cluster is expanded into a diagonal trail across the whole grid: the motif is repeatedly echoed in successive offset positions, preserving which cells belong to the lighter foreground color versus the darker foreground color. The original pattern stays in place, and the output is the superposition of these repeated shifted instances, clipped where they would extend past the grid edges.

The input contains a uniform background with one special horizontal stripe that spans the full width of the grid. In the output, the grid layout and position of that stripe stay exactly the same, but the stripe’s color is changed to a new highlight color while the background remains unchanged.

The grid is re-formatted by cutting the input into consecutive 12-column vertical slices and stacking those slices one above the next. The first 12 columns become the top half of the output, and the next 12 columns become the bottom half, while all colors and internal pixel patterns are preserved exactly. Any extra columns beyond these two 12-column sections on the far right are ignored.

The input is made of several equal-sized picture panels placed side by side, with each panel separated by a vertical strip of blank cells. The transformation removes the blank separator columns and keeps only the far-right panel. That chosen panel is copied exactly into the output, with all internal colors and structure unchanged.

The grid is divided into repeated sections, each containing the same larger patterned object, plus fixed corner markers and scattered single-cell specks. Compare the vertical positions of those larger objects across sections, find the one that already sits highest, and move every other matching object straight upward so all of their top edges align to that same row. Everything else stays in place, except any specks that fall under a moved object are covered, and the object's old location is erased to background.

The output is made by placing five horizontal copies of the entire input grid side by side, preserving the same tiled wall/background pattern and the same fixed marker cells. The only nontrivial changes happen inside the small multicolored structure near the center: each copy shows the same structure in a different stage of a short animation, where the small side protrusion(s) shift position or disappear and the middle bar is partially emptied/rearranged in the last stage. In other words, the result is a 5-panel horizontal sequence of the original scene with the central gadget evolving from panel to panel while the rest of the grid stays the same.

The background-colored divider lines stay fixed, so the grid remains split into the same horizontal rectangular compartments. For each compartment, inspect its non-background cells and find the color that occurs most often; then repaint the entire compartment as a solid block of that color. If several colors tie for most frequent, the chosen one is the tied color that appears first when reading that compartment from left to right.

The input is a solid field cut by one full horizontal line and one full vertical line of the other color, forming a cross. In the output, the whole original grid is repeated side-by-side several times, so the height stays the same but the width grows by horizontal tiling.

These repeated copies are then masked symmetrically: for rows near the top and bottom, some central tiles are replaced entirely by the cross color, while rows closer to the middle keep more copies. This creates a horizontally centered diamond/hourglass-shaped band of the cross color, and the original full horizontal divider becomes a single full-width line across the enlarged grid.

The picture is divided into equal vertical panels laid side by side on a uniform background. Each panel contains one of two fixed multicolor motifs: one motif uses a small upper feature, a larger lower mass, and a sparse marker column in one palette, while the other panel type is the corresponding motif in a different palette and layout. In the output, every panel is replaced by the opposite motif template in the same panel position, and all untouched background cells stay the same.

The input contains a single symmetric diamond-like blob on an otherwise empty canvas. The output is made by stacking multiple full-size copies of the canvas vertically; in each copy, the blob is replaced by one concentric version of itself, shrinking by removing one outer layer at a time from the original down to the smallest 3-row diamond, then growing back through the same intermediate sizes. The object keeps its color and horizontal position in every stacked panel, while all other cells remain background.

Identify the unique center marker and the one-sided colored arm attached to it: moving outward from the center, there is a run of one arm color followed by a short terminal block of a second color. Use that outward sequence as a template to build a full four-direction cross centered on the marker, copying the same pattern left, right, up, and down. Existing segments are kept, and missing directions are filled so the cross is rotationally symmetric, with the terminal color always at the far ends of each arm.

The grid contains one large main object and two smaller detached clusters of the same original color. The main object is left unchanged, while each detached cluster keeps its exact shape and position but is recolored: the higher cluster becomes one highlight color, and the lower cluster becomes the other highlight color. In effect, the task labels the two satellite pieces by vertical order.

The input consists of many identical rows, each repeating the same left-to-right color sequence. In the output, those repeated rows are turned into a vertically symmetric left-aligned staircase: the top row keeps only the first color, each lower row reveals one more color from the shared sequence until the middle reaches the full sequence, and then the visible prefix shrinks by one color per row. All cells to the right of the kept prefix are replaced by the background color.

The output places four copies of the entire input scene side by side, making the grid four times wider while keeping the same height. Each copy is the whole input rotated by a different quarter-turn about the canvas center, covering all four orientations (0°, 90°, 180°, 270°), with colors unchanged. When the arrangement or the motif is symmetric, some panels look identical; when it is not, the objects shift or flip between horizontal and vertical forms.

The grid keeps the background unchanged while recoloring the entire sparse patterned figure made of the main foreground color into a new output color. Any cells of the second foreground color that sit directly edge-adjacent to that figure are treated as part of it and are recolored the same way, effectively filling interruptions inside the shape. All other cells of that second foreground color, when isolated from the figure, remain unchanged.

The grid’s geometry stays exactly the same: all objects keep their shapes and positions, including the black region and the filled shape pieces. The only change is a recoloring of the widespread surrounding field color into a new highlight color, while the black cells and the other foreground/object color are left untouched.

Treat the grid as three side-by-side square panels, each as wide as the grid is tall. The output appends a fourth panel on the far right that is an exact copy of the leftmost panel, while the middle two panels remain unchanged. In other words, the pattern of foreground cells and contrasting marked cells from the first square block is duplicated at the end.

The foreground shape is decomposed column by column from left to right. For each input column, make a new block with the same height as the original grid, copy that column’s foreground/background pattern into only the leftmost column of the block, and leave all other cells in the block as background. Stack these blocks vertically, so the output height becomes the input height multiplied by the input width while the width stays the same.
