The left-side figure made from the dominant foreground color is thickened and regularized: gaps between nearby foreground cells are filled so the shape becomes more solid and continuous. Newly filled cells that belong to the body/interior of this enlarged figure take the same foreground color, while newly added cells that lie on the outside edge of the expansion are marked with a different highlight color. Other pre-existing colored cells, including the small marker colors and the separate right-side bands, are preserved in place.

The input contains two separate rectangular mosaics made from the same main fill color, some accent cells, and several contrasting marker cells, with a small 3-cell bar beneath each one. Compare the two mosaics and keep the one that has more of the contrasting marker-color cells. The output is a horizontal crop containing only that chosen mosaic and its matching 3-cell bar below, while all other columns—including the other mosaic and the gap between them—are removed; the row positions and empty rows stay the same.

The input contains several small pictures stacked vertically, each surrounded by the same solid border color and separated by bands of that same border color; any blank columns outside this framed area are irrelevant. The transformation cuts out each picture’s interior by removing the surrounding frame, then places those interior grids next to one another from left to right in the same top-to-bottom order they appeared in the input. The interior patterns themselves are copied unchanged, including their background cells and colored shapes.

The input is a very wide grid containing repeated copies of simple one-cell-thick line patterns in a single source color: a full middle horizontal line, one or more full vertical lines, and sometimes diagonals slanting in each direction. The output compresses this into a square whose size matches the input height, keeping just one centered canonical copy of each pattern type: the middle horizontal line, the middle vertical line, the top-left to bottom-right diagonal, and the top-right to bottom-left diagonal. Repeated instances are merged, and the surviving line types are recolored by role so different directions/features use different output colors.

The input contains several full-width horizontal bars of one non-background color, separated by background-only rows. The output keeps this original pattern, then appends a series of copies of the same row structure: in each appended copy, every full-width bar stays unchanged, but each formerly empty row is replaced by a single cell of the bar color placed in one fixed column. These appended copies sweep that single-cell column from left to right across the grid, one column per copy.

The output keeps the same height but triples the width by placing three horizontal copies of the whole input side by side. The left and right sections are exact copies of the original grid, while the middle section is its color-inverted version: every background cell becomes the single foreground color, and every foreground cell becomes background. This is done row-for-row across the entire canvas, so sparse marks turn into a negative image in the center band.

The wide input is made of several equal-width panels placed side by side; the output compresses these repeated panels into a single panel of that width while keeping the full height. For each cell position inside the panel, compare the corresponding cells across all repeated copies: if every panel has the same non-background color there, keep that color in the output; if the panels disagree, replace that position with background. As a result, unchanged repeated shapes remain, while varying marker corners or altered cells are erased except for any parts that are common to every copy.

The wide input grid is folded horizontally into a square whose width equals the input height. Each marked cell keeps its row, but its column is reduced modulo the grid height, so columns separated by one full grid-height stack onto the same output column. The output is the overlap/union of all these folded copies, leaving a single square image of the marked pixels.

The long input grid is split into several equal square panels placed side by side. These panels show the same background-colored canvas with a foreground-colored symmetric shape, but the outer panels are only partial/clipped copies while one central panel contains the complete figure. The output removes the repeated side panels and keeps just that single full square pattern.

The output is formed by stacking four same-width panels vertically, each panel having the original input’s height. The first panel is the input unchanged, and the third panel is the same scene except that the small patterned object just left of the full-height divider is flipped vertically in place. The second and fourth panels are transformed versions of the first and third: the solid block on the divider’s right is cut down to only its top square cap (keeping as many top rows as the block is wide, and clearing the rest below), and the nearby small motif is reduced to its 3-row core and pushed one step into/across the divider.

The nonblank part of the grid is split into four consecutive horizontal bands, each with its own texture/background pattern and embedded colored objects. In the output, each band is translated horizontally to the right by a different amount: the top band shifts by 1 cell, the next by 2, the third by 3, and the fourth by 4, with wraparound at the left/right edges. All colors and internal arrangements inside a band stay the same relative to each other; only their band-wise cyclic horizontal position changes. The empty rows below remain unchanged.

The input is made of large solid rectangular regions of a few colors. In the output, each straight horizontal change between one region and the region below is replaced by a 45-degree staircase: the upper region keeps a stepped triangular wedge that descends to the right, and the lower region fills the complementary wedge underneath it. As a result, rectangular blocks are turned into interlocking diagonal/triangular bands, and when a block sits above plain background, that same descending staircase continues into the background area.

The colored cells form a row of equally spaced rectangular glyph-objects on a large background, with each glyph made from a solid body plus a small internal hole pattern. The output leaves every existing glyph unchanged and fills the blank slot at the far right with one more glyph, chosen to continue the visible repeating sequence of glyph types and vertical offsets across the row. In other words, the pattern is extended by one final tile into the last available position.

The input contains a mostly empty background, a single marker cell near the upper right, and a small staircase-shaped cluster near the lower right. The output keeps the same width but extends downward by stacking repeated copies of this whole right-side motif, preserving the marker/cluster geometry and letting repeated copies overlap into a continuous vertical pattern.

The number of stacked repetitions depends on how far the marker sits from the right edge: if the marker is farther left, more repeated bands are created. Aside from this vertical expansion and repetition, the background stays unchanged and the non-background cells keep their original roles and relative arrangement.

The non-background cells form a rectangular patch containing two colors. In the input, the left side already shows an alternating checkerboard pattern between these two colors, while the remaining cells in the patch are mostly filled with just one of the colors. The output completes the checkerboard across the entire rectangle, recoloring those uniform trailing cells so every row and column continues the same alternation established at the left edge.

The input is a single horizontal bar, and the output turns it into a larger same-colored comb/zigzag structure built around that bar. The bar is extended horizontally on one side, and then short vertical prongs (about three cells tall) are attached at alternating positions along the bar, alternating above and below it. The direction of the horizontal extension is chosen so the expanded figure fits the available surrounding space.

The input is a horizontal strip made of several equal-size square panels placed side by side. The transformation cuts the grid into these square panels, preserving each panel’s internal pattern and colors, and then restacks them vertically in the same left-to-right order. Nothing inside a panel changes; only the overall layout changes from one row of panels to one column of panels.

The grid keeps the same height but is stretched horizontally into a much wider canvas, with the background color filling all new space. The original foreground-dot motif is then repeated across this wider canvas in several horizontally separated copies: one copy stays at the far left, one at the far right, and additional copies appear between them as the motif shifts sideways by one cell per row, producing inward-facing diagonal/symmetric bands. In other words, the output is a horizontally expanded, tiled-and-slid version of the same sparse pattern, preserving the original spacing of the marked cells within each copy.

The grid contains two separate non-background objects made from a main color with contrasting tip/edge cells. In the output, these two whole objects exchange positions: the left object is translated to the right object's location, and the right object is translated to the left object's location, while each object keeps its exact internal shape, orientation, and colors. Everything else stays as background.

Each input has two key patterns: a solid horizontal bar in the top row and several identical lower rows made of evenly spaced single cells. In the output, the grid keeps the same height but becomes much wider, using the top bar’s length as the horizontal expansion factor; every lower patterned row is turned into a 2-row band, while the original top bar row itself disappears. In each band, the upper row is recolored to a new highlight color and shows the lower-row spacing pattern replicated according to the top bar, while the lower row keeps the original color and shows the top-bar pattern replicated according to the lower-row cells; all other cells stay background.

The wide input contains several separated copies of the same foreground pattern on a uniform background. Some copies are plain, while others include an extra strip in a third color along one side; that strip indicates that the true pattern is shifted within its local frame (for example up, down, or sideways), and the strip itself is not part of the final shape. The output shrinks to a square canvas and overlays all copies into one common position, keeping only the foreground cells that all copies share in common after those shifts are accounted for; all other cells become background.

The full-width horizontal separator and the short horizontal block beneath it are turned into a 3-row motif. The separator shifts up by one row, the row containing the lower short block is filled across with a new accent color while keeping that short block unchanged, and the row immediately below receives a copy of the short block in the separator’s color. All other cells, including the separate short block in the upper area, stay unchanged.

The shape of the grid does not change at all: the vertical divider and the horizontal band structure stay fixed, and no cells move. Instead, the puzzle applies a global color substitution, cycling the active colors so that every instance of one color is replaced by the next color in a palette order, while the divider color stays unchanged. In some examples this cycle also swaps the two large band/background colors on the left; in others those large bands remain as they are, but the right-hand mosaic is still recolored by the same uniform palette shift.

Inside the solid rectangular panel, keep the scattered marker cells and the short horizontal base strip near the bottom, while leaving the outer noisy background unchanged. From each marker, draw a descending staircase path toward the center column of the base strip: each step goes one row down and shifts one column horizontally toward that center until aligned, then continues straight down. Newly drawn path cells use ordered trail colors to show increasing step distance from the marker (first step, second step, then base-reaching/later steps), and if multiple paths would cover the same panel cell, the shorter-distance trail color is what remains.

The grid is built from several vertically stacked copies of the same small cross/T-shaped template, with repeating full-width patterned rows acting as separators rather than part of the answer. One color serves as a temporary scaffold/placeholder inside these templates, while the other colored cells are clues; the output combines those clue placements to form the resolved final pattern, removing the separator rows and discarding the placeholder color. In the simpler example where the repeated template is already concrete everywhere, this same resolution appears as turning the whole scaffolded pattern into the single final foreground color.

Each non-background object is a concentric square made of an ordered stack of ring colors plus a center cell. The three input objects are the same pattern under successive cyclic shifts: from one object to the next, the previous center color becomes the new outer ring and every other ring moves one step inward. In the output, the three given objects are cropped and arranged left-to-right on the top row, and a second row is added containing the next three cyclic shifts, completing all six possible rotations of the ring/color order.

The output is made by stretching the picture into four equal-width panels placed side by side, as if showing four time-steps of the same scene. In each panel, the large uniform separator/header rows stay unchanged, while the non-uniform horizontal bands are vertically advanced from one panel to the next: the upper band containing the solid strip and blob-like shape is scrolled through its rows, and the lower band below the blank separator likewise cycles its patterned rows. Thus the result is a horizontal sequence of row-shifted copies of the original bands, with wrapping inside each active band but unchanged solid divider rows.

The output keeps the same rows but stretches the picture horizontally by placing many side-by-side copies of each input row, one copy for each column of the original grid. In rows that contain only the background and the two main colored regions, each copy is identical; but in rows containing the extra accent color, those accent cells shift one step to the right in each successive copy, wrapping cyclically within the row while the other cells stay fixed. This turns the accent-color interruptions into an animation-like horizontal sweep across repeated copies of the original scene.

The input is a sequence of equal-width picture frames placed side by side, with the uniform strip along the bottom acting as a separator that is discarded. The transformation collapses this strip of snapshots into one frame-sized image that represents the final/latest scene: it keeps the arrangement from the last frame (including the special colored marker when present) rather than the earlier repeated copies. In effect, repeated earlier states are removed and the output is the single resolved end-state image, with the moving shape appearing in its final position.

The input contains one irregular foreground drawing made of a single non-background color, sometimes with an unrelated full-width horizontal divider elsewhere in the grid. In the output, the drawing keeps exactly the same shape and position, but every cell of that drawing is recolored to a different foreground color. The background stays unchanged, and any separator line is removed by turning it into background.

The output keeps the same height but stretches the scene to four times the width by placing four copies of the original canvas side by side. In the 2nd and 4th positions, the small multicolored motif is copied exactly as it appears in the input; in the 1st and 3rd positions, that motif is modified by shifting its small standout marker cells by one square into adjacent background spaces, with the 1st copy using one direction pattern and the 3rd copy using the opposite pattern. The background color stays unchanged everywhere else.

The output keeps the same height but stretches the grid to four times its original width by placing four identical copies of the entire input side by side. Every cell pattern is repeated in the same left-to-right order, so any foreground shapes and background areas reappear unchanged in each quarter of the output. If the input is uniform, the result is simply a uniformly colored grid that is four times wider.

The non-background cells form repeated 3-row motif bands on a plain background. In the output, the canvas is expanded to four equal-width panels placed side by side, and each original motif band is copied into all four panels with the same internal shape and horizontal pattern. The only change is vertical placement: each copy is shifted up, down, or left unchanged by one row in a repeating staggered/zigzag phase, so the bands appear to ripple diagonally across the four panels while the rest stays background.

The grid is divided into horizontal spans by full-height divider columns, and each span contains the same vertical motif: a main stem with a few small colored side attachments at fixed rows. In the output, the divider-and-motif sequence is extended by one more span to the right, adding one new divider column and one new copy of the motif. The motif placements inside the spans are adjusted into a stronger zigzag: after the first copy, successive copies are shifted alternately one cell left and one cell right within their spans, and the newly added last span repeats the first copy’s placement.

The output is made by placing four horizontal copies of the entire input scene side by side, so the grid becomes four times wider while heights and object layouts stay the same within each copy. In each copy, the small scattered marker shapes and the secondary-colored part of the large central composite object may be recolored, while the large object's main/base color is preserved. Specifically, the 2nd and 4th copies keep the original colors, the 1st copy changes both the markers and the large object's secondary region to one new highlight color, and the 3rd copy changes the markers to another highlight color and the large object's secondary region to a different matching highlight.

The grid contains a large solid rectangle of one dominant color running through the middle columns, with narrower side bands of background and marker cells on the left and right. The transformation does not alter any row internally; instead, it cyclically shifts the row order downward, moving the last k rows to the top, where k is the width of the side band before the central solid block begins. In other words, the amount of row rotation matches the horizontal thickness of the non-central border region.

The wide input is made of three horizontal repetitions of the same motif, so the output compresses these repeats into a single copy, reducing the width to one third while keeping the same height and background. Within that retained motif, each small corner-shaped 3-cell object is reoriented so that a single-above-pair shape becomes a pair-above-single shape, while the isolated marker cell remains a lone cell in the corresponding part of the pattern.

Each input has two solid 3×3 reference blocks on the left: one near the top and one near the bottom. On the right there is a hollow rectangular frame whose upper-left corner is marked with the top reference color and whose lower-right corner is marked with the bottom reference color; in the output, these two marked corners are expanded inward, with the area just above the frame copied downward into the top of the rectangle and the frame color pushed left/up from the lower-right side as an inward L-shape. Small remnants of the two marker colors appear along these inward fronts, positioned according to the horizontal spacing between the two left reference blocks, while all other cells stay unchanged.

The output is made by placing three same-sized panels side by side, so the width becomes three times the input width while the height stays the same. The left panel is the original grid unchanged; the middle panel contains the entire non-background drawing rotated 90 degrees counterclockwise, and the right panel contains the same drawing rotated 180 degrees, each surrounded by background in a same-size canvas. The relative arrangement of the separate foreground parts is preserved within each rotated copy, so a small piece that was below the main shape moves to its rotated position (for example, to the right in the middle panel and above in the right panel).

The input contains several horizontally repeated copies of the same small motif on a uniform background; the output keeps just one copy-sized window (the leftmost repeat region), preserving the motif’s horizontal bar in its original object color. The special marker column that appears in the repeats at different vertical offsets is merged into this single kept motif: the marker occurrence above the bar is changed to the bar’s color, the marker on the bar’s row is recolored with a new highlight color, and the marker occurrence below is recolored with another new color. In effect, the repeated variants are collapsed into one canonical motif that summarizes all three vertical marker positions.

The input is split into three equal vertical panels: the two outer panels contain the same small foreground shape, while the center panel contains that same shape expanded by one cell in all directions. In the output, these panels are rearranged into a vertical stack. The top two stacked copies show the small shape, but every cell that belongs to the expanded center version and not to the small shape is recolored with a highlight color, making the added one-cell border visible; the bottom copy is just the original small shape on the background.

The two larger same-colored shapes define a horizontal repeat interval, and the output extends the canvas to the right by one more such interval. A third copy of that large shape is placed at the new position, continuing the left-to-right spacing pattern.

The smaller marker-colored shapes are also adjusted: the horizontal marker beside the left instance is shortened by removing its rightmost cell, and the vertical marker beside the right instance is shortened by removing its top cell. That shortened vertical marker is then copied again beside the newly added third large shape.

Each non-background object is a horizontal run on its own row, with different rows containing runs of different colors and lengths. In the output, every such run is extended straight to the right, keeping its original row, left endpoint, and color, until it reaches the grid’s right border. Background cells and empty rows remain unchanged.

The whole input grid is copied three times side-by-side, preserving the same row structure, divider lines, and spacing. The left and right copies stay unchanged, while in the middle copy every filled block inside the compartments is recolored to a new highlight color, with the background and the thick frame/grid lines left the same. The result is a horizontal triptych: original pattern, recolored version, original pattern.

The input contains a solid rectangle in the upper field, sitting above a horizontal divider line, and sometimes a matching lower rectangle already exists beneath it. In the output, that upper rectangle is copied to the horizontally mirrored position on the opposite side of the grid, keeping the same size and height. A second copy is then placed directly below this new upper copy by shifting it downward by exactly its own height, and this lower copy is recolored to the lower-object color, even if it overlaps the divider row.

The input contains a small symmetric motif: several identical outer pixels arranged around one distinct center pixel, with everything else as background. The output keeps the same height but turns the picture into a horizontal strip of 12 side-by-side copies of the whole input grid. In the first 6 copies, the pattern is unchanged; in the last 6 copies, only the single center pixel changes to a new color while all surrounding pixels and background stay the same.

The picture contains one or more outlined shapes drawn in a single foreground color on a uniform background. The shapes do not move or change form; instead, any foreground cell that lies on every third row of the grid (rows 3, 6, 9, ... from the top) is recolored to a second marker color, creating horizontal stripe-like highlights through the existing figure. All other foreground cells and the background stay the same.

The output is formed by placing five same-sized panels side by side, each panel having the same height and width as the input. The 1st, 3rd, and 5th panels copy the input silhouette exactly, while the 2nd and 4th panels are right-aligned triangular/staircase masks in the foreground color: one grows by one cell per row from top to bottom, and the other shrinks by one cell per row in the opposite progression. The background stays unchanged elsewhere.

The input is a horizontal sequence of equally spaced motif slots built from the same scaffold: a vertical line pattern above and below, and a central crossbar row. Most slots contain distinct inner symbols, but one slot type appears as the repeated/plain template at both ends (or as the duplicated motif among the set). The output extends the canvas to the right by one more full slot and copies that repeated template motif into the new rightmost position, along with the matching vertical scaffold around it.

Inside the fixed outer border, there are two active structures: a vertical line of one color, and a small motif made of a 3-cell horizontal bar with a single cell of another color centered directly above it. In the output, that single upper cell is expanded sideways into its own 3-cell horizontal bar, aligned exactly over the lower bar. Separately, the vertical line is erased except for its bottommost cell, and from that bottom cell a down-right diagonal staircase of the same color is continued until it touches the border.

The large connected shape is the only structure that matters; the smaller scattered marks are removed. A new highlight color is then placed in the background cells immediately outside the large shape’s perimeter, forming a dotted outline that follows its full outer contour, including slants and step-like edges. This outline uses every other available perimeter-adjacent cell, creating an alternating/checkerboard-style border around the shape.

The output is formed by transposing the whole input grid onto a new canvas: each input row becomes an output column, and each input column becomes an output row, with one extra row added at the top. The transposed picture is copied exactly in the lower part of the output, keeping the background color and all dark shape cells in their new swapped coordinates. In the new top row, a single marker cell is placed above the center column of each connected dark object from the input (which corresponds to that object's center row after transposition).

The input is divided into four equal rectangular quadrants, with similar frame-like vertical border patterns repeated in each section. The output is simply the lower-right quadrant of the input: cut the full grid in half horizontally and vertically, then keep only the bottom-right quarter. This selected quarter is recognizable because its top row contains the two special marker cells, and all cells inside it are copied unchanged.

The grid is divided into several equal-width vertical panels laid out side by side on a uniform background. Each panel contains the same kind of shape pattern, but drawn in a different foreground color. The output performs a one-step cyclic shift of these panels to the left: every panel moves into the position of the next one, and the leftmost panel is moved to the far right. The internal pixels of each panel stay unchanged; only the panel order changes.

The input is split into several equal square panels laid side by side, and the output is a single square panel of that size made by comparing corresponding cells across all panels. Any non-background symbol that appears in the same location in every panel is kept unchanged, while the positions of one wandering marker type are unioned across panels and recolored into one new highlight color, and the positions of a second wandering marker type are unioned and recolored into another new highlight color. Other symbols that do not occur consistently in all panels are discarded, unless their cell is taken by one of the two highlighted unions.

Find the large solid-colored horizontal band and treat the background-colored cells near its top as the key template positions, repeated across equal-width horizontal sections. In the output, the differently colored marker cells are removed and replaced by a standardized motif tied to those template positions: the holes are reproduced lower in the band, and in the taller example a marker is also placed one cell above-right of each reproduced hole. If the input contains extra repeated horizontal sections, the output keeps only the canonical repeated portion of the band.

The input is a tall 2-column strip containing several identical marker cells in the right column, separated by blank rows. In the output, the grid keeps the same height but widens, and those marker cells are repositioned along a descending diagonal so that the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, etc. markers appear at rows 2, 4, 6, ... and columns 2, 4, 6, ... . In each blank row immediately below a marker, a horizontal 3-cell bar is added starting at that marker’s column; these bars use successive auxiliary colors, while any bar that would extend past the right edge is omitted.

The input is a wide image made of three equal subgrids placed side by side, each with the same background and internal divider columns. The output is obtained by cropping out and keeping only the rightmost subgrid exactly as it appears, including its small colored staircase/diagonal figure and the bottom-left bar. Nothing inside that chosen subgrid is altered; the other two subgrids are simply discarded.

The picture is split into three side-by-side 9×9 motifs built from the same diagonal diamond/X outline. The output cleans up these motifs by completing any partial attachments on the upper half into solid, regular wedge-like triangular fills: the left motif remains the plain outline, the middle motif becomes the outline plus a completed wedge on its left side, and the right motif becomes the outline plus completed wedges on both left and right sides. Grid size, positions, and background stay unchanged; only the foreground pixels needed to finish those canonical shapes are added or adjusted.

The input is split into three equal rectangular panels placed side by side, each filled with a different non-background color and containing the same kind of symmetric cutout motif made of background cells. The first and third panels share one version of that motif, while the middle panel shows the alternate, slightly more expanded/shifted version. The output appends a fourth panel on the right: it uses the fill color of the first panel, but the background-hole pattern of the middle panel, continuing the A-B-A-B motif pattern and repeating the first panel’s color at the end.

The input is a stack of full-width horizontal bands, each band having a color and a thickness. The output is made by stacking several copies of this band-height template, but in each copy the band colors are cyclically rotated: first the original order, then shifted by one band, then shifted again, and so on. The widths stay unchanged, and each band position keeps its original thickness even when a different band color moves into that position.

The tall input contains a large symmetric reference motif in the middle and isolated single cells of the same foreground color above and below it. The output crops the scene down to the top square region, using the full input width as both the new width and height. Within that cropped region, the upper single cell is expanded into a solid 3×3 block centered on its original position, matching the filled central core suggested by the middle motif.

The non-background cells form one or more sparse clusters made of short horizontal strokes on different rows. Each cluster is redrawn as a simplified connected “comb/bracket” version of itself: a vertical backbone is created through the cluster’s full height, and every row that originally contained a stroke becomes a horizontal arm extending from that backbone, with the arm length chosen from the original row’s width/offset pattern. If this reconstructed backbone would fall outside the grid because the cluster is flush with an edge, only the in-bounds arm portion is visible in the output.

The output expands the scene into three side-by-side panels, each as wide as the original grid. In the middle panel, the single non-background figure is copied unchanged, but shifted upward so its topmost occupied row touches the top edge of the panel. In the left and right panels, the same figure is copied in its original position, except every cell of the secondary accent color is turned into background, leaving only the main body color.

The input contains one repeated monochrome pattern, plus a small color key on the bottom row: the pattern’s own color followed by three new colors. In the output, that key row is cleared, the original pattern stays in place, and three additional copies of the same pattern are stacked below it in separate bands of the same layout. Each added copy is recolored uniformly using one of the three key colors, taken in left-to-right order from the bottom-row key.

The input is made of three equal-width vertical panels placed side by side, each showing the same overall pattern but with a different main object color. The output is simply the rightmost panel cropped out and kept unchanged, including its small accent marks, divider cells, and bottom-row pattern.

The grid contains a few dense colored clusters embedded in a background, plus many isolated guide pixels of other colors scattered above, below, and around them. In the output, these fragmented colored traces are extended straight through the background—primarily as vertical continuations—so that isolated guide marks become connected into long continuous bands aligned with the nearby clusters, while the original cluster shapes remain recognizable. Overall, the task turns a sparse, broken arrangement of colored pieces into column-aligned continuous structures.

The input contains four matching patterned motifs, one in each quadrant around a blank horizontal-and-vertical cross. For each quadrant, take the color of the motif’s inner corner cell closest to the central cross, and replace that whole motif with a solid square of that color that extends one cell farther outward than the original motif while keeping the central blank row and column unchanged. All other colors and nested structure are removed, leaving four uniform blocks separated by the same cross-shaped gap.

The input is a horizontal sequence of 6x6 panels, separated by single background columns. The output turns this into a vertical stack of 6x6 slots (one slot for each original panel), copies the leftmost 6x6 panel unchanged into the top slot, and leaves every remaining slot entirely background. Any foreground and accent cells inside that first panel are preserved exactly.

Treat the tall input as a stack of equal-sized square panels: the panel size is the grid’s width, so the height is split into several width-by-width blocks. The output rearranges these blocks from a vertical stack into a single horizontal strip, placing the top square first, then the next square to its right, and so on. Inside each square, the two-color stepped boundary pattern is preserved exactly; only the large-scale layout of the square blocks changes.

The output turns the single colored figure into a long horizontal strip of same-sized frames. Each frame shows the overlap of the figure with a copy of itself as that copy is shifted one step at a time along a diagonal direction, so the first frame is the full original shape, then the visible overlap shrinks until it disappears, and the sequence is repeated symmetrically for the opposite diagonal shift. The figure’s color stays the same and all empty space remains background.

The input contains a single horizontal bar on an otherwise uniform background. The output keeps the same height but stretches the picture into a long horizontal strip made by placing many row-sized frames side by side; rows that were only background stay only background in every frame. In the row with the bar, the bar is turned into a step-by-step trace/animation: cells already passed over become a trail color, the current moving edge is marked with a distinct highlight color, and the remaining/not-yet-passed part keeps the bar’s original color.

The grid layout does not change: the background stays the same, the full-height divider columns stay the same, and every small colored marker remains in exactly the same cell. The only transformation is a recoloring of those non-divider marker cells by a fixed substitution rule, applied consistently across examples. In other words, the task is to keep all positions and structure unchanged while permuting the marker colors.

The grid contains a repeating dotted pattern made from three stripe-colors arranged in a 6-row cycle. In the output, every patterned dot is shifted two cells to the right, wrapping around to the left edge when it passes the border, and its color is cycled to the next stripe-color in the repeating order. The lone special marker in the top-right corner does not move; it loses its special status and is recolored into the lowest stripe-color.

Each tall grid is reduced to a single row of the same width by examining columns independently. If every cell in a column is the same color from top to bottom, that column’s shared color is copied into the output; if the column contains any variation at all, it is replaced by the empty color in the output. This preserves only perfectly uniform vertical stripes and removes columns disrupted by scattered noise cells.

The wide input canvas contains a single small L-shaped figure near the upper-left, with the rest of the extra space consisting only of empty background. The output discards the unused right-side area and keeps only the left square region whose width matches the input’s height, preserving the figure’s position inside that square. The figure’s shape stays unchanged, but its original foreground color is replaced by a different foreground color.

Inside the hollow rectangular frame, the only interior clue is a two-cell horizontal pair near the upper-left corner: a fixed marker cell followed immediately by a colored seed cell. The output keeps that pair unchanged, then extends the seed color downward to fill the full interior height beneath the pair, making a solid 2-column vertical strip from the row below the pair down to the row just above the bottom border. All other cells, including the frame and background, stay the same.

The input is a long strip made of three equal-width panels, each showing the same underlying shape, but some copies are drawn in an alternate object color and many cells are corrupted by small stray marker pixels. The output extracts a single canonical panel for the shape drawn in the target object color, with a uniform plain background. All stray marker pixels are removed, and any damaged cells are repaired so the shape matches the shared silhouette seen across the copies.

The solid rectangular block attached to the left edge stays where it is, and a new vertical stripe is added on the far-right column. This stripe begins on the same row as the top of the left block and continues downward to the bottom of the grid. On the row containing the marker pieces, a horizontal connection is drawn toward the right: it is filled mostly with one new color and ends with a different terminal color at its right end. When the original markers are wider groups, the outermost left cell of the left group and the outermost right cell of the right group are left unchanged, while the interior between them is replaced by the new connection.

The input is divided into three equal-height horizontal bands, and the output is a single band formed by overlaying those three bands cell-by-cell. For each position, if all three stacked cells have the same color, that shared color is kept; if any of the three differs, the cell is replaced with a new highlight color. Thus the output compresses the height to one third while marking every disagreement between the three versions.

Identify the compact non-background motif on the left, take its full bounding square, and copy it unchanged. Create a new square background canvas and place this motif exactly in the center. The empty border added on each side is as thick as the motif’s side length plus one cell, so the output is just a much larger centered version of the same pattern with all colors preserved.

The input contains a single symmetric diagonal skeleton centered in the grid, like an X/diamond made of isolated pixels. In the output, every cell of this original skeleton is recolored to one new color, and a second color is added to form a larger concentric outline around it: the same symmetry is preserved, but the new outline expands outward until it reaches the grid edges, creating top and bottom horizontal stretches and matching left/right side segments. The background remains unchanged.

The output keeps every cell in place but simplifies the color roles. The existing filled shape color and the separate line/scaffold color are merged into a single common color, so all cells of those two structures become one unified object while preserving their exact positions. The small marker/path color is deleted entirely, turning those cells into background; all other background cells stay unchanged.

The input contains three equal-length line objects near the top: a vertical line, a diagonal that slopes down-left toward it, and a diagonal that slopes down-right away from it. In the output, the vertical line is rotated into a top-row horizontal line of the same length, and the down-left diagonal is mirrored into a down-right diagonal while keeping its lower endpoint in the same place. The down-right diagonal is converted into a down-left diagonal placed flush against the bottom edge, with its topmost original cell left behind in its original top-row position.

The input contains three horizontally separated copies of the same sparse checkerboard-like rectangle in one foreground color, with blank rows between its colored rows. The center copy is the undistorted/upright one, while the left and right copies are shifted sideways as they go downward. The output crops out just that central copy, preserving its full height, width, alternating pattern, and color while discarding the surrounding empty space and the two side copies.

The input is a vertical stack of four same-sized mini-grids separated by blank rows. These four panels are reassembled into a 2×2 layout with the third panel in the top-left, the second in the top-right, the fourth in the bottom-left, and the first in the bottom-right, and the blank separator rows are removed. Before placement, the panels are rotated according to their destination: top-left gets a 180° turn, top-right a 90° clockwise turn, bottom-left a 90° counterclockwise turn, and bottom-right stays unchanged.

The solid horizontal divider stays fixed, and the fully formed multicolor row-pattern just above it is treated as a template block. The partial copies of that block at the left and right are extended so that the whole area above the divider is filled with side-by-side repetitions of the same block, completing the missing intermediate copies. In the upper parts where neighboring copies have different visible heights, the divider color is used as a transitional filler, producing stepped/diagonal connector cells instead of leaving background gaps.

Each input has a colored upper structure, then a blank horizontal separator, then a lower repetition of the narrow top part. The output throws away the separator and everything below it, and keeps only the first as-many rows of the upper structure as the input has columns. Those kept rows stay unchanged and are placed at the top-left of a new wider canvas, with all newly added cells filled with the background color.

Ignore the thick outer border of the dominant background color and extract the inner rectangular panel filled with alternating vertical stripes of two non-background colors. The output keeps this panel’s height and preserves its striped content at the left, but widens the canvas to four times the panel’s original width by adding empty background-colored space to the right. Thus the result is the cropped striped rectangle followed by three equally wide background-only sections.

Each input has two wide vertical bands of one color separated by a central block; in the output, those wide bands are trimmed down to only their inner two columns, the columns closest to the center. The remaining cells are rewritten according to the row pattern: ordinary rows become plain background, the row that had side segments of the accent color gets that accent spread across all non-band areas (including the center gap), and the row that had an accent segment only in the center turns that whole center span into the band color while the outer areas revert to background. The single isolated marker in the middle block stays in place.

Each grid contains several separate copies of the same fork/K-shaped object: a fixed thick vertical stem on the left with two diagonal arms and a middle bar extending to the right. The objects stay in the same places, but the cells on the right-hand arms are locally adjusted according to the specially colored marker cells: those marker cells are shifted onto nearby branch positions, and neighboring main-color arm pixels are added or removed so the right side becomes a cleaner, more regular version of the shape. The left stem and the overall layout do not change; each repeated object is processed independently.

The sparse non-background cells are treated as several horizontal groups. In the left-side group, the output completes the implied figure by adding many cells in a new highlight color along the straight bridges between existing marks, especially diagonal/horizontal continuations, so the scattered seeds become a dense connected pattern. A separate group on the far right is left as its original seeds but gets surrounded by a one-cell-thick rectangular frame in another new color, while background elsewhere stays unchanged.

The input is a wide grid split into three equal vertical panels by two full-height separator columns in a contrasting color. The output removes those separator columns and reassembles the three panels by stacking them vertically from top to bottom in the same left-to-right order. All patterns inside each panel stay unchanged; they are only moved into their new stacked positions.

The scattered shapes in the movable color are translated horizontally to the right by one fixed offset for the whole grid, keeping their internal row-by-row structure; parts that land on the small upper-right clue cells can overwrite them, and parts that go past the right edge disappear. The large block of the other main color stays in place, and an extra small remnant of the movable color is then drawn immediately above that block, attached along its top edge. Aside from this rightward shift and the added top attachment, the background and the anchored objects do not change.

Each grid is a solid field cut by full-length separator lines of the other color, running across entire rows and entire columns. The output keeps the same size and colors, but repositions those separator lines by one cell in a zig-zag/alternating way along each axis, so successive vertical dividers shift oppositely and the horizontal dividers are similarly nudged. As a result, some gaps between separators shrink or disappear while neighboring bands widen, but no new colors or object types are introduced.

The upper part of the input is a small motif repeated horizontally several times across the grid, while the lower part is empty except for a horizontal divider row made mostly of one solid color with two marker cells in the motif’s accent color. The distance between those two marker cells gives the width of a single repeated motif. The output keeps only one copy of the motif (the leftmost tile), shortens the divider to that same width with its final cell shown in the accent color, and mirrors/copies the upper motif into the empty area below the divider.

Ignore the position of the figure in the large field and crop the minimal bounding box containing the non-background pattern. Make three horizontal copies of this cropped pattern, each enlarged only by adding a 1-cell frame around it: the left and right copies get a frame in the overall background color, while the middle copy gets a frame in the pattern’s main solid color. Internal details of the pattern, including holes and background-colored interruptions inside it, are preserved exactly.

The input is a vertical stack of three rectangular panels separated by two full-width separator bands. Each panel contains the same small accent-colored shape in the same position, but on three different panel background colors. The output keeps the whole stack unchanged and then appends one more separator band plus a duplicate of the middle panel at the bottom, preserving the same width and internal pattern.

Inside a rectangular hole cut out of the main filled area, there is a small cluster made of one marker cell and several companion cells. The output keeps the whole scene unchanged except that the marker is relocated to the geometric center of that rectangular hole, exchanging places with whichever companion cell is currently there. If the hole has no single center because of even dimensions, the chosen center position is the lower-left one among the central cells.

The output keeps the same height but becomes three times as wide by placing three versions of the input side by side. The first panel is the original grid unchanged, the second panel is a recolored copy where the three colors are rotated in a fixed 3-cycle, and the third panel applies that same color rotation one more time. So the structure and positions of all cells stay identical in each panel; only the color labels cycle from panel to panel.

The input is made of several repeated square motifs placed side by side: one motif is a centered cross/plus made of one color, and the other is a centered diagonal X made of another color. The output collapses these separated motifs into a single square by superimposing all copies at the same center position. For each cell, the color that appears in more aligned copies is kept; if both colors would occupy the same cell equally often, the diagonal-X color takes precedence.

The small 2x2 block near the top is used to create a new vertical bar of the same color exactly two columns to its left. This new bar runs downward through the empty region until it reaches the upper edge of the lower solid rectangle, overwriting any cells in its path and replacing the left edge of the large solid blocks where it intersects them. Because the original 2x2 block stays in place, the top becomes a 4-cell-wide cap, while the alternating patterned strip on the far right remains unchanged.

The input is a square picture with a uniform background and a single solid rectangular block. The output keeps the same height but becomes five times wider by placing five copies of the whole square side by side.

These five panels alternate between the original picture and its transpose (equivalently, a reflection across the main top-left to bottom-right diagonal), starting and ending with the original: original, transposed, original, transposed, original. Because of that, the rectangle stays in its original position in panels 1, 3, and 5, while in panels 2 and 4 its row/column offsets and dimensions are swapped.

The tall input contains several vertically separated partial snapshots of the same centered figure being built row by row: an upward-pointing triangular fan whose rows widen symmetrically until they become a full horizontal base across the whole width. The output discards the repeated stacked snapshots and normalizes them into a square canvas whose size matches the input width, placing one completed version of that figure at the top. Thus the non-background cells form a centered symmetric pyramid/triangle in the upper half, with the remaining lower rows left blank.

The input is split into several equal-sized panels placed side by side, and these panels show successive stages of repainting the same pattern. The output keeps only the final/rightmost stage, then finishes it by changing any remaining cells of the original scaffold color into the main repaint color, while leaving blank cells and the separate accent-colored band/region unchanged. In effect, the result is the completed version of the rightmost frame.

The grid is split into three horizontal bands of equal height, each band keeping its internal row order and contents unchanged. The transformation performs a vertical cyclic shift of these bands: the bottom band is moved to the top, while the original top and middle bands slide down by one band. No objects are redrawn or recolored; only the large-scale band ordering changes.

The colored shape is preserved exactly—same outline, same internal holes, and no recoloring—but it is repositioned within the background so that it is centered more precisely in the frame. In the even-sized examples, the whole figure shifts one cell up and one cell left, moving the extra empty margin from the top/left side to the bottom/right side; in the odd-sized example, the figure is already centered, so the output stays unchanged.

The grid contains one or more vertical line-like structures made mostly of a single dominant color. Some cells on these vertical structures are replaced by other colors, but in the output those interruptions are repaired so each affected column becomes a continuous solid line of the dominant color again. All non-line background cells stay unchanged, and the stray non-dominant colors on the lines are simply overwritten.

Each input has a background, one full-width separator row in a second non-background color, and one or more solid foreground blocks above and below that separator. The output keeps the original grid unchanged as the leftmost quarter, then appends three more same-sized panels to the right. Those added panels are schematic summaries of the upper and lower foreground blocks and the separator row: they convert the blocks’ row/column extents, gaps, and shared or extra spans into simplified rectangular stripe patterns using the same three roles of color (background, foreground, separator).

The output keeps every row of the input unchanged, preserving all colors, object shapes, and their left/right placement. Then the entire input grid is duplicated directly underneath itself, so the height doubles while the width stays the same. In other words, the full vertical pattern is repeated once more as a second copy stacked below the first.

The input is split into three equal-width panels placed side by side, each containing a copy of the same sparse foreground pattern plus a lower composite shape. Only one panel is special: in its lower shape, the terminal cell at the end of the horizontal bar is a distinct highlight color, while the other two panels have only the ordinary attachment color there. The output is formed by cropping out that one special panel and discarding the other two, preserving the panel’s contents exactly.

The input is a horizontally striped pattern whose rows are all identical, so the whole grid can be treated as one row-pattern repeated downward. In the output, that entire original grid is copied side-by-side multiple times, with the number of horizontal copies equal to the input grid’s height. No colors or internal stripe order change; only the width expands by repeating the full original pattern across each row.

The outer rectangular frame stays exactly the same. Inside that frame, every cell belonging to the colored diagonal or slanted shape is erased and turned into the interior background color. The result is simply an empty background-filled interior surrounded by the original border.

The input grid is a vertical stack of three equally sized panels containing foreground shapes on a background. The output is simply the top panel copied exactly, with the same width and one-third of the input height. No objects are modified inside that panel; the lower two panels are discarded entirely.

Identify the smallest rectangular patch that contains every non-background cell in the input, preserving all colors and the exact internal pattern inside that rectangle. In the output, clear the rest of the grid and place four copies of this cropped patch flush with the four corners of the original canvas: top-left, top-right, bottom-left, and bottom-right. The grid size stays the same, and the original central occurrence is not kept unless it overlaps one of those corner placements.

The output keeps the same width but expands the height from N rows to N×N rows, using N-row blocks. The single non-empty horizontal pattern from the input is copied unchanged onto selected rows of these blocks, while all other rows stay background. Across the blocks, the copied rows form a centered vertical diamond/hourglass with band thicknesses 1, 3, 5, …, N, …, 5, 3, 1, so the original multicolor stripe appears repeatedly in that symmetric shape.

The transformation keeps the height and colors the same, but extends the picture horizontally into a longer strip. It identifies the existing vertical motif of the foreground shape—its solid lobes and rectangular background cutouts—and repeats those modules side by side so the same row-wise pattern continues across a wider canvas. The result is a horizontally tiled/continued version of the original structure, preserving its symmetry and internal gaps.

The input contains a fixed 3-column-wide stacked block made of six horizontal strips, and this multicolored block stays unchanged. The output adds a new marker color in an L-shaped extension on the block’s lower-right side: a vertical line is placed immediately to the right of the stack, starting beside the second strip and continuing down to the bottom strip, and then a horizontal line is placed one row below the stack from under its middle column to the new right-side column. In other words, the transformation decorates the stack with a lower-right border/hook while preserving all original colored strips.

The input is a tall grid with a uniform background and several solid foreground rectangles placed at different heights; as you go downward, the rectangles get larger. The transformation keeps only the bottom-most, largest rectangle and removes all higher rectangles by taking the bottom square portion of the grid (the last as-many rows as the grid is wide). Within that cropped area, the rectangle stays in the same horizontal position, with only background above it.

The grid is widened to three times its original width, while keeping the height the same. The left third is just the original picture, which consists of a solid lower block and a short horizontal strip sitting one row above it. In the middle third, that short strip is re-expressed as a descending diagonal of the same length (running from its original right end down to its original left end), and in the right third it is re-expressed as a vertical line of the same length at the strip’s original left column. The solid lower block remains solid across the entire widened output, effectively extending straight through all three thirds.

The output is made by duplicating the entire input grid horizontally. Every filled shape and every empty gap keeps the same size and row position, and an identical copy is placed immediately to the right of the original, so the output has the same height but twice the width. Background cells remain background everywhere else.

The input contains several horizontally separated copies of the same large pattern, all on the same background. One copy is intact, using only the pattern’s normal colors, while the other copies are contaminated by extra foreign-colored cells inserted into them. The output is the vertical strip containing the intact copy: it keeps the original rows and background, but crops away the other repeated copies so only the clean exemplar remains.

The non-background shape is isolated by cropping to its tight bounding box, removing all the extra empty space around it. That cropped shape is then rotated 90 degrees counterclockwise. The shape’s colored cells and internal empty cells are preserved exactly; only the frame is reduced and the orientation changes.

Ignore the empty top and bottom rows; each filled row is made from 5-cell motifs consisting of a 3-cell bar in the main color, with either a contrasting marker on the left end, a contrasting marker on the right end, or no marker. The output keeps the original rows and extends them to the right by repeating the earlier motifs in reverse order, excluding the final motif, so the full sequence of motifs becomes a horizontal palindrome. The same row transformation is applied identically to every non-empty row.

The grid is divided into several equal-height horizontal sections, taken in order from top to bottom. The output rearranges these sections side by side from left to right, turning a vertical stack into a single horizontal strip. Within each section, the pattern of background, the large main-color shape, and the smaller accent-color marks is preserved rather than redrawn.

The grid is built from a vertically repeating two-color pattern, and some later rows are “tampered with” by replacing part of the pattern with a short run of a different marker color. Use the first such altered row as a split point: keep the untouched rows above it as one block, then take an equally tall block starting at that altered row. If that lower block exists in full, place the upper block on the left and the lower block on the right; if not, just output the untouched top block and discard the incomplete marked tail.

Each input is treated as a single tile containing two parts: a left rectangular checkerboard-like region in one foreground color and a small T-shaped figure in a second foreground color on the right. The output is made by concatenating exact copies of this whole tile side by side across the row, so the canvas becomes much wider while the height stays unchanged. Nothing inside a tile is altered; the alternating block and the T-shape are simply repeated horizontally a task-specific number of times determined by the source tile’s layout.

The grid is made of repeated vertical blocks, each containing the same right-edge stem and one centered horizontal arm of varying length: a shortest version, a medium version, and a longest version marked by a special leftmost tip. In the output, these motif-blocks are reordered by arm length from largest to smallest, so all longest/wider motifs move above the narrower ones while keeping the same internal shape and spacing. Then one extra block is added at the bottom: a duplicate of the largest motif, so the tallest/widest pattern appears both first and last.

The only changing object is the small three-row motif made of the accent color, consisting of three identical cross-like marks arranged horizontally in the lower background region. This motif is shifted vertically by exactly one row while keeping its horizontal position and shape unchanged: if it is directly touching the full-width separator line beneath it, it moves up one row; if there is a background row between the motif and that separator line, it moves down one row to touch the separator. The large top block and the separator row themselves stay fixed.

The large structured motif in the middle is kept unchanged and acts as the reference object. The only thing that changes is the lone isolated cell of the extra marker color outside that motif: it is shifted and sometimes duplicated to one or more corresponding perimeter positions around the motif, using the motif’s bounding box/outline as the guide. In other words, the marker color gets redistributed to matching edge or corner locations around the central symmetric figure, while everything else stays the same.

The wide input is made of three equal panels placed side by side. All three panels have the same frame and the same main shape; only the small accent-colored cells inside that shape vary from panel to panel.

The output keeps a single panel-sized copy of the shared frame/shape and places the accent cells in the completed consensus position implied by the three variants. In effect, the three input panels show different partial placements around the same central figure, and the output resolves them into the one remaining consistent highlight pattern while leaving the rest of the object unchanged.

Each input contains one large solid rectangular block in a single color, plus a separate smaller multicolored figure elsewhere on the background. The transformation deletes the smaller disconnected figure completely, repainting its cells with the background color. The large rectangle and the rest of the grid stay unchanged.

The non-background cells form fragments of one ordered, repeating color sequence that is meant to trace a clockwise path: first across the top edge, then down the right edge, then leftward along the bottom edge. The output compacts these scattered fragments into a square canvas whose top row is the concatenated upper horizontal run, whose rightmost column contains the vertical run beneath it, and whose bottom row continues from the lower horizontal run so the color cycle stays continuous around the corner. Empty space inside the square remains background.

The top fully populated rows act as a reference pattern, and they remain unchanged. In the sparse rows below, each surviving non-background cell or fragment is treated as an anchor, and the output restores the missing horizontally adjacent motif from the reference at the same columns, so partial traces become complete short pattern segments while untouched background stays blank. Any large irregular shape already drawn in the lower area is preserved; only the missing template pieces around it are filled in.

All original colored objects are discarded; only the total number of non-background cells matters. Starting at the center of the grid (the top-left cell of the lower-right quadrant), the output places that many cells as a single clockwise border-following path: first across to the right edge, then downward on the right edge, and then leftward along the bottom edge if more cells are still needed. The filled cells use the three input colors in a fixed repeating cycle, so the output becomes a regular striped path rather than preserving any input shape.

The input always has two large background regions meeting near the middle, with a band/object color sitting on their boundary and sometimes a smaller inner core color inside that band. In the output, the original scene is replaced across the full same-sized grid by a regular checkerboard-like weave: every other cell becomes the right-side background color, while the remaining cells alternate between the left-side background color and the boundary/object color in diagonal repetition. The inner core color is generally removed, but if that core has a single clear center, it is kept as one central pixel within the new pattern.

The grid is split into stacked mini-panels by full-width separator rows. In each panel, the large central shape stays the same, but the three distinctive cells around it—the top protruding cell, the bottom protruding cell, and the single marker cell—can appear in different left/middle/right arrangements. The output finds the one panel whose arrangement is out of sequence and replaces that entire panel with an exact copy of the panel immediately above it, while leaving all other panels and separators unchanged.

The whole grid is rewritten row-by-row using a fixed repeating vertical pattern: rows follow a 6-row cycle of horizontal offsets and stripe insertion. In that cycle, some rows are shifted one cell right, some are shifted one cell left, and the 2nd and 5th rows of each 6-row block are special: after shifting left, every other cell starting from the first column is replaced by a new highlight color, creating vertical stripe rows. All original motif colors, including any accent-colored segments, otherwise keep their row shapes and simply move with the row shift, while the emptied edge is filled with background.

The input is made of full-height vertical color bands, each with a specific width. The output stacks several full-size versions of this band pattern: first the original, then after a blank separator row each successive cyclic rotation of the band-color order; the band widths stay tied to the same positions in the rotation.
When the appended version is in vertical form, it looks like the original layout but with the colors rotated among the bands; when it is in horizontal form, those same band widths are converted into stripe heights, producing full-width horizontal stripes in the rotated color order. The output includes all nontrivial rotations, separated by blank rows, alternating horizontal and vertical presentations.

Each input shows two same-sized framed pictures placed side by side on a blank canvas. The output removes the large canvas and keeps only a narrow summary strip, aligned to the original rows, that captures the part of the two pictures that overlaps or matches structurally; cells that do not belong to this shared portion are replaced by background. When the two pictures share very little, the summary collapses to a few simple frame-columns, while stronger similarity preserves more interior detail.

The input is a wide strip made of multiple horizontally repeated panels built on the same diagonal/scaffold pattern, with a few colored symbols placed inside the panels. The transformation crops out the single panel at the far right and discards all earlier repeated panels and any separator space between them. The output keeps that rightmost panel unchanged, with the same height as the input.

The input is a solid rectangular block made of one repeated color, with 2 rows and 3 columns. The output keeps the same color and the same height, but stretches the block horizontally by repeating the 3-cell row pattern until the width becomes 18 columns. In effect, the rectangle is extended sideways while nothing else changes.

The input consists of several same-sized framed rooms placed side by side, separated by narrow background-colored spacer columns. The output removes the spacers and extra copies, keeping just one room-sized frame whose interior is the coordinate-wise overlay of all rooms: every marked cell from any panel is copied into the corresponding position in the single result, while empty cells and the border stay unchanged.

The large solid rectangles made of the same fill color are the only objects that change: they are repainted into the marker color seen in small cells positioned just above their top edge. When a rectangle has multiple such marker cells above it, the whole rectangle is recolored; when it has exactly one aligned marker above it, every cell in the rectangle changes except the single top-edge cell directly underneath that marker, which stays in the original fill color. All other scattered symbols, the background, and the top border row remain unchanged.

The input is composed of three equal-sized panels placed side by side, each containing the same main vertical divider and a similar arrangement of rows, bars, and small colored objects. The transformation crops away the first two panels and keeps only the rightmost panel. Any full-width horizontal bands and small accent cells are preserved exactly as they appear inside that rightmost section.

Each input contains a main patterned field plus a few solid rectangular insertions near the top and sometimes on the right. The output turns to empty/background the large orthogonal region spanned by these inserted blocks: a broad corridor/box starting at the large upper block and extending across the grid until it reaches the other inserted block(s) or the outer side, so any patterned or border cells inside that footprint are erased. Everything outside this zeroed region is left unchanged.

The input contains the same small figure repeated across the row at a fixed horizontal spacing, with some copies carrying extra side or corner marker cells while others do not. The output compresses this strip of repeats into a single representative tile by aligning the copies by their repeat period and superimposing them, so the result shows the base figure plus every marker that appears in any aligned copy. The grid keeps the original height, but the width is reduced to just the bounding box of one merged repeat; rows that were empty remain empty.

The picture is a horizontal sequence of repeating composite motifs built from the same small mound/diamond-like shape in three foreground colors, with the three shapes overlapping in a consistent staggered arrangement. In each input, the sequence reaches the right border in the middle of one motif, so the motif is truncated. The output keeps the existing grid unchanged, extends the canvas to the right, and draws the missing cells needed to finish that final partial motif according to the same pattern seen in the earlier complete motifs.

The main large filled wedge in the upper part is kept unchanged. In the lower part, the input contains a right-aligned descending staircase/triangle mixed with extra duplicate fragments of the same color farther left (and sometimes a small extra attachment at the top of that staircase); the output removes those stray fragments and regularizes the lower figure into one clean right-edge staircase. Overall, the transformation is a cleanup that preserves the big top mass and keeps only the single coherent lower-right continuation.

The input is divided into two equal vertical halves, each containing a similar pattern on the same background, with a full-width horizontal divider stripe near the bottom. The output is simply the right half of the input: discard the entire left half and keep the right-side figure, along with the matching portion of the divider row and the background rows. In other words, this is a vertical crop that preserves only the larger/right-hand version of the motif.

The non-background cells act as waypoints: they are kept in place, and extra cells of the same color are added to join them into continuous linework. The added cells follow straight/staircase rasterized segments between neighboring points according to their spatial order (especially left-to-right), so isolated dots become connected polylines while the background stays unchanged.

Ignore the large outer background and focus on the aligned hollow rectangular outlines made of the foreground color. The output keeps only the shared rectangle width, using a block whose top part is the upper rectangle exactly, then appending the extra bottom rows needed to match the height of the lower rectangle; if the lower rectangle contains a separate interior foreground cell, its row is included in this appended part. This resulting narrow block is then stacked vertically once for each separate foreground connected component in the input.

The input contains several separate composite figures made from a top-colored cap, a middle/support color, and a lower color. In the output, these figures are first extracted and repacked side-by-side in left-to-right order with a one-cell gap, while keeping each figure’s internal row structure and relative vertical offset.

To the right of that packed copy, each figure appears again in a normalized form: the top-colored cells stay where they are, the lower color is converted into the support color, and nearby empty cells in the support region are filled so that the non-top part becomes a more solid/complete connected support shape around and beneath the top part.

The entire input grid is repeated three times side-by-side, so the output has the same height but triple the width. Most of the repeated pattern stays identical, including the background border and the alternating two-color field inside. The only special object is the small cluster of accent-colored cells embedded in that field: it appears unchanged in the left and right copies, while in the middle copy the same cluster is vertically mirrored within its panel.

The input is a very wide image composed of four equal-width panels laid side by side. The transformation removes the repeated horizontal panels and keeps only the leftmost panel, copying its pixels exactly into the output. As a result, the height stays the same while the width is reduced to one quarter of the input.

The single non-background shape is kept with the same geometry and row positions, but the canvas is expanded horizontally to four times its original width. The shape is copied unchanged into four side-by-side panels, each placed at the same offset it had in the original grid. The four copies are recolored into four fixed output colors in a consistent left-to-right order, while the input color itself is ignored and all other cells remain background.

Treat the input as several equal-width panels placed side by side on a common background. Compare the panels cell-by-cell at matching relative positions, and produce a single panel of the same height and one-panel width that keeps only the cells whose color is identical in every panel. Any position where the panels differ is replaced by the background/frame color.

Ignore the solid monochrome top row, then split the rest of the input into consecutive 3-row motifs. The output is a long vertical catalog made by repeatedly stacking the full motif list in the same order: first all motifs unchanged, then for each motif from top to second-last, add two stacks where that motif is replaced by a 3-row blank block while every earlier motif is in a modified form, followed by one stack where that motif is also modified. The modified form keeps the solid middle row the same, but shifts the colored cells in the sparse top and bottom rows one cell left so they occupy the former blank positions.

The small accent-colored shapes inside the large lower field are transformed into downward "drops": for each such shape, only its lowest occupied cells are kept, and those cells reappear one row lower while the rest of that shape is erased.
