In addition, the accent-colored shape that is nearest the inner corner of the L-shaped border is copied into the horizontal arm of that border, snug against its right end. The other colored structures, including the right-side bar/object and the frame itself, otherwise stay fixed.

The picture is organized into stacked horizontal bands, each containing a small narrow symbol (three columns wide) and, farther right, a wider symbol of another color. In each band, the output keeps everything already present, then fills the empty far-right area with the wider-form version of the narrow symbol, drawn in the same color as the existing wide symbol. The left marker shapes do not change; the only new cells are this rightmost converted copy, clipped if the grid edge cuts it off.

The grid is made of several vertically stacked copies of the same object pattern, where each section uses one main color and a small connector pattern introduces the next color in the sequence. The transformation merges the first two colors in that chain: every cell of the second introduced color, wherever it appears in the whole grid, is recolored to the top section’s main color. All other colors, object shapes, and positions stay unchanged.

Each input is a striped template made of three solid vertical blocks repeated across all rows: a left block, then a gap column, then a middle block, then another gap column, then a right block. The output places three copies of this whole template side by side: the left and right copies stay unchanged, while in the center copy only the middle block is recolored to a new highlight color. The gap columns and the left and right blocks remain in the same positions within each copy, and the height is unchanged while the width triples.

The grid contains a full-width horizontal band and, below it, a small 2×2 block of another non-background color. In the output, that small block is modified by adding exactly one new cell immediately to the right of its top row, turning it into a right-pointing step/L-like shape. The horizontal band and all other background cells remain unchanged.

The input consists of several repeated picture blocks laid out horizontally, with each block separated by a vertical divider of one distinctive color. In the output, everything from the left edge up through the last divider is overwritten with that divider color, creating one large solid rectangle. Only the final block to the right of the last divider is preserved unchanged in its original position.

Identify the solid rectangular block and the separate marker-colored cells placed around it. The block itself is unchanged, while the marker cells are completed into a full symmetric halo/outline around the block: every given marker implies the missing matching markers in the corresponding opposite or mirrored positions around the rectangle, so the surrounding pattern becomes balanced and complete. Background cells remain unchanged.

The input contains several horizontally repeated copies of the same non-background pattern: a 6-row symbol in the upper part and a matching 1-row bar in the bottom row, separated by large stretches of empty background. The transformation removes all the wide empty gaps, crops each repeated block to its tight width, and packs the repeated blocks directly next to each other in a compact strip. One redundant repeated copy is omitted, so the output shows three side-by-side copies of the same upper symbol and three matching bottom bars, while the blank rows between them stay blank.

The input is divided into equal vertical chambers by a repeated wall color; only the small foreground patterns near the bottom of each chamber matter. In the output, the wall/grid structure is erased and each chamber’s bottom pattern is copied onto a blank canvas as a separate block, preserving its exact shape and orientation. These blocks are arranged in chamber order from left to right, then followed by the same blocks again in reverse order except for the final chamber, so the overall sequence becomes palindromic.

Inside the fixed outer frame, the main cluster of contrasting cells located in the upper part of the filled region is translated exactly one column to the left. Any part of that cluster that would cross the left interior edge is clipped away, and the cells it leaves behind on the right are restored to the surrounding fill color. Other elements, such as isolated cells elsewhere and the small marker pair at bottom right, remain unchanged.

The non-background cells form an L-shaped arrangement: repeated objects run down the right side and across the bottom. In the output, those border objects stay in place, and the empty interior near the lower-right corner is filled with the same color to create a diagonal staircase/triangular wedge that bridges the inner side of the right-hand sequence to the inner side of the bottom sequence. The added region grows step by step down-left, matching the spacing or block structure already implied by the border pattern.

The input contains a single non-background seed cell centered in an odd-sized square, and the output keeps the same width but stacks many copies vertically so the height becomes the square of the original size. Each stacked block is a centered stamp in the seed’s color: it starts as the original 1-cell seed, then grows through odd sizes (3, 5, 7, …) up to the full width, then shrinks symmetrically back to 1. For size 5 and larger, the stamp is a star made from the center row, center column, and both diagonals; for size 3 this coincides with a solid 3×3 block.

The image keeps the same horizontal band structure, but the canvas is extended to the right. Each row is continued by repeating its existing left-to-right pattern, so the striped regions simply keep going and the lower patterned row preserves its regular spacing. As part of that continuation, the small solid rectangular patch in the upper band reappears one repeated cycle farther right, and the same patch is also repeated in the bottom band when it exists there.

The input is three vertically stacked 8-row bands sharing the same guide marks on the right, and each band contains one solid 3x3 block. The output keeps only a single 8-row band: it uses the top band’s layout, but the 3x3 block area is replaced by the color of the block that is repeated in the lower two bands (the duplicated block color among the three bands). The small vertical 3-cell marker near the top is also transformed into a 4-cell vertical marker whose top half is one fixed color and bottom half is another fixed color, while the nearby special guide cells remain aligned. If the selected repeated block color is already used by the output’s marker/frame colors, that 3x3 block area is left as background instead of being drawn.

The output places four versions of the input side by side, so the width becomes 4 times larger while the height stays the same. The first panel is the original grid, and in the next three panels the distinctive non-background picture region is progressively narrowed from both left and right edges, replacing the removed outer columns with blank cells while leaving the surrounding checker/frame pattern unchanged. In other words, the important object is shown in successive horizontal “erosion” stages, keeping only its increasingly central columns.

The wide input is divided into several equal square panels laid side by side, where each panel has the same height as the whole grid. Compare the panels position-by-position, treating both non-background colors as simply "filled" cells: if a location is filled in a strict majority of the panels, that location becomes filled in the output; otherwise it stays background. The output is a single square of the same height, and every surviving filled cell is redrawn in one uniform foreground color rather than preserving which of the two input marker colors appeared there.

Each input contains two bordered panels on the same row, plus an unrelated single marker near the upper left. The output keeps those original panels unchanged and extends the canvas to the right by adding a third panel of the same size and border. The new rightmost panel is filled with a left-right mirror image of the contents of the left panel, while the background and the lone marker stay the same.

The input is a tall sparse grid containing many separate horizontal bars of the foreground color, all flush against the right edge and appearing only on a repeating set of row levels. These bars are not all kept: the output extracts the short base motif that generates the larger vertical pattern, places only that motif in the topmost corresponding rows, and turns all remaining bar-rows below it into background. The surviving bars stay right-aligned, but their lengths are the canonical lengths from the recovered motif rather than the full repeated/expanded sequence seen in the input.

The output is made by taking the entire input grid and duplicating it horizontally. An exact copy of every object, including the frame-like structures and the small contrasting marks inside them, is placed immediately to the right of the original, so the height stays the same while the width doubles. The background cells are copied as part of this full-scene repetition.

The single full-height marker column stays in the same place, and the output is made by placing several same-sized copies of the input side by side. In those copies, a centered diamond/lozenge-shaped zone grows outward from the marker near the middle rows, repainting whatever cells it covers while the rest of the pattern stays unchanged; the zone is shown in a symmetric size sequence from small to medium to largest and back to medium and small, using three highlight colors. The last panel is the untouched original again, and when the height has two middle rows the expanding shape is mirrored across those two central rows.

Each grid contains a left-to-right progression of non-background motif blocks: a patterned top edge, matching vertical color-columns beneath it, a matching lower edge, and a solid footer band. In the input this shrinking sequence stops early, and the output continues it into the blank space by appending the missing smaller blocks at the same horizontal spacing pattern until the progression reaches its final tiny block. The newly added blocks keep the same internal row structure and corresponding color roles as the earlier blocks, just at the next reduced sizes in the series.

The input is divided into several equal-width vertical panels placed side by side, each identified by the same tall separator line in the same relative column. The output keeps just one panel-sized frame and overlays all of those panels on top of each other, aligned so the separator lines coincide. Any non-background cell from any panel is preserved in the merged result, so scattered markers and colored blocks from different copies accumulate into one combined picture.

Each input is made of a smaller rectangular pattern that is already repeated side-by-side across the row direction. The output keeps every row exactly the same but extends the image further to the right by continuing that same repeating block until there are four horizontal copies of the fundamental motif. No cells change color within the existing area; the task is purely horizontal pattern continuation/tiling.

The input is a hollow rectangular frame whose border is mostly one color, with a few special marker cells on that border in a second color. The output builds a sequence of concentric versions of that same frame: repeatedly remove one layer from all four sides to make a smaller inner frame, keeping any marker cells that still lie on the surviving border. These frames are then placed on a larger blank canvas in order from largest to smallest, shifted progressively to the right and one row downward so they form a diagonal cascade of nested-border snapshots.

The input is a wide grid made of three equal vertical thirds, with a regular striped/checker-like background pattern running across the whole image. In the left part, that background is disrupted by an extra multicolored shape, while the rightmost third remains an untouched example of the underlying pattern. The output is produced by cropping away the first two thirds and keeping only the clean rightmost third as the full result.

The grid is mostly background, with one small 3×3 patch made of a main object color and a single different-colored cell embedded in it. In the output, that lone different-colored cell is propagated to fill the entire 3×3 patch, so the mixed patch becomes a solid square of the marker color. Everything outside that square stays unchanged.

The unchanged background contains one or more copies of a special all-different “guide” sequence, plus nearby solid rectangular regions and smaller attached fragments. In the output, each guide sequence is expanded outward into a staircase/diagonal 2D pattern: the ordered colors of the guide are propagated into adjacent empty space and across neighboring solid blocks, so those plain rectangles become bands or wedges colored by successive later entries of the guide rather than staying uniform. When multiple guide copies touch the same structure, their propagated patterns meet and merge, but the canvas size and the original overall placement of objects stay the same.

The picture is made of three repeated copies of the same motif placed side by side on a uniform background; the output extends this horizontal repetition by adding a fourth copy of the motif on the right. In addition, only the leftmost copy is modified: a new highlight color is drawn as a vertical stroke in the column immediately adjacent to the motif’s single marker cell, following the motif’s downward stem and continuing straight down to the bottom of that panel. The other existing copies, and the newly appended copy, keep their original structure and marker cell unchanged.

The wide input is divided into equal square panels whose side length is the grid height. Each panel is copied unchanged, but instead of being arranged side-by-side across one row, the panels are stacked vertically in the same left-to-right order. So the content inside each panel stays identical; only the overall layout changes from a horizontal strip of squares to a vertical column of squares.

The grid keeps the background and the vertical divider unchanged. On the main side of the divider, every fragment drawn in the secondary accent color is repainted into the same color as the large solid block, so all those scattered pieces merge by color with the dominant filled region while staying in place.

Separately, each small 2x2 marker block is removed and replaced by a 1x2 horizontal segment directly one row below its former location, keeping the same columns. No other cells change.

The output keeps the same height but becomes 6 times wider, arranged as six side-by-side panels, each panel the size of the original grid. The fourth panel is an exact copy of the input, while the first panel is a full recolored copy of every non-background object. The other panels show aligned same-column echoes of those objects: vertical pieces are selectively kept and extended into nearby empty rows (especially around run ends, gaps, or toward the border), and these auxiliary copies use a fixed set of alternate colors while preserving the original rows and columns.

The input contains two short diagonal line segments in different colors: one slants down-left from the upper-right area, and the other slants down-right toward the lower-right area. In the output, each segment is extended along the same diagonal direction until it reaches the grid borders, producing the full top-right-to-bottom-left diagonal and the full top-left-to-bottom-right diagonal. Where those two diagonals meet in the middle, the cell is kept in the color of the down-left diagonal, so the other diagonal is broken at that point.

The input contains several horizontally separated monochrome motifs that are all partial versions of the same centered line framework: a square box-sized pattern made from the two diagonals, the middle row, and/or the middle column. The output collapses these separated motifs into one shared bounding box of that common size, keeping the same vertical placement in the grid while removing the wide horizontal spacing. Each distinct partial motif is recolored with its own role-color and overlaid, so the final small figure shows how the different source pieces combine into one composite star/cross pattern.

The input consists of three equal-width copies of the same scene laid out side by side, with the copies separated only by repetition rather than drawn borders. The transformation crops the grid to a single panel by keeping only the rightmost third and discarding the left and middle copies. All colors and object arrangements inside that kept panel stay unchanged, including any top border/header row.

The input is made of several vertically repeated panels of the same layout, separated by solid horizontal divider bands. Each panel contains the same central multicolor motif and some scattered marker cells or lower shape pieces, but different panels are missing different parts.

The transformation overlays all corresponding panels position-by-position, taking the union of every non-background cell to reconstruct one complete panel. The output is just this single merged panel, with all recovered markers and shape extensions combined into their fullest version.

Find the horizontal row that contains the main set of non-background cells. On that row, ignore any cells that are just a symmetric left/right pair around another cell on the same row; those side companions stay in the original color, while the remaining cells are the significant markers (either isolated dots or the centers of vertical/cross-like structures). Recolor these significant markers from left to right with a fixed sequence of highlight colors, while leaving all other cells unchanged, including any vertical extensions above or below them.

The picture is split into equal-width vertical panels made of a dominant background color with small contrasting cutout-like shapes. The input shows two such panels side by side; the output extends the canvas to the right by one more panel-width and places an exact copy of the entire left panel at the far right, while leaving the original two panels unchanged.

The input is a vertical stack of repeated panels separated by a marker row; across these panels, the same 3-row tall block of a special color shifts horizontally while other scaffold shapes stay mostly fixed. The output keeps only the top panel (through its separator row and the one row below it), then erases from that top panel every column-position that the shifting block ever occupies anywhere in the full stack. Any scaffold cells that lie in those visited columns are removed too, while all other cells remain unchanged.

The background and the overall diagonal outline made of the main non-background color stay unchanged. Each differently colored marker cell is shifted by one step along the connected diagonal border/path of that shape, and the cell it leaves behind is restored to the main shape color. When there are multiple markers, each one moves independently on its own arm of the pattern.

Locate the solid 3×3 square near the middle of the large canvas and keep only a square crop centered on that area, so the output has the same height as the input but reduced width. Then replace the center cell of the 3×3 square with the color of the isolated marker on the right, while the isolated marker on the left is discarded along with the rest of the background. The rest of the 3×3 square stays unchanged.

The grid contains a single large solid shape in one color and two cells of a second highlight color: one near the upper-left of the shape and one farther down on the right side. The transformation draws a descending down-right diagonal connection from the upper highlight toward the right-side highlight, recoloring each crossed shape cell into the highlight color until it reaches the existing right-side highlight. All other cells, including the background and the rest of the shape, stay unchanged.

The input is a wide grid made of three equal-sized panels placed side by side, each showing the same overall pattern on a background but at different stages of a color progression. The transformation simply extracts the final stage: crop out the entire rightmost panel and use it as the output. Nothing inside that chosen panel is changed; all other panels are discarded.

The input consists of several sparse diagonal patterns placed in horizontal bands, with blank rows separating the bands. In each band, the colored cells already form the final shape; the transformation keeps every marked cell in exactly the same position but discards all original color differences. All non-background cells are recolored to one single uniform foreground color, while the background and separating blank rows remain unchanged.

A solid horizontal band at the very top of the grid is moved down by exactly one row, and the newly exposed top row becomes background. All other cells stay where they are, so any part of another object that was originally in the row directly under the band gets covered/erased by the shifted band, while objects farther below remain unchanged.

The grid is split into two equal-height halves showing the same motif in two different encodings. Use the lower half to identify the filled interior of the central wedge/triangle-like object, then keep only the upper half and erase those corresponding interior cells there to the empty background color. Everything else in the upper half—the striped scaffold and the small guide/outline cells around the shape—remains unchanged.

The input is a striped wallpaper made of multiple side-by-side vertical panels, but the non-background figure appears as duplicated or partial fragments across those panels. The output reduces the grid to a single panel of that same striped background, keeping only one coherent copy of the figure: use the panel with the most complete version, or combine complementary fragments if the full figure is split across panels, while discarding the redundant copies. Any marker cells that only belonged to cut-off fragment edges are replaced by the surrounding fill or background stripe color so the remaining shape is clean and continuous.

The upper patterned rectangle is turned into a full-width horizontal banner: its internal row/column motif is extended and effectively repeated side-by-side so the patterned area spans the whole upper section, often making the grid wider while keeping the height the same. The single standout marker cell inside that pattern is not kept unique; it is propagated into multiple copies that follow the same repeated pattern, appearing along a down-right diagonal through the expanded banner. Plain background rows above/between regions and the solid block at the bottom keep their original roles and colors, only being widened when the canvas widens.

Split the tall input into equal horizontal panels using the full-width separator rows, then collapse those panels into one output panel of the same size as a single section. Compare the same cell position across all panels: if every panel has background there, leave background; if every panel has the separator/empty color there, keep that separator color; otherwise mark that position with a single canonical filled color, regardless of which object color(s) appeared there. As a result, only unanimous background and unanimous empty holes survive unchanged, while all object placements and partial overlaps are merged into one standardized shape.

The input contains several horizontally repeated motifs, each marked by a small 2x2 cue block and sometimes also connected to a larger dark shape below. In the output, each motif is reduced to its standardized right-end piece: a 2-cell strip in one highlight color on the upper row, with a 2x2 block of another highlight color directly below it, all placed on a blank background. If the lower dark shape includes a 5-cell-wide rectangular body immediately to the left of that right-end piece, that body is preserved in its original dark color; everything else is removed.

The square input scene is copied four times and laid out side by side in a single horizontal strip, so the output keeps the same height but has four times the width. These four panels show the entire original pattern—including the corner-like shapes, the diagonal marker cells, and any other colored object—at rotations of 0°, 90° counterclockwise, 180°, and 90° clockwise, in that order from left to right.

Treat the picture as a horizontal tile: the repeated spacing is defined by the vertical divider line and the matching full-width divider rows. The output extends/repeats this tile so there are seven divider positions across the width, copying the top/bottom background bands and separator structure into each new section. In the single mixed middle row, the small colored block that sits to the right of a marker cell is advanced around the seven available post-marker slots, filling in the missing intermediate states from the input so that all seven cyclic placements of that block appear across the repeated sections.

The input contains a single-color cross: one full vertical line and one full horizontal line intersecting at the center of a square background. In the output, the cross itself is unchanged and stays in the same left-side position, but the canvas is widened by adding a large blank background region to the right while keeping the height the same. No new colored cells are added outside the original cross; the transformation is purely a horizontal frame extension filled with background.

The input contains several separate two-color motifs arranged from left to right; one earlier motif and one later motif already form a matched pair because the later one is a vertical flip of the earlier one. Another motif in the middle has no partner yet, so the output extends the canvas to the right and adds that missing partner as a left-right mirror of the middle motif, using the same two colors and keeping its vertical placement. All existing shapes stay unchanged; only the extra mirrored copy is appended in the empty space on the right.

Everything above the bottom banner is reduced row-by-row to a two-color pattern. In each row, the row’s identifying color (shown at the far left in the examples) is treated as the "keep" color and all cells of that color are converted to one output color, while every other cell in that row is converted to the other output color, collapsing the original multi-color palette into a binary image. The horizontal footer with the central solid bar stays unchanged.

The whole picture is stretched horizontally by duplicating the entire input side-by-side once. Every row is copied exactly and appended to its own right edge, so the width doubles while the height stays the same. This includes the solid top border row and all lower patterned objects, preserving their colors, shapes, and spacing within each repeated half.

The input contains a large solid rectangular block and one horizontal row where a different accent color appears across the left margin (and also on the far right outside the block). In the output, that accent color is propagated into several parallel descending diagonals running from the upper-left region toward the lower-right region; these diagonals continue straight through both the background and the large block, recoloring the cells they pass through. The original rectangle and the original accented row remain in place, and the right-side accent segment is preserved rather than expanded.

The input contains several solid diamond-shaped objects of the same color, usually increasing in size from left to right, plus a few small marker cells in another color between them. In the output, all diamonds are erased except the largest one, and that largest diamond is shifted to the position of the leftmost/smallest diamond, keeping the grid size unchanged. The marker-colored cells are otherwise left where they were, but any that fall under the moved large diamond disappear because they are overwritten.

The large grid is divided into equal vertical panels by a repeated divider color. A small target motif appears twice, once near the left side and once again in the far-right panel, while the other panels are mostly empty. The output keeps the full height but crops away everything except the far-right 6-column region containing that right-hand copy of the motif together with its adjacent divider cells.

The grid contains several repeated copies of the same main shape made from the dominant foreground color, plus some small scattered marker cells in other colors. Identify the rightmost copy of that repeated shape and draw a new rectangular highlight around it using the new accent color, tightly surrounding that shape’s occupied area. All existing cells, including the other repeated shapes and the small marker colors, stay unchanged.

The output stacks four same-width panels vertically, separated by solid full-width divider rows in a new color. The top panel is just the original picture, while the lower panels reduce each cross-shaped object to its single center cell. Among those reduced panels, the first shows the centers of the two crosses that are vertically aligned in the same column, the next shows only the lower center from that aligned pair, and the last shows the centers of all crosses.

The output crops the grid down to just the occupied drawing area, removing the large empty background region. In these examples, all colored cells are packed at the top, so the transformation simply deletes every fully blank row beneath the last row that contains any non-background cell. The remaining top block is kept exactly as-is, including any background holes inside the pattern.

The solid background border is not preserved. Instead, take the rectangular block containing the two non-background colors, and treat it as a repeating tile. The output fills the entire original canvas by wrapping that interior pattern horizontally and vertically, so rows continue cyclically past the right edge and columns continue cyclically past the bottom/top padding areas.

The grid contains one or more patterned regions separated by a distinctive guide/barrier color that forms a vertical divider (sometimes as part of a larger frame). The output is made by cropping out only the region immediately to the right of the rightmost such divider, keeping that divider itself as the new leftmost column. All other copies/regions and empty space are discarded, while the selected pattern’s internal pixels and row alignment stay unchanged.

The input is split into several equal-sized panels by full-height divider columns. Compare those panels cell-by-cell at the same relative positions, and keep only the positions that are occupied in every panel, ignoring the specific panel colors and discarding all extra pixels that are not shared by all panels. The output is one clean panel showing this common overlap pattern, drawn in the foreground color of the leftmost panel and without the divider columns.

The whole input grid is copied as a complete rectangular tile and repeated in a 2-by-2 arrangement. This doubles both the width and the height: the original pattern appears unchanged in the top-left, top-right, bottom-left, and bottom-right quadrants of the output. All background areas and colored motifs keep their exact internal layout; nothing is recolored or rearranged, only replicated.

The input is divided by full background-colored separator rows into several equal-height panels. One panel shows a plain template/frame, other repeated panels show the same template in a different color scheme with an extra interior shape added, and the last panel is the template with that interior shape transferred into it and recolored to the target accent color. The output is simply this final completed panel, cropped out from the larger stacked input.

A small reference object near the top stays unchanged: a horizontal bar of one color with two stacked marker cells at its right end. On the row directly below it, a different single marker cell also stays fixed, while every cell of the scattered foreground color on that row is shifted one step to the left, treating the row cyclically so cells can wrap from the left edge to the right edge. Nothing else in the grid changes, and if a shifted foreground cell would land on the fixed marker, that position remains occupied by the marker instead.

The grid contains several identical mound-like/triangular filled figures repeated at regular horizontal intervals. In the input, the first few repeats are complete, while the far-right repeat is only partially present, showing mainly its lower portion. The output completes that last repeat by copying the same full figure shape, size, and alignment as the earlier complete ones, leaving all existing cells unchanged otherwise.

The output widens the canvas to three times its original width by placing three side-by-side copies of the input scene. The left and right sections are unchanged copies of the original grid, including the same foreground figure in its original color and position relative to each section. The middle section is another copy of the same scene, but the non-background figure is recolored to a different highlight color while the background stays the same.

The output widens the scene to three times its original width and uses that space to show three consecutive horizontal snapshots of the same configuration. In the first third, the input is preserved; in the second third, the unique marker from the patterned lower row has moved up to the row above and sits immediately to the left of the upper bar; in the third third, that marker moves one step farther right so it replaces the upper bar’s leftmost cell. Across the enlarged bottom row, the repeating stripe pattern is continued/tiled, and once the marker leaves its original lower-row position that spot is turned into background.

The picture is built from a fixed-width horizontal tile repeated side by side: each tile contains the same top divider segment and the same lower arrangement of markers and a small multicolor pattern. The output keeps the existing tiles unchanged and extends the canvas to the right by copying that whole tile pattern repeatedly, so every row continues with the same periodic structure. Across the examples, the number of repeated tiles is expanded to the next power-of-two count (for example 3 tiles become 4, and 5 tiles become 8).

The layout does not change: the outer frame, the large uniform interior, and all small embedded shapes stay in the same places with the same sizes. The dominant interior background color is the only one left unchanged, while every other color—including the border color and each accent object color—is recolored by moving one step forward in a fixed global color cycle. Thus the task is purely a consistent palette substitution, not a shape or position transformation.

Each input shows a same-color figure that is only partially present: there is a central core plus a few sparse cells that act like hints for the missing parts. The transformation completes this into a larger centered figure with four-way symmetry, by copying the existing motif through reflections/quarter-turn symmetry around the shape’s center and then connecting the copies into one continuous region. The original colored cells stay in place, and only additional cells of that same foreground color are added on the background.

The input consists of several equal-width copies of the same scene placed side by side, with thin vertical separator columns between them. The output removes the separators and collapses the repeated copies into a single panel of that width. To make that panel, align the copies cell-by-cell and overlay them: wherever any copy has a foreground pixel instead of the panel background, that pixel is kept in the result, so the shared main figure stays the same and the differing small marks from all copies are combined into one image.

The full-width solid row splits the input into an upper half and a lower half of equal height. Build the output by pairing corresponding rows from these two halves, superimposing them into a single half-height image: start from the upper row, then copy any non-background cells from the lower row on top of it so the lower half wins wherever both halves contain something. After this row-by-row merge, shift the entire merged picture one cell to the right, leaving the new leftmost column blank.

The non-background cells are small equal-sized tiles arranged in sparse motifs that run diagonally down-left. In the output, these diagonal motifs are condensed: their wide spacing is removed and each motif is rewritten as a compact axis-aligned signature made of short bars or filled rectangles, with repeated-color tiles merged together. The background stays the same, while some colors from the original diagonal pattern disappear and the surviving colors are kept only in these packed summary shapes.

The input is made of several equal-sized square panels placed side by side in one horizontal strip. The output cuts those panels apart and restacks them vertically in the same left-to-right order, so the first panel becomes the top block, the second becomes the next block down, and so on. The contents of each panel stay unchanged; only the layout of the panels is rearranged from a row of blocks into a column of blocks.

The grid is mostly unchanged: the blocky shapes above the bottom solid strip stay exactly where they are, and the background remains the same. The only transformation is that each small marker cell inside or between the upper shapes is recolored to match the bottom horizontal ground strip, as if the ground color is being copied into those marked positions. In examples with multiple marker cells, all of them change this way.

Each input contains a rectangular outline on the right with a smaller filled block tucked into its upper-left interior, using the same fill color as the separate solid rectangle elsewhere. The output adds a second copy/continuation of that filled block toward the opposite lower-right side of the outlined rectangle, as if echoing the inner block across the frame. Parts of this echoed block that overlap the existing outline or other already-filled cells are absorbed, so in some examples only a thin strip or short bar is newly visible.

The input contains a single solid, centrally placed blob of one non-background color on a uniform background. In the output, that blob is hollowed out: all interior cells of the shape are changed back to the background, while the outermost one-cell-thick boundary of the original shape is preserved in the same foreground color. The canvas size and the shape’s position stay the same; only filled area is removed to leave an outline.

The output places three copies of the input side by side, keeping the same height and tripling the width. The left and right copies are unchanged from the input, while the middle copy keeps the exact same shape pattern but recolors every non-background cell into the color of the interior filled object; background cells stay background. In other words, the framed scene is duplicated as original–monochrome-object-color–original.

The input contains several vertically repeated copies of the same scene: a small 2x2 marker block on the right and, on the left, a three-row shape whose top is fixed while one lower pixel shifts farther left in each lower copy. The output keeps only the top scene (effectively the first 6-row band) and removes the lower repetitions. In that retained top copy, the bottom horizontal part of the left shape is extended leftward to the furthest left position reached by any of the lower copies, filling the whole span continuously, while the right marker block and the background stay unchanged.

The key change is applied to the solid rectangular block: it is replaced by a larger panel whose top-left corner moves one cell up and one cell left, while the panel’s proportions are rebuilt from the original block’s dimensions (new height comes from the old width, and new width comes from the old height, with an added border). This new panel has an outer border in the block’s original color and a centered inner rectangle in a new highlight color, leaving thicker side margins than top/bottom margins. The tall strip on the left and the isolated single cell remain unchanged except where the enlarged panel overlaps them.

The grid contains a rectangular frame in one color, with the same color also forming a vertically symmetric diagonal/X-like motif inside it on a contrasting background. The output places four panels of the original size side by side: the original pattern, then a version where the inner motif is shifted upward as far as it can go so its top portion extends beyond the frame, then the original again, then a version where the motif is shifted downward so its bottom portion extends beyond the frame. In those shifted panels, the diagonal arms keep their natural outward slant outside the box, and the frame row moves inward to fill the space left behind.

The output is formed by placing four same-sized copies of the input side by side in one row, so the height stays the same and the width becomes four times larger. The first copy is the original shape, and each next copy is the previous one rotated 90 degrees counterclockwise. Because the large filled square block is rotationally symmetric, the visible change is mainly that the single-cell attachment moves around the outside of the block from one side/corner position to the next.

The grid is made of repeated small track-like motifs arranged in three columns, with one highlighted marker in an upper motif and one in a lower motif of each column. The dark track cells and the plain background stay fixed; only the highlighted marker moves to the next position in that motif’s cycle. Because the three columns show different phases of the same cycle, the marker moves straight down in the left column, diagonally up-left in the middle column, and diagonally up-right in the right column.

The input contains the same picture repeated side-by-side across the width several times, separated only by being copied into equal-width horizontal tiles. The transformation removes this horizontal repetition and keeps just one representative tile—the leftmost copy—while preserving the full height and the exact arrangement of foreground cells inside that single block. In effect, the canvas is cropped from a repeated strip down to one original pattern unit.

The input is a regular rectangular lattice: one foreground color forms evenly spaced horizontal and vertical divider lines, and the other color fills the gaps between them. In the output, that same lattice is redrawn in a slanted/isometric way, where each straight divider line becomes a staircase-like diagonal, so the square/rectangular cells turn into rhombus-like cells. The canvas becomes taller while keeping the same width, and triangular background regions appear around the projected shape where the tilted grid no longer fills the corners.

The input contains a maze-like grid made of separator lines, with one distinct foreground figure drawn inside and across those compartments. The output is formed by stacking three copies of the whole input vertically: the top and bottom copies stay unchanged, while the middle copy has the foreground figure removed and replaced by empty space, leaving the separator framework intact. In other words, it creates an original / erased / original vertical sequence.

The small 3×3 seed made of an outer ring and a different center is animated growing outward one layer at a time into a larger axis-aligned square. In each new frame, the newly added perimeter uses the seed’s border color while everything inside that perimeter becomes the seed’s center color; growth is clipped by the grid edges and continues until the expanded square reaches the cells marked by the corner indicator color. The output is the whole time sequence laid out as equal-sized frames concatenated side by side, with the indicator cells staying fixed in every frame.

The wide input is made of three equal-width vertical panels placed side by side. Each panel contains the same sparse pattern on the same background, but the marked cells are shifted one column farther to the right from panel to panel. The output collapses these three panels into a single panel by superimposing them cell-for-cell, keeping the background elsewhere and preserving the two marker colors where they appear.

The input is a row of several equal-sized panels separated by single divider columns, each panel showing the same main scene with small variations. The output keeps just one panel (dropping the divider columns and all duplicate panels). Within that retained panel, the solid rectangular block on the left stays unchanged, the small diagonal marker near the bottom is removed entirely, and the cross-like figure on the right is reduced to its smaller central version by trimming one cell from each arm.

The wide input should be split into equal square panels whose width matches the grid height, then those panels are folded/overlaid into a single square output by keeping each cell’s row and its within-panel column (equivalently, columns are taken modulo the panel size). Each non-background shape keeps its exact geometry and local placement from its own panel, but it is recolored to indicate which panel it came from, with separate recolorings for the two original foreground color families. Where multiple panels land on the same output position, the overlaid result uses the corresponding remapped overlap color instead of background.

The input contains a single sparse foreground motif on an empty background, and the output is formed by expanding that motif through self-overlap. Conceptually, each foreground cell serves as a placement point for another translated copy of the whole motif, and all of those copies are merged together. This creates a much larger, denser version of the same overall structure, with thick central regions and extended diagonal/side features that preserve the original shape’s symmetry or skew.

The input consists of two side-by-side versions of the same scene, and the output keeps only the right-hand version, repositioned into a single 15-column panel. In that kept panel, the small loose shape in the empty area is copied exactly, while the framed structure is normalized by changing the uniquely highlighted inner block to the standard fill color. That highlighted inner block is also expanded by one column toward the center, replacing the first divider column so the left interior region becomes one cell wider.

Each input is a grid with a large left background region, a large right background region, and one asymmetric highlighted motif sitting across their boundary. The output places five same-size panels side by side: the first panel is the original grid, the next three panels show that asymmetric motif rotated through successive quarter-turns to give its other orientations, and the fifth panel repeats the original orientation. Outside the rotated motif, cells are filled back in with whichever of the two background regions they belong to.

The output is made by placing four copies of the original striped scene side by side, so the height stays the same while the width becomes four times larger. In the first panel the small motif is unchanged; in the next three panels, the motif built around the special pivot cell in the middle band is rotated around that pivot by 90° counterclockwise, 180°, and 90° clockwise. The surrounding background bands stay fixed, while both the hole-shaped pattern and the other marked cell move together as one rigid configuration, even if that carries the marked cell into a different band.

The input contains a long horizontal band built from two alternating scaffold colors with occasional background holes, plus a small 3-by-3 block near the lower middle. In the output, that entire patterned band is regularized into one solid rectangle spanning the same overall left-to-right extent: all internal alternation and holes are replaced by the marker/fill color already present in the band. Only the outermost left and right columns of the band remain as a single border color, and the small lower 3-by-3 block is kept unchanged.

The grid keeps the same width but is expanded vertically to three times its original height, with the original top row staying at the very top and an identical copy of that patterned row placed at the very bottom. The background color continues to fill almost everything, but additional cells of the top-row accent color are inserted in the lower area to form a centered, vertically symmetric recursive triangular/diamond pattern beneath the alternating top-row marks. In other words, the sparse alternating border pattern is echoed downward into a Sierpiński-like interior and then repeated again on the bottom edge.

The alternating two-color background stays in place, while the connected foreground pattern made of the main solid color plus a single highlighted tip color is advanced to a different phase of its repeating motion cycle. In the output, some foreground cells disappear and reveal the underlying checker/stripe background, while corresponding new foreground cells appear farther along the motif’s path, preserving the same overall shape progression. The canvas size and background pattern do not change; only the position/phase of the moving foreground figure changes.

The grid contains a single vertical separator line in a third color that stays exactly where it is. Ignore that separator and group the remaining cells into vertical bands two columns wide; the band that includes the separator’s neighboring column is left unchanged, and then as you move outward to either side, every other 2-column band has its two main colors swapped while the alternating bands in between are kept the same. No cells move, and the separator column itself is unchanged.

Split the input into two equal vertical halves and treat the left half as the base tile. Find the prominent centered shape in the left half and the corresponding centered shape in the right half; make a second version of the left half where only the center cell of that left shape is recolored to the right shape’s color, while all other right-half content is ignored. The output is built by repeating these two half-width tiles across the row in an alternating pattern: original left tile, center-recolored left tile, then the same pair again.

The output places three horizontal copies of the entire input side by side, preserving the two background regions, the vertical marker columns, and the small symbol in the upper region unchanged in each copy. The only evolving part is the solid rectangular block in the lower region: in the first copy its right half is replaced by a new color and its left half is continued downward for two more rows, in the second copy only the block’s upper-left 2-cell piece remains while the rest of its original footprint becomes the new color, and in the third copy the block disappears completely, with its original footprint fully turned into that new color.

The tall input is divided into consecutive square panels whose side length equals the input width; each panel contains the same kind of motif, sometimes with an internal hole pattern. These panels are not altered in structure, but are reassembled side-by-side from left to right in the same top-to-bottom order, turning the vertical strip into a horizontal strip. After that rearrangement, every background cell that touches a motif cell by an edge is recolored to a new highlight color, creating a one-cell outline around the copied shapes while leaving the original motif color and hole color unchanged.

The output is made by taking the entire input picture and copying it once directly below itself, producing a grid with the same width and exactly double the height. Every colored object, background cell, and spatial arrangement is preserved exactly in both copies, with no recoloring, rotation, or resizing.

The grid has two horizontal zones inside the side frame: an upper zone filled with a placeholder background color, and a lower zone with empty space plus some objects. In the output, every cell of that upper-zone placeholder background is recolored to the prominent pattern color already present there, effectively turning the whole upper compartment into one solid region of that color. The frame, the lower zone, and any other non-placeholder cells in the upper zone (such as differently colored blocks) stay unchanged.

The grid is split into three boxed panels by narrow separator columns. The left and right panels contain the same decorative accent attached to the top edge, while the center panel lacks that top-edge accent; the output copies that shared top-edge accent into the center panel in the matching position and shape. At the same time, the small horizontal three-cell marker lower inside the center panel is removed by recoloring it to the separator/empty color, while the other interior pattern in the center panel stays unchanged.

The input is a row of equal-sized square panels separated by single vertical divider lines in a third color. Across these panels, the same foreground shape on a uniform background is shown in successive growth stages, with each panel adding one more row to the pattern. The output removes the dividers and earlier snapshots, keeping only one square panel: the final, most complete stage from the rightmost panel.

The grid is horizontally extended by one more repeat of the central window-like motif: the four identical corner blocks are copied to the right at the same vertical level and with the same spacing pattern. The long top and bottom border stripes are extended to cover the new width, and a blank separator column is inserted between repeated sections wherever the frame uses such dividers. The single cell at the center of each repeated motif alternates between the two accent-marker colors, so a lone first-marker motif gains a second-marker copy, and an existing first/second sequence becomes first/second/first.

The output is a tall vertical filmstrip made by stacking successive frames of the same scene, with one frame for each input row. In these frames, the cells of the thin marker color are the only moving object: they shift straight downward by one row per frame, keeping the same columns and overall pattern, while the launch marker appears only in the first frame and the horizontal bar / bottom target shapes stay fixed. Where the falling marker passes through other shapes it is drawn on top of them, and when it reaches the bottom target level it becomes part of the target color, leaving settled target-colored cells there.

The input is a vertical strip made of several repeated framed scenes, separated by blank rows. Each framed scene keeps the same border and most of the same interior structure, while a small colored piece changes position/orientation from one copy to the next. The transformation cuts these scene-sized blocks out of the vertical stack and repacks them into a wider, more compact layout, placing the successive copies next to each other instead of only below each other, while preserving each block’s contents and frame.

Each input is a grid made of two solid horizontal regions: one color filling the upper rows and another color filling the lower rows. The output collapses this whole scene to a 1×1 status cell that indicates whether the upper region is perfectly uniform or contains an extra stray cell of a different color. If there is a lone contrasting marker embedded in the upper band, the output is the same marker-present status color; if the two bands are completely clean and uniform, the output is a different status color.

The grid is cleaned and recolored by role: the scattered noise cells are removed, the plus-shaped object is kept in the same location but recolored, and the two background regions are normalized. Every cell of the empty background becomes a uniform light fill color, while the pre-existing solid field region keeps its original background color. The plus/cross object changes to a new highlight color, and the isolated marker cells of the other non-background color disappear into whichever background surrounds them.

The grid is divided into several same-width colored subgrids by full horizontal background rows. The transformation keeps only the bottommost subgrid, but shifts its contents down by one row inside a frame of the same size: a new background row is inserted at the top, the original top-through-next-to-last rows are preserved underneath, and the subgrid’s last row is discarded.

The input contains a single special seed cell on an otherwise uniform background. In the output, that seed stays in place, its 8 neighboring cells become a solid 3x3 halo of a new color, and then larger concentric square rings centered on it are created according to Chebyshev distance. These outer rings alternate between a drawn ring color and the original background color, continuing outward until they hit the grid boundaries, so the pattern is clipped by the frame if the seed is off-center.

The grid contains two kinds of full divider lines: one color forms the regular row/column separators, and another color forms occasional solid horizontal bands. These structural lines stay exactly where they are and do not change. Inside the remaining cells, the two non-divider colors are completely swapped: the dominant fill color becomes the accent-dot color, and every accent-dot cell becomes the fill color.

The grid is built from a vertically repeating row-block: a background field, a full-width horizontal stripe, and a few single-cell marker pixels at fixed columns arranged in a symmetric pattern around that stripe. The output keeps the entire input unchanged and extends the canvas downward by appending exactly one more copy of the same repeating row-block. The added rows use the same background color, the same separator stripe color, and the same marker positions as the earlier blocks.

Treat the input as several equal square blocks stacked vertically, where each block’s height matches the full grid width. The output rearranges these same blocks side-by-side in the same top-to-bottom order, turning a single vertical column of tiles into a single horizontal row of tiles. Each block’s internal pattern of foreground and background cells is preserved exactly; only the placement of the blocks changes.

The output keeps the entire input grid unchanged, then appends an extra block underneath it. That extra block is made from the input with its bottom strip removed, where the removed strip has the same height as the grid’s width; the remaining upper part is rotated by 180 degrees and stacked below the original. As a result, the vertical line pattern and any horizontal bars reappear in the added section in upside-down and left-right-reversed positions.

Each input is made of identical rows containing two alternating non-background colors separated by background gaps. Most neighboring colored cells are spaced the same way, but a few intervals are one background cell longer; identify which color most often appears immediately before these longer gaps. The output collapses the pattern to a 1-cell-wide column whose height matches the input, filled entirely with that selected color.

The grid contains several separate objects, but only the central hook/L-shaped figure and the lone marker beside it are changed. The hook is lifted upward by exactly one row, and the previously detached marker is absorbed into the hook, becoming the second cell from the top on its vertical segment; the marker’s old location is cleared. All other objects stay fixed, except that if the raised hook overlaps another shape, the hook overwrites the overlapped cell.

Treat the picture as a row of square panels, where each panel’s width equals the full grid height. Inside these panels, a fixed multicolor 3x3 emblem and some single-cell marker dots follow a step-by-step positional progression from left to right, with the emblem moving up or down between panels. The output extends the strip to the right by continuing that progression as a bounce-back/reverse sequence: after the last given panel, the later panels retrace the earlier offsets in reverse order while keeping the same internal shapes and orientations.

The grid contains a horizontal strip made of equal-width repeating tiles, visible because a marker-colored cell appears at the same position in every tile. One tile is a special variant: on the upper active row it has a different arrangement of the foreground cells than the standard tile, while the lower active row keeps the same marker pattern. The output widens the grid by repeating the standard tile so that this special tile ends up exactly in the center, with matching numbers of standard tiles copied to its left and right; all other background cells stay unchanged.

The filled foreground shape is replaced by a thin plus-sign skeleton. The output keeps only the midpoint row and the single central/right spine column of the original figure, drawing a horizontal bar and a vertical bar that cross at the figure’s center. The bars extend symmetrically, with arm length determined by how wide the input shape gets at its widest point.

Find the single foreground shape and crop to its tight bounding box. The output is a vertical stack of five recolored versions of that crop: the middle copy keeps the original foreground color, the two copies next to it use a second color, and the top and bottom copies use a third color, arranged symmetrically. The farther a copy is from the center, the more it is vertically thinned by omitting some horizontal rows and leaving background padding, so the center is the fullest version and the outer copies are the most reduced.

Among the disconnected non-background objects, the smaller isolated motif is selected while the larger shape is left unchanged. In the output, a solid rectangular halo of a new color is placed behind that small motif, covering the motif’s bounding box expanded by exactly one cell in every direction. The original motif’s cells stay as they were, so the new color fills only the surrounding cells of that enlarged rectangle.

The only changing parts are the scattered cells of one foreground color in the upper region. In each row, every contiguous horizontal run of that color has its rightmost cell shifted one square to the right, while the rest of the run stays fixed; isolated single cells are treated the same way, except runs already touching the right border cannot extend further. The background, the separate marker-colored shape lower down, and the solid bottom band remain unchanged.

Treat all non-background cells as one motif: take the full bounding rectangle containing the main shape and the special marker, change the marker into the motif’s normal color, and if there is room below it, extend it one more cell downward in that same color. Then use this completed motif as a tile and repeat it in a 3-by-3 array, copying it side-by-side and top-to-bottom with no gaps. The output is just this enlarged tiled pattern on a background field.

The output keeps the same number of rows but reduces the width to the smallest horizontal block that can generate the entire input by repeating side to side. In other words, the grid is compressed to one full repeating unit of the row pattern shared across the whole image. If every column is identical, this minimal unit is just a single column.

The output keeps the same height but shrinks the width to one third of the input. Horizontally, the input is folded/stacked into three equal vertical sections: cells whose columns differ by one section width are placed onto the same output column, so parts of a shape that extend past the first section wrap around to the left edge of the output. The colored shapes themselves are otherwise preserved, with empty background staying empty.

The repeated maze-like/frame-like objects are multiple centered size variants of the same blueprint, arranged vertically and separated by solid divider rows. The output throws away the whole stack and divider rows, keeps a single canvas around the largest variant, and overlays all size variants on top of each other so that overlap depth becomes colored layers: largest-only cells form the outer band, cells shared with smaller variants form progressively deeper inner bands, and the original empty holes stay empty. The isolated guide dots around the stack are also kept as single reference dots on the corresponding sides of the output.

The large background stays the same, but the hollow rectangular region becomes the place where the loose shapes from below are brought inside. The small 2-cell bar near the top of that region is lifted up to the region’s top row, and its old cells are turned back into background. The other two colored shapes that were hanging beneath the rectangle are redrawn inside it: the compact cluster is moved upward into the lower-middle of the rectangle, while the diagonal chain is continued upward-right through the rectangle, avoiding cells already occupied by the moved cluster.

The large canvas contains several small rectangular panels embedded in a uniform background; each panel is a same-sized window filled mostly with a secondary interior color plus a few colored marks. The output removes the wide background gaps between these panels, extracts each panel exactly, and places the panels side by side in their original left-to-right order. The rows above and below the panel band remain as uniform background, so the overall effect is a horizontal compression of the meaningful windows only.

The single foreground pattern in the input is duplicated horizontally to make four identical copies placed side by side. The output keeps the same height and colors, but its width becomes four times the original width because each row is repeated across from left to right. Nothing inside the motif is altered: the border-like and corridor-like structure is preserved exactly in every copy, and the background stays background.

The input is divided into three equal-width panels placed side by side, each showing the same general scene structure but with small object placements varying from panel to panel. The transformation simply crops out the rightmost panel and returns it as the whole output, preserving all of its colors, rows, and object positions exactly while discarding the left and middle panels.

Each input is a same-sized picture with background, a fixed outline/ring color forming the border shape, and a multicolored interior pattern. The output is made by placing nine copies of that picture side by side: the first copy is unchanged, and in each later copy the interior non-background cells are recolored by moving one step farther along the same repeating color cycle, while all shapes and positions stay identical. The background stays background, and the border/ring itself stays the same border color even though that color can appear inside later copies as a result of the recoloring cycle.

The input contains several same-sized solid square blocks of different colors, all aligned in one vertical column on a uniform background. The output rearranges these blocks into a single horizontal row, keeping their top-to-bottom order from the input as left-to-right order in the output. Each block is placed inside its own full-width background frame matching the original horizontal placement, and these frames are concatenated side by side; vertically, only the background band around one block is kept.

The existing colored shapes are preserved exactly as they are; nothing in the main scene is moved, recolored, or resized. The only change is the addition of a horizontal marker strip on the second row, beginning just inside the left border and extending to the right edge. This strip is split into five consecutive color blocks in a fixed order, normally three cells per block, with the last block shortened or lengthened as needed to fit the available width.

The filled pattern is decomposed into its separate shape pieces, and each piece keeps the same color, orientation, and internal geometry. The arrangement is then rebuilt in the empty right side of the grid with the vertical bands effectively swapped: pieces from the lower part of the input are moved into an upper-right cluster, while pieces from the upper part are moved into a lower/right cluster. In the new layout the pieces are packed much more tightly than before, so original blank gaps are removed and same-colored pieces may end up touching or merging visually.

Each grid starts as a two-color checkerboard with a small motif of two non-background marker colors arranged around a single central cell that stays as background. The output grows that motif into long straight lines centered on the same point, extending every indicated horizontal, vertical, and diagonal direction all the way to the edges. The two marker colors continue in the same phase/order they already show in the seed pattern, so the added cells follow the checkerboard alignment while the center itself remains unchanged.

The output builds a tall vertical stack of repeated versions of the input, keeping the two long horizontal header stripes the same in each repetition. From one repetition to the next, every other colored object below those stripes is shifted upward by one more row, so the small markers disappear once they would overlap the header, and the process continues until the large lower block has been shifted as high as possible without touching the lower header stripe. The repetitions are placed one under another with a one-row gap in their starting positions, so the bottom of the final stack may be cropped by the output boundary.

Each input has a large framed structure with a filled upper block, a smaller filled lower block, and one single marker cell sitting outside the frame on the left. In the output, the frame and the upper block are removed, and only a left-hand portion of the lower block is kept and recolored to a new highlight color; the amount kept depends on the outside marker’s vertical position, as if that marker defines a diagonal cutoff through the structure. The lone marker is also transferred to the output near the right/below end of the kept lower piece, unless that implied landing position would fall off the grid.

The wide input consists of several equal-width panels placed side by side, all showing the same overall symbol but with some parts shifted within each panel. The output compresses these repeated panels into a single panel of the same height by overlaying corresponding cells from all panels and taking the union of their colored marks, while leaving background cells unchanged. In other words, any position that is occupied by a given feature color in at least one repeated copy becomes occupied in the final single composite.

The large irregular foreground shape remains where it is, and only certain small accent pieces are transformed. Any non-background, non-foreground marker that forms a 3-cell corner/L shape is removed from its original location and redrawn as a solid 2×2 block in a vertical stack on the left side of the main figure, with the different marker types placed in a consistent order. Other colored marks that are not this 3-cell corner pattern stay unchanged, and the single isolated bottom marker is simply recolored into its output color.

The input is split into several equal-height horizontal panels stacked vertically, all sharing the same overall layout but with a few cells or small pieces changing from panel to panel. The output collapses these panels into a single panel of that base height, keeping the original width. In that reduced panel, every position whose color differs across the stacked copies is marked with a single highlight color, while every position that stays the same in all copies is turned into background.

The grid is split into several equal-width vertical sections, each containing a small isolated marker near the top and a larger multicolored pattern near the bottom. Among these repeated bottom patterns, one section is different from the others because it contains extra/altered colored cells in its upper part. The output keeps the full height but crops away all other sections, leaving only the unique section together with its top marker in the same relative position.

A single non-background colored cell appears somewhere inside a rectangular room bounded by a contrasting border. In the output, that cell’s color spreads to fill the entire interior of the bordered rectangle, replacing all empty interior cells while leaving the outer frame unchanged. The exact position of the original seed cell does not matter; it only determines the fill color for the enclosed area.

The grid contains one large shape made of the main object color, with a single special-colored cell near one corner acting as a corner marker. That marker implies a 5-cell plus-shaped stamp whose center lies just outside the object at that corner, with the given special cell as the inward arm of the plus. In the output, the same corner stamp is mirrored to the corresponding positions at all four corners of the object's overall extent, recoloring any overlapped cells there to the special color while leaving the rest of the shape and background unchanged.

The input is divided into several same-width picture blocks stacked vertically, with completely blank horizontal rows separating them. The transformation removes those blank separator rows and places the nonblank blocks side by side from left to right, preserving each block’s contents exactly. The output therefore has the original block height, while its width becomes the sum of the widths of all stacked blocks.

The output keeps the same height but becomes four times wider, by placing four horizontal versions of the entire input side by side. These four panels are the original grid, then the whole grid cyclically shifted left by about one quarter, one half, and three quarters of the input width; anything that moves past the left edge wraps around to the right edge. The colored shapes themselves do not change color or structure—only their horizontal starting position within each repeated panel changes.

The input is converted into a horizontal strip of equal-sized panels: the height stays the same, and the width becomes the original width repeated for each upward step (one panel per row-to-row step). Each panel continues the alternating checkerboard phase, while any places where the input breaks that checkerboard are carried through the strip as step-by-step diagonal traces, so the special same-color runs appear to march through successive frames. In other words, the output is a side-by-side time sequence built from the input pattern rather than a single enlarged picture.

The input consists of three equal-sized subgrids placed side by side, and the output is formed by collapsing them into a single grid of that same subgrid size. Corresponding cells from the three panels are overlaid: background stays background, and if only one non-background color is present there (or the same color repeats), that original color is kept. When two different source colors overlap, the cell is changed to a specific merge color for that pair, and when all three source colors appear together, a separate merge color is used.

The grid is expanded horizontally into five equal-width panels placed side by side, while the background color stays unchanged everywhere else. In each panel, every original 3-cell horizontal marker is redrawn as the same ordered 3-cell line but with a different orientation: one descending diagonal, one vertical stack, one ascending diagonal, one unchanged horizontal line, and a final repeat of the descending-diagonal version. The three non-background colors keep their relative order along each new line, and all such markers are transformed the same way for every row where they appear.

Each input contains one distinguished object: a single-cell-thick diagonal of one color running from the top-left downward one step per row. The output keeps the entire original grid unchanged, then widens the canvas by exactly the grid height and places a second copy of that same diagonal in the new right-hand space, with the same slope and row alignment. All other colored cells stay where they were, and the added columns are otherwise empty.

The input is a tall grid made of three equal-height horizontal sections stacked vertically. The output keeps each section unchanged—preserving all patterns, background framing, and the small colored marker blocks—and rearranges them side by side from left to right in the same top-to-bottom order they had in the input. In effect, the whole figure is converted from a vertical stack of three panels into a single horizontal row of three panels.

The single foreground-color marks are treated as partial straight arms of a larger figure, and the output completes those arms by extending them inward until they meet or overlap in a common interior region. Existing diagonal fragments continue along the same diagonal, while horizontal or vertical fragments turn into diagonal stair-step continuations aimed toward that meeting area; isolated single cells behave like one-cell diagonal arms. The output keeps the same height, uses a wider canvas, and leaves the added space on the right empty.

A diagonal two-color trail runs through the empty area of the grid, while the large upper region, the lower horizontal band, and the small block inside that band act as unchanged scenery. The transformation deletes this trail everywhere except where it touches the left edge: only the leftmost-column endpoint cells of the two-color trail are kept, and all other trail cells are turned into the empty color.

Each input is a wide strip containing several separated diamond/cross-shaped clusters in different colors. The transformation keeps only the cluster in the middle color position—the central diamond—and deletes all other side clusters and stray pixels. The output is a square window whose height matches the original grid height and whose width is chosen as the same size, centered on the kept object so that this central diamond remains in the middle with surrounding background preserved.

The grid contains a horizontal sequence of identical 3-cell-wide block motifs, each with a small attached single cell aligned to one of its columns, and one motif is marked by a unique contrasting cell inside it. The motifs are cyclically reordered so that the marked motif becomes the leftmost motif in the sequence; its contrasting cell appears there, and its original location is restored to an ordinary motif. The attached single cells move with their corresponding motifs to the new order, while the rest of the scene (background, separator/marker row, and base row) stays the same.

Each input has a large left area made from an alternating two-color checkerboard and a large uniform filler area on the right.
