The only meaningful feature is the connected patch where the checkerboard’s active color expands into an irregular wedge/blob, breaking the alternating pattern near the boundary with the filler area. The output discards the original canvas size and position information, isolates that same kind of disturbance, and replaces it with one fixed, small vertical template: a mostly solid active-color shape with a specific arrangement of accent colors along its edge.

Treat the input as 2 or 3 square layers stacked vertically, each layer having the same width as the whole input’s column count. Build the output by replacing each cell position of these layers with a 2×2 block: if all layers are background there, the block stays background; if only one non-background color appears there (even if repeated across layers), the whole 2×2 block is filled with that color; if two different non-background colors appear there, the block records both by putting the main/body color and the secondary/accent color across the top row, with the bottom row left background. The result is therefore a square output of double width and double height that merges the stacked layers position-by-position.

The input consists of several symbol-like pattern blocks placed side by side, separated by single vertical divider columns in a distinct separator color. The transformation removes every such divider column and shifts the remaining blocks together horizontally, preserving their order. The shapes inside each block are unchanged; only the frame becomes narrower because the separator columns are deleted.

The multicolored central figure stays in place, along with the large background regions and the side border strip. The sparse marker-colored cells that form a diamond/halo around the figure are deleted from their original positions and redrawn as the same pattern shifted into the lower-right open area, with any shifted cells that would land on existing non-background parts simply not appearing. Separately, the lone figure-colored cell in the dark bottom band grows into a small 2-by-3 block centered on that seed.

Each input is made of three equal-width panels placed side by side, showing the same overall figure but with different cells filled in. The output shrinks the image to one panel by superimposing the three panels cell-by-cell: wherever any panel contains a more specific feature, that feature is kept, while generic fill, border, and finally background are used only if no higher-priority feature is present. In effect, the result is the fully combined version of the repeated figure, preserving the detailed top pattern, the small side marker, the lower band, and all blank areas in their shared positions.

The input contains a single horizontal bar made of one distinguished endpoint cell followed by a run of identical body cells. In the output, the canvas is enlarged and this bar is reproduced four times: first in its original orientation, then rotated so the body extends upward from the marked cell, then flipped so the body extends leftward, and finally rotated so the body extends downward. These four versions are placed at separated positions in the larger frame, with all marked endpoint cells aligned on the same central column and each body segment pointing outward from that alignment.

The input is a vertical stack of repeated scene frames separated by solid horizontal divider rows. Across the stacked frames, a single marker in one column appears progressively lower, ending inside the centered rectangular block; the output collapses this animation to just the top frame region (up to before the next divider) and removes the extra repeated copies. In that kept frame, the marker’s whole straight downward path is drawn as a vertical line from its first position to its final destination, overwriting the cells it passes through, while all other objects remain in place.

The whole input grid is repeated side-by-side three times, creating a new grid with the same height and triple the width. The left and right copies stay exactly the same as the input, including the large patterned structures and any small marker cells. In the middle copy, the main shapes remain unchanged, but every small isolated marker cell is recolored to a new highlight color while keeping its position.

The input shows a repeated 3-row motif placed at regular vertical intervals on an alternating two-color striped background. In each motif, the top and bottom rows contain a 3-cell bar of one object color, while the middle row contains a left-extending run of a second object color immediately adjacent to that bar; across the given motifs, this run grows step by step (length 1, then 2, then 3, etc.).

The output keeps the original grid unchanged and extends it downward by continuing the stripe pattern and adding the same motifs in reverse order of that growth. In other words, after the longest middle-row run, the sequence is mirrored vertically below: longest again, then shorter, until it returns to the smallest run.

The colored cells form the lower part of a branching shape: a vertical stem with one or two diagonal arms attached near its top. In the output, each diagonal arm is extended upward in the same direction, one step sideways for each step upward, until it reaches the grid boundary. The original stem and all existing colored cells stay unchanged, and the background remains empty.

Ignore the scattered single marker dots and the permanent frame/wall color, and focus on the compact multicolored motif near the middle. That motif is merged into one object, its gaps are filled, and it is thickened outward into a larger rounded/octagonal mass painted in a single standard fill color, even replacing internal wall cells where the mass extends. Everything else stays in place, with only occasional protruding tip cells of the original motif left visible.

The input shows two single-cell traces of different colors forming opposing diagonals across the fixed-width grid: one moves from the left edge toward the right and back, while the other moves symmetrically from the right toward the left and back. The output keeps the width unchanged and extends the picture downward by continuing this same row-by-row oscillating diagonal pattern, preserving the periodic bounce and the center-row overlap behavior where only one of the two colors appears when they meet. The completed output contains repeated full cycles of this vertical motion rather than stopping at the input’s last row.

The input contains a 3-row motif: on the lowest active row there are three copies of a small centered pattern (a highlighted center cell flanked by two guard cells), on the row above there is one guard cell above each copy, and on the top active row there is a single highlighted cell above one of those columns. The output greatly widens the canvas and turns the lower 3-row structure into a long horizontal repetition of the same motif with regular spacing, so the bottom pattern and its one-row-above markers become an evenly tiled strip. The lone top highlighted cell is then placed above the corresponding repeated column, while all other cells remain background.

Find the single foreground shape, crop it to its tight bounding box, and use that cropped height as the output height. The output places three same-sized panels side by side: first a one-step orthogonal expansion of the shape (every foreground cell grows up/down/left/right, clipped to the crop), then a one-step orthogonal erosion of the shape (only the inner cells remain), and finally the original cropped shape unchanged. The background color stays background throughout.

The upper section is unchanged: the plain background and the solid rectangular block stay exactly as they are. In the lower section, the irregular object is extended/replicated in the direction of the nearby diamond-like object, creating a trail or bridge of that object's color across the gap. As this growth reaches the diamond, some of the diamond's cells are overwritten by the advancing color, while any untouched parts of the diamond remain visible.

The output keeps the pattern unchanged vertically but extends the canvas horizontally by placing several identical copies of the entire input next to each other. Every object in the input—including the long horizontal bar and the vertical bar(s) on the background—is duplicated with the same spacing and shape, producing four side-by-side repeats of the original grid.

The input is divided into horizontal bands separated by plain background rows, and each band contains identical sparse marker positions repeated across the row. The top band uses one accent color for those markers, while lower bands repeat the same row pattern but with different accent colors. The output is formed by cropping away all lower bands and keeping only the full top band: every row from the top down to just before the first row whose markers switch to a new color is preserved unchanged.

The wide input is split into several equal-sized vertical panels by full-height divider columns. One panel is marked as the bad/corrupted copy by a single isolated marker cell; this entire marked panel is ignored. The output is a single panel formed by superimposing all of the remaining panels cell-by-cell, keeping any non-background content that appears in any unmarked copy and dropping the divider columns.

The input is a single rectangular panel with a border-colored frame pattern around a solid interior, and the output turns it into a horizontal strip of five same-height panels. The middle panel is the original, the two outer panels are horizontal reflections of it, and the 2nd and 4th panels are a simplified inward version where the vertical side borders shift one cell toward the center and the thicker top/bottom corner runs are reduced to just their innermost border cells. When the original is already left-right symmetric, the reflected panels look the same as the original.

The output makes the grid five times wider by placing five side-by-side copies of the original scene. The 3x3 object on the right of each pair is repeated unchanged in every copy, while the 3x3 object on the left alternates through its two observed forms: the sparse diamond/X-like form and the fuller square-ring form. Different left objects can start at different phases of this 5-copy cycle, so one occurrence may appear as X→ring→ring→ring→X while another appears as ring→X→ring→X→ring; if a shape is cut off by the border, that truncation is preserved.

The picture is divided into horizontal color bands, and within each band the columns are arranged as a repeating fixed-width tile pattern. The output keeps the entire input unchanged and extends the grid to the right by one more copy of that same tile, so every band continues its horizontal repetition for one additional cycle. All holes/cutouts inside the repeated shapes are copied exactly, and nothing is altered vertically.

Each grid shows a regular stepped layout built from a separator color, empty cells, and filled cells, forming a repeated staircase/triangular pattern across the board; the small accent-colored cells near the top are part of the original design and stay where they are. The cells in the odd marker color are defects inserted into that design. The output repairs those defects by replacing each marked cell with whatever role fits the surrounding pattern at that position: separator line, empty background, or filled interior.

The output isolates the cells of the filled region color and deletes every other colored structure. All non-background cells that are not this region color—such as the repeated vertical marker lines or other small colored bars—are turned into background, while the region color stays in exactly the same positions and shape.

The colored cells form two matching 3-point side shapes: a left and a right chevron, where the top and bottom occupied rows line up and the middle occupied row is shifted sideways. The output keeps those original anchor cells and adds more cells of the same color between the left and right sides, placing them at proportional intermediate positions so the zigzag/chevron pattern continues inward as smaller nested bends. Only the upper two occupied rows are extended this way; the lowest occupied row stays unchanged.

The input shows several vertically stacked copies of the same two-part block pattern, where each lower copy has more of its upper-left area removed. The output extracts only the lowest copy of this evolving shape, keeping its silhouette of filled cells and blanks. After isolating it, the grid is cropped to the tight bounding box around that shape, and all non-background cells are recolored to a single uniform color.

The grid is expanded horizontally into four equal-width panels, each panel being a copy of the original canvas background. In these four panels, the single small foreground symbol is shown in all four quarter-turn orientations: the first panel keeps the original orientation, and the next three panels contain the 90°, 180°, and 270° rotations of that same symbol. Only that symbol changes orientation and placement within its panel; the background color and overall panel size stay the same.

The full-width marker rows split the input into stacked panels. Take the top panel as the base, then copy the large block from the bottom panel onto it, preserving the block’s exact position within its panel; this pasted block overwrites any cells in the top panel that it covers. The output is just this overlaid top panel, so only parts of the original top pattern that lie outside the pasted block remain visible.

The grid is split into horizontal panels by full-width divider rows in a distinct separator color. The output keeps only the bottommost panel: everything above the last divider and the divider row itself is removed, while the remaining panel stays the same width and preserves its internal pattern, object positions, and colors against the background. If earlier panels contain similar shapes, they are ignored.

The output widens the canvas to three equal-width panels and places two unchanged copies of the input figure in the left and right panels. In the center panel, the same-colored diagonal/symmetric figure is re-expressed in a rectified, axis-aligned form: its slanted structure is straightened into a compact centered pattern of horizontal bars and vertical posts. The background stays empty, and only this added middle reconstruction changes the scene.

The input is made of three equal-width copies of the same small pattern placed side by side. In each copy, the bottom part is the same growing triangular wedge, while the top part is a solid block with a vertical gap and a different fill color for each copy. The output crops out and keeps only the rightmost copy, preserving its top block, its internal gap, and the wedge underneath exactly as they appear.

A single descending diagonal object is made of two non-background colors: most of the diagonal is one color, but a few cells on that same diagonal are already marked with a second color. In the output, the entire connected diagonal is recolored to the marker color, so every cell along that diagonal becomes uniform. The small 2x2 block on the right side and all other background cells stay unchanged.

The input is a sparse lattice of single-cell markers of one foreground color, and the output turns it into a long horizontal strip of cropped copies of that same lattice. Each copy shows the pattern shifted to one of the relative self-alignments obtained by matching one marker position against another marker position; cells that would fall outside the original frame are simply clipped. The height stays the same, the marker color stays the same, and the new width comes from concatenating all of these self-aligned shifted versions side by side.

The square input is expanded horizontally into five equal-width panels, all using the original colors unchanged. For each row position, the output concatenates: that row from the input, the matching column counted from the right side, the matching row counted from the bottom but reversed left-to-right, the matching column counted from the left but read bottom-to-top, and then the original row again. In effect, the output is a horizontal “unwrapping” of the square from top, right, bottom, left, and back to top.

The output is made by stacking three full-height copies of the scene vertically. The first copy is the original input, while in the second and third copies the widespread ‘flood’ color that occupies the lower part of the grid (and any disconnected patches of that same color elsewhere) is shifted one row upward or one row downward relative to the fixed objects and neutral background. When this shift would go out of bounds, the shape is clipped/padded by the grid edge, and the other colored structures remain in place.

The input is a one-color comb/E-like figure: a left vertical spine, with certain rows turning into long horizontal bars. In the output, those bar-rows are re-encoded into a small fixed-width motif that is repeated across the width, while the original color becomes the motif’s scaffold/outline rather than one continuous solid bar. Each original full bar also produces two colored 2x2 echoes in every motif: one shifted 3 rows upward into an upper-right slot and one shifted 3 rows downward into a lower-left slot, with anything outside the grid simply clipped.

The input is made of several small framed subgrids laid out side by side, with each subgrid separated from the next by a single vertical strip of empty background. The transformation simply deletes those separator strips and packs the framed subgrids tightly together in the same order. Each subgrid’s internal pattern and border stay unchanged; only the blank columns between them are removed.

The input contains several same-sized patterned panels placed side by side in a horizontal strip, with empty background rows above and below. The transformation removes the empty outer background and keeps only the rightmost panel, copying that panel exactly as it appears, including its interior markings and irregular cells. All panels to the left are discarded.

Each row contains a horizontal color pattern that is shown once completely at the left, then shown a second time with one position replaced by the blank/delimiter color. The output keeps the grid height the same, preserves that damaged second copy exactly as-is, and extends the width by appending one more full copy of the original left-hand pattern to the far right. In other words, the rows are continued periodically using the intact first segment as the repeating unit.

The non-background line pattern is reduced to its overall outer extent: all internal gaps, partitions, and grid-like structure are removed, leaving a solid rectangle in the line color. The output keeps the input height but expands horizontally to a width equal to the input’s total cell count, then places this solid rectangle flush left with the same height and width as the original input grid; everything to the right is background.

Each non-background figure keeps exactly the same shape, size, and position, but its two internal colors are rearranged. In every row of a figure, the occupied cells stay in place while the side-block of the secondary color that was on the right is moved to the left, and the main color shifts to the right; rows containing only the main color stay unchanged. This is applied independently to every repeated copy of the motif across the grid.

The output keeps the grid size the same but removes two kinds of structure: the thin scaffold/guide lines and the large central blob attached to them. Everything belonging to those two main colors is turned into background. Only the smaller independent colored objects away from that central mass—such as the little block or staircase-like shape near the lower side areas—are preserved exactly in their original positions.

The sparse foreground motif is copied within its original-sized canvas after being shifted diagonally down-right by an offset equal to its empty margin from the top and from the left. Any parts pushed past the bottom or right edge are clipped away.

This shifted canvas is then repeated horizontally five times, with a single background column separating each copy, while all other cells remain the background color.

A large jagged object in one non-background color is treated as the main figure: when it is a clean standalone object, it is moved to a standard position near the top of the grid; when it is polluted by cells of the other non-background color, that main figure is not kept. The smaller objects in the second non-background color are then normalized by shape (bar-like pieces stay bars, triangular/wedge-like pieces become a small triangle) and placed into fixed aligned slots below or within the standardized main figure, while extra or nonmatching pieces are discarded.

The non-background cells are not just kept as they are; the foreground pattern is self-replicated. Treat each foreground cell as an anchor and overlay translated copies of the foreground shapes so that the pattern is stamped onto the positions of its own occupied cells, merging overlaps into the same foreground color. The output is therefore a larger-looking superposition of repeated copies of the original clusters, while the grid size and background stay unchanged.

The grid contains several fixed structures—a long descending diagonal of single cells, some larger colored regions near the top/left, and a solid bottom border—that stay in place. Every isolated marker of another color is translated exactly one cell down and one cell left (southwest), and its original cell is cleared to the surrounding background. If a moved marker lands on an existing non-background cell, it simply replaces that cell.

The input consists of several equal rectangular panels placed side by side, separated by single vertical divider columns. The transformation extracts only the far-right panel and outputs it unchanged, dropping all panels to its left and removing the divider columns.

The tall scene is vertically compressed into a much shorter grid while keeping the same width, the lone marker in the upper-left, and the solid border column on the right. Each filled rectangular foreground block is replaced by a slanted staircase/triangular silhouette rather than a solid rectangle, keeping its horizontal placement and size information in a tapered form. The different block-silhouettes appear in the same top-to-bottom order as the original rectangles, with large empty vertical gaps collapsed to little or no space.

The input is a row of three same-sized framed panels separated by the border color. Each panel has the same filled rectangle, but the small dark motif near the bottom differs: the left panel shows the motif’s left branch, the middle panel shows its central vertical stem, and the right panel shows its right branch. The output collapses these three panels into one single panel and overlays those three motif variants in the same interior: the left-branch cells stay dark, the stem and right-branch cells are recolored to a new highlight color, and the top cell of the stem is given a distinct marker color; everything else in the frame stays the same.

The grid is split into several equal-width panels by thin vertical divider columns, and those divider columns stay unchanged. In each panel, the same underlying wall-and-space pattern appears, but some cells have been overwritten by an extra foreground color that forms different shapes in different panels. The output removes that foreground overlay and restores the hidden wall/space cells so that every panel becomes a clean identical copy of the shared template.

The lone special marker slides horizontally to the far-right end of its row. Then, for each column, find the highest non-background cell in that column among the ordinary shapes or, if the column is otherwise empty, the top of the solid bottom band; place a new highlight cell one step above that topmost cell, or on that cell itself if it already touches the top border. The only column not given such a highlight is the special marker’s original column.

The input contains a single solid foreground rectangle on an otherwise empty background, and the output ignores its original location and rebuilds it as a compact canonical pattern near the top-left. The rectangle’s cells are rearranged into two overlapping stair-step wedges separated by a descending diagonal gap: a shrinking wedge anchored at the upper right of the main cluster and a growing wedge anchored at the lower left. A single extra foreground cell is then placed alone in the output’s bottom-right corner, with all remaining cells left as background.

The tall input is made of five equal-height panels stacked vertically; the output keeps only one panel’s height, with the same width and the same constant right-edge stripe. The decorative patterned block near the top is discarded, and the relevant content comes from the bottom panel: any small markers on the left are shifted down by one row, while the isolated marker near the right side stays in place. All other cells revert to the plain background.

The descending diagonal marker made of a leading cell and a trailing cell is shifted one row downward, so its topmost segment disappears and a new lowest segment is added one step farther down-right. The separate horizontal bar is then redrawn on its original row so that it begins under the shifted diagonal’s first leading cell and spans the sequence of the diagonal’s leading-cell positions. The vertical guide line, the ground row, and the other support/block shapes stay in place; if the shifted diagonal reaches the bar’s row, the bar overwrites the diagonal’s leading cell while the trailing cell remains visible to its right.

The input is a vertical stack of same-sized panels, with each panel separated by a full-width divider row. Each panel contains a short top band on a solid background with one or two small marker cells, and below it a larger region showing a block of empty cells embedded in background; the output keeps each panel unchanged internally but removes the divider rows. Then all panels are laid out side by side in their original top-to-bottom order, producing one wide grid whose height matches a single panel and whose width is the sum of all panel widths.

The grid contains a full-width horizontal separator line in a distinct color. The output is formed by cutting the grid at that separator and keeping only the portion below it, with the lower pattern preserved exactly in the same columns while everything above the line, including the separator itself, is discarded.

The output is made by vertically duplicating the entire input grid. Every colored structure and blank band stays unchanged, and a second identical copy of the whole scene is placed directly underneath the first one. This keeps the width the same while doubling the height.

The output keeps every object’s shape, size, and position exactly the same; only the colors change, while the background remains unchanged. The recoloring is a fixed substitution across the whole grid: one foreground color is converted into a second, that second is converted into a third, the small accent color used by the tiny cross/marker object is converted into the first, and the third color stays as it is. In other words, this task is purely a palette remapping with no geometric modification.

The input contains one hollow rectangular frame in a border color, with four special colored markers at fixed roles: one on the top edge, one on the bottom edge, one on the left midpoint, and one on the right midpoint where a short horizontal stub extends outward. The output widens the canvas and places four copies of this same framed figure side by side. In the first copy the markers stay as given, and in each next copy the four marker colors shift one position around the frame in a cycle: right marker goes to top, top goes to left, left goes to bottom, and bottom goes to right; the frame, background, and stub shape do not change.

The grid contains one region that is supposed to be a regular two-color checkerboard/alternating pattern, but in that region a single cell has the wrong color. The output fixes exactly that one intruding cell by recoloring it to whichever of the two checkerboard colors is needed to preserve the alternation with its neighbors. All other regions, including solid blocks and unrelated shapes, stay unchanged.

The input is a row of same-height subgrids placed side by side, with each block separated by a single vertical divider line in a distinct separator color. The transformation removes the divider columns and keeps only the leftmost subgrid. In other words, the output is just a crop of the first panel, unchanged internally.

The output is made by placing six horizontal copies of the entire input scene side by side. Across these copies, the large central rectangular panel cycles through three interior states: its secondary alternating cells are kept as in the input, replaced by the panel’s main fill color, or replaced by the color of the surrounding arch/outline. At the same time, the two small auxiliary right-side/bottom-right objects alternate between their original colors and a single new shared color, so the six copies show all combinations of the 3 panel states with the 2 auxiliary-color states.

The input contains several evenly spaced vertical guide columns, plus a few small attached block-shaped patterns made of a second color; each such pattern contains exactly one distinctive marker cell. In the output, all of the small patterns are removed and all guide columns except the leftmost one are erased to background. The leftmost guide column is kept, and on every row where any pattern’s distinctive marker appeared, that cell on the leftmost guide column is changed into the marker color.

The input is a vertical stack of three equal-height horizontal bands. Each band shows the same main right-side shape, while a small secondary marker on the left appears in a different band each time. The transformation simply crops away the top two bands and keeps the bottom band exactly as it is.

The output is a horizontal strip of repeated snapshots of the entire input scene. The number of snapshots is one more than the height of the thin vertical yellow stack in the middle; all other structures (background, dark posts, floor/base region, and the magenta marker pattern) are simply copied unchanged into every snapshot. What changes from frame to frame is that this yellow vertical stack collapses into a right-shifted diagonal: after the first frame, the top yellow cell disappears, the remaining yellow cells are arranged as a lower-left to upper-right diagonal just above the yellow base, and this diagonal loses one cell each step until it vanishes completely.

The input contains one solid rectangular patch on a uniform background, and the output keeps that original patch as the leftmost part of a much wider canvas with the same height. To the right, the rectangle is unfolded into many successive staggered echoes: its filled rows/columns are extended as repeating rightward traces, so the solid block turns into sparse, regularly spaced marks that appear on different rows as the trace progresses. Overall, the transformation is a horizontal time-strip or trail of the rectangle rather than a single moved copy.

The input contains a single foreground pattern on a blank background. In the output, that entire grid is repeated two more times to the right, preserving the exact shape and row/column structure each time. The first copy keeps the original foreground color, the second copy recolors all foreground cells with one new color, and the third copy recolors them with another new color, while background cells remain unchanged.

The grid layout stays the same: all objects keep their exact shapes and positions, including the long horizontal bar and the background. Only the three recurring marker colors are rotated in a fixed cycle, so every cell of the first marker color becomes the second, the second becomes the third, and the third becomes the first. This recoloring applies both to the side-frame strips and to the small interior symbols, while the background color and the special bar color are unchanged.

The wide input is made of three horizontal repeats of the same panel, with one repeat containing an alternate marker; the output keeps just one normal panel (equivalently, one repeated block, matching the copies with the true marker rather than the odd alternate one). In that kept panel, find the special marker near the bottom and paint a solid 2-by-3 rectangle of a new color directly above it, centered on the marker’s column so it covers the two rows above and the marker’s column plus its left and right neighbors. Everything else stays as in the chosen panel, even if the new rectangle overwrites existing cells.

The input contains one fixed four-part motif centered on a cross, with four differently colored lobes occupying the top, right, bottom, and left directions. The output places four copies of this same shape side by side, keeping the background and geometry identical in every copy. In the first copy the colors stay as they were, and in each next copy the four lobe-colors are cyclically reassigned to the neighboring direction (top takes the former right color, right takes the former bottom color, bottom takes the former left color, and left takes the former top color).

The input contains a sparse pattern made from two persistent foreground colors plus a third, temporary-looking color. In the output, every temporary-colored cell is recolored to match the existing path/outline color, while the other foreground color and all positions stay unchanged.
After this recoloring, the entire completed grid is copied and stacked vertically as identical repeats, producing a much taller output with the same width.

Identify the only structured subpicture at the left side of the input, with the rest of the grid being uniform background, and repeat that entire subpicture horizontally multiple times to make a long strip. The internal layout of background cells and empty cells stays identical in every copy. The only thing that changes from copy to copy is the small highlighted shape/object: its original color is kept in the first copy, then it cycles through three other highlight colors, repeating that 4-color cycle across the row.

The grid keeps the same height but becomes wider by adding a new strip on the right whose width equals the number of rows. That new right-hand strip is an exact copy of the leftmost square section of the input: take the first N columns, where N is the grid height, and duplicate them to the far right. All marked cells and background cells within that copied block are preserved in the same row positions.

The grid is horizontally cropped: the leftmost and rightmost columns are removed, while everything else stays in the same order. All horizontal color bands keep their colors, heights, and vertical positions, so the only change is that the picture becomes two cells narrower with the side edges trimmed away.

The input is a set of full-height vertical stripes on a blank background, with a repeating left-to-right color order of first stripe color, second stripe color, third stripe color, then the first stripe color again. The output keeps the height the same but triples the width by placing three horizontal copies of the stripe spacing pattern side by side. In the first copy the stripes stay unchanged, in the second copy each stripe’s color advances one step through the three-color order, and in the third copy it advances one more step, while all background cells remain background.

The input contains a single two-part figure on a uniform background: an upper motif in one color sitting directly above a lower solid rectangular block in another color. In the output, this whole figure is stretched/extruded horizontally to the right from its original left edge, occupying most or all of the remaining space, while the background elsewhere stays unchanged. The lower block becomes a longer solid rectangle, and the upper motif is extended row-by-row so its existing silhouette/indentation pattern is propagated across the new width.

The grid contains a connected foreground drawing in one color laid across two different background regions, with a few cells in a second accent color marking key nodes of that drawing. In the output, this drawing is completed by extending its existing bars, bends, and branch-like/stair-step continuations into adjacent empty cells, following the same local geometry already present. When an extended branch reaches a position analogous to an existing marked node, a new accent-colored node is placed there; the two background fields themselves remain unchanged.

The colored cells define a common center and act as sparse samples of a digital circular/octagonal outline. In the output, the main non-background color is extended to fill the missing perimeter points of that same outline, so the sparse ring becomes a fuller symmetric contour around the center. The special color is then added at the matching quarter-rotated positions on the next larger companion ring, keeping all original cells and omitting any placements that would fall outside the grid.

A boxed pattern near the bottom, outlined in a single border color, is treated as the reference object; the scattered colored cells above are an unboxed copy of its meaningful contents. Compare the upper copy to the boxed one row-by-row using only the non-background, non-border colored tokens: any upper tokens that match the boxed pattern are removed, and if an upper row contains extra/wrong tokens, those extras are deleted so the remaining tokens in that row shift left to match the boxed row’s color sequence. The boxed region stays unchanged, and the output shows only any corrected leftover token(s) from the upper copy, which is often nothing at all.

The foreground cells form a motif built from 45-degree diagonal strokes, but one stroke is incomplete. In the output, background cells are added along a single straight diagonal so that this unfinished part is completed: the new cells continue an existing slanted line or supply the missing arm that makes the diagonal pattern consistent with the rest of the figure. All original foreground cells stay in place and the rest of the grid is unchanged.

The output is made by extending the canvas horizontally to three side-by-side sections of the original width. The left and right sections contain an unchanged copy of the input figure in the same position.
In the middle section, that same small diagonal-cross/X-shaped object is replaced by a larger expanded version centered on the same middle cell: its center becomes a 3-cell horizontal bar, a single cell remains directly above and below that bar, and the top and bottom corner cells move outward by one step, making a taller and wider version of the motif.

The sparse marker-colored cells are treated as special points that are erased in the result, becoming background holes. Around them, the surrounding area is painted with a single new foreground color; each marker contributes its touching neighborhood, and overlapping neighborhoods merge into one larger region. In the smaller examples this creates compact clusters around the markers, while in the larger example the merged painted region ends up covering the whole canvas except for the original marker positions.

The input contains a single non-background seed cell. In the output, that seed becomes the center of the largest odd-sized square that can be centered on it while staying inside the grid, and this square is filled as concentric square rings. The rings alternate between the seed’s color and a newly introduced second color, with the exact center staying the seed color; equivalently, cells at even square-distance from the center use the seed color and cells at odd square-distance use the new color. Everything outside this centered square remains background.

The output keeps the original striped square unchanged on the left, then adds a second block of the same size immediately to its right. This added block is the transpose of the input: the input’s vertical stripe pattern becomes horizontal bands, so columns of the original become rows in the new block. The dominant filled color and the background gap color stay the same; only the orientation changes.

The input consists of several same-sized subgrids placed side by side, separated by full vertical divider columns. Each subgrid contains a shape drawn in one foreground color on a common background, and the output removes the dividers and overlays all subgrids into a single grid of that shared size. Any cell occupied by the shape in any subgrid is kept in the merged result, with the foreground recolored to a new output color while the background stays unchanged.

The input contains a single diagonal chain of same-colored cells, which represents one side of a diamond-shaped outline tilted at 45 degrees. The output completes that diamond by adding the three missing diagonal sides, using the given segment as one edge and reflecting/extending it symmetrically around the diamond’s center. The original cells stay in place, and only matching-color cells are added to form the full hollow rhombus.

The output keeps the same height but makes the canvas five times wider; only the leftmost block the size of the original grid is used, and the rest stays background. Inside that left block, the pattern is transformed within the subgrid that excludes the top row and leftmost column: the foreground cells are copied by reflecting them across the descending diagonal of that subgrid (from its top-right corner to its bottom-left corner) and overlaid with the original. This turns the original right-edge vertical stroke into a matching top horizontal stroke and completes the motif with its diagonal mirror, while the top row outside that subgrid stays as it was.

The grid is organized into repeated horizontal panels marked by a full-width divider line. Take the equal-height strip immediately above each divider, align those strips row-for-row and column-for-column, and merge them onto the top strip so that any cell occupied in any panel becomes occupied in the first panel. The output then keeps only the top part of the grid up to just before the second divider (including the first divider and its blank spacer rows), while all lower repeated panels are discarded.

The output is formed by taking the entire input image and appending an exact horizontal copy of it to the right. This doubles the grid’s width while keeping the height unchanged, so every panel, separator gap, and small internal colored detail appears again in the same order. No objects are moved, recolored, or reshaped within each half; the whole scene is simply tiled once more side by side.

The wide input is made of the same column pattern repeated several times across the row, so the output collapses the grid to a single repeating block while keeping the original row positions. All copies are overlaid modulo the repetition width, producing one compact motif that contains the combined non-background cells from the repeated columns. During this reduction, the various guide/marker colors that act like structural anchors are normalized into one common marker color, while the distinctive motif colors and the bottom anchor color remain unchanged.

The grid is extended horizontally by adding one more same-sized panel on the right. This new panel keeps the exact object/frame pattern of the existing panel motif, but the colors are rotated among the structural roles: the outer frame takes the previous inner color, the inner region takes the next color in the cycle, and so on. In the two-color examples this is just a swap of frame and center colors; in the three-color example it continues the left-to-right color-role cycle across the repeated square patterns.

The sparse non-background pattern is copied repeatedly into side-by-side panels, so the output keeps the same height but becomes much wider. From left to right, each whole-panel copy is vertically offset in a symmetric staircase: first unshifted, then shifted down by 1 row, then by 2, and so on up to a middle maximum, then the shifts reverse back up to 0. Background stays background, and any part of a shifted copy that would fall outside the top or bottom edge is simply clipped.

Each input is a 3-row background field containing exactly two isolated accent cells on the middle row. The output keeps the same width but expands the grid to 9 rows, and draws that accent pair three times on rows 1, 5, and 9. In each repeated row, the left accent cell is placed in the third column and the right accent cell is placed in the second-from-last column; every other cell remains background.

The tall input is divided into several same-sized panels by full-width separator rows. Compare these panels and identify the recurring foreground template: keep only the cells whose colored contents line up in the same relative positions across the repeated instances, while removing panel-specific extra shapes and decorations. The output is one panel-sized grid showing just this shared pattern on the background.

The output keeps the same width and background color, but makes the grid four times taller by stacking repeated copies of the entire input underneath each other. Every colored object — the block, the vertical marks, and the small pair near the bottom — stays in exactly the same horizontal position within each copy. In other words, the whole input image is tiled vertically 4 times with no horizontal changes.

The input contains several separated one-cell-thick strokes of the same foreground color: a vertical line, a left-to-right descending diagonal, a full horizontal line, and a right-to-left descending diagonal segment. The output rebuilds these scattered pieces into one compact square whose side length matches the stroke length, translating the pieces so they overlap in their natural shared crossing pattern. In the result, the vertical and horizontal lines form a central cross, and the two diagonals are placed to meet that same center, producing a star/asterisk-like figure.

The grid contains one compact 3×3 block of assorted non-background colors and a separate single-cell marker elsewhere. In the output, that entire 3×3 block is preserved in the same position and size but every cell in it is recolored to one uniform fill color, while the isolated marker cell and the background stay unchanged.

Find the smallest rectangular crop that contains the entire non-background figure, keeping both the figure pixels and any background pixels inside that crop. The output is made by taking that cropped rectangle and repeating it unchanged four times side by side in a single horizontal strip. The surrounding empty border from the original grid is removed, and there is no vertical repetition.

Each input has a small bordered box containing a solid inner block, plus a separate large solid rectangle elsewhere. In the output, the inner block’s color is extended from the small box toward the upper-right as a slanted ribbon/parallelogram with staircase diagonal ends; where this ribbon passes through the small box, any crossed border cells are changed to the inner color as well. The large solid rectangle stays in place, only being overwritten where the ribbon reaches it, and the ribbon’s overall extent is determined by the size of that large rectangle.

The large grid is partitioned into four equal quadrants containing two example pairs arranged in a 2×2 layout. The output is simply the lower-right quadrant copied exactly, preserving all colors and shapes in that panel while discarding the other three quadrants.

Inside the unchanged rectangular frame, the sparse foreground pattern is a diagonal/zigzag line made of single cells. The entire foreground pattern is translated straight downward, without changing its shape or columns, until its lowest cell sits on the last row inside the frame. Its original cells are cleared back to the background color, while the frame and all other background cells remain unchanged.

The input is partitioned into several equal-width vertical panels, each with its own solid background color and small overlaid markings. Across these panels, a bright foreground block made of the same highlight color appears as a progression, growing from a smaller version in earlier panels to a larger completed version in the far-right panel. The output is simply that final rightmost panel, cropped out exactly as it appears, with its background and the completed highlight shape preserved.

The grid is expanded horizontally into five side-by-side copies of the original background bands: the upper field, the single middle stripe, and the lower field are all repeated unchanged across the full width. The small non-band figure is treated specially: in the leftmost copy it is moved one cell to the right, and any cells it leaves behind are filled with the upper-field color. In the other four copies, that figure is removed entirely by repainting its original cells with the upper-field color, so it only remains visibly present in the first panel.

The input is split into two equal side-by-side parts: a left multicolor diamond-like motif and a right single-color diamond-like guide. The output is formed by turning the guide’s successive horizontal layers (from outer to inner, ignoring layers that would produce nothing) into filtered copies of the left motif, laid out side by side; inner guide layers keep more of the left motif, while outer guide layers leave only smaller core subsets. Because the guide is vertically symmetric, these filtered copies appear in a symmetric horizontal sequence, with an unchanged/full left motif at the center when that layer is present.

The output places four side-by-side copies of the entire input grid, keeping the height the same and quadrupling the width. In each copy, the cross-shaped connector and the framed 3x3 endpoint tiles stay in the same locations, but the single special marker inside every endpoint tile rotates around the tile’s central hub: first at the top as in the input, then on the right, then at the bottom, then on the left.

The framed picture is divided into a regular grid of 3×3 interior tiles, and each tile is treated as its own small object. The output places four full framed copies side by side: first the original image, then a version where every 3×3 tile is rotated a quarter-turn left, then a half-turn, then a quarter-turn right, while each tile stays in the same tile position in the overall layout. The background and the outer frame color are preserved, so the panel boundaries appear as repeated frame columns.

The output is made by placing four full-width copies of the input side by side, with the vertical separator stripe kept in the same relative position in every copy. The first copy is unchanged; in the second, the entire upper horizontal band is recolored to a new fill color, the small rectangle inside that band is recolored to its own new color, and the entire bottom band is replaced by the separator color. In the third copy, the upper band is recolored to match the middle band and the small rectangle is recolored again, while the bottom band stays original; in the fourth copy, the top stays as in the input but the bottom band is again fully replaced by the separator color.

The grid is made of repeated panels containing small reference symbols above and larger composite shapes below. In the output, every cell of the secondary filler color inside the larger lower shapes is erased to the background, while the outline color and the other meaningful colored parts are left exactly where they were. The top reference symbols remain unchanged, and there is no shifting or resizing—only removal of that one filler color.

The grids contain several separate blocky, character-like shapes drawn in one foreground color on an empty background. The output keeps every shape in the same place but repairs/completes it by adding foreground cells where strokes are missing, so each damaged glyph becomes a fuller, more standard-looking symbol. No objects are moved or removed; the change is only the insertion of extra pixels adjacent to the existing strokes.

The input contains a single cross shape made of one foreground-colored full row and one foreground-colored full column on a blank square background. The output creates a new blank canvas with double the input height and double the input width, then places the entire original cross pattern unchanged inside it, centered so that the cross sits in the middle of the larger frame. No recoloring or reshaping happens; only the surrounding blank border is enlarged.

The picture’s geometry stays exactly the same; only colors are reassigned. Specifically, the three non-background colors that make up the large filled regions are rotated in a 3-cycle: the color used for one main mass changes to the second main-region color, that one changes to the third, and the third changes back to the first. All other colors—background, the long horizontal bar, the vertical stem, and the small marker cells—remain unchanged.

The grid is divided into equal-width panels by full-height separator columns. The output keeps only the leftmost panel as the base picture, removes the separators and other duplicate panels, and then copies over any cells of the special accent color from the other panels into the same panel-relative positions on that base. All other colors/shapes stay as they are in the leftmost panel; only those accent-colored marks are merged in.

The input consists of three horizontal stripe-bands, each filled with its own alternating two-color pattern. The output makes the grid five times wider by repeating each original row as five side-by-side tiles; the top band stays entirely tiled with the top pattern, and the bottom band stays entirely tiled with the bottom pattern. Only the middle band is edited: in its first two rows, centered tiles are replaced by the top-band pattern in a 3-then-1 taper, and in its last two rows, centered tiles are replaced by the bottom-band pattern in a 1-then-3 taper, while any middle rows between those remain the original middle pattern.

The wide input contains several copies of the same-sized motif placed side by side across the middle, separated by background columns, with a solid horizontal strip at the bottom. The transformation cuts the image into equal vertical sections, each section centered on one motif and keeping its local background padding and the bottom strip segment of the same width. These cropped sections are then stacked vertically in left-to-right order, so the output is a tall column of the original repeated units.

The grid is expanded to twice its original height and width, using the long cross in the separator color as the reference landmark. The original picture is kept in the upper-left, and three more copies of the entire scene are added around it: one rotated 90° clockwise on the right, one rotated 90° counterclockwise below, and one rotated 180° in the lower-right. As a result, every non-background object reappears in the corresponding rotated positions, and the separator-colored cross continues through the enlarged layout to align the four versions.

The grid is divided into three equal-height horizontal panels, each containing one foreground figure on a plain background. The output keeps only the bottom panel, preserving its width and the exact arrangement of foreground cells within that panel. In other words, the top two repeated panels are discarded and the lowest copy becomes the whole output.

The input contains a noisy black/foreground pattern split by straight divider lines of a third color, plus solid full-width rows of that same divider color at the top and bottom. In the output, the top and bottom solid divider rows are removed entirely, reducing the height by 2. All remaining divider-color cells inside the picture (the vertical separator columns) are recolored to the foreground color, so the separated sections become one continuous pattern while background cells stay unchanged.

The input is a vertical stack of repeated frames showing the same scene in two alternating states. To form the output, keep one base frame and superimpose later frames only in places where they add new non-background cells; if a later frame merely changes the color of an already occupied cell, the base frame’s color stays. As a result, the lower outlined-and-filled shape gains the extra connecting/left-edge cells seen in the alternate state, while the upper shape keeps its original bar color instead of the alternate recolor.

The wide input is partitioned by blank separator columns into five separate 3×3 pattern blocks. Among those five blocks, one pattern is repeated and the others are distinct, so the transformation reduces the whole set to a single horizontal strip whose length equals the number of distinct blocks. That strip is filled uniformly with a new output color, ignoring the original pattern colors and internal details.

Each input contains several separated copies of the same framed motif, with a small corner marker indicating its orientation; some orientations are present directly and one orientation may be missing while another is duplicated. The task crops these motifs, uses 180° rotation on copies when needed so that all four corner-marker orientations are represented exactly once, and places the four tiles side by side with no blank gaps. The left-to-right order is by the marker moving around the corners in counterclockwise order.

The entire picture is reflected left-to-right across the grid’s vertical centerline. Every non-background cell keeps its color, but each row’s colored pattern appears in reverse horizontal order at the mirrored columns, including the solid separator bands and the isolated single cells near the top and bottom. The background stays unchanged.

The picture is divided into equal-width vertical tiles, where each tile is a small repeated motif made of background, patterned cells, and occasional marker cells. The output keeps the original row content unchanged, then extends the grid to the right by appending the interior tiles in reverse order: copy the second-to-last tile, then the one before it, and so on, stopping at the second tile. In effect, the first and last original tiles stay unique end pieces, while the middle sequence is mirrored onto the right side.

The input is an odd-sized square made of alternating full horizontal bands of one color and rows where that same color appears in every other cell, leaving regularly spaced cells of a second color. In the output, this whole square pattern is copied unchanged at the top. The canvas is then extended downward to five times the original height while keeping the same width, and all newly added rows are filled entirely with the second, gap/background color.

The wide input is split into three equal horizontal panels, all sharing the same background and the same small bottom block pattern. In each panel, locate the single highlighted cell; the output keeps just one panel-sized canvas and preserves the shared background/bottom pattern. Then draw the highlighted color along straight connections from the first panel’s highlighted cell to the second’s, and from the second’s to the third’s, while all dark guide marks used inside the panels are removed.

The non-background cells act as sparse anchor points for one symmetric, jagged geometric figure. The output completes that figure by adding the missing same-colored cells along the stepped straight sides between the anchors, filling skipped rows/columns so the sloping edges become continuous and balanced left-to-right. Where the completed sides meet or overlap, extra cells appear as a short top cap or a horizontal bridge across the middle.

The scattered cells in the second row are collapsed to a single vertical pillar: keep only the second cell of the leftmost horizontal block of that color, erase the rest of that row’s cells of that color, and extend the kept cell straight downward through the solid lower region. The lone marker from the top row is removed from the top and reappears inside the lower solid region immediately to the left of this pillar. Its vertical position is set by how many cells remain from its original column to the right end of the upper block it was above, counting that aligned cell.

The grid has a uniform background, one special center cell, and several cells of another color forming only part of a stair-stepped outline around that center. The output completes this partial outline into a full figure centered on the special cell by copying the given pattern through rotational/mirror symmetry around the center, so matching arms/arcs appear in all directions. The special center cell stays unchanged, and only the outline color is added.

The picture is a row of equal-sized repeated panels. The output keeps every panel unchanged except the rightmost one, which is edited so it becomes an exact copy of the panel immediately to its left. In these examples, that correction only affects the small accent-colored vertical marker in the last panel: its top cell is removed and a new bottom cell is added so the marker sits one row lower, while the other colored structures stay fixed.

The input is preserved and the grid is extended downward. The rows are organized in horizontal bands whose height matches the grid width, and the output continues the sparse two-color motif sequence already established by the earlier bands, copying the same row patterns in the same columns and leaving empty rows empty. The extension stops when the total height reaches seven such width-sized bands.

The grid is a checkerboard-like frame: one background color fills the separator rows and columns, while the cells at the alternating positions contain a small matrix of values. Compare these value-columns by adding the entries in each column, and identify the column with the smallest total. In the output, the separator/background stays unchanged, every cell in the minimum-sum column is replaced by the empty/dark cell color, and every cell in all other value-columns is replaced by a single highlight color.

The entire input scene is copied and stacked vertically multiple times, using the original grid as a repeating frame. In each stacked copy, the small floating rectangle is shifted one cell to the right while the long top bar and the bottom platform/floor structure stay unchanged. The number of copies equals the number of rightward positions available until that small rectangle reaches the right edge of the grid.

The output is a horizontal strip of four same-sized panels. In each panel, the background-like cells are filled uniformly (the first panel keeps the original background, while the next three use new flat background colors), and the dark path/holes pattern stays in its original place; the other foreground shape is then reproduced with a one-cell offset in a different direction from panel to panel (up, left, down, right). When that shifted shape would land on cells belonging to the dark pattern, the dark pattern remains visible instead of being replaced.

The output widens the canvas to three times the original width and places three side-by-side copies of the input scene on the same rows. The left and right copies are unchanged, while the middle copy modifies the small non-background pattern by swapping every adjacent pair of columns within that pattern’s horizontal span (1st with 2nd, 3rd with 4th, etc.). All other cells remain the uniform background color.

The foreground pattern is copied into a new canvas made of four equal-width panels placed side by side, while the height stays the same. The first panel keeps the original centered figure, and the next three panels show the same figure rotated around its center by equal 45-degree steps, so the arms/lines through the center cycle through the four directions (diagonal, vertical, opposite diagonal, horizontal). Background cells remain unchanged and only the foreground shape is reoriented.

The corner/frame pieces stay unchanged. In the middle area there are two similar patterned blocks; the transformation removes the left-hand block while leaving the right-hand block exactly as it is. If the left block extends into the same columns as the left frame/corner band, only that overlapping leftmost strip is preserved and the rest of the block is turned into background.

The non-background cells in the input all lie on the right border, and their row positions are the main thing being extracted. The output keeps the same height but becomes four input-width panels placed side by side; in each panel, every occupied input row also creates a full vertical stripe at the column whose index matches that row, with the stripe color depending on that row’s order among the marked rows and on which panel it is in. The original right-edge cells are then echoed inside each panel as recolored traces starting from the same border positions, forming copies/descending down-left diagonal continuations so that the four panels show four transformed versions of the same border-column pattern.

The wide input is split into three equal subgrids, and the output is a single subgrid of that same size. The non-background shapes in the panels are treated as fragments or stages of one figure: their matching parts are overlaid, and the main-colored region is completed so the relevant pieces form one coherent connected shape. Small auxiliary-colored marks are ignored if they are just separate indicators, but any auxiliary piece that belongs to the final connected composite is kept in place.

The grid contains three repeated lower clusters beneath three identical horizontal header bars. Each lower cluster keeps the same 3-cell body and bottom-center accent, but the single cell directly above the body is the only part that can vary between the body color and the accent color.
In the output, those three upper single-cell markers are reassigned so that the only body-colored one is placed on the leftmost cluster, while the other two clusters use the accent color there. Everything else remains unchanged.

The grid is divided into three vertical compartments by separator columns, and almost everything stays fixed. In each compartment, look at the short 3-cell horizontal bar below the long horizontal divider: only its middle cell changes, becoming the color of the small separate 2-cell block found elsewhere in that same compartment. If a compartment has no such 2-cell block, the middle cell of its 3-cell bar is replaced by the background instead.

The large patterned block and the small foreground shape stay unchanged; the only change is in the set of isolated marker cells of another color. Those markers already lie on a single straight horizontal or vertical line with a constant spacing, except that one position in the sequence is missing, and the output fills in exactly that missing marker cell so the line becomes evenly spaced.

The scattered input objects are ignored and the entire grid is replaced by a centered set of 1-cell-thick concentric square frames, like a bullseye made of nested square rings. The rings use a fixed color progression from outermost to innermost; larger odd-sized grids show more outer layers, while smaller ones show only the inner suffix of the same progression. The innermost non-background layer is always a 3-by-3 ring, leaving a single background cell at the exact center.

The input is made of four equal-sized panels placed in a single row or a single column on a uniform background. Each panel contains the same foreground pattern, but the pattern is rotated through the four quarter-turn orientations. The output keeps only one panel: the first panel in reading order (leftmost if the panels are horizontal, topmost if they are vertical), preserving its full local background frame and discarding the other three rotated copies.

The grid keeps the same height but is extended to the right by one horizontal period, where the period is the spacing between the isolated foreground dots in the upper sparse row. In the added columns, the solid foreground stripe continues straight across, the upper sparse row gets one more dot at the same interval, and the lower mixed row continues by repeating its leftmost period-sized segment. All other rows remain background in the new area.

Each input has a small patterned patch (mostly one interior color with a few accent cells) and a separate larger shape marked in a different placeholder color, all on a uniform background. In the output, the background is recolored, the placeholder shape is turned into a scaled-up copy of the small patch, and the patch’s row/column pattern is enlarged proportionally by repeating rows and columns so its accent cells keep the same relative arrangement. Any holes, notches, or missing cells in the larger target shape remain background, and the original small patch location is cleared into the new background.

The input contains two separate figures made from two foreground colors: a small clustered motif near the top and a larger line-based drawing near the bottom. In the output, both figures keep exactly the same shape, position, and occupied cells, but all of their non-background cells are recolored into one single uniform foreground color. This turns each mixed-color figure into a solid monochrome version of itself.

The non-background reference pieces stay unchanged: the horizontal bar in the upper left, the small block in the upper right, and the small block in the lower left are all preserved exactly. Among the several disconnected middle objects made of the same foreground color, only the rightmost one is kept, and every other object of that color is erased. The kept object does not move or change shape; it is simply isolated from the rest.

The wide input is split into three equal square sections placed side by side, each containing one foreground figure on a blank background. The output keeps only the middle square section, but the figure inside it is transposed: its rows and columns are swapped, as if reflected across the square’s top-left to bottom-right diagonal, while staying in the same local position within that square.

The input is made of two equal-width side-by-side panels containing the same object pattern, with the right panel acting as a mirrored counterpart of the left. To produce the output, collapse these two panels into one by keeping a single half-width version of the pattern, effectively superimposing the left half with a horizontally flipped right half. The thin accent-colored cells are not preserved as a separate color; they are converted into the main object color, while the background stays unchanged.

The input shows a square border in the background color around a large region of another color, with a connected spiral/maze-like intrusion of the background color reaching inward. In the output, that whole internal intrusion is overwritten by the region color, except for one single background-colored cell left at the exact center of the grid. The original bottom-edge opening is kept, and three matching one-cell openings are added on the other sides so there is one opening per side, arranged around the center with the same one-cell offset pattern.

The wide input is made of five equal square panels placed side by side. To form the output, these five panels are collapsed/overlaid into a single square by aligning corresponding cells, keeping the background unchanged and preserving any non-background cell that appears in any panel.
Across the panels, the same small structure repeats: two side blocks of one object color stay fixed, while a highlighted color occupies a different column of the central 5-cell-wide region in each panel. When all five panels are superimposed, those shifted highlights combine into one solid central 5×5 block between the two side blocks.

The input is a vertical stack of same-sized panels separated by one blank row, like frames in a filmstrip. The output converts that framing into a horizontal strip: it keeps the panel height, creates enough width for all frame positions with one blank column between them, and places only the topmost nonblank panel unchanged in the leftmost position. Everything else in the new strip is left as blank background.

The grid contains a regularly spaced lattice of anchor cells; in the output this anchor lattice is redrawn one column to the right, so the leftmost anchor column disappears and a blank column is left at the far left. The scattered foreground pixels are treated as connected diagonal/branching shapes and are re-placed horizontally relative to the shifted anchor lattice while keeping each shape’s structure. One distinguished shape (the left/first one) is recolored with the new highlight color, while the other foreground shape(s) stay in the original foreground color.

The input contains several same-colored hollow rectangles arranged in order along one axis, with each successive rectangle becoming narrower and taller. The output keeps all existing rectangles and adds one more rectangle after the last/smallest one in the same direction of the sequence: this new rectangle is a copy of the first, widest-and-shortest rectangle. If there is not enough room, the grid is extended in that direction to fit the added copy.

The input is a row-wise repetition of the same horizontal tile, which can be recognized from the repeated 2-row band near the bottom. The output keeps just one copy of that tile (the leftmost repeat), preserves its background and bottom band, and removes the repeated upper foreground blocks. The single contrasting cells associated with those upper blocks are then overlaid into this one tile and turned into a new highlight color, with the result shown as a connected step/diagonal path linking the projected marked positions from the repeated tiles.

The grid is transposed: rows become columns, so the whole figure is reflected across the main diagonal and the output’s height and width are swapped relative to the input. At the same time, the two non-background colors exchange roles everywhere, while the background stays unchanged. This means the central cross/diamond structure and its extending lines keep the same relative shape after diagonal reflection, but every cell of one foreground color becomes the other foreground color and vice versa.

The object in the second foreground color stays exactly where it is and keeps its shape; only the scattered cells/patches of the first foreground color are expanded. Each first-color cell is propagated along descending diagonals through empty space, so the output becomes filled with repeated diagonal streaks or copies derived from the original first-color placements. Where these diagonal traces meet the preserved second-color structure, that structure remains unchanged rather than being overwritten.

The background stays unchanged, while each cluster of marked cells is redrawn in a new color as a larger, thicker version of itself. The redraw preserves the cluster’s local structure—single cells become small square blocks, and neighboring cells merge into wider bars or stair-step patches so the same connectivity pattern is visible at a heavier 2-cell thickness. Each component is expanded in place with slight outward growth, replacing the original sparse marks with solid filled regions.

The input contains one small multi-part symbol near the top and a solid vertical border on the far right. The output is made by stacking many copies of the original-height frame vertically; in each stacked band, that symbol is reproduced shifted to the right by the same amount as its original offset from the left, while the right border stays fixed. Across successive bands, a new highlight color forms a horizontal trail that grows one cell longer each band (clipped by the border), and the symbol’s small detached side cells are echoed near the right side as repeated markers.

Each row is a single-color horizontal band containing a few blank cells near the left that reveal that row’s repeating horizontal template. The output completes that template across the full row: blank cells are added farther to the right at the same phase(s) and spacing suggested by the starting segment, while all nonblank cells keep the row’s original color. Rows that already show an every-other-cell blank pattern are extended as full alternations, while rows with a longer repeating block just get periodic extra blanks in the matching positions.

The input is a horizontal row of equal-sized square panels, each panel as wide as the grid is tall. The output keeps all existing panels unchanged and enlarges the grid by adding one more panel on the far right. That new rightmost panel is an exact copy of the leftmost panel, including its background cells, mixed foreground pattern, and bottom stripe.

The output is a vertical stack of four same-width panels separated by solid separator rows. The first panel is the input unchanged; the next three keep the large symmetric outer shape in place but redraw the inner asymmetric line-pattern in its other orientations: one version is mirrored left-right, and the other two are the 90°-rotated forms, which appear as a full horizontal middle bar with the diagonal part placed above or below it. In other words, the result enumerates the original inner motif together with its horizontal reflection and its two quarter-turn variants, all shown inside the same outer frame.

A uniformly filled input grid is turned into a much wider grid of the same height, with the original fill color still used as the background everywhere else. In each row, a short horizontal dashed strip is added: it alternates between a new dark color and the background color, starts with the dark color, and has length one more than the input width. That dashed strip shifts right by a constant amount from one row to the next (specifically by one less than the input width), so the strips trace a descending diagonal across the enlarged canvas.

The sparse markers are expanded into an alternating checkerboard pattern across a large region of the grid, with the phase aligned to the distinguished single-cell marker so that its parity fixes which squares get which checker color. Then diagonal wedge-shaped corner regions are trimmed according to the other marker cells (and the reference cell’s placement relative to the borders): some wedges are cut back to background, while others have one checker parity overwritten so the wedge becomes a solid triangle of one checker color. Everything outside those diagonal edits remains in the same alternating pattern.

Inside the large plain panel, there is a 3-row decorative strip made from two accent colors, often repeating the same checker-like 3x3 motif several times from left to right. The output preserves only the rightmost complete motif, while the repeated material to its left is weakened/erased: the cells of one accent color are replaced by the surrounding non-accent background, leaving at most the other accent color as a partial trace. Overall, the transformation reduces a repeated chain of motifs to a single surviving terminal motif on the right.
