The non-background content consists of two aligned side fragments, one on the left and one on the right, embedded in a uniform field. These two fragments are treated as partial horizontal pieces of one motif: they are merged into a wider strip by joining them through their shared blank edge/column, preserving the same vertical row pattern of blank rows and filled rows. The completed strip is then written back at both side locations as a left-right mirrored pair, while the rest of the grid stays unchanged.

Find the vertical object made of the distinctive marker color in the upper part of the grid, above the solid horizontal divider. In the lower dark-colored band beneath that divider, mark the same column by placing one cell of that marker color in the top row of the band and one cell of a new endpoint color in the bottom row of the band. All other cells, including the divider and the scattered small marks, remain unchanged.

The output stretches the scene into four equal-width panels arranged side by side. The large bordered rectangle is copied into each panel in the same relative place, preserving its border and the non-highlight interior pattern, while the highlight-colored shapes are treated separately as movable overlays: across the four panels they are shown in different panel-specific placements/variants, so highlight cells inside the rectangle may disappear in some copies and detached highlight shapes outside the rectangle shift between panels. Small isolated marker cells outside the main rectangle are only repeated in the panels where their shifted copy remains on the canvas.

The grid is split into equal-width vertical panels by full-height separator columns in the contrasting cutout color. The output extends the image to the right by reflecting the panel sequence around the last existing panel: keep the input unchanged, then append the earlier panels again in reverse order, inserting the same separator columns between them. As a result, a sequence like panel1–panel2 becomes panel1–panel2–panel1, and panel1–panel2–panel1 becomes panel1–panel2–panel1–panel2–panel1.

The grid contains a filled diamond on the left and a large solid block on the right with a messy background-colored cutout inside it. In the output, the left diamond is used as a template to redraw the right-side cutout: the cutout is cleaned into the same diamond silhouette/scale, but represented only by regularly spaced diagonal background cells (a striped/sampled version of the diamond) inside the solid right block. All other irregular holes in the right block are filled back in, while the left object and the overall frame stay in place.

The grid has a top band with three short horizontal bars and a bottom band with three small 2x3 rectangles, each accompanied by a single marker cell on the last row. Find the rectangle whose marker is directly underneath the rectangle itself, while the other two markers sit just outside their rectangles on the left or right. The output keeps all rows but crops the image horizontally to the narrow column range around that matched rectangle/marker pair, which also preserves the corresponding bar above and removes the other two groups.

The input is a row of equal-sized subgrids separated by black divider columns, and the output collapses them back to a single subgrid. Start from the rightmost subgrid as the base, then merge the earlier subgrids only into the upper region that uses the top background color: treat that top background as transparent, so any colored marks from earlier panels are stamped in, and if multiple non-background marks overlap, the later panel in left-to-right order wins. The lower region, which uses a different background color, is not accumulated; it is copied exactly from the rightmost panel.

The grid contains a single repeating zigzag/diagonal trace in one foreground color on a uniform background. A few cells that should belong to that trace are shown in a different marker color instead of the trace color. In the output, those marker-colored interruptions are converted to the trace color, restoring one continuous repeating path while everything else stays unchanged.

The input is built by repeating a top-left template along one axis, so the output first isolates that single fundamental top-left block and erases the extra repeated continuation beyond it. Within the kept block, the top row is preserved exactly as it appears, while every cell in the rows below is turned into the foreground color, making the rest of the block a solid filled rectangle. Everything outside that retained block becomes background.

The wide input is made of three identical copies of the same smaller picture placed side by side. The output removes the duplication and keeps just one single copy, equivalent to cropping the grid to one third of its original width. All rows and internal details of that one tile are preserved, including the mostly uniform upper area, the short patterned row near the bottom, and the solid bottom band.

The input consists of several vertically separated copies of the same foreground motif on a plain background, with a few isolated single-cell accents in a third color. These repeated copies are collapsed into one output strip whose height matches one motif, combining the information from all copies to reconstruct a more complete version of the shape where missing parts in one copy are supplied by the others. The background remains unchanged, and any accent cells that belong to the collapsed strip are kept in their corresponding relative positions.

The wide input grid is made from several equal-width panels placed side by side on the same background, each panel containing the same basic small figure or a slight variant of it. The transformation extracts a single panel and discards the horizontal repetition, so the output has the same height but only one motif-width. When one panel is the distinct variant among the repeats, that differing panel is kept; otherwise the repeated unit itself is returned unchanged.

The input is a vertically symmetric motif: an inner diamond/hourglass made of single cells lies between two long horizontal bars that each have a one-cell gap at the center, sometimes with a single connector cell just inside that gap. The output makes the grid three times taller and stacks three versions of this motif one under another. The middle copy is unchanged; in the top copy, each broken bar is split so its outer end segments stay on the original row while the rest shifts one row inward toward the diamond, and in the bottom copy the opposite completion is shown: each bar’s center gap is filled into a solid full bar and the adjacent connector cell is removed.

The colored cells depict a skewed 3D-like structure: a long top strip, edge/scaffold cells, and a few marked face cells. The output redraws the same object from the opposite/back side, so the long top strip becomes a short centered ridge, the scaffold/edge cells are repositioned to the back-facing outline, and the marked cells keep their colors but move to the corresponding rear-visible locations. The background stays the same.

The single non-background cell marks the center of the output pattern and keeps its original color. The entire grid is then filled with concentric, axis-aligned square rings centered on that cell, each ring one cell thick and extending to the edges of the canvas. These rings alternate between the center cell’s color and a second color, producing a square target-like pattern across the whole board.

The input is a horizontal strip of several equal-sized square panels, each showing a noisy version of the same two-color pattern on a background. Split the strip into those square panels, then overlay them cell-by-cell to make one output panel of the same square size. For each position, keep the background only if all panels are background there; otherwise choose the foreground color that appears most often at that position, with ties consistently resolved in favor of one of the two foreground colors.

The input is divided into several horizontally framed panels separated by blank rows; they all show the same template, with one line-shaped gap inside a filled interior, and a few copies also contain a special marker color. The output keeps just a single copy of the template and enlarges that interior gap by one cell in every orthogonal direction, so a thin horizontal or vertical opening becomes a thicker diamond/capsule-like shape while the outer frame stays unchanged. The marker-bearing duplicate panels act as the cue that this one-step growth of the gap should be performed.

The output is made by placing three copies of the input side by side, tripling the width. The left and right copies are unchanged, while the center copy is the input reflected vertically (top-to-bottom): the bottom horizontal region moves to the top, the top region moves to the bottom, and all embedded patterns keep their columns but appear in reversed row order. Uniform background bands stay uniform, while the small motif objects in the middle and lower sections are mirrored vertically within that central panel.

The input contains one complete framed rectangle with a solid interior, plus a second matching frame on the right that is open at the top and initially empty inside. The output places three horizontal copies of the whole scene side by side. Across these three copies, the right-hand open frame is progressively filled from the bottom upward with the same interior color as the left rectangle: first still empty, then only the lowest interior band filled, then a larger lower portion filled, while all borders and other background cells remain unchanged.

The input has a big solid region on the left, an empty region on the right, and a few small marked shapes embedded in the solid region. In the output, the empty area is no longer a full right half: it is compressed into a smaller upper-left patch, while the solid color spreads across most of the grid. The non-background marked shapes from the original solid side are then redrawn inside this expanded solid field as enlarged rectangular copies, preserving their top-vs-bottom ordering: small top markers become 2-by-2 style blocks, and the bottom strip becomes a larger doubled block shifted toward the right.

Each input has a large hollow square frame on the far left, a separate complex symbol in the middle, and an empty region on the far right. The transformation copies the left hollow frame and places an identical copy into the empty space on the right, aligned with the same top and bottom rows. The middle symbol and all existing cells stay unchanged, so the central figure ends up framed symmetrically by matching square borders on both sides.

The input is split into three same-width vertical panels separated by single blank columns. The output extends this strip to five panels by reflecting the panel sequence horizontally: keep the original first, second, and third panels, then append a copy of the second panel and a copy of the first panel, with the same blank separator columns between panels. All cell patterns inside each panel are copied exactly, so the final layout is a left-right palindrome around the original third panel.

The input is arranged as three equal-width vertical panels placed side by side. The output keeps only the middle panel, preserving its height and the relative positions of its main colored blocks, while removing the scattered single-cell marker pixels and leaving only background around the remaining larger shapes.

The input contains two side-by-side copies of the same large patterned figure, with a blank divider column or gap between the left copy and the right copy. Small rectangular patches in other colors are embedded inside these figures; these are treated as foreign inserts and are erased back to the background. The output keeps only the left-hand copy of the main figure, with those inserted colored blocks removed, and turns the entire right copy (and everything to its right) into background.

The input contains a small cross/plus-shaped figure made of the foreground color, with one extra foreground dot on the same horizontal line at equal distance to the left and right of the cross’s center. The output keeps all existing marks unchanged, extends the canvas to the right, and places one additional foreground dot on that same row one more equal spacing beyond the right-hand extra dot. In effect, the symmetric left/right pair around the central cross is continued by one more step to the right.

The whole input canvas is expanded into a 2×2 layout, repeating the same border structure and empty padding in each quadrant. The figure inside the frame is copied unchanged in the upper-left and lower-right quadrants, while the other two quadrants show derived versions of its lower body: the lower-left quadrant enlarges the lower-colored body by thickening/doubling that region, and the upper-right quadrant shows a compact, distorted version of that same body-growth while keeping the small top accent block. In short, the output is a framed 2×2 composition with two original copies on the main diagonal and two body-expanded variants on the other diagonal.

The output is four side-by-side copies of the original square grid, so the width becomes four times larger while the height stays the same. In each copy, the main connected figure is completed into a fully four-way rotationally symmetric pattern by taking the original main-color shape and adding its 90°, 180°, and 270° rotations around its center. The other non-background cells—the three isolated marker colors and any accent-color cells—are not merged this way; instead, each horizontal copy shows them rotated by 0, 90, 180, or 270 degrees around the same center, overlaid on top of the completed main figure.

The input contains one large foreground figure drawn as a sparse or perforated outline, symmetric across both axes, on an otherwise empty background. In the output, that same figure is solidified: for each row occupied by the figure, every background cell between the leftmost and rightmost foreground cells is filled with the foreground color. The overall outer silhouette, size, and position stay the same; only internal gaps and row-wise breaks are filled in.

The output expands the grid into four equal-width panels placed side by side. In the first panel the original triangular/pyramidal objects are copied unchanged; in the second, each such object is reduced to its left half (including the center column) and recolored with the new highlight color. The third panel contains the original objects flipped vertically within their own bounding boxes, and the fourth panel contains the same vertical flip applied to the recolored left-half versions.

Each grid has a small multicolored block near the boundary between an upper background area and a lower background area, plus a one-cell-wide trail extending upward from that block through the upper area. The output leaves the backgrounds and the multicolored block unchanged, and continues that trail upward by following its existing diagonal zigzag pattern until it reaches the top edge. In other words, the sparse trail color is completed upward in the same path shape already implied by the input.

Each input has a large solid rectangle of one color surrounded by a different background color. In the output, the solid rectangle is carved from the inside using the background color to make concentric rectangular rings, beginning two cells in from the rectangle’s edge and repeating inward with one-cell-thick bands of the original rectangle color left between rings. The outer frame/background stays unchanged, and if the innermost ring collapses because space is small, it becomes a filled central bar/block of the background color.

The input grid is made from a smaller vertical tile that repeats exactly across the width. The output keeps the height and all colors unchanged, but extends the grid to the right by continuing that same horizontal repetition until the tile appears four times total. In other words, nothing inside the motif is edited; the pattern is simply completed by adding more copies of the repeating block.

The key change happens to the hanging, frame-colored container attached to a vertical post inside the bordered room. Its upper rim stays fixed, but its lower part is pulled downward through the bottom of the room: the old bottom edge is removed, the side walls extend lower, and a new lower section of the container appears below, carrying its hollow interior with it.

Any small colored cells that were inside this container move upward by one row within the container (so pieces already just under the roof disappear), while colored marks elsewhere in the room remain unchanged.

Treat the tall input as a stack of square panels whose side length is the grid width; each panel contains one foreground shape on the background, and a final panel may be slightly truncated at the bottom. The output places these square panels side by side from left to right in the same top-to-bottom order, preserving each panel’s internal pattern and orientation. A single vertical separator in the foreground color is inserted between neighboring panels, and the first panel is repeated once more at the far right.

The non-background content is made from repeated 3x3 motifs using two roles: a preserved accent color and a second structural color. In the output, the accent color stays unchanged while the structural color is replaced by a new output-only color, and the resulting figure is redrawn in a canonical middle region of the grid. If the motifs already form one connected horizontal chain, that chain is kept with its same spacing/overlap; if the motifs are separated copies, the distinct motif types are overlaid into a single centered composite symbol.

The output doubles the canvas in both height and width, forming a 2×2 arrangement of transformed copies of the entire input grid. The upper-left quadrant is the original grid unchanged, the upper-right is the whole input rotated 90° clockwise, the lower-left is the whole input reflected top-to-bottom, and the lower-right is the corresponding rotated/reflected version (equivalently a 90° counterclockwise rotation of the original). Background stays background; only the foreground pattern is re-expressed in these four orientations.

The input contains two vertically stacked copies of a scene: an upper clean version and a lower repeated/altered version. The output keeps only the upper scene, cropping the grid at the end of the first complete arrangement and discarding everything below it. In that kept scene, the small left-hand marker shape and the right-hand motif of a small accent-color cluster above a solid rectangular block are preserved exactly.

The grid has a fixed top border row, a large wedge near the top, several scattered single-cell markers, and a separate compact block lower down. In the output, every scattered marker is moved vertically up into the first row below the border, staying in the same column, and its original location is cleared back to the background; if a marker lands on part of the wedge, it overwrites that cell. Separately, the lower compact block is recolored to a new highlight color while preserving its exact shape and any interior hole/opening.

Each input is made of identical rows, so the task is effectively to pick a horizontal slice of the picture. There are several colored runs: some runs of one non-background color, and some runs of another non-background color; the left occurrences are mixed with or adjacent to the first non-background color, while the far-right occurrence is a standalone block of the second non-background color. The output keeps only that isolated rightmost block and the contiguous background space immediately to its left, cropped across the full height of the grid.

The entire input grid is duplicated by tiling it once to the right and once downward, producing a grid with double the original width and double the original height. In other words, the output is a 2×2 arrangement of four identical copies of the input. All colored cells, including the sparse special markers on the uniform background, keep the same internal positions within each copy.

The wide input is divided into equal horizontal blocks, one block per output column/row. Inside each block, there are two relevant colors: a repeated "marker" color that appears as a single pixel in the same internal column of the non-feature rows, and a dominant color that fills most of the feature row within that block. The output compresses these blocks into a smaller square: along one distinguished row it places each block’s dominant color in order, and along the corresponding distinguished column it places each block’s marker color in order; every other cell remains background, with the row/column intersection following the horizontal sequence.

The input contains a cross-shaped divider, and the only other colored clues form an L-shape in the lower-left: a vertical list on the left edge below the divider and a horizontal list on the bottom edge left of the divider. Together these clues specify a repeating cyclic order of the non-divider colors.

In the output, that cycle is extended to fill the entire outer frame: the left edge and bottom edge continue the cycle in the same direction, while the top edge and right edge use the reversed order of that same cycle. The interior stays unchanged (empty background plus the central cross), aside from border cells where the new frame values overwrite the edge ends of the cross.

The input is divided into three equal horizontal panels stacked top-to-bottom, each panel containing one foreground shape on a background. The output rearranges these same three panels side-by-side in left-to-right order, preserving every panel’s internal contents exactly, including the shape’s position within its panel and all surrounding blank space. In other words, a 3-by-1 strip of panels becomes a 1-by-3 strip.

The picture is made of equal-width horizontal tiles containing the same foreground motif on a uniform background, except that one tile is distinguished by a small extra lower extension. The output keeps the height the same but widens the grid by continuing this tiling pattern horizontally, adding more copies of the regular motif. The distinguished motif is placed so that its extra lower extension sits in the horizontal middle of the enlarged strip, with matching repetitions filling the remaining space on both sides.

The whole input grid is copied horizontally to make a second identical copy on the right. A single vertical strip of background cells is inserted between the two copies, so the height stays the same while the width becomes twice the original width plus one blank column. Any internal features, including the repeating scaffold pattern and any extra colored blocks, are preserved exactly in both halves.

The grid contains a small row-pattern embedded in a uniform background, and the rows of that pattern continue downward until the sequence starts over from the top. The output keeps only the first full, non-repeated block of rows and removes the repeated continuation at the bottom. No cells are recolored and the width stays the same; the change is only a vertical crop that stops just before the top row pattern reappears.

Each input contains one main multicolored shape and one isolated single-cell marker elsewhere on the grid. The main shape is translated so that the marker’s location lines up with the position in the shape’s bounding box at the bottom row, one cell in from the right edge; the shape’s internal pattern and colors stay unchanged. The original copy of the shape is removed, and the marker is absorbed into the moved shape—remaining visible only if that aligned position was empty in the original shape.

The input contains the same 1-row horizontal color pattern repeated down the whole grid. The output keeps the width the same but stacks four vertical copies of this repeated-row block: first the original pattern, then the same pattern shifted one cell to the right with background padding, then the original pattern again, and finally the pattern shifted one cell to the left with background padding. Thus the height becomes four times the input height while the colored sequence is only horizontally offset in the second and fourth bands.

Ignore the blank padding on the right and take the leftmost square subgrid whose side length equals the grid height. From that square, make four transformed copies covering the four orientations/symmetry variants of the contained pattern (so the small foreground objects, including the line-shaped one, are rotated/reflected accordingly), and in each copy the special marker color appears at the square’s four corners. Place these four square copies side by side with a single background column between them.

The entire picture is scrolled upward by one row: empty space at the top is removed, a new empty row appears at the bottom, and the compact blocky shapes in the lower part keep exactly the same form while moving up with the scroll. In the upper sparse pattern, the single unique marker is removed and converted into the same color as the adjacent highlighted cells, producing a short vertical two-cell marker. The surrounding scattered foreground pixels are then redrawn into a tighter stepped/zigzag outline in the same general neighborhood rather than staying in their original sparse positions.

The input is split into three equal-width vertical panels that depict the same scene template side by side. The output shrinks the canvas to one panel’s width and merges those three panels by superimposing corresponding cells: objects shared by all panels remain, objects that appear in only some panels are added, and if two panels place different non-background colors in the same spot, the version from the rightward repeated panels is the one kept. This creates one consolidated scene containing the common large block plus the combined smaller markers and bars.

Each input contains a large symmetric solid shape in one main color, with a contrasting-color plus sign running through its center vertically and horizontally. In the output, that plus sign is erased to background everywhere except the exact center cell, which stays contrasting-colored. Then new contrasting-colored cells are drawn as the four diagonal arms of an X, starting next to the center and extending outward one step per row/column through the main-colored shape, so the original filled shape is cut by a horizontal/vertical gap and decorated with a centered diagonal cross.

The grid contains several foreground motifs stacked vertically on a uniform background; most are solid block-like shapes, but one is a smaller irregular symbol made of separated/branched pixels. The output keeps only the horizontal band that starts at the blank row immediately above this unique irregular symbol and ends at the isolated horizontal foreground bar below it, preserving the full width and all blank rows inside that band. Everything else above and below this selected band is removed.

The input shows one small foreground shape on a uniform background. In the output, the grid keeps the same height but becomes five times wider, forming five horizontal slots; the middle slot contains a completed version of the shape as a 7-cell cross/T-like motif, with the same orientation and anchored near the same location as the original object. The two slots next to the center show a smaller 3-cell elbow taken from that motif, and the two outermost slots show just a single tip cell, with everything else left as background.

The grid contains many isolated cells or small groups in one foreground color, plus a separate compact pattern in another color. The transformation simply removes every cell of that second-color pattern, turning those cells into background while leaving the first-color marks exactly where they were. The grid size and all remaining objects stay unchanged.

The full-height columns in a special divider color split the input into equal-width panels. The first two panels define a repeating alternation of panel-types, and the later panels already continue that same alternation. In the output, the divider columns are removed and the two panel-types are copied in alternating order to extend the sequence horizontally, keeping all objects inside each panel in the same relative positions.

The input is a vertical stack of several similar mini-grids, separated by full-width horizontal divider rows in a special separator color. Each mini-grid contains the same kind of two-part horizontal block on the background, but with different widths. The transformation crops away everything except the bottommost mini-grid, leaving that last section unchanged, including its surrounding background border.

The grid contains several separate colored objects, and the output is made by deleting exactly one of them: the smallest connected monochrome object in the whole scene. That object is replaced with background cells, while every other object—including larger solid blocks and multi-part or enclosing structures—stays in the same position and keeps its shape unchanged.

The input is a tall grid made of several vertically stacked snapshots of a foreground pattern, all using the same width; the output keeps only the final snapshot at the bottom. Concretely, take the bottom square section whose height equals the grid’s width and discard everything above it. This preserves that lowest pattern exactly, including any background holes inside it.

A roof-and-walls structure stays in place, and only the hollow interior of the wall rectangle is changed. The small marker shapes below it are read from left to right: each connected group of marker-colored cells becomes a horizontal stripe inside the rectangle, with stripe height equal to the number of marker cells in that group and stripe color taken from the non-marker cell attached to the group; if a marker group has no attached payload color, that stripe is left as background. These stripes are stretched across the full inner width of the rectangle, and if the encoded stack is taller than the available interior, only the final part of the stack is kept.

The input is a horizontal strip made from several cyclically shifted copies of a smaller hidden picture, with one foreground shape staying fixed while another darker pattern appears shifted from copy to copy. The transformation aligns these repeated blocks to recover the underlying figure, then compresses it to a single-column vertical summary by reading the relevant recovered column/row state for each height level. In that summary, empty/background rows are replaced by a new neutral color, rows belonging only to the fixed lighter shape keep that lighter color, and rows where the darker pattern is the meaningful content are marked with the darker color.

The input contains several vertically stacked sections, and the top section is the only complete one: it begins with a small marker block in the upper-left and includes the repeating interior stripe pattern across the full width. The transformation crops the grid to keep exactly this first full section, stopping just before the next lower row pair where the left marker reappears but the rest of the row is only background. No recoloring or rearrangement happens inside the kept section; everything below it is discarded.

The foreground pixels form outline-diamonds / X-like motifs on a blank background, with two such motifs shown one repeating-width apart. The second motif is the same repeating pattern but vertically shifted upward relative to the first, so the output continues this horizontal progression by placing more copies at the same spacing and with the same stepwise vertical offset from one copy to the next. The completed output becomes a wider, horizontally extended strip that is symmetric across the full sequence, while any parts of the repeated motifs that would go beyond the top or bottom edge are simply clipped by the unchanged height.

Each input is made of several copies of the same patterned tile, where only the tile’s outer/outline color changes; the background and the shared interior fill color are irrelevant. The output compresses the scene to a single row containing one cell for each distinct outline color that appears. These colors are not kept in spatial order from the input; they are listed in one fixed canonical color order, skipping any colors that are absent.

The input is split into three equal vertical panels. The leftmost and rightmost panels are identical complete pictures: a small sparse pattern on the left, attached to a solid rectangular block on the right, with a single special marker at the top-left edge of that block. The middle panel is a different partial/distractor panel, so the output keeps just one copy of the repeated complete panel and discards the center panel and the duplicate copy.

Each input consists of two equal-width panels placed side by side under a solid border row, with the same multi-colored arrangement repeated in both halves. The output discards the duplicate half and keeps one single panel—the intact/full copy when there is a slight mismatch between the two—so the result is just half the original width with the border and all objects preserved in the same within-panel positions.

The input is a wide grid containing two same-sized patterned figures, one on the left and one on the right, separated by background. The output turns this into a vertical filmstrip on a half-width canvas: it stacks one frame per figure-column, beginning with the full left figure and ending with the full right figure, while the intermediate frames show only the progressively overlapping central vertical slice so the visible shape shrinks toward the middle and then expands again. Any cells that use the figure’s internal background/cutout color are converted to the outer background color in the output.

The input grid is split into three horizontal bands of equal height, all with the same width. The output keeps only the bottom band exactly as it appears, preserving the background and marked cells unchanged, while the upper two bands are removed.

The input is split into three equal-width vertical panels, each containing one instance of the same kind of composite motif plus any scattered background markers. The output keeps the whole original image unchanged, then horizontally appends an exact copy of the last two panels from the input. In effect, the panel sequence becomes first–middle–last–middle–last.

The wide input is divided into four equal vertical sections, each the same height as the output and each containing part of the same foreground pattern. These four sections are folded/overlaid into one square grid, so the output keeps the original height but reduces the width to one quarter, combining the foreground marks from the sections into a single compact motif. The foreground color does not change; only the layout is compressed from a long strip into one centered composite image.

The output keeps the grid height, enlarges the width, and uses the more solid/filled shape as a bookend: that shape is copied unchanged on the far left and again on the far right. The other shape, the one whose middle rows split into separate left and right pieces, is unfolded into four equal-width panels placed between them: first the top single-piece rows, then the left pieces from the split rows, then the right pieces from the split rows, and finally the bottom single-piece rows. Within each panel, the extracted row fragments keep their original row order and horizontal form inside a square frame.

The non-background cells on the three populated input rows form diagonal progressions for each foreground color, as if they are fragments of longer slanted lines continuing beyond the visible area. Extend those diagonal chains leftward until they meet the left border of a square canvas whose size matches the input width. The output is otherwise blank and keeps only the left-edge entry cell(s): a mark in the top-left corner for a line that would enter from above, and/or a mark in the bottom-left corner for a line that would enter from below, using the color of that line.

Treat the non-background content as one whole picture and rotate that picture around the center of the grid by quarter turns. The output is the overlay of the original scene plus its 90°, 180°, and 270° rotations, drawn on the same background. As a result, each input object reappears in the other rotationally corresponding locations, and overlapping rotated copies can modify areas where they land.

The input contains several solid diamond/rhombus blobs of the non-background color, arranged across a background field. In the output, all of these foreground shapes are deleted so the grid becomes entirely background-colored, while the width stays the same and the height is rebuilt to equal the sum of the diamonds’ full sizes (their top-to-bottom spans, which match their widths).

The input is a wide grid made of three equal square sections placed side by side, each containing the same kind of motif: a vertical line crossing a horizontal line, with the horizontal line capped by two different marker colors. The middle section shows an expanded version of this motif, while the two outer sections show the smaller shared version. The output keeps just one square section containing that common outer motif (effectively the leftmost third of the input) and discards the other two sections.

Across the whole grid, the three common background/noise colors are cyclically relabeled, while the distinct object colors and the frame color stay the same. The frame-colored border marks a special interior region: starting from the first row just inside the frame, the contents are converted into an alternating pattern where one interior row becomes scaffold-color / empty / scaffold-color / empty, and the next interior row becomes empty / original cell / empty / original cell, repeating downward. Thus the framed area turns into a checkerboard-like weave of a new empty color and a repeating scaffold color, with every second row preserving the original symbols only on the kept parity positions.

The output keeps the entire input unchanged and extends it horizontally. It takes the leftmost square block of the grid (its width equals the grid’s full height) and copies that block to the far right as a new appended section. The copied section preserves the exact pattern of the two background regions and the contrasting marker cells from that left edge block.

The input is made of three equal-width panels placed side by side, each showing the same checkerboard-like scene with a few colored shapes, but with occasional cell-by-cell discrepancies between the copies. The output compresses this triptych into a single panel by keeping the leftmost copy as the base image. Any position where the three corresponding panels do not all match is recolored with a new highlight color, while all matching cells and all existing shapes otherwise remain unchanged.

The large grid contains many scattered candidate fragments, but only a compatible subset belongs to one hidden small picture. Those chosen fragments are normalized to the same bounding box, aligned on top of each other, and merged into a single compact output, with inner/more specific fragments taking precedence where layers overlap. All other scattered objects act as distractors and are ignored, so the output is just the reconstructed small composite image.

The vertical separator splits the input into two equal panels, each containing one framed motif with a highlighted center. In the output, the canvas is widened into four equal panels with the same separator repeated between them: the first two panels are the original left and right panels, then the right panel’s motif is copied into the third panel and the left panel’s motif is copied into the fourth. These two new copies are not placed at the exact same coordinates: their placement uses the relative offset between the original motifs, rotated clockwise, so a downward offset between the originals becomes a rightward shift in the copies, and any horizontal offset becomes a vertical shift.

The grid contains two separate rectangular patterned blocks on a blank background. The output keeps the rows unchanged and preserves each block exactly, including the body color, the two distinct colors at the top corners, and the single contrasting interior cell in each block. All unnecessary blank columns at the far left, between the blocks, and at the far right are removed so the two blocks are packed side by side with just one blank column separating them.

The entire input picture is duplicated horizontally. The output keeps the same height, doubles the width, and places an exact copy of the full input grid immediately to the right of the original, including the background, the lower band, and the patterned block shapes above it. No objects are recolored, moved vertically, or altered internally; the scene is simply tiled side-by-side once.

The upper pattern is the control: the row of evenly spaced single guide dots determines how many vertical two-cell markers must appear in the bottom band, while the short horizontal bar tells where their spacing should bend. In the output, the lower paired markers are redrawn from left to right as one pair per guide dot, no longer at their original columns: the regular guide spacing is expanded by one column for the early gaps, then compressed by one column for the later gaps, with the switch happening around the horizontal bar’s position. Everything else in the grid, including the entire upper section and the separator row, remains unchanged.

The output keeps the entire input grid unchanged as its top half, then appends a new block of the same height underneath, so the total height doubles. To build this added block, split the input in half horizontally and look only at the upper half; collect every column that contains any non-background cell there. In the appended block, those columns become solid vertical bands across both appended halves: the first appended half uses a highlight color, and the second appended half uses the grid’s main foreground/bar color, while all other cells stay background.

The grid contains a horizontally repeating motif: a vertical bar running through all rows, with a full-width middle row of the bar color and neighboring rows that place accent cells on both sides of each bar. In the input, several copies of this motif are already present, followed by unfinished background-only space on the right. The output completes that right-side gap by extending the same horizontal repetition at the same spacing until the grid width is filled, leaving all existing cells unchanged.

The grid contains one unique special seed cell, and the output adds a new highlight color along empty horizontal and/or vertical gaps centered on that seed. These added cells extend from the seed through clear space to connect with the nearest existing non-background cell or to run out to the edge, sometimes absorbing an endpoint cell of the secondary color into the new segment. Everything else in the picture remains unchanged, so the result is just a small line or L-shaped extension anchored at the seed.

Each example has a large solid block of one dominant foreground color, plus a smaller patch of another color embedded in or touching that block. The transformation leaves the whole grid unchanged except for that smaller patch, which is mirrored horizontally across the vertical centerline of the large block, replacing symmetric cells of the dominant color on the opposite side. All surrounding multicolored marker shapes and stray cells stay in place.

The full-height vertical line stays unchanged and serves as a central divider. In any row that contains mirrored single cells on the two sides, use the same-colored pair closest to the divider, then extend each member outward away from the divider along its row in that same color. The extension is an alternating trail: the first new cell is the immediately outer neighbor, then additional cells are filled every other step until the side runs out, overwriting any farther-out cells already on that path.

The whole picture is extended horizontally by placing an exact copy of the entire input grid immediately to its right. Every row is duplicated end-to-end, so the output keeps the same height, doubles the width, and preserves all object shapes, gaps, and special marker cells in the same relative positions within each half. There is no recoloring or rearrangement; it is a side-by-side horizontal repetition of the original scene.

The non-background cells form a single right-pointing wedge/arrow outline on an empty background. The rule grows/completes this outline outward: the two slanted arms are extended, the shape becomes taller and wider, and the right side is completed as a straighter vertical edge. When more than one growth stage fits, those successive enlarged/completed versions are laid out side by side in horizontal blocks, so the output can become much wider than the input.

The wide grid is reduced to a 1-cell-wide vertical summary while keeping the same height. Rows belonging to the solid full-width horizontal bar are preserved as a vertical run of the bar’s color, and all horizontal placement information is discarded. For the other non-background color, only the bottommost two rows where that color appears anywhere in the input are marked in the output; all remaining rows become background, so matching copies above the bar are ignored.

The input shows a single symmetric figure made from one foreground color, with thick horizontal and vertical stretches around the center. In the output, the size and overall symmetry stay the same, but the figure is re-expressed as alternating one-cell-thick bands: moving inward, filled blocks are converted into zigzag/checkerboard-like contour layers instead of solid masses. In other words, the transformation turns the original thick symmetric motif into nested alternating foreground/background rings that preserve the same centered structure.

The input consists of several same-sized panels stacked vertically, each surrounded and separated by blank rows/columns; the output removes this framing and keeps a single panel-sized grid. Across the panels, one accent color is accumulated by superimposing all of its occurrences in their original coordinates, so every position containing that color in any panel appears in the output. The other accent color forms a 3-cell arrow/triangle in different orientations; only the upward-pointing version is kept, and if more than one panel has that upward shape, the one taken is the panel with the most cells of the first accent color.

The small accent-colored marks are treated as directional seeds only when they already form a 2-cell segment: a horizontal pair grows into a full horizontal ray to the right, and a vertical pair grows into a full vertical ray downward. Each ray is drawn through the empty background until it reaches the grid edge or the main multicolored block, while isolated single accent cells do not grow. The large block and the left-side border stay in place; only the new extensions in the accent color are added, sometimes touching or replacing the block’s thin top stripe at the contact point.

The input is a stack of picture frames separated by full-width divider rows. Convert this vertical sequence into a horizontal strip: take each non-divider frame in order, place them side by side left-to-right, and then append the first frame once more at the far right to close the sequence. The background stays the same, and a single full-width divider row is kept as the bottom row of the final output.

The input is divided into two equal vertical halves, and the output keeps the same height but only one half-width canvas. The two halves are superimposed cell-by-cell: any cell occupied by the main foreground shape in either half becomes foreground in the output, while cells that are only background or the secondary filler/noise color become background. In effect, the task merges two partial/occluded copies of the same shape into a single completed silhouette.

The decorative top band and the solid bottom border stay unchanged; only the single middle row containing a horizontal run of plain cells plus two special marker colors is modified. Use the two markers to define a horizontal span, then reflect that span to the left of the left-hand marker so that the marker becomes the center of a larger symmetric interval, and recolor that whole interval with the new highlight color. Any plain cells outside the highlighted interval stay plain, with border-touching cases clipped at the row edge and effectively spilling to the far right in the examples.

The large solid rectangular blocks stay fixed, and each single marker sitting above a block gets a new cell added directly above it, creating a two-cell vertical marker. The mixed small symbols in the row immediately above the blocks and the scattered small symbols in the row immediately below are then regularized: symbols are cleared, recolored, or repositioned relative to each block so the noisy input becomes a clean, repeated decoration pattern around the blocks. In short, the task standardizes the accents around each rectangle while leaving the rectangles themselves unchanged.

The input is a vertical sequence of scene snapshots separated by full-width horizontal divider lines in the border color. The transformation keeps only the final snapshot: everything above the last divider is discarded, and the output is exactly the rectangular block of rows below that divider. This preserves the last scene’s horizontal platform segment and the small 2x2 object in their final positions on the same-width background.

The large picture is composed of several smaller framed panels placed side by side, all using the same solid border color for their outer frame and separators. The transformation cuts these horizontal panels apart and restacks them vertically in left-to-right order, keeping each panel’s internal pattern unchanged and upright. Because each panel keeps its own frame, the stacked result shows consecutive full border rows between neighboring panels.

The scene contains a vertical stem standing directly above a 3×3 square that is filled with one dominant color except for a single contrasting cell. In the output, the stem is lengthened upward from its existing top while keeping its bottom attached in the same place above the square, so it grows toward the top edge of the grid. At the same time, the contrasting cell inside the 3×3 square shifts one step counterclockwise around the square’s perimeter (for example, from the right-middle position to the top-middle position, or from top-middle to left-middle).

The grid contains a single compact block floating above a stack of full-width horizontal colored bands at the bottom. The transformation keeps the bottom bands unchanged and moves the floating block straight downward, without changing its shape or horizontal position, until its bottom edge sits directly on top of the uppermost band. All other cells remain background.

The input contains several glyph-like objects stacked vertically, separated by full blank rows. Each object is isolated, stripped of the vertical spacing, and converted into a sideways/horizontal version of the same silhouette: the main solid block stays together while the single-cell protrusion is repositioned consistently according to that reorientation. The output is a single short strip where these transformed glyphs are placed left-to-right in the same top-to-bottom order as they appeared in the input.

The grid is organized into 3-row horizontal strips, and each strip is treated as four 7-column compartments. Inside each compartment, all cells of the same color are taken as one local shape: that shape is shifted horizontally to the left side of the compartment (keeping its row positions), then duplicated on the right side after replacing it by its filled bounding rectangle; the two copies are separated by one background column. If multiple colors appear in the same compartment, this is done for each color and the results are overlaid, while the blank separator rows stay blank.

The background is a regular lattice of one line color running in evenly spaced horizontal and vertical stripes, with a multicolored rectangular figure placed over part of it. In the input, some lattice cells inside the figure’s surrounding area have been erased to the plain background color; the output restores those missing stripe segments wherever they pass through empty space. The colored figure itself stays unchanged, and only the blank cells that should belong to the underlying grid are recolored to reconnect the interrupted horizontal and vertical lines.

The output makes a 2×2 mosaic of the entire input grid, so the canvas doubles in both height and width. The upper-left tile is the original scene, the upper-right tile is the scene rotated 90° counterclockwise, the lower-left tile is rotated 90° clockwise, and the lower-right tile is rotated 180°. Both the large foreground shape and the small three-cell corner marker are copied with these same rotations, preserving their internal structure and relative placement within each rotated tile.

Any row that contains at least one non-background cell is transformed into a solid horizontal stripe spanning the entire width of the grid, using that same foreground color. The original segment length and position within the row do not matter: a short bar, long bar, or even a single cell all become full-row bands. Rows containing only background remain unchanged.

The picture is organized as consecutive vertical bands: an all-left band, then a band containing the next main color plus a small patch color, then a band containing the next two main colors, and finally the far-right band that stays unchanged. In the output, the main stripe colors are shifted one band to the left: the second band’s main color fills the first band, the third band’s left-side color fills the second band, and the third band’s right-side color fills the whole next band, while the rightmost band remains the same. The small patch color is preserved only as a flat segment on the bottom row at the same columns, and the single marker cell is kept on its original row but moved to the right edge of the newly expanded penultimate band.

Inside the bordered area, a solid horizontal block sits above a descending diagonal staircase made from the same structural color as the inner side walls, and a two-cell colored marker starts near the staircase’s lower-left end. The transformation moves that two-cell marker to the row immediately below the solid block, horizontally centered under that block (its left cell at the block’s midpoint), while keeping the marker’s left-to-right color order unchanged. The marker’s original bottom position is then filled in with the staircase/wall color so the staircase end looks completed there.

The output keeps the same height but stretches the canvas to five times the original width. The entire input image is copied side-by-side five times in a row, so the lone solid figure and all surrounding background repeat at equal horizontal intervals. No recoloring or reshaping happens within each copy; this is a horizontal tiling of the whole grid.

All fixed structures stay in place: the long horizontal bars, vertical bar, marker dots, and compact block on the right are unchanged. The only changing cells are the loose cells of the main movable color that appear as scattered singletons or diagonals; each row’s movable cells slide horizontally to the right as far as possible, stopping at the grid edge or just before the first occupied cell in that row. If a row has several movable cells, they end up packed together immediately to the left of that obstacle while keeping the same row positions.

The entire input picture is duplicated side-by-side across the row direction. Every row is copied exactly four times in sequence, so the output keeps the same height but becomes four times wider, repeating the full framed motif—including the outer border, the interior background, and the foreground pattern—without any other changes.

The input consists of several horizontal repeats of the same framed panel. The output collapses these repeats into a single panel, preserving the border/background and the colored blocks that are common to all copies, while reconstructing the small black shape from the differing copies into the most complete coherent connected version. In other words, the repeated panels are alternative/partial versions of one picture, and the result is the one-panel template with the completed black mark.

The solid horizontal separator bars are turned into a column-summary of the main patterned objects. For every separator row, mark with the primary object color every column where that same color appears anywhere else in the grid, while leaving the other separator cells unchanged. All non-separator rows, including the secondary accent-color pixels and the existing objects, stay exactly as they were.

The input is split into several equal-sized vertical panels by thin divider columns. The output collapses these panels into a single panel of the same height by comparing corresponding cells across all panels: if every panel has the same value there, that shared value is kept, while cells where some panels show the solid object color and others show empty background are replaced by the divider color. In other words, the divider color is reused to mark disagreements between aligned panel contents, and the divider columns themselves disappear.

The input is divided into three equal vertical panels, each showing a noisy version of the same underlying two-color picture: a left-side staircase/wedge of one color expanding downward against a second background color. The scattered third-color cells are noise or damage marks, so the output shrinks to a single panel width and reconstructs the clean intended two-color pattern, removing all of those marks. In other words, the three side-by-side copies are used as redundant evidence to recover the undisturbed staircase boundary.

The grid is split into a striped header and a dark lower field; the only meaningful object is the small path-like figure in the lower field made of the path color plus one distinguished marker cell, while the scattered dot color stays fixed as background noise. The output stacks many full-height copies of the original frame vertically, and in each successive copy the marker is advanced through the path figure (starting from the opposite end), with the figure re-drawn at the corresponding offset. As this progression is unrolled through the stacked copies, parts of the figure can appear in the striped header of a copy, but the alternating stripe pattern and the dot-color cells otherwise remain unchanged.

The input is a single solid rectangle filled entirely with one uniform background color, with no internal objects or markings. The output keeps exactly the same color and full solidity, but the rectangle’s dimensions are swapped: its height becomes the original width and its width becomes the original height. In effect, the whole grid is turned so the long and short sides exchange roles.

The input contains a single symmetric shape on an otherwise empty grid. Find that shape’s bounding box, imagine sliding that box straight downward until it is bottom-aligned with the grid, and then place only two cells of the original object color on the top row of that bottom-aligned box. Those two kept positions are the horizontal midpoint of the box and its rightmost column.

The output is built only from the right-hand portion of the input: take the block from the midpoint to the right edge (for odd widths, this includes the center column). Then make a horizontally mirrored copy of that block and arrange the four pieces across the output as: original right block, mirrored copy, mirrored copy again, original right block. All colors and internal patterns in that chosen right-side block are preserved; the left part of the input is not used.

The input is a 5-row banner made of many small character-like shapes arranged in fixed 4-column slots. The output places four full copies of this banner side by side; in copy 1, each shape’s leftmost occupied vertical stroke is recolored to the highlight color, in copy 2 its second occupied stroke is recolored, in copy 3 its third occupied stroke is recolored, and in copy 4 its fourth occupied stroke is recolored if it has one. All other foreground cells keep their original color and the background stays unchanged.

The input contains one prominent hollow frame in the foreground color, plus additional smaller foreground structures nested inside it. In the output, all inner structures are discarded and only a single hollow frame remains. That frame is expanded or shifted so that it becomes the border of the entire grid, with the whole interior left as background.

The grid contains a small foreground object made of the non-background color on a uniform background. In the output, that object is moved rigidly to the upper-left corner so that its bounding box touches the top edge and left edge, while its exact shape and orientation stay the same. The original location is erased back to the background color.

The input is a rectangular wall-frame split into two equal rooms by a single vertical wall, and the output redraws this same wall system as a tall, vertically unfolded strip. Each output row is one of three cross-sections: all wall, outer-frame-plus-center-wall, or center-wall-only; the strip starts and ends with the full frame pattern, while the middle contains shorter center-wall-only runs separated by solid wall bands. The output keeps the wall/background colors, makes the output width equal to the input height, and uses the lengths of the stacked runs to reflect the original horizontal spans of the outer frame and the two side rooms.

The grid is a vertical stack of repeated scene-frames, each containing the same fixed scaffold: a pair of matching markers near the top, a left-side anchor, a horizontal bar near the bottom, and sometimes a right-edge endpoint. One extra single cell acts as the moving token, and its position relative to the scaffold changes from frame to frame.

The output performs a cyclic shift of these frames downward by one: each frame is replaced by the frame that was immediately above it, and the top frame is replaced by the former bottom frame. In other words, the whole repeated panel content is rotated by one step, preserving each frame’s internal layout exactly.

The input contains a background with one foreground color arranged as several full horizontal bars and vertical traces. In the output, that same foreground color is propagated to cover every remaining background cell, turning the entire rectangular grid into a solid block of the foreground color. Nothing is moved or resized; the rule is simply to complete/fill the whole canvas with the existing non-background color.

First, treat the small marker-colored cells as temporary annotations and erase them, replacing each one with the surrounding background so that only the main shape color remains. Then copy this cleaned whole grid five times in a vertical stack: the 1st, 3rd, and 5th copies keep the original background color, while the 2nd and 4th copies change every background cell to a different alternate background color. The shape cells stay in the same positions in every copy.

The grid is kept the same except for the lowest row inside the outer background border. That entire interior bottom row, which is originally filled with the main body color, is recolored into a new highlight color from the left inner edge to the right inner edge, while all other objects (the scattered holes, the diagonal markers, and the small special-colored pieces) remain unchanged.

The solid outer frame stays unchanged, and the thin inner border with the two alternating border colors is restored to its regular alternation wherever it was disturbed. The large central square, which is mostly a single fill color in the input, is replaced by a completed diagonal repeating pattern that cycles through four colors: the two accent/clue colors, one of the border colors, and the original interior fill color. In other words, the output cleans up stray clue cells on the border and expands the hinted periodic motif to fill the entire central 6×6 area.

The input is a tall stack of equal-height horizontal blocks: each block contains a mostly blank field with one central vertical line that alternates between two colors, plus one full-width striped row made from two other alternating colors. These blocks repeat down the grid in an alternating ABAB pattern, where the striped row flips phase from one block type to the other. The output crops the grid down to just one full block, keeping the first occurrence of the same block type that appears at the very bottom of the input; the width stays the same.

The input is a vertical stack of equal-sized square panels: the grid’s width gives the side length of each panel, and the full height is an exact multiple of that size. The output rearranges these panels from a top-to-bottom stack into a left-to-right row, preserving every panel’s internal pattern exactly, including the background, scattered foreground cells, and any special marker-colored cells. No cells are recolored or edited; only the layout of whole square sections changes.

The slanted chain leading into the corner is discarded, and the cornered shape is normalized into a horizontal bar made in the diagonal’s color, placed where the original corner row was. The two other colored arms are treated as attachments of length one less than in the input, and the output stacks six same-width copies of the scene vertically, each copy showing the attachments in a different successive position around that fixed bar (a six-step rotation/orbit around its left end). In short: remove the diagonal guide, turn the corner into a horizontal bar, then display six vertically stacked animation frames of the remaining two colored arms moving around it.

The input is a short horizontal stripe pattern made of equal-width color blocks, repeated multiple times side by side across all rows. The output crops the grid to just one full repeat of that pattern, keeping the same height and preserving the block order and colors. In other words, the frame is narrowed to the smallest horizontally repeating unit.

The input’s left-aligned filled bar/stripe pattern is used as a template, and the output enlarges the scene only vertically by stacking multiple full-height copies of the original layout. In each successive stacked copy, the region that was empty on the right is populated by a self-similar echo of the input’s own filled-vs-empty row pattern, creating a recursive/fractal-looking extension toward the lower right. The background rows remain background, the left filled structure stays anchored in place in every block, and the single special marker is preserved at the far lower-right edge of the enlarged result.

Each input has a staircase-shaped wedge in the upper left made of one non-background color, a matching staircase-shaped wedge in the lower right made of another non-background color, and a final solid blank row. The output widens the grid to the right and continues the same row-by-row staircase progression into the new columns, using the same step size seen in the original wedges. As a result, the upper wedge extends/echoes into the added top-right area, the lower wedge extends through the added bottom-right area, and all other cells are filled by the original background or blank-row color.

The large multicolored cluster near the top is normalized into a standard shaded version of the same shape: its cells are recolored by structural role rather than by their original colors, with a solid horizontal band through the middle, one color for the upper/left mass, another for the upper-right edge, and another for the lower-right/bottom side. The object’s placement and general silhouette are preserved, but the original palette is discarded in favor of this fixed role-based palette. The separate staggered stripe pattern at the bottom is also rewritten using the same standardized colors, turning the simple repeated blocks into a taller repeating multicolor band aligned to the same columns while leaving background empty cells unchanged.

The output keeps the input’s height but stretches the canvas to four times the original width, creating four equal side-by-side panels. Each panel is completely filled with the color of the input’s vertical bar, and the original background is removed except for a tiny background-colored mark placed in the two rows immediately above where that bar begins and centered horizontally within each panel. From left to right, these four marks show successive growth stages of a 2×2 block: one cell, then a vertical pair, then an L-shape, then a full 2×2 square.

Each input is expanded into five horizontal tiles: the whole scene is copied side by side so the output width becomes five times the input width while height stays the same. The large lower object and the single isolated bottom marker are repeated unchanged in every tile, but the small top object is recolored differently from tile to tile. The isolated marker acts like a code that chooses the phase of a fixed 5-step recoloring cycle for that top object, so different examples show different shifted color sequences across the five copies.

The input contains a single foreground blob on an empty background, and the output keeps that blob while enlarging it by filling nearby empty cells that continue the blob’s existing stepped outline. In effect, short horizontal/diagonal edge patterns are extended outward to complete the implied shape, smoothing jagged boundary notches and adding connected mass above, below, or to the right where the local contour suggests it. The result is a larger, more solid version of the same object, with no changes to the background elsewhere.

The grid is split into two stacked parts: an upper block that stays unchanged, and a lower block that begins where the lower patterned object appears. The entire lower block is shifted one column to the left as a whole, carrying along both the main shape and the alternating marker pattern around it. Cells that move past the left edge are discarded, and the newly opened cells at the right edge are filled with background.

First isolate the single non-background figure by cropping away all empty rows and columns, and place this cropped figure unchanged on the left side of the output. Then place a second copy of the figure immediately to its right, but reoriented by a diagonal row/column swap (a transposed or diagonal-mirrored version rather than a left-right or top-bottom flip). The color stays the same, while notches and holes move to the corresponding diagonal positions in the right-hand copy.

The input consists of several same-sized square panels arranged side by side, separated by single columns of the separator color. Each panel has the same outer border color and contains its own interior pattern made from the two motif colors. The output keeps every panel unchanged but rearranges the panels into a vertical stack in the same left-to-right order, inserting a single full-width separator-colored row between consecutive panels.

Each input is a short horizontal strip made of several identical vertical panels arranged periodically, with thin divider columns in the frame color between them; neighboring panels effectively share some border columns. The output extends this same periodic strip across a much greater width, repeating the panel pattern to the right while making the divider/border columns explicit so the repeated panels no longer overlap. All internal details of each panel, including the top holes and the contrasting bottom band, are copied unchanged in every repeated panel.

The whole input grid is duplicated side-by-side: the output keeps the same height, places an exact copy of the original on the left, then adds a single blank/background-colored vertical separator column, then places the same grid again on the right. No internal objects are edited or recolored; every row pattern, including the existing repeated motifs and separators, is preserved exactly within each copy.

The grid is based on an alternating two-color checkerboard, with some cells in the upper part modified to form a shape or pattern. The output keeps only the top half of the input rows, then lays out four equal-width horizontal panels separated by one checkerboard column: panel 1 is the cropped top half exactly as given, panel 2 is the same area restored to a clean checkerboard, panel 3 repeats panel 1, and panel 4 repeats the clean checkerboard. In other words, the upper half is duplicated twice, with blank checkerboard copies alternating between them, while the entire lower half is discarded.

One non-background color acts as a temporary filler/noise color and is removed from the scene. It is recolored to the color of the larger region that should absorb it: when it splits or sits inside a bigger object, it becomes that object's color, and when it is just a standalone patch in empty space, it becomes the background. This replacement is applied to every patch of that filler color, while all other colored objects keep their shapes and positions.

The single non-background pattern is duplicated into four equal-width panels placed side by side, so the output keeps the same height but becomes four times wider. From left to right, these panels show the motif in its original orientation, then rotated 90° counterclockwise, then rotated 180°, and then rotated 270° counterclockwise. Only the foreground shape is copied and rotated; the background cells stay unchanged.

The picture is split into several same-sized panels placed side by side, with blank separator columns between them and blank rows above and below. The output reduces these repeated panels to one panel of that width by overlaying them cell-by-cell: if any panel has a colored cell at a position, that color is kept there, and only positions that are blank in every panel stay blank. In effect, the repeated incomplete copies are merged into one complete motif, preserving all non-background colors and the original vertical extent.

Use the special marker above one candidate shape to choose the target region. Keep the full height of the grid, but crop a square window centered on that marker column, so the output is the selected local scene only. Inside this cropped scene, the large block under the marker is regularized into a solid rectangle of its main color: contrasting cells that lie inside the rectangle are replaced, while contrasting cells that protrude outside the rectangle (and the marker itself) are preserved.

The input is a vertical stack of several candidate panels, separated by full horizontal divider rows. Across the panels, one larger shape stays fixed while a smaller block shifts step by step sideways toward it; the output keeps only the single panel showing the final position of that moving block (the furthest-right/closest-to-contact state). The chosen panel is copied exactly, along with its bottom divider row.

The output is made by placing four copies of the input grid side by side, so the height stays the same while the width becomes four times larger. In each copy, the scattered hole/marker cells on the mostly uniform background are kept in the same places, but the main compact multicolored figure is shown in a different orientation: first as given, then rotated 90°, 180°, and 270° across the four panels. The result is a horizontal gallery of the same scene, with only that central figure changing orientation from panel to panel.

Find the row containing two separated objects of the same color, one on the left and one on the right. Extend that color horizontally so the two objects become one continuous bar spanning from the left object to the right object, leaving all other rows unchanged. Then recolor the midpoint of this new bar with a second accent color: one cell if the span has odd length, or the two central cells if it has even length.

Each input contains a 3-by-3 block, a horizontal strip on the block’s middle row, and a single marker cell lower down. The 3-by-3 block is shifted left by exactly the same number of columns as the vertical gap from the block’s top row to that lone marker; any nearby strip cells that end up immediately touching the moved block remain, while overlapped cells are replaced by the block. The lone marker is expanded into a 5-cell horizontal bar on its own row, aligned under the moved block, and a new 2-by-7 rectangle of a new color is added three rows below it, centered under that moved block.

The non-background cells are sparse guide marks for straight border lines, mostly along diagonals and sometimes a central vertical axis. In the output, those partial line fragments are completed by extending and mirroring them into a full large shape that reaches the frame edges when appropriate. The interior of that completed diagonal polygonal region is then filled solidly with the same foreground color, while the outside remains background.

The input contains a blank background with a few isolated marker cells of different roles; in the output, all of those markers are converted into one common highlight color and expanded into 1-cell-wide rays/segments. These segments follow straight horizontal or 45-degree diagonal directions, linking markers that line up in those directions and otherwise continuing until they meet another segment or the grid edge. The background stays unchanged, while the result is a sparse line-drawing built from the original singleton points.

Each input is organized into vertical content bands separated by a special divider color. In the output, the row patterns inside each content band are preserved, but the colors are remapped by swapping the empty/background color with the dark fill color and swapping the other two content colors with each other, while the divider color stays the same. The divider columns are also repositioned to act as framing columns around the recolored bands, so the output begins with divider cells and keeps divider-colored boundaries between the transformed sections.

Each input contains a background, a rectangular outline made of one non-background color, and a second color occupying the area inside that outline; sometimes that inner-color also extends outside the frame. The output removes the entire outline and also deletes any cells of the inner color that lie outside the framed area. Only the rectangular region strictly enclosed by the frame is kept, in the same position, with everything else turned into background.

The input is split into three equal vertical sections, each containing the same small foreground shape in the same relative position, but with a different color. The output keeps only the leftmost third of the grid and discards the other two thirds, preserving the background and the shape exactly as it appears in that first section. In effect, the result is a crop to the first repeated panel.
