The large repeated foreground shapes stay fixed in place, along with the background. Only the small single-cell marker color changes: markers that occupy corresponding relative positions around/inside each repeated shape are cyclically reassigned from one copy of the shape to the next copy on its left, with wraparound from the leftmost copy to the rightmost. In effect, each shape keeps the same geometry, but inherits the marker arrangement that previously belonged to its right-hand neighbor.

The input is a wall-and-space floorplan with a fixed outer frame, internal vertical dividers, and a few special gaps/openings in those walls. The output keeps the same height but stretches the picture into a long horizontal strip by placing one full-width copy of the layout for each original row. Across these repeated copies, the pattern is progressively offset/skewed so that the notable openings and broken wall segments march diagonally through the strip, while the basic wall/empty structure of each copy stays the same.

The non-background cells remain single-pixel dots, and the grid keeps the same size and the same total number of dots. What changes is their placement: every foreground dot is relocated to a new coordinate by the same global position-remapping rule, so the whole sparse constellation is scrambled into a different arrangement while background cells stay background. In other words, the task is a frame-wide coordinate permutation of the dot pattern, not the creation of larger shapes or recoloring.

The wide input is split into consecutive square panels, each panel having the same width as the grid’s height. The output is formed by collapsing those panels onto one another into a single square: cells in the same relative position within each panel are superimposed, and any non-background mark is kept there. In effect, repeated motifs, small marker dots, and partial shapes scattered across different horizontal panels are merged into one combined square picture.

The output is formed by cropping the input down to the smallest rectangle that contains all non-background cells. In these examples, the meaningful figure sits at the far left, so all trailing background-only columns on the right are removed while the rows stay the same. The main foreground shape and its single differently colored marked cell are preserved exactly in their relative positions.

The input grid is divided into three equal-width vertical panels. The output keeps those three panels unchanged, then extends the grid to the right by copying the middle panel and then the left panel, producing a five-panel sequence: left, middle, right, middle, left. Nothing inside a panel is altered or mirrored cell-by-cell; whole panels are repeated in that order, so the final grid becomes horizontally symmetric at the panel level.

The input is divided into equal-width vertical panels, each identified by one marker cell in the upper sparse row; the marker sits in the same relative column within every panel. Each panel includes the full height of the grid, keeping the background, the marker, and any special cells in the lower solid region unchanged. The output is made by extracting these panels from left to right and stacking them vertically, so the original wide strip becomes a tall column of smaller subgrids.

The grid is made of several equal-sized panels placed side by side, separated by the background color, and all panels share the same decorative frame and internal template. Inside each panel, a small multicolor motif is accompanied by one special marker that can occupy one of four directional/orientation states around that motif; the output reconstructs a full set of four panels in a fixed progression, copying the given examples and filling in the missing variant(s). In each completed panel, the template cells next to that orientation are cut out to background, while the rest of the frame and repeated pattern remain unchanged.

The output discards the whole interior picture and keeps only the grid’s left edge. It crops the input down to a single column with the same height, copying each cell from the original first column in order from top to bottom. All other columns, including the large blocky shapes on the right, are removed.

The output keeps the background and the foreground shapes in the same places, but adds one new highlighted horizontal band through the foreground area. This band is placed on the row that acts like the shape’s transition row—the point where a solid cap/base gives way to a different internal pattern—and every cell across each foreground piece’s full width on that row is overwritten with the highlight color, even if those cells were previously holes or other colors. All other rows remain unchanged.

The output expands the canvas horizontally to twice the original width while keeping the height unchanged. The entire input pattern is copied into the left half unchanged, and an exact duplicate of it is placed in the right half directly beside it. Thus each colored cell/object reappears at the same row and same relative column position within the new right-hand half, with the background filling all other spaces.

The output places several horizontal copies of the input side by side, keeping the same height. In each successive copy, the small left-side block stays fixed, while the large block on the right (including any differently colored marker cells inside it) is shifted one cell farther to the right. The copies continue for every possible rightward position of that right-hand block, stopping when its right edge reaches the grid border; the unchanged background fills everything else.

The non-background cells form a small hooked/diagonal shape with a clear pivot: the rightmost cell in its top occupied row, which is also the top of the vertical stem. The output keeps the original shape and adds three more copies of that same shape rotated 90°, 180°, and 270° around this pivot cell. Overlapping copies merge, producing a four-way rotationally symmetric figure while the background stays unchanged.

Find the single non-background object, which is a hollow rectangular outline, and discard all surrounding empty space by cropping to that object’s height. The output becomes a horizontal strip made by repeating that outline motif five times side by side across the width, using the same outline color and background color. In other words, one isolated box-like shape in the input is turned into a tightly framed row of repeated box/zero-like copies in the output.

The input is divided into several vertical subpictures arranged side by side, separated by one-column divider strips. The output removes those dividers, takes each subpicture in left-to-right order, and stacks them vertically on a blank canvas of the original width, keeping each subpicture’s internal pixels unchanged and left-aligned. Between consecutive stacked subpictures, a fixed two-row upward-pointing marker made from the marker color is inserted in the middle of the blank area.

The large picture is made of identical framed mini-panels arranged in separated horizontal groups, with a small marker above each group. The outer canvas, the markers, and all panel frames stay fixed; only the colored interior pattern inside each 2-panel group is reassigned. The interior contents shift cyclically one group to the left, so each group is replaced by the pattern from the next group, and the last group wraps around to the first position.

Inside the small framed area, one color acts as a fixed pivot point and another color forms a pattern around it. The output keeps the frame, the side markers, and the pivot unchanged, but rotates the surrounding pattern 90 degrees counterclockwise around that pivot. Everything outside this local structure stays the same.

The non-background cells form rough, partially drawn two-color blobs that are completed into larger, smoother diagonal/rounded shapes. Gaps, holes, and short breaks between nearby fragments are filled so each local group becomes a solid connected mass, and nearby pieces that belong to the same overall form are grown until they join. The more interior-looking color spreads through the filled body, while the other color is kept mainly on the outer rim or tips as the shape’s accent/edge.

The grid contains a repeating scaffold of background cells and thin separator marks, with some scaffold positions occupied by identical solid rectangular blocks and one position occupied by a distinctive hollow rectangular block. The output appends a second full copy of this whole arrangement in the direction of the grid’s longer axis: if the canvas is taller than it is wide, the entire picture is repeated below; if it is wider than tall, the entire picture is repeated to the right. All objects, including the unique hollow block, keep the same relative placement inside the repeated scaffold.

The large wedge/triangle-shaped main object and the separate vertical border line on the far right stay unchanged. The only change is to the small two-color marker attached on the left side of the main object: extend it two columns further left, making the first new column an exact copy of the marker’s current leftmost column and the second new column a color-swapped version of that column. Thus the marker becomes a wider leftward band built from its left edge, while all other cells remain the same.

The tall input grid is split into four equal square sections stacked vertically, each using the same foreground-on-background pattern. The output rearranges these four sections into a single horizontal strip, placing the top section first, then the second, third, and fourth section side by side. The contents of each section are copied exactly; only the overall layout changes from vertical stacking to horizontal concatenation.

The transformation removes the large solid blob located in the upper/middle area of the grid by repainting all of its cells to the background color. The smaller structured shapes near the bottom—one blocky symbol on the left and one tiny cluster on the right—stay exactly unchanged. In other words, the output keeps the bottom objects and erases only the big floating mass.

Each input contains a checkerboard-like rectangular border in one color and a centered orthogonal cross in a second color. The output completes this partial pattern into solid, nested rectangular rings covering the same bounding box: the dotted border becomes a continuous outer ring, the interior rings alternate between the two colors, and the cross color is expanded from its plus shape into the full ring at its distance from the edge. Any space inside the innermost completed ring remains background.

The input contains a single foreground L-shape anchored at the upper-left corner. In the output, this L is propagated to the right in repeating 2-part blocks: first a left-facing/right-facing mirrored pair that shares a continuous top bar, then an upside-down mirrored pair that shares a continuous bottom bar, and this alternation continues across the row. If the grid is too short for the next full 2-L block but still has room for one L, a final copy of the original upper-left L is placed and any leftover cells remain background.

The grid contains exactly two non-background objects, each possibly made of several colors and having its own bounding box. The transformation swaps these two whole patterns by moving each object so that its bounding box’s top-left corner lands at the other object’s original top-left corner, preserving the objects’ internal pixel arrangement and colors. Their original locations are cleared to background, and if a swapped object would extend beyond the grid edge, the overflowing part is simply clipped.

The output keeps the same height but makes the canvas five times wider, then places five copies of the single non-background figure across it at equal horizontal intervals. In each copy, the special bottom tip cell is preserved, and the long stem/top-bar shape is redrawn as a variant where the connection up to the horizontal cap is shifted sideways, so some stems stay vertical while others lean diagonally left or right. The repeated variants can overlap at their top bars, creating merged horizontal runs where neighboring copies touch.

The input contains three horizontally repeated copies of the same foreground figure on a uniform background. Each copy shares the same core shape, but each one has a different extra single-cell attachment in one direction (for example above, below, or to the side). The output collapses these three copies into one centered figure on a canvas the size of a single section, keeping the common core and adding all of the distinct attachments together into that one figure.

The input contains one or more horizontal bars in a single foreground color on an otherwise empty background. In the output, every foreground bar stays exactly the same size, shape, and position, but its color is changed to a different foreground color. Nothing else in the grid is altered.

The grid has two parts: an upper field where each row contains one standout cell on a uniform background, and a lower two-row guide band with evenly spaced vertical markers. Remove the guide band, then compress the upper field horizontally by treating each region between consecutive guide markers (including the left edge region and the final right-edge region) as a single output column. In the output, each row keeps its standout cell, placed in the column corresponding to the region that contained it, while the rest stays the upper background color.

Each input has a large symmetric guide pattern of dark cells on a uniform background, plus a smaller L-shaped colored object near the middle. The output keeps the guide and background unchanged, and adds two same-sized copies of that L in the upper-left region of the original: one copy is flipped so it has a top bar with a left-side vertical, and the other is rotated so it has a left-side vertical with a bottom bar. These two added copies use two new colors and are positioned so they meet at the original object's upper-left corner, even overwriting that corner cell.

The background and the existing main stroke color stay unchanged. The differently colored single-cell markers act as anchors for missing straight segments: using the shape/orientation of the nearby main-color line, infer the unfinished direction and extend a one-cell-wide line of the marker color from that anchor until it reaches the border or another marker anchor. Depending on the figure, this adds a horizontal closing edge or diagonal continuations that complete the partial line pattern.

Only the narrow 5-row header band at the top is edited; the scattered single cells in the large lower field are left unchanged. In any header row that contains one or more special marker cells, each marker is turned into the start of a horizontal tail extending to the right edge, where the row is rewritten as an alternating sequence of the marker color and a new fill color. Header rows without such markers stay as solid bands, and if a row has multiple markers, the alternating tail can restart or shift phase around the later marker positions.

The input grid is divided into three equal-width vertical panels, each containing the same silhouette drawn in a different non-background color. The output keeps those three panels unchanged and extends the canvas by one more panel of the same width on the right. This new rightmost panel is an exact copy of the middle panel, including both its shape and its color, while all remaining cells stay as background.

The input contains several large solid rectangles of the same color arranged horizontally near the bottom, each with a small marker pattern floating above it. The output crops out just the rightmost such rectangle together with the space directly above it, preserving the small marker that belongs to that rectangle and removing all other repeated blocks. The result is a smaller grid whose width matches that one rectangle and whose height spans from the top of its marker area down through the full rectangle.

The single framed square is replicated horizontally five times, preserving its position within each repeated canvas-sized block and leaving the background empty elsewhere. In every copy, the lone interior marker is expanded into a full cross: a horizontal bar across the frame’s interior row and a vertical bar across the frame’s interior column, both centered on the original marker’s location. The cross color alternates from copy to copy—marker color in the 1st, 3rd, and 5th copies, and frame color in the 2nd and 4th—while the frame itself stays unchanged.

The non-background figure contains a main-colored wedge attached to a special-colored tip/short vertical tip segment. Using the upper special-colored cell as the bottom-right vertex, extend the figure’s two implied boundary rays through empty space: one goes straight upward and the other goes diagonally up-left, filling those added cells with the main object color. The final new cell at the top of each ray is marked with a separate highlight color, while all original cells stay as they are.

The grid has a solid-colored band across the top, an empty lower field, and one differently colored object sitting in that lower field. In the output, that object is removed from its original position and redrawn in the same color as a centered, compact normalized version that straddles the boundary between the top band and the lower field. Its overall filled/empty structure is preserved in simplified form, while the two background regions stay the same everywhere else.

First, take the minimal square bounding box that contains all non-background cells; this box defines a single centered four-sided motif made of marks on the top, bottom, left, and right sides. Then build an output strip whose height is that box size and whose width is that size repeated once per box column: each box-sized block is a concentric variant of the same motif, with the side segments changing symmetrically from outermost/longest to innermost/shortest and back again. The original pattern is one member of this sequence, appearing at the offset(s) that match its side-segment placement inside the bounding box.

The output keeps only the motif-colored shape from the input and places three copies of it side by side, so the canvas becomes three times as wide while keeping the same height. In the middle third, that same motif color is also used to draw a large cross: a full-height vertical line on the center column of the middle panel, and a long horizontal line on a row determined by the other marker objects in the input. The background stays the same, and the other colored objects themselves disappear.

The input contains a single non-background marker on an otherwise uniform grid. In the output, that marker becomes the center of a 7-cell-wide starburst: the marker color is extended 3 cells outward horizontally, vertically, and along both diagonals, so the full horizontal row, full vertical column, and the two diagonals through the center are drawn. If this star would go past the grid edge, it is simply clipped by the boundary.

The grid is split into several vertical sections by full-height divider columns in a distinct separator color. The output removes those divider columns entirely and slides the remaining sections together, concatenating them horizontally into one continuous grid. All other cells and objects, including the small emblem at the far left and the scattered foreground shapes inside each section, keep their original row positions and their positions relative to their own section.

The filled shape is an asymmetric cross/plus, and the grid is organized as equal-width horizontal panels placed side by side. From one panel to the next, the same cross is rotated 90 degrees counterclockwise around its intersection point; the output keeps the given panels and extends the sequence until there are four panels total. Any part of a rotated cross that would fall outside its panel is simply cut off at that panel’s border.

The whole input grid is duplicated four times side-by-side, so the output keeps the same height and becomes four times wider with the original background spacing preserved in each copy. Most cells stay identical in every copy, but the small accent cells inside the large solid rectangle behave like animation frames: the two aligned upper accent cells alternate between their original color and a new accent color in successive copies, while the single lower accent cell cycles through three colors across the four copies, returning to its starting color in the last copy.

The input is split into horizontal bands by the rows that begin with a short left-edge run of marker cells; each such run gives that band its starting column, and the rest of the band is filled by one of the two main colors. In the output, the marker color disappears and the grid is reset to a blank background, then each band is replaced by a 1-cell-wide diagonal of its fill color passing through the band’s vertical midpoint and starting at the same left indent. Bands of the upper/main first color draw diagonals down-right, while bands of the other main color draw diagonals up-right; if several consecutive bands have the same fill color, their diagonal direction alternates between successive bands.

The input is a horizontal strip of repeated 8-column scenes separated by blank spacer columns; each repeated scene shows the same small picture at a later stage of growth. The output keeps only the final stage, i.e. the rightmost repeated scene, and removes the spacer columns and all earlier copies. In that kept scene, the fixed bars and paired blocks stay in place while the changing object is the one that progressively extends across the sequence and appears at its maximum extent in the output.

The grid is split into three equal vertical panels by separator columns, and each panel contains the same kind of foreground emblem placed on a colored background band. From input to output, the emblem pattern in each panel is shifted one panel to the left with wraparound: the left panel takes the middle panel’s version, the middle panel takes the right panel’s version, and the right panel takes the left panel’s version. Only these foreground emblem cells move; the panel backgrounds, empty separator columns, and overall layout stay unchanged.

The large central field is transformed by cyclically shifting every scattered accent dot four columns to the left, wrapping around at the edges; the uniform top band and the solid lower bands otherwise stay the same. The special marker near the bottom of the central field does not stay as itself: its four-left shifted position becomes a blank cell, and the lone contrasting cell in the first lower strip row is moved to a column two steps further left than that blank (six columns left from its original position, with wraparound). If that destination column already contains a shifted accent dot in the row above, that dot is replaced by the special marker.

The output is made by placing three same-height copies of the scene side by side, so the width becomes triple. The left copy is the original input unchanged; the middle copy keeps the background and the secondary foreground pieces in the same places, but replaces the solid rectangular block with a horizontal repeating three-color stripe pattern; the right copy keeps only the secondary foreground pieces and removes that rectangle back to background. In other words, the rectangle is split into three presentations: original, recolored/patterned, and absent, while the other foreground object acts as a fixed reference repeated across the panels.

The grid is a checkerboard-like background split into repeated horizontal tiles. In each tile, the top/bottom marked row contains one of two alternating signal colors, while the middle marked row contains the other signal color next to a fixed anchor color. The transformation swaps those two signal colors between the top/bottom marker and the middle-row marker within each consecutive 2-tile group, so the alternating order flips; if a final tile has no partner, it remains unchanged.

The grid is divided into three horizontal picture bands separated by blank rows, and the bands are cyclically reordered so the bottom band moves to the top, the top band moves to the middle, and the middle band moves to the bottom; the blank separator rows stay in place. Inside each moved band, its entire outer border is overwritten with a solid frame color chosen from that band’s own content (the dominant non-background color already appearing on its perimeter), while the interior pattern is otherwise preserved. Finally, the geometric center cell of each band is replaced by a single special marker color.

Find the single non-background square region in the grid, including its internal color pattern, and treat it as a rotatable tile. The output is four copies of the whole canvas placed side by side, where that square appears in the four 90-degree rotational orientations (original plus the three quarter-turn rotations), each kept in the same relative position within its own panel and with the rest left as background.

The output turns the single input board into a horizontal filmstrip of five full-board snapshots, with each snapshot separated by a one-cell blank column. Across these snapshots, the small plus-shaped marker in the moving accent color advances one step at a time along the connected trail/region of the path color, temporarily replacing those path cells while everything else on the board stays fixed. The other special plus-shaped marker remains in place and serves as the reference/end of the route, and the border/background are preserved in every frame.

The wide input is divided into three equal vertical panels, and these panels are collapsed onto each other by matching cells with the same row and the same position inside each panel; the output therefore has the same height but one-third the width. The identical solid square/rectangle that appears in all three panels at the same local position is kept in its original color, while all the other marks collected from the panels are overlaid in the reduced canvas and recolored to a different highlight color. Background cells stay background.

The grid contains a fixed cross-shaped scaffold in one common color, with four diagonal rays extending away from its center into the four quadrants. The shape and positions of all rays stay the same, but the ray colors are reassigned as if the quadrant-color pattern is rotated one step clockwise: the lower-left ray’s color moves to the upper-left ray, the upper-left moves to the upper-right, the upper-right moves to the lower-right, and the lower-right moves to the lower-left. The scaffold itself, including the center cell and the anchor points on the border, does not change.

The entire input picture is kept unchanged, but the canvas is stretched horizontally. The output has the same height as the input and a width four times larger, with the original grid placed flush against the left edge in exactly the same positions. All newly added columns on the right are filled only with the background color; no existing object, marker, or internal pattern is moved or recolored.

The grid contains three distinct motifs placed left-to-right inside the framed upper area: a larger irregular pattern made from empty cells and top-band-colored cells, a solid rectangular block whose left part is one accent color and right part is another, and a smaller solid block in that second accent color. The output cyclically shifts these three motifs one position to the left: the two-color block moves into the left slot, the small solid block moves into the middle slot, and the irregular patterned motif is copied into the right slot. All framing, separators, the top band, and the lower empty strip stay unchanged.

A full divider row and a full divider column in the contrasting separator color split the input into four rectangular quadrants. Remove that row and column, then keep each quadrant unchanged and place the quadrants side by side in clockwise order starting from the upper-left: upper-left, upper-right, lower-right, lower-left. The background and any internal cells inside each quadrant are preserved exactly during this rearrangement.

The entire input pattern is preserved unchanged and placed flush against the left side of the output. The canvas is widened to four times the original width while keeping the same height, and all newly added columns on the right are filled entirely with the background color. In other words, the maze-like framed shape is not altered; it is simply given a large blank extension to its right.

The input contains a large plus-shaped object in one main color on a plain background, with small marker-color pixels placed at the four tips of the plus. The output keeps the same height but expands the canvas to four original-width panels laid side by side, using the plus’s center and tip markers as a template for repeated traces. In the leftmost panel, the marker color spreads along the arms so that only a small central core of the plus remains in its original color; in the other panels, additional marker-color echoes of the same geometry appear as aligned vertical, horizontal, and diagonal traces across the tiled strip.

The output consists of five side-by-side copies of the input grid, so the height stays the same while the width becomes five times larger. In each copy, all cells keep the same positions and shapes, and the background color never changes; only the non-background colors are recolored. Moving from left to right, every non-background color advances one step through a fixed four-color cycle, so the first panel is the original, the next three are successive recolorings, and the fifth panel returns to the original coloring.

Each input contains a small cross centered on a distinct central marker, with one arm color around it on a uniform background. The output completes this into a full, centered plus sign: the vertical arm is extended straight up and down through the center until it spans the grid’s full height, and the horizontal arm is extended left and right so its total length matches that full vertical span. The center marker remains unchanged while only the arm color expands over the background.

The colored figure is a symmetric, thick cross-like blob, and the output replaces it with a 1-cell-wide skeleton: the middle horizontal and vertical axes are preserved, while each bulky filled block is thinned into diagonal branches that meet the center. Small corner protrusions collapse to single diagonal traces instead of solid wedges. If the original figure has empty padding around it, the output widens into several side-by-side panels showing the skeleton at each allowable degree of outward extension within that padding, with symmetric repetition and only one panel when no padding exists.

Ignore the top strip and the divider/frame color: the remaining three motif colors define a cyclic order based on their first appearance when scanning the input from left to right, top to bottom. The output places three horizontal copies of the whole patterned area side by side, keeping all frame/divider cells unchanged; the first copy is unchanged, the second copy advances every motif color to the next color in that discovered cycle, and the third copy advances them one more step. The solid top strip is extended across the full new width.

The input contains a single straight bar on an otherwise empty grid. The output adds that bar’s mirror image across the grid’s vertical middle line, using a second color for the mirrored copy while keeping any original cells that are not covered by the reflection. Where the reflected copy overlaps the original, the overlap is shown in the new color, so an object lying entirely on the center line is simply recolored.

The grid contains four repeated vertical motifs arranged left to right: an upper single marker, a middle row with a left-right pair of two different colors around the motif’s center column, and a lower single marker on the same center column. In the output, these four motif-patterns are reassigned by adjacent-pair swapping: the 1st and 2nd motifs exchange their internal layout, and the 3rd and 4th motifs do the same. Thus the center columns stay fixed, but each column now carries the top height, bottom height, and middle pair spacing that originally belonged to its neighbor within the pair.

The input is a vertical stack of several copies of the same framed scene, separated by repeated header rows and a blank spacer row. Compare the copies position-by-position and keep only the cells that are consistently present in every copy, so any cell that changes between an object color and background across the stack is removed. The output is then a single copy of this stable/common scene, cropped to one panel without the extra bottom spacer row.

The output keeps the input’s height the same but stretches the canvas horizontally by placing multiple exact side-by-side copies of the whole input image. In each example, the small patterned block made of a dominant color with a few contrasting cells is repeated unchanged, along with all surrounding background, so the entire original grid appears tiled across the row direction. No colors are altered and no objects are moved within each copy; the transformation is a horizontal repetition of the full scene.

The figure is a single non-background structure made of a long horizontal bar crossing a long central vertical bar, with two shorter vertical side-posts sitting on the horizontal bar, one on the left and one on the right. The output keeps the whole structure the same except on the left side, where extra cells are added to turn the left side-post and the left end of the horizontal bar into a small filled wedge/triangle attached to that end. Nothing is added on the right side, and no existing non-background cells are removed.

Ignore the large background and isolate each separate foreground object. Sort these objects from left to right by their leftmost occupied column, then replace each one with a tiny 2-cell signature that depends only on whether its bounding box is narrow (one column wide) or wide (two columns wide, including bent shapes that still span two columns). Pack those signatures tightly together into the small output summary grid, using the background color for the missing cell in the narrower/wider marker.

The entire input grid is duplicated horizontally: the output keeps the same height but becomes three times as wide. Every row is repeated side-by-side three times, so the full pattern—including background, empty space, and the multicolored object near the bottom—appears as three identical copies in a row. No cells are altered within a copy; only horizontal tiling is applied.

Each input has one solid, centered foreground shape made of contiguous horizontal bars. The output redraws this shape as a transposed profile of its horizontal reach: moving from the outside of the shape toward its vertical centerline, each output row’s length equals how many input rows still extend that far inward. The result is a tighter, narrower silhouette in the same foreground color on the same background, with any single unmatched center column of the original effectively omitted rather than doubled.

The marked cells form one or more repeating diagonal bands, where parts of the same band are wrapped within the original frame. The output keeps the original grid at the top, then extends the canvas downward and copies the marked cells into new lower rows so those wrapped diagonal continuations are laid out explicitly instead of being folded back into the same short height. The background stays unchanged, the width is preserved, and the result is a tall unwrapped view of the same diagonal pattern.

The tall input is split into equal-sized horizontal bands, each band containing one separated pattern on the common background. These bands are then rearranged from vertical stacking into a single horizontal row by placing the full band images side by side in their original top-to-bottom order, preserving every cell exactly. Finally, that whole horizontal sequence is duplicated once, so the row of bands appears twice across the output.

Find the long horizontal bar and use its length as the width of a new output canvas, while keeping the original height. Every non-background cell from the input is copied to the same row but its column is wrapped into this new width cyclically, as if the large grid were folded into equal-width vertical strips of the bar’s size. The wrapped copies are then superimposed, so when different objects land in the same output cell, the visible cell is the one shown in the examples.

The special color in the last row marks the ends of equal-width horizontal sections, while the other non-background color forms a repeating vertical-column motif that is identical in every row except the solid horizontal bar row and the marked bottom row. The grid is extended to the right by adding more sections of the same width, continuing the section-by-section motif in a back-and-forth mirrored progression so the sequence of section patterns becomes symmetric/oscillatory rather than introducing a new design. The full-width bar row is stretched across the new width, and the bottom-row markers are continued at the same spacing at the end of each added section.

The grid is mostly unchanged: a background area is bounded by a border-colored left edge and a mostly border-colored right edge, but the right edge contains a short segment in the same color as a small horizontal bar inside the grid. In the output, a single new marker cell is added on the row of that interior horizontal bar, placed in the empty cell immediately to the left of the matching-colored cell on the right edge. All other cells stay the same.

Treat the large filled rectangle (including the smaller embedded rectangle) as one row-wise pattern inside its original bounding box. Starting from the top row of that rectangle, shift successive rows horizontally by offsets following a sideways wave: 0, then right by 1, right by 2, right by 1, back to 0, then left by 1, left by 2, left by 1, repeating as needed; the smaller inner rectangle moves along with its rows. Any parts shifted past the rectangle’s original left or right edge are clipped away, and the vacated cells become background.

The large input is a row of equal-sized mini-grids separated by the frame color; the output collapses this strip into one mini-grid of the same size. Align all mini-grids on top of each other: the shape cells that are present in every mini-grid remain in the original object color, while extra cells that appear only in some mini-grids are kept at their positions but recolored with auxiliary colors to distinguish the different partial variants/layers. The outer border and empty background are preserved.

The input is a tall stack of square panels: if the grid width is n, the rows can be split into consecutive n-by-n sections. The output rearranges these sections from a vertical stack into a horizontal strip, keeping every panel’s contents exactly the same, including the zigzag trail and the special marker cells. Then that whole horizontal strip is repeated a second time to the right, so the ordered sequence of panels appears twice side by side.

The single colored horizontal bar is treated as one stage in a sequence of bars that all lie on the same row-position pattern: start from the shortest same-colored bar aligned with the original bar’s left end, increase its length in steps of two until reaching the input bar, then keep extending toward the borders until a full-width bar is reached. The input grid itself stays unchanged at the top, and beneath it the output appends a run-length/rotated encoding of each stage: for each bar, write its left empty margin as blank rows, then its bar length as full-width colored rows, then its remaining right empty margin as blank rows. Concatenating those encodings produces the long striped block under the original grid.

Treat each solid full-width line as a separator between tall subgrids, where each subgrid contains one foreground cell per row forming a zigzag/bouncing diagonal across the columns. The given subgrids are consecutive overlapping snapshots of one longer periodic diagonal motion, so the output reconstructs the complete sequence by generating every one-row-shifted snapshot of that motion, keeping the same subgrid height and inserting a separator line between each snapshot. In other words, the output fills in all missing phases of the oscillation so the diagonal pattern is shown step-by-step through its whole cycle.

The centered multicolor diamond-like figure is copied horizontally into a strip of four adjacent panels, with no gaps, so the output keeps the same height but has four times the width. The 1st and 3rd panels are exact copies of the input, while the 2nd and 4th panels show the same figure rotated 90 degrees counterclockwise. The background stays unchanged around each copy.

The input contains two same-colored figures stacked vertically: an upper symmetric hollow motif and, below a blank separator row, a large hollow rectangular frame. The output keeps both original figures unchanged, then extends the grid downward by adding another blank separator row and placing an exact copy of the upper motif beneath the rectangular frame. In effect, the final layout becomes: top motif, empty row, rectangle, empty row, repeated top motif.

The input has two identical sparse marker strips (one near the top and one near the bottom) and, between them, a horizontal band of repeated 5x5 framed motifs whose interiors contain a few accent cells. In the output, this whole non-background content is cyclically scrolled upward: the motif band moves toward the top, while the top marker strip wraps around to the bottom area and joins the lower copy. The repeated 5x5 motifs keep their internal shapes, but the motif sequence can also rotate sideways with wraparound, so a motif that falls off the right end reappears at the far left one row lower in the shifted band.

Each row is transformed independently by a one-cell cyclic shift to the left. The color at the far left edge of a row is removed from the front and wrapped around to become the new far-right cell, while all other cells in that row slide left by one position. This preserves the row lengths and keeps the same sequence of colored vertical bands, just with each row rotated.

The wide input is made of three same-sized square panels placed side by side. These three panels are collapsed into one square output by aligning them cell-for-cell and superimposing their foreground shapes. For each position, the output keeps a foreground cell if that position is filled in any of the three input panels; otherwise it stays background.

The output keeps the same rows and all non-background cells, but removes every column that is entirely background. This horizontally compresses the picture so separated colored pieces slide together left-to-right while preserving their vertical positions, row structure, and the order of the nonempty columns. Background-only space above/below objects is unchanged; only empty columns are deleted.

The input contains two same-colored objects: a short vertical marker near the left edge, and a longer one-cell-wide path farther right that places one cell in each row. In the output, the marker disappears, and the long path is redrawn so that its cells are shifted horizontally by an amount equal to the marker’s height, alternating by row: top row of the path shifts right, next row shifts left, then right again, and so on. If a leftward shift would run off the grid, the cell is kept at the nearest in-bounds position.

The wide input grid is split into several adjacent square panels of equal size, each panel having the same height as the whole grid. The output is simply the far-right panel copied out as its own square grid, with all cells preserved exactly. No objects are moved or recolored inside that selected panel; only the framing changes by cropping away the earlier panels.

The output is the left half of the input grid: all rows are kept, but the grid is cropped vertically at the midpoint so the repeated structure on the right is discarded. Within the kept half, the small cluster around the horizontal separator is preserved except that the single odd-colored cell at the top middle of the cluster is removed and replaced with background, leaving two matching cells separated by a gap. The long horizontal separator line remains spanning the new cropped width.

The input is made of several equally sized panels arranged left-to-right, separated by background, with the same small left emblem and a right-side shape that changes progressively across the sequence. The output keeps only the first panel and the last panel, cropping each one to a single-panel width and discarding the middle panels. These two preserved panels are then stacked vertically in a new grid, with the leftmost panel placed in the top half and the rightmost panel placed in the bottom half, while their internal patterns and blank margins stay unchanged.

The input contains four single colored cells placed at the midpoint of the top, left, right, and bottom edges of an otherwise blank square. The output stretches the grid horizontally into five equal-width copies of that square placed side by side. In each copy, the four cells stay in those same four edge-midpoint positions, but their colors rotate around the positions by one step each time: the top color moves to the left, the left to the bottom, the bottom to the right, and the right to the top. The fifth copy therefore matches the original arrangement again.

Read the picture as a left-to-right sequence of nonempty vertical column-clusters, where each cluster is a maximal band of columns containing any colored cells and clusters are separated by completely blank columns. Rebuild the grid by removing all leading/trailing blank columns and shrinking every gap between consecutive clusters to exactly one blank column, while keeping each cluster’s internal pattern unchanged. After this compaction, append one more copy of the entire leftmost cluster at the far right, separated from the previous cluster by one blank column.

The input is a regular lattice: solid divider rows and columns surround identical empty rectangular compartments. In the output, the empty/background color is discarded and each row of the original grid is turned into the solid divider color, leaving only a single full-height column marked in a new highlight color.
The output is formed by stacking many same-width copies of this simplified grid vertically, one copy per column position, with the highlighted column shifting one step to the right from copy to copy and wrapping around after the last column. The starting column depends on the phase/alignment of the original lattice.

Each input has a guide structure in one color: a full horizontal bar with a short vertical stem rising to it, plus a separate motif in another color placed below it. The output preserves the original arrangement and propagates it diagonally down-right, recreating the same guide/motif relationship again in the empty space; when a repeated copy would go off the grid, it is clipped to the visible area. Overlaps are allowed, so parts of the repeated motif may be covered by the guide color, leaving partial bars, stems, and truncated motif fragments.

Each input shows a single colored 1-cell-wide zigzag path running downward through the grid, oscillating between nearby columns on a blank background. The output keeps the same height but stretches the canvas to four times the width and places four side-by-side copies of that path. These four copies are phase-shifted versions of the same zigzag: each copy is the pattern advanced by one row-step relative to the previous one, so across any row you see four consecutive positions of the oscillation.

The input is divided into three equal vertical panels that contain corresponding copies of the same small shape on the same background. The output collapses these three panels into a single panel by comparing aligned cells: if all three cells are background, keep background; if all three are part of the shape, keep the shape color; if some panels have shape and others have background, mark that cell with a new highlight color. This makes the shared solid body stay unchanged while the differing cells in the top edge are emphasized.

Take the leftmost square section of the input, where the square’s width equals the grid height; this square contains the full pattern to use. The output keeps the same height and repeats that square panel four times side by side, copying every cell exactly, including the background, the main figure, and any marker-colored cells inside that square. Any additional columns to the right in the input are not interpreted as separate content; they are replaced by these repeated copies of the left square.

The input contains a pattern made of one foreground color on a blank background, possibly with several disconnected pieces; the output repeats the entire input scene as horizontal tiles. The canvas width is multiplied by 7, and each tile keeps the same cell positions and background while recoloring all foreground cells through a fixed 7-color cycle, starting with the original foreground color in the first tile and then continuing with the next colors in that cycle in the remaining tiles. Thus every object, including stray single cells, is duplicated unchanged in shape and placement, only shifted into the next tile and recolored.

The grid has two large horizontal background bands: an upper band and a lower band, and only the upper band contains a small horizontal bar in a third color. In the output, that bar is normalized into a 3-cell horizontal bar of the same color and placed at the center of the upper band, using the upper/left-centered position when the band has even dimensions. The two background bands themselves remain unchanged.

The full-width horizontal bar and the scattered lower markers stay unchanged; only the connected figure made from the path-colored cells together with the single special marker is modified. Treat that figure as a traced path and extend its rightmost end by a two-cell tail: first a new highlighted cell, then one more path-colored cell. If the special marker is already sitting at that rightmost endpoint, it is converted into the highlighted cell and the extra path-colored cell is placed immediately to its right.

The top row repeats the same motif, which divides the grid into equal-width vertical strips. Each strip keeps its own contents, but the strips are reordered left-to-right based on the checkerboard pattern inside them: strips with the regular phase are grouped first, strips with the phase-swapped version come after, and strip(s) that contain the transition/misaligned seam are placed last. The colored markers in the header and the special marker inside a strip move only as part of their whole strip.

Each input is a stack of solid-colored horizontal bands, where every band contains the same centered non-background block inside a wider background frame. The output keeps the same band order, heights, and colors, but extends the picture horizontally by placing side-by-side copies of that framed block while expanding the colored part outward symmetrically by one cell per side in each successive copy until it fills the whole frame, then shrinking back in reverse. Thus each band becomes a left-to-right width progression from its original thickness to maximum width and back, with background padding preserved within each repeated frame.

The output is formed by cutting out a square from the far right side of the input. The square’s width equals the input’s height, so the result is the rightmost height-by-height block of cells, copied exactly with all colors and patterns preserved. No objects are moved or recolored; everything outside that right-edge square is discarded.

The output keeps the same height as the input but stretches the canvas into eight side-by-side copies of the input’s width. In each width-sized block, the larger 5x5 symbol is copied in place using only its main stroke color while its other internal/accent color is turned into background, and the smaller 3x3 symbol is copied in place using only that accent color while its stroke color is turned into background. Thus the result is a horizontal tiling of a color-filtered version of the two input objects.

The grid is stretched only horizontally: its height stays the same, while the width is multiplied by the number of regularly spaced marker columns in the patterned upper band. That upper band is treated as a repeating left-to-right motif, so its divider/gap pattern is continued across the new width (adjacent copies blend into one long periodic strip). Any rows that are uniform background or a single solid fill color keep their row color and simply extend across the widened image.

The output is made by stacking eight full copies of the input grid vertically, each copy acting like a successive frame. In each frame, one entire interior column near the left side is recolored to the highlight color, and this highlighted column moves one step to the right from frame to frame across the striped field; the original tall marker stays in place, except that the separator just to its right flips to a second accent color in the frames where the moving column is on the opposite stripe phase. If there is already a block made from the highlight color on the right, that block is shifted sideways by one cell to match the current phase, while any internal pattern inside it is preserved.

The input contains three vertically separated copies of the same fixed scaffold: a small top marker next to a vertical bar, plus a lower reference marker. These scaffold parts stay in place, while the other scattered markers around them are treated as successive positions of a moving pattern from the first copy to the second to the third. In the output, those changing markers are recolored into a single trace color and all intermediate cells are filled so the pattern is connected across the copies by straight/diagonal paths, including turning the lower reference-marker positions into a continuous vertical trace.

The wide input grid is divided into three equal vertical panels of the same height. These three panels are then collapsed onto one another, aligning cells by their relative row and column positions inside each panel, so the output has the same height but only one third of the width. Marks from the left and middle panels keep their original foreground color, while marks coming from the rightmost panel are recolored to a new highlight color before being overlaid.

The solid full-width divider rows split the tall input into several equal-height horizontal panels. The output is formed by removing the divider rows and keeping only the bottommost panel, preserving its width and the exact positions of any colored cells inside it. All other panels above are discarded.

The input is made of several vertically separated copies of the same kind of composite symbol: an upper block in one color with a single marker cell, and a lower block in a second color, sometimes with extra stray cells or misaligned rows. The output treats each copy independently and repairs it into a cleaner, more regular version by removing dangling/off-pattern cells and replacing bad rows with a consistent continuation of the symbol’s valid row pattern, often extending that corrected pattern into nearby blank spacer rows. If the marker or edge cells are slightly displaced, they are shifted so the top and bottom parts line up with the repaired structure.

The grid contains several separate colored motifs, and the only change is that the leftmost motif is duplicated. A copy of that entire object, with the same shape, size, color, and row alignment, is placed in the empty space at the far right of the grid. All original objects remain unchanged and nothing else is modified.

The non-background content is isolated, tightly cropped, and then reproduced as five horizontal variants placed side by side. In every variant, the rectangular pattern stays the same except for the vertical contrasting bar in the lower rows: it is moved horizontally through five positions from left-shifted to centered to right-shifted, and the cells it leaves behind become background. The detached single cell above the rectangle, as well as the rectangle’s other colored rows and corner cell, remain fixed and are repeated identically in each copy.

The grid is expanded horizontally to three equal-width copies of the original. The left and right sections are exact copies of the input, while the middle section keeps the same cell layout but swaps the two colors everywhere, turning each color into the other. Nothing moves spatially within a section; only the width changes by concatenating original, color-swapped, original.

The grid contains several identical non-background rectangles placed in separate horizontal bands. In the output, the rectangles keep the same size, color, and row bands, but their horizontal placements are reassigned so that from top to bottom they are ordered from rightmost to leftmost. In other words, sort the objects by column position in descending order and place that sorted sequence into the existing vertical slots.

The output keeps the same height but becomes five times wider by placing five versions of the entire input grid side by side. These copies are, from left to right: the original grid, the grid rotated a quarter-turn clockwise, the grid rotated a half-turn, the grid rotated a quarter-turn counterclockwise, and the original grid again. The background frame and all colored cells are transformed together as one whole picture.

The input is a long strip made of four same-size square panels placed side by side, with a single background-colored separator column between neighboring panels. The transformation extracts each square panel intact and stacks them vertically in the same left-to-right order, removing the separator columns but preserving every color pattern inside each panel. After placing panels 1 through 4, the first panel is repeated again at the bottom.

The output is made by repeating the entire input image horizontally four times in a row. Nothing inside each copy changes: the bordered rectangle, its inner fill, and any surrounding background all stay in the same vertical position and are duplicated exactly. The height remains the same while the width becomes four times larger.

The grid’s checkerboard background is preserved, and the whole scene is repeated several times side by side to make a much wider strip; any lone corner marker is repeated in the same corner of each repeated panel. The main non-background shape is then propagated across these horizontal repeats: copies of the shape appear in neighboring panels and overlap, producing a broader merged version of that same shape in the middle of the strip while unchanged panels still retain the original placement. In short, the output is a horizontal tiling of the input with the foreground object echoed/overlapped across the tiled copies.

The large grid contains a mostly empty background, and near the bottom there is the same composite motif repeated several times side-by-side at regular spacing. The output removes the repeated copies and keeps just one repeat block (the middle representative copy), preserving its vertical position and the small differently colored marker associated with it. All other columns are discarded, so the result has the same height but a much narrower width consisting of a single motif-width segment.

The input consists of two same-sized patterns placed side by side, separated only by the midpoint of the grid. The output is formed by overlaying the right pattern onto the left pattern cell-by-cell, using the non-background mark wherever either half contains one. In other words, the result is a single half-width grid that is the union/superposition of the two horizontal halves.

The grid is made of identical pattern panels stacked vertically, separated by full-width divider rows; these divider rows stay unchanged. Keep the first panel exactly as the reference, then for each later panel take the reference panel’s marked cells and shift them downward by an increasing number of rows (1 row in the second panel, 2 in the third, etc.), wrapping within that panel’s interior. In each shifted panel, shifted marks that land on cells occupied by the original reference pattern are shown in the original mark color, while shifted marks landing elsewhere are shown in the dark separator color; all other interior cells are the plain background color.

The input consists of several equal-sized square panels placed side by side, all drawn on the same background color. The output collapses these panels into a single square of that same size by overlaying them cell-for-cell: any position that contains a foreground mark in at least one panel becomes foreground in the output, while positions that are background in every panel stay background. No objects move within a panel; the rule is just horizontal partitioning followed by a pixelwise union.

The input is a set of nested rectangular layers, and the output turns it into a much wider strip by reusing the input’s vertical slices as rows. For each position, the output row is formed from the corresponding input column, then the next input column, then a left-right mirror of that next column, and finally a mirror of the first one, with the “next” column wrapping around at the end. In these examples this creates four side-by-side mirrored repeats of the same layered frame pattern.

The input contains a fixed motif: a solid inner block surrounded by a sparse ring of another color. In the output, that surrounding color is extended outward as one or more stepped diagonal rays that continue the existing slanted arm/corner structure of the motif into nearby empty background. The inner block stays in place, while the added cells follow the same diagonal spacing as the ring and may, in larger layouts, continue through the motif and emerge on the opposite side.

The input is made of several identical copies of the same picture placed side by side across the row direction. The transformation removes the redundant horizontal repetitions and keeps just one full copy of the repeated pattern, producing a narrower grid with the same height. The foreground and background cells inside that kept copy are unchanged.

The input contains one distinctive 3x3 anchor object near the upper-left: a block of one color with a single contrasting center cell, plus several separate sparse marker patterns made of the contrasting color elsewhere in the grid. Each of those marker patterns is shifted so that its own center aligns with the center of the 3x3 anchor, and all shifted patterns are superimposed together. Finally, the anchor’s center is filled to make it a solid 3x3 block, and the result is shown on a square output centered on that block.

The input is divided into equal square panels placed side by side on the same background. The transformation copies the entire leftmost panel exactly, including its background cells and the small contrasting marker cells inside it, and appends that copy as a new panel at the far right. All original panels stay unchanged; only the canvas widens by one panel to hold the duplicate.

The output is formed from the lower half of the input only, keeping the same width but discarding the upper half. The large uniform field on the right is preserved row-for-row, along with any embedded colored patches there, while the small rectangular block that touches the boundary between the left strip and the right field is redrawn one column farther left so it sits compactly inside the left strip. The scattered marker-colored cells in that left strip are also consolidated into a tighter connected pattern, so isolated markers become short linked clusters next to the shifted block.

Inside the bordered field, the existing three-cell horizontal bar is kept as a fixed anchor. The lone marker above the bar is transformed into a new horizontal segment of length 4, starting at that marker’s position and extending to the right, while the lone marker below-right of the bar is transformed into a new vertical segment of length 2, starting there and extending downward. The anchor bar, the outer frame, the top stripe, and the rest of the background remain unchanged.

The wide input is divided into four equal horizontal panels, marked by evenly spaced small anchor cells near the top. Each panel contains a similar dark shape with slight variations; the output shrinks the scene to a single panel-width canvas and combines the panel contents into one aligned summary motif, using the same background and the same anchor-relative placement. Repeated structure is collapsed, while the differing parts from the panel variants are merged into one composite pattern.

A diagonal chain of single cells in one persistent color runs through the scene and intersects several compact block-like objects. In the output, each of those larger objects is recolored to a single common target color, regardless of its original fill color, while the diagonal chain itself stays unchanged even where it passes through the objects. Background and any isolated non-block marker cells are preserved.

The grid contains a tall vertical line in one non-background color, next to a fixed alternating pattern of another color on its right. A single odd marker cell appears immediately to the left of that vertical line on one specific row. In the output, that marker and the vertical-line cell directly beside it on the same row are both erased to background, while the rest of the pattern stays unchanged.

The input is split into equal-sized panels, arranged either vertically or horizontally. In each panel, the same corner marker blocks stay fixed while the central foreground figure grows step by step from a small plus into a larger diamond-like shape; the output is simply the panel with the most expanded version of that figure. In other words, discard the earlier smaller stages and crop out the final largest stage unchanged.

The two main non-background shapes are cut out by their tight bounding boxes, then superimposed by aligning their upper-left corners. In the merged figure, cells belonging only to the first shape keep that shape’s color, cells belonging only to the second shape keep the second shape’s color, and cells where both shapes occupy the same position are recolored with a third highlight color. This composite is then moved to the top of the grid, horizontally centered, while the original copies of the shapes disappear and the small bar at the lower left remains unchanged.

The output is formed by stacking four same-sized copies of the input grid vertically. In these four panels, the distinguished anchor cell stays in the same relative position, while the attached cells of the other non-background color are rotated around it through 0°, 90°, 180°, and 270° orientations. If a rotated part would leave a panel at an edge, it wraps around to the opposite side of that panel, and all background cells remain unchanged.

The large grid is split by separator columns into several equal-sized small boards that show noisy variants of the same figure. The output condenses these variants into one clean 10×10 board by keeping the stable core of the figure, preserving the marker-colored cells that belong to its interior course, and deleting protruding or inconsistent cells along the outer edges and tails. In other words, repeated versions are compared to recover a simplified consensus shape with stray extensions removed.

The input is a horizontal strip of identical framed blocks on a plain background; each block has the same outer frame color, but some contain a smaller accent-colored shape in a particular position. The output extends the canvas to the right and appends one more block after the same gap size used between the existing blocks. This new rightmost block is an exact copy of the leftmost existing block, including both its frame and its internal accent pattern, while everything already present stays unchanged.

The input is split into three horizontal background bands, with a solid rectangular patch of a fourth color embedded in the bottom band. The output makes the grid three times wider by placing three side-by-side copies of the entire input pattern.

In addition, above the rectangular patch in the middle copy only, that patch’s color grows upward into a centered tapered wedge/pyramid: it starts from the copied bottom rectangle and narrows as it rises, ending in a single-cell tip in the higher bands. The left and right copies stay as plain repetitions of the original scene.

A lone marker cell sits at the top of a vertical border-like column of another color; that marker is extended by placing more cells of the same marker color to the lower right. The new markers form a growing staircase: from each marker, go 1 row down and 1 column right for the first new cell, then 2 rows down and 1 column right, then 3 down and 1 right, and so on (triangular row offsets). Add these markers only while the landing cell is empty; if the next landing spot would hit the existing patterned cells or go out of bounds, stop, and leave all other cells unchanged.

The input contains one main rectangular picture made of a dominant object color with a few contrasting detail cells inside it, plus several separate marker segments in another color scattered around the canvas. The transformation keeps the main picture exactly as it is and deletes all of those separate marker segments by repainting them to the background color. The overall grid size and the solid bottom border row remain unchanged.

The input is a vertical stack of same-sized framed panels, separated by single blank rows. Across the stack, the highlighted shape inside the frame shrinks step by step toward the center or disappears; the output is simply the last panel in this sequence, copied exactly with its frame and interior pattern.

The top area stays fixed, but the large lower plus-shaped marker is used as a hub: it is removed and replaced by a set of spokes consisting of the vertical line through its center and both diagonals through that same center. These spokes are drawn outward across the surrounding empty area and through the nearby upper block, repainting crossed cells into the lower block’s color while leaving the other small shapes mostly intact except where a spoke passes. Where the spokes pass through the horizontal band of identical cells, that band is converted into a patterned strip of a new color instead of keeping the original plus-sign.

The grid’s canvas is reshaped by swapping its width and height, turning a very wide board into a tall one. All non-background objects keep the same positions relative to the top-left corner, so their shapes and colors do not change; the only effect is that the unused empty space on the right is removed and replaced by empty space below.

The grid is divided into equal-width vertical blocks: the input shows two copies of the same block, and the output adds a third copy to the right. In the top two rows, the small foreground pattern is repeated one more time exactly; in the large lower region, the solid field color is extended across the new block. The bottom row also continues its per-block marker pattern, placing the same special marker at the corresponding position in the newly added rightmost block.

The long multicolored stripe marks that the picture is split horizontally into equal-width time-frames; the output adds one more frame to the right, repeating that divider pattern for the new frame as well. For every other row, the contents of the first frame are treated as the row’s base template: all non-background, non-moving cells from that first frame are copied into the same positions in every frame, while rows whose first frame is empty become entirely empty. If a row contains the unique moving marker, its column shift from frame to frame is continued with the same constant horizontal step, so the marker is placed in the newly added rightmost frame at the next position in the sequence.

The grid is made of identical horizontal rows, so the transformation is applied to the row pattern and then repeated unchanged down the whole grid. Two regularly alternating backbone colors stay fixed in place, while the other three colors are globally remapped in a cycle: the first accent color becomes the second, the second becomes the third, and the third becomes the first. The grid size and all positions stay the same; only this color substitution changes.

The two non-background colors represent two separate staggered triangular patterns. The single-cell markers form a downward-pointing triangle, so the output adds the next missing row above it with the same spacing; the 4-cell horizontal bars form a left-pointing triangle, so the output adds the next missing layer farther to the left with the same stagger. All original objects stay in place, and if a newly added bar and marker would overlap, the single-cell marker remains visible.

The input contains four single-cell colored markers arranged in a plus shape around an empty center. In the output, those four colors are reassigned by rotating them one step counterclockwise around the center: the right color moves to the top, the top moves to the left, the left moves to the bottom, and the bottom moves to the right. The background and the occupied locations stay the same; only which color sits at each arm of the cross changes.

The grid contains one foreground line-shape on a uniform background. If that shape is a centered vertical spine with a single diagonal branch coming in from the upper right, the output completes it into a fully symmetric diamond/hourglass-like figure by mirroring the branch across the spine and then mirroring the whole upper part downward, using the same foreground color. In the other examples, the foreground shape is not in that valid centered form, so it is erased and the output becomes all background.

The grid contains four small colored clusters arranged left-to-right on the same rows, separated by wide vertical bands of background. In the output, each cluster keeps exactly the same internal pattern and colors, but the empty space between neighboring clusters is reduced by one column each time, so the 2nd cluster shifts left by 1, the 3rd by 2, and the 4th by 3. Equivalently, one blank column is removed from each of the three separator gaps while everything else stays unchanged.

The grid contains a small foreground pattern made of the contrasting color embedded in a wide field of background color. The output keeps the full vertical extent of the original grid, but trims away all-empty background columns on the left and right so that only the minimal column range containing the pattern remains. The foreground shape itself is unchanged, staying in the same rows, with the remaining space still filled by the background color.

The input contains a single central marker and a few scattered cells that are fragments of a larger diamond-shaped pattern around it. In the output, that incomplete pattern is completed into a fully symmetric set of concentric Manhattan-distance layers centered on the marker: the farthest diamond ring uses the outer color, the next ring inward uses the second color, and the next ring inward uses the third color. The center stays unchanged, and the four orthogonally adjacent cells to the center remain background, creating a small cross-shaped gap around the center.

The grid keeps the same size and background, but each connected foreground patch is reduced to a thinner, skeletal trace rather than staying as a solid blob. Cells that remain as the main surviving trace are split into two roles: most of the preserved path is recolored with the new highlight color, while a smaller set of key anchor/junction/corner cells keep the original foreground color; all other original foreground cells are erased.

The large uniform background/empty color is globally replaced by a different fill color across the entire grid. All other elements stay fixed: the dark border-and-divider structure, the solid rectangular regions, and the small accent marks keep their shapes, positions, and colors, while only the previously empty spaces both inside and outside the structure are recolored.

Each non-background shape is replaced by its tight axis-aligned bounding rectangle, drawn as a border in a new highlight color. The border of that rectangle overwrites whatever was on the rectangle’s edge, while any cells strictly inside the rectangle keep their original contents, including the object’s original color and any interior background holes. Everything outside these bounding rectangles stays unchanged.

The grid is split into three vertical parts: a large left background region, a single divider column, and an unchanged right region. A short horizontal marker bar that begins on the top row is copied downward through the left region, keeping the same color and length, while its horizontal position follows a repeating zigzag: it stays aligned for one extra row, then shifts left step by step, then reverses and shifts right step by step, repeating this wave pattern down the rows. When part of the bar would go past the left edge or into the divider, that part is simply clipped, while everything else remains unchanged.

The input is a row of evenly spaced mini-scenes: each scene has the same fixed lower structure (a small dark cavity above a short platform) plus a brighter T-shaped marker at some vertical stage. The output completes the repeating vertical-motion pattern of that marker within the scenes, filling the missing intermediate placements so the marker continues downward through/into the lower structure where the cycle requires. It also extends the strip by one more scene on the right, keeping the same spacing and using the next state of the same repeating pattern.

Treat the wide input as several equal square panels laid side by side, where the panel width equals the grid height; the leftmost column is a fixed vertical border and is preserved. The output is a single square built from the first panel, keeping its border and foreground cells in the same relative positions. Then scan the remaining panels to the right: if a foreground cell occurs in the same non-border column position in more than one of those later panels, copy only the cells from the rightmost such panel into the output at that column position; foreground cells that appear only once in the later panels are ignored.

The only change is in the single horizontal row made from two alternating stripe colors plus some misplaced cells of a third color. That row is regularized into a perfect left-to-right alternation of the two stripe colors, continuing the existing pattern so every odd-position cell matches the first stripe color and every even-position cell matches the second. All other colored shapes and the background stay unchanged.

The full-width horizontal bars stay unchanged, and the stepped foreground structure between them is preserved.
