The output adds a set of 2-cell-tall marker columns across the upper part of that middle band, positioned according to the staircase’s horizontal step rhythm and extended one more position beyond the existing structure; if a marker lands on the shape, those cells are recolored. The leftmost marker uses the original shape color, while the later markers use a fixed sequence of distinct highlight colors.

The input consists of four same-sized solid squares arranged in a 2×2 layout with a blank row and blank column separating them. The upper-left square stays unchanged, while the other three squares grow inward toward the central gap using their own colors: the upper-right square extends leftward from its inner bottom corner, the lower-left square extends upward from its inner top corner, and the lower-right square extends both upward and leftward from its inner top-left corner. The added inward arms have thickness 1 and length equal to half the square’s side, so they partially fill the central cross-shaped space and meet near the center.

Each grid has a large framed area with a uniform upper block, and a lower strip split into two adjacent colored regions: a left region and a right region. In the output, the entire lower strip is repainted to the left region’s color and extended downward to fill the former bottom frame row, creating one solid bottom rectangle beneath the unchanged upper block. The right region’s color is removed from that strip and kept only as a single marker placed in the top-left corner of the outer frame.

The non-background content near the upper-left is a stack of horizontal motifs: each row has a left anchor cell and then an alternating two-color run extending to the right. In the output, these motifs are unpacked into a diagonal staircase: the top anchor stays where it is while the lower motifs are moved to progressively lower-and-right positions, with larger offsets for lower rows, and their original locations are cleared back to background. The left-side vertical strip remains in place, and any shifted motif may appear only as the surviving visible part of its alternating run if its leading cells are discarded.

Divide the input horizontally into equal square panels whose width equals the grid height; the foreground marks form one motif per panel. Keep the whole original grid unchanged, then append to its right a copy of the center panel band: for an even number of panels, copy the two middle panels, and for an odd number of panels, copy the three middle panels. The copied panels keep the same pixel patterns and vertical positions, just shifted to the new right-side extension.

The whole input grid is duplicated horizontally: make three identical side-by-side copies of the entire original image. The output keeps the same height but triples the width, preserving every object, separator line, marker, and empty-space pattern in exactly the same rows and relative positions within each repeated block. In other words, columns are tiled 3 times left-to-right with no other edits.

The grid contains several horizontally separated copies of the same motif, each drawn with a solid foreground color and a hole/interior color, but each copy is incomplete or slightly distorted in a different way. The output widens the canvas to the right and adds one more copy: a reconstructed/clean version of the motif, assembled by combining the evidence from the existing copies so that missing foreground pieces are restored and only the true interior holes remain. All original copies stay where they are, and only this new synthesized motif is appended on the right against the same background.

The upper striped divider and the large two-color patterned block beneath it stay unchanged; the action happens only in the smaller symbol cluster lower in the grid. In that lower cluster, the scaffold/support-colored cells remain fixed, while the other marker cells fall straight downward within their own columns until they reach the bottom or the first occupied cell below them, using the original layout as the obstruction pattern. A stray extra accent cell that is not part of the scaffold or falling markers is removed.

The input has two key objects: a hollow 3x3 frame and, lower down, a separate 2-cell horizontal marker made of two different colors. The output stacks four same-width scenes vertically, with the lower three scenes beginning with a full-width separator bar in the frame’s original color. These scenes are: the original picture, then a copy where the frame is recolored to a new auxiliary color, then a composite where the frame returns to its original color and its center is filled with the marker’s left-hand color while an auxiliary-colored copy of the hollow frame appears below, and finally the original picture again.

Each input contains three single-cell markers: one upper marker somewhere above, plus two side markers placed on the same row near the left and right edges. In the output, the upper marker is extended into a full vertical line using its own color, and the row defined by the two side markers is filled completely across with a different line color, creating a cross. The two side markers themselves are replaced by that horizontal bar, and at the crossing point the horizontal bar’s color takes precedence.

The grid layout stays exactly the same: every cell keeps its position, and the background remains unchanged. The only transformation is a global recoloring of all non-background cells: list the non-background colors that appear in the input in increasing order, then replace each one with the next color in that list, with the highest used color wrapping around to the lowest used color. Thus all shapes and patterns are preserved, but their colors are shifted forward by one step in the task’s active palette.

The grid is a horizontal repeating strip: a foreground color forms evenly spaced vertical posts on a background, with one special row where those posts widen sideways into a repeating bump pattern, and the bottom row remains empty background. The output keeps the height and the existing left part unchanged, but extends the strip to the right by continuing the same periodic motif for several more repeats. In other words, it horizontally tiles the established post spacing and the special-row thickening pattern across a wider canvas.

The lone non-background figure is not recolored or replaced by new objects; instead, it is redrawn in a skewed, stair-stepped form. Straight vertical, horizontal, and diagonal strokes are reprojected into a right-leaning/isometric-looking version, so branches and bars shift across nearby rows and columns while preserving the figure’s overall connectivity and general silhouette. In effect, the output is a slanted re-rendering of the same shape rather than a crop, fill, or mirror.

The input is divided into horizontal bands where each band is made of several identical rows, and each band contains a different short color pattern. The transformation takes one representative row from each band, keeps the bands in top-to-bottom order, and concatenates those row patterns left-to-right into one long row. That long row is then repeated the same number of times as each original band’s row repetition count, producing a short wide output.

The scattered single-color noise cells stay in place, while the three uniquely colored clue cells are replaced by a constructed figure centered on the anchor clue cell. The row or column in which those clue cells are aligned determines the figure’s orientation: a straight bar is drawn through the anchor in that direction, with its interior filled by a new color and both ends capped by another color. In addition, the two cells immediately perpendicular to the anchor are marked with the cap color, creating a small cross/I-shaped symbol whose length is inferred from the original clue spacing and mirrored to be centered on the anchor.

The non-background colored marks are short boundary hints for a larger shape: each hint is extended outward in the same orientation it already has (horizontal, vertical, or diagonal), even across the grid’s separator bars, until it reaches the full implied contour. When multiple colored hints are present, they become different sides/corners of one completed region, and the empty space enclosed between those extended sides is filled with a single new interior color. Cells outside this completed region stay as they were.

The wide input is made of four equal-width panels placed side by side, each showing a partial version of the same scene. The output reduces this to one panel by superimposing the four panels cell-for-cell, keeping every non-background part so the missing pieces from one copy are supplied by the others. When different objects overlap, the same visible layering is used consistently: the right-hand block takes precedence over the central band, which takes precedence over the two left-side piece colors; the small top header strip is kept once in the merged panel.

The main non-background shape is a fixed orthogonal line/outline network, and the only changes involve the small set of highlighted marker cells that sit on that network. In the output, a marker is moved by one step to an adjacent cell along the existing line, following the local path of the structure (including around turns), while its old cell becomes an ordinary line cell again. Markers that are already effectively in the correct/backward position on their local segment stay where they are.

The wide input is split into several equal-sized square panels laid out from left to right on a common background. The rule is to extract the final panel on the far right and use it unchanged as the output. The earlier panels show a step-by-step sequence of overlapping or handoff between colored shapes, and the output is simply that sequence’s last frame.

The input contains a solid full-width horizontal band of the non-background color attached to the bottom, with empty background above it. In the output, that same band is repeated upward in a vertical pattern: copies of the band appear every other band-height, with a background gap of the same height between filled bands. This upward repetition continues from the bottom band and is clipped by the top edge if a full copy does not fit.

The input contains a hollow rectangular frame in one non-background color. In the output, the empty area inside that frame is replaced by concentric rectangular layers: the layer immediately inside the original frame is filled with a second color, the next inner layer switches back to the frame color, and the colors keep alternating as the rectangles shrink inward. The original outer frame and the outside background stay unchanged, and if the nesting reaches a single center cell, that center remains background.

The bottom multicolor base/marker structure stays exactly the same. The only changing object is the sparse diagonal chain of single cells in the upper field: it is shifted one step downward along its own diagonal direction, so a diagonal slanting right moves down-right and a diagonal slanting left moves down-left. Equivalently, the topmost cell of that diagonal disappears and one new cell is added at the lower end to continue the same line.

The output is a horizontal strip of animation frames made by repeating the entire input grid side by side. In each frame, the fixed background structures repeat unchanged, but the small highlighted piece inside the horizontal patterned region is shifted one cell horizontally, moving through all allowed positions until it reaches an end, then reversing to create a back-and-forth sequence. The moving piece can cover cells of the other shapes where it passes, so only its position changes from frame to frame while the diagonal marker pattern and other static objects are copied into every frame.

There are two non-background structures above the solid bottom border: a small compact block and, lower down, a darker support/container shape that may include a different interior fill. The transformation removes these from their original locations and recreates the arrangement at the bottom of the grid, with the support shifted down to the floor area and any interior fill cleared out. Where the relocated structure reaches the bottom border, that border is overwritten or opened up, and the compact block may occupy part of the final bottom-side footprint.

The output keeps the same height but expands the grid to three equal-width panels placed side by side. The left and right panels are exact copies of the input, while the middle panel is a horizontal mirror image taken with respect to the input’s distinctive vertical divider line, so that this divider moves to the opposite side of the panel and every colored object/bar flips across it. Background cells remain background.

The single solid foreground rectangle is duplicated downward multiple times while keeping its width, shape, and horizontal position unchanged. The grid becomes four times as tall, and the same pattern reappears as four vertical copies stacked one under another, with background-only rows preserved so the copies are separated by the same empty spacing implied by the original top/bottom margins.

The input is split into three equal-width panels placed side by side, and the output is a single panel with the same height and one-third the width. For each cell position, compare the three corresponding cells from the three panels: if all three panels contain the same color there, keep that color in the output; if they differ, replace that position with the background color. In effect, the output is the cellwise intersection/common pattern shared by the three noisy copies.

Split the input into three equal vertical tiles, and in each tile discard the always-empty first column so only the meaningful 7/8-column picture remains. Stack these cropped tiles vertically in reverse left-to-right order: right tile, then middle tile, then left tile, keeping every colored pattern unchanged. Then add one extra stacked tile made by splitting at the horizontal midpoint and combining the lower part of the leftmost tile with the upper part of the rightmost tile, creating a wraparound transition block.

The grid contains a repeated two-cell motif made from two special colors: one cell sits above/right of the other, and the lowest copy already has a surrounding halo of a fourth color. In the output, that halo pattern is copied onto the next higher copy of the same motif, positioned relative to its two special cells in the same way. The original lowest haloed motif is then grown outward by one additional layer of that same fourth color, while the side borders and the matching marker cells at the very top and bottom remain unchanged.

The grid keeps all existing non-background objects exactly where they are: the line/point objects in one color and the patterned shape in another color do not move or change. Every empty background cell is recolored to the special fill color already present in the input, so the whole canvas becomes that fill color except where the original objects remain visible. This effectively turns the former background into a solid field behind the existing shapes.

The grid has an upper field and a lower field with different background colors, plus several identical 2×2 accent-color blocks near the bottom of the upper field. The transformation keeps only the leftmost of these 2×2 blocks and erases all the other copies. In the lower field, the original accent-color markers are removed and replaced by a 2-cell descending diagonal placed in the top two rows of the lower field, immediately to the right of the surviving upper block.

A hollow rectangular/U-shaped outline is identified along with a small two-cell vertical marker below it. In the output, the outline is recolored to a new color, the lower marker is erased, and the two special cells on the top edge are replaced by a single special cell centered between them. Additionally, two new interior cells appear on the row just below the top edge, placed symmetrically one step inward from the left and right sides near where those top-edge special cells had been.

The transformation simply recolors the entire non-background drawing. Every cell belonging to the lone connected figure is changed from its original shape color to a different output color, while the background is left untouched. The figure’s outline, internal gaps, extensions, and exact position remain exactly the same.

The input is split by thin background-colored separator columns into several equal-width panels that are mostly horizontal repeats of the same row pattern. The output removes the separators and keeps just one panel’s width: for each row, it copies the panel that is different from the others when a unique panel appears, and otherwise copies the shared repeated panel. The distinguishing feature is a small left-side marker/bar shape, which occurs in different panel positions across the rows, so the output preserves that moving marked version instead of the redundant repeats.

The grid keeps the same height, but it becomes wider: the rows above the solid base row are extended horizontally by continuing the same 1D pattern of filled blocks and blank gaps that is already present. In other words, the top strip acts like a repeating/cyclic horizontal motif, and the output shows more of that motif to the right. The bottom full-width bar is extended to match the new width, while nothing changes vertically.

The vertical divider stays fixed and the two sides are updated separately. On the left side, the horizontal bar-shaped marker color is shifted downward by one row as a whole (clipped if it would go past the bottom), while the other left-side marks stay in place. On the right side, each scattered dot moves exactly one row vertically according to its column position measured from the divider: dots in the 1st, 3rd, 5th, etc. columns move up, while dots in the 2nd, 4th, 6th, etc. columns move down; any dot pushed out of the grid disappears.

The only changing color is the mid-tone structural color: every occurrence of it is recolored, while the background, the existing foreground pattern, and the small marker dots stay in place. Most of those structural cells—including the large block/frame around the foreground region and most scattered single cells—become one new color. A small subset of detached outlier cells at the extreme outer sides are distinguished and become a second new color instead.

The input is divided into equal vertical stripe blocks, with a few horizontal bands that contain special motifs: in each block there is a small framed pattern whose center identifies that block, and some bands are just a uniform filler across all blocks. The output wipes the grid to background, keeps the original stripe row at the very bottom, and keeps only the portion of each special horizontal band that lies inside the rightmost stripe block, in its original position. A new summary row is placed at the top: each stripe block is recolored to the center color of that block’s small motif, except when that block’s normal stripe color is the same as the motif frame color, in which case the frame color is shown instead.

The input contains two same-shaped pyramid/triangle-like figures made of different non-background colors, both resting on a solid horizontal base strip at the bottom. The transformation keeps only the left figure and removes the matching figure on the right. The grid is then cropped to the left figure’s full width, preserving its shape, the background around it, and the corresponding segment of the bottom base strip.

The output keeps the original square pattern as the leftmost panel, then places three transformed copies of the same pattern to its right, making a strip four grids wide and the same height. These copies show the shape in its other orientations: one reflected across a diagonal (equivalently a quarter-turn for these symmetric examples), one turned upside down, and one reflected across the other diagonal. No recoloring happens; the foreground and background stay the same, only the whole picture is reoriented and concatenated side by side.

The input is split into four equal square panels placed side by side, each containing the same foreground line segment but in a different rotated/shifted phase inside its square. These four phases form a cycle: right-shifted horizontal, lower vertical, left-shifted horizontal, upper vertical. The output stacks the panels vertically in that canonical cyclic order, starting from the right-shifted horizontal phase regardless of the input order, and then repeats that first phase once more at the bottom to close the cycle.

Each input contains a single solid rectangular block in a foreground color placed on a uniform background. The output keeps that rectangle exactly the same size, shape, color, and position, but changes every background cell to a new blank color. In other words, only the background is recolored while the lone rectangle is preserved unchanged.

The whole grid is reflected vertically, so every row is reversed top-to-bottom while columns stay the same. After this flip, all cells belonging to the large mass/diagonal line color are recolored into the accent line color, while the plain background color and the small special marker colors stay unchanged. As a result, the big lower block becomes a solid accent-colored block at the top, and the diagonal made from the mass color reappears in mirrored position as an accent-colored diagonal beneath it.

The input is divided into three equal vertical panels, and the output keeps the same height but shrinks to the width of one panel. The three panels are superimposed onto one another at matching coordinates: first the left panel, then the middle panel on top of it, then the right panel on top, so any non-background cell from a later panel overrides what was underneath. Full-width horizontal bands such as the divider row near the top and the footer rows at the bottom are preserved, just shortened to the new one-panel width.

The output is a four-panel horizontal strip: the input canvas is repeated side by side four times, so each panel has the same size as the original grid. In each successive panel, the tall left-hand rectangle is copied again but placed progressively lower, creating a downward staircase across the strip, while the smaller right-hand stacked rectangles stay in the same local position in every panel. In the repeated panels, the upper right small rectangle is also accented by a few extra marker cells placed just outside its left and right corners, like a partial bracket/frame.

The input is a full-height grid made of several equal-width vertical panels placed side by side, sometimes with a blank spacer column between them. The output is obtained by cropping out only the far-right panel and discarding every panel to its left. All rows, internal shapes, empty cells, and the original object colors inside that last panel are preserved exactly.

The input contains several identical copies of the same small colored pattern repeated side by side across the wide grid, with empty background columns between copies. The output keeps just one copy of that repeated pattern—effectively cropping to the minimal set of columns occupied by a single instance, using the leftmost instance as the template. The row count stays the same, so empty rows above or below the pattern are preserved while the extra repeated horizontal copies are removed.

The input contains a large plus-shaped non-background figure: a vertical bar spanning the full height and a horizontal bar spanning the full width, crossing in a central rectangular overlap. The output is a centered crop around that overlap, keeping the overlap itself plus exactly one cell of surrounding thickness on all four sides. In other words, it extracts the inner rectangle made from the crossing region and the immediately adjacent layer from each arm, with all cell colors preserved.

The input is divided into several equal-width vertical panels that repeat the same general figure, plus a solid horizontal band at the bottom. The panel indicated by the marker-colored cells is extracted, the marker cells themselves are removed to background, and the remaining figure is flipped left-to-right. The output is just that single panel, with the bottom solid band kept unchanged but cropped to the same width.

The input is split into several framed subgrids laid out left to right, with narrow blank columns between them. The transformation removes the outer frame from each subgrid, keeps the inner contents in the same positions, and converts every cell of the dark bar/stripe color inside those subgrids into blank background while leaving the main fill color and any special accent pixels unchanged. The cropped interiors are then reassembled side by side in the same order, still separated by single blank columns.

The input contains a single solid isosceles triangle pointing upward on an otherwise empty background. The output keeps the same height but makes the canvas four times wider, splitting it into four equal panels: the original upward triangle, then the same triangle turned to point left, then turned to point down, then turned to point right. In each panel the reoriented copy is anchored at the original triangle’s tip position within that panel, so rotated versions may extend downward and can be clipped by the panel’s bounds.

The large hollow rectangle with its interior pattern stays unchanged, as does any solid patch that is connected to that larger structure. The only edited pieces are separate small objects made from the same border color: a 3x3 plus-like motif is column-compressed upward inside its own 3x3 box, turning it into a top-heavy T-shape, and any isolated solid 3x3 block is recolored to a new highlight color. In other words, detached auxiliary objects are transformed, while the main framed figure is left alone.

The input is mostly a uniform background made of vertical color bands, repeated row after row, but a localized staircase-like disturbance is drawn across a few middle rows using a marker color and short horizontal bars of another color. The transformation ignores this overlaid disturbance and recovers the underlying clean banded row pattern. The output is a new 4-row grid formed by repeating that restored background row four times.

The input is divided into three identical horizontal bands, each ending with a solid full-width separator row and containing three equal-width mini-patterns above it. Treat each mini-pattern as a 2-row tile; scan the nine tiles from left to right, top band to bottom band, keep only the first occurrence of each distinct tile, and discard repeated copies. The output is a single band formed by concatenating those unique tiles in that order, keeping their internal colors and structure unchanged and retaining the matching solid separator row underneath.

The wide input is split into several equal square panels placed side by side, with each panel being a copy or partial variant of the same centered motif. The output collapses these panels into one square by superimposing them cell-for-cell: any non-background mark that appears in any panel is kept, while the background stays only where all panels are empty. In effect, repeated identical panels reduce to one copy, and shifted/incomplete versions combine to form a more complete composite figure.

The grid has an upper template made of a short vertical bar plus several isolated hole-colored cells, a full-width horizontal separator, and a smaller matching motif below. The output leaves the separator and most existing objects unchanged, but copies the arrangement of the isolated hole-colored cells from the upper template into the lower region, preserving their relative spacing and stamping them around the lower motif. This copied hole pattern is positioned next to the lower motif with a one-cell leftward offset, and any cells it lands on are replaced by holes.

The picture is split into repeated horizontal strips: every row that contains a horizontal bar (ending at the same right-edge boundary cell) determines one copy of the whole input, and these copies are concatenated side by side. In each copy, almost everything is unchanged, except that one bar-row is selected in cyclic order starting from the row containing the special marker and then moving downward through the bar-rows, wrapping to the top. On the selected row, the marker is absorbed into the bar color and the bar is extended one extra cell to the left, while the right boundary column and all blank separator rows stay the same.

The input is made of three vertically stacked bands of equal height. The top and bottom bands are identical clean copies of one pattern, while the middle band is a disrupted/shifted version of that same pattern, with pieces pushed sideways and edge filler appearing.
The output keeps just the undistorted repeated band: it crops the grid to one third of the original height and reproduces the clean top/bottom pattern at full width. In other words, the transformation extracts the stable template and discards the corrupted middle copy.

The input is split into three equal-width vertical panels placed side by side, each with a dominant background color and a small internal pattern made from accent cells. The output keeps the original three panels unchanged, then appends a second copy of them to the right in reverse panel order: right panel first, then the middle panel, then the left panel. Nothing inside a panel is altered or mirrored; only the large panel order is reversed, so the grid becomes twice as wide while keeping the same height.

The grid is divided into equal framed panels arranged horizontally. The leftmost panel contains the reference figure, while the panel(s) to its right contain a distorted or different version of that figure. In the output, every other panel is replaced by an exact copy of the leftmost framed panel, so the final image is a horizontal strip made entirely of identical repeats of the left-hand template.

The image keeps the background and the compact symbol-shaped object in place, but all cells of the auxiliary “empty/placeholder” color are erased to background. The long scaffold/track-colored pieces are then horizontally phase-shifted by row: as you go downward, rows of that color follow a repeating pattern of move one cell right, stay, move one cell left, stay, then repeat. This makes the scaffold look like a sideways oscillation, while the symbol itself is simply cleaned of its placeholder holes.

The input is divided into several vertical panels by a separator color. In each panel, there is a small pattern made from a foreground color plus another internal color that acts like holes/transparent cells; only the foreground cells are kept, while separator and background are ignored. The output places these panel-patterns onto one blank grid in panel order, with each next pattern shifted one cell down and one cell to the right from the previous one, so their foreground pixels overlap into a single diagonal composite in the upper-left.

The wide input is made of several equal-width panels placed side by side, each panel containing the same guide pattern in one color and some short horizontal bars in another color. To form the output, these panels are collapsed onto a single panel-sized grid by overlaying corresponding positions: if a bar appears in any panel at a given cell, it is kept there in the result. The guide-colored pixels are only used to show the repeated panel structure/alignment and are removed, so the output contains just the combined bar pattern on an otherwise empty background.

The input consists of four same-sized scene blocks stacked vertically, separated by blank horizontal bands. Each block is kept unchanged, but the blank separators are removed and the four blocks are rearranged side by side into one long row. The left-to-right order is determined by the state of the central framed motif: sort the variants by the position/progression of the missing frame segment and the small marker inside, so they form the motif’s natural sequence rather than the original top-to-bottom order.

The input is made of repeated side-by-side copies of the same staircase-like silhouette, drawn in one main foreground color on a background, with a smaller accent-colored wedge attached at one location in some copies. The transformation first treats the silhouette itself as a reusable template, then creates additional horizontal copies in which the accent wedge is removed back to the main color in some copies and, in others, that wedge is transplanted/expanded onto a copy of the silhouette in the same diagonal/stair-step orientation. The output is therefore a long horizontal catalog of these silhouette variants and accent-placement combinations, while the underlying object shapes and background stay unchanged.

The input is divided into several horizontal sections separated by completely blank rows. Each section contains the same shape pattern drawn in a different non-background color, sometimes with holes/cutouts made of the background color. The output removes the blank separator rows, crops each section to its actual motif, and arranges those colored motif sections side by side from left to right in the same top-to-bottom order they had in the input.

The entire input grid is duplicated horizontally to make three side-by-side copies of the original picture. Height stays the same while width becomes three times larger, and every object—including the small vertical segment above the larger rectangular block—reappears at the same rows in each of the three repeated sections, with the background repeated as well.

The input contains a left-to-right sequence of same-height foreground motifs whose horizontal size decreases step by step, ending at the smallest terminal motif near the right edge. The output widens the grid and appends the complementary sequence of motifs to the right, increasing in size again in the same style and spacing, so the size progression becomes symmetric around the smallest motif. The original part is kept unchanged; only this right-side continuation is added.

The full-width row in the special separator color divides the input into several equal-width panels stacked vertically. Remove those separator rows, then place the panels side by side from left to right in the same top-to-bottom order they originally appeared. Each panel’s contents, including its background and any shifted internal rows, are preserved exactly; only the layout changes from vertical stacking to horizontal concatenation.

The picture consists of several same-sized hollow rectangular frames lined up horizontally, each in its own color, with some frames containing a small embedded mark near the lower part. The transformation appends one more frame to the far right: it is an exact copy of the leftmost frame, using the same border color and the same internal mark pattern. All original frames and background cells stay unchanged.

The tall grid is split by separator rows into four 7×7 panels. Any empty panel is completed by copying the two shapes from the nearest filled panel: the left-side shape is rotated 90° clockwise, the right-side shape is rotated 90° counterclockwise, and these rotated results are stacked inside the empty panel with the rotated right-hand shape in the upper part and the rotated left-hand shape in the lower part. Panels that already contain these rotated shapes remain unchanged, and the separator rows stay unchanged as well.

The main change happens to the multicolored structure near the bottom: relative to the top of its central vertical stem, a fixed up-right staircase/arc of cells in the large block’s color is added. At the same time, the lone cell of that same color above the stem is removed, and the small accent pieces attached to the structure are shifted/reconfigured toward the right. All isolated marker-colored cells elsewhere stay where they are, and the large bottom block is kept except that if a marker is embedded in its top row, the surrounding cells of that row are removed.

The input contains a mostly uniform background with a small contrasting connected shape, usually a vertical stroke with short side protrusions. In the output, that contrasting shape is completely removed so every cell becomes the background color. The grid keeps the same width but its height is expanded to four times the input height, producing a taller all-background rectangle.

The top patterned block, which contains a contrasting vertical stripe, is preserved exactly and acts like a key. The small plus-shaped marker below is shifted upward by one row, and the lower solid rectangle is no longer kept rectangular: its left edge is lifted upward so that one or more of its leftmost columns move up by one cell, creating a stepped/slanted shape. The number of columns that get lifted appears to be determined by the highlighted stripe in the top block.

The grid contains three small motif-shaped objects in a single accent color near the top, and a large solid rectangular block in a different color lower down that acts like an occluder. In the output, that solid rectangle is removed back to background, and the lower area is completed so it shows a second row of the same three motifs as 180-degree rotated copies of the top-row motifs. Any parts of those lower rotated motifs that were hidden by the rectangle are restored.

A single long vertical line acts as a fixed spine, and a second-colored shape attached to it is expanded upward into a fuller connected form. The existing attachment pattern is projected upward along diagonals from the side branches, creating new rows above the original cluster; within those rows, gaps between the new left edge and the existing branch cells are filled in to make a solid attached section. The spine stays unchanged outside this grown area, but spine cells that fall inside the newly completed shape can be replaced by the shape color.

The grid is extended horizontally to four copies of the original width while keeping the height unchanged. In each width-sized block, the same central vertical stripe is reproduced in the same place, and the mirrored slanting/diagonal point pattern on both sides is continued with the same row-by-row phase so the motif reads as a seamless horizontal repetition. The diagonal pattern’s color alternates by block: first and third blocks keep the original diagonal color, while second and fourth blocks use a new color; the background stays unchanged.

Treat the tall image as a vertical stack of equal square panels, each showing the same star-like frame: two diagonals plus a central row and column, with colored arms around one center cell. The output rebuilds these panels into the correct progression starting from the first panel: from one panel to the next, the eight outer arm colors move one step clockwise around the center, and the color that was on the bottom arm becomes the new center color. Any repeated or out-of-order panels in the input are replaced by the missing intermediate states so the stack forms one complete ordered cycle.

Find the single non-background object: a hollow rectangular frame whose border is one color and whose interior is a second color. Crop to that object’s bounding box, then duplicate the entire rectangle once to the right and once below, producing a 2-by-2 tiled block of four identical copies. The surrounding empty background is discarded, so the output is just this larger repeated pattern.

The grid is divided into equal-width panels by single vertical divider columns of a distinct separator color. The transformation appends one more divider and then duplicates the entire rightmost panel exactly, placing that copy immediately to the right. All marked cells inside earlier panels stay unchanged; only the canvas is widened by repeating the last panel.

The input contains a horizontal sequence of equally spaced single colored cells on an otherwise empty background. In the output, these cells are processed left to right in a repeating cycle of three centered motifs: the first stays a single cell, the second expands into a solid 3×3 block, and the third expands into a larger symmetric 5×5 motif with a full middle row, 3-cell rows just above and below it, and three separated cells on the top and bottom rows. This 1st/2nd/3rd pattern repeats across the whole sequence, while the grid size and background remain unchanged.

Inside the bordered rectangular room, the lone odd interior cell is removed by changing it back to the room’s normal fill color. Then a new border-colored L-shape is drawn inside the room from the top-left inner corner: a vertical segment goes downward to the former special cell’s row, and a horizontal segment goes rightward across the top interior row with the same length, forming the top and left sides of a square-like corner mark. The bottom-border marker and the outer background stay unchanged.

The input contains three same-shaped pixel patterns placed side by side, separated by background columns. Two of the patterns share the same foreground color while the middle one uses a different color; the output keeps just one full copy of the repeated-color pattern. Specifically, the result is the leftmost repeated pattern, preserving its exact shape and its surrounding background margin, while the other two side-by-side copies are discarded.

The output is formed by making a second copy of the entire input picture and placing it directly to the right of the original. Nothing inside the pattern is changed: all foreground shapes, gaps, and background cells stay exactly the same. The result is a horizontal doubling of the whole grid, producing two identical side-by-side copies.

The output is made by placing five full copies of the entire input side by side, so the height stays the same while the width becomes five times larger. The first copy is unchanged, and each next copy keeps all shapes and positions identical but shifts every cell’s color one step forward through a fixed 5-color palette cycle; this includes the background, so a previously absent fifth color appears in later copies. Nothing moves, rotates, or changes size—only horizontal concatenation and global recoloring occur.

Each input contains a solid rectangular block of one color on the background, with a contrasting color marking the block’s upper-left corner and sometimes the first part of a down-right diagonal. The output completes that diagonal inside the rectangle: starting at the marked upper-left cell, every step one row down and one column right is recolored with the contrasting color until the diagonal reaches the rectangle’s bottom or right edge. Everything else, including the background and the remaining cells of the block, stays unchanged.

The tall input grid is composed of several vertically stacked repeats of the same scene segment, separated by background rows. The transformation removes the repeated lower copies and keeps only the topmost complete segment, with all objects inside it unchanged. That retained segment contains the original arrangement of a solid block near the top, a framed block beneath it, and a smaller solid block farther down, all in the same positions relative to one another.

The grid is divided into repeated sub-images by full-height blank separator columns, and each sub-image contains a special marker near the bottom that belongs to the main figure. In each sub-image, the figure is completed to be horizontally symmetric about its middle: mirrored row pairs are compared, treating the marker as if it were a normal filled cell, and any filled cell present on one side is copied into the corresponding blank position on the other side. No filled cells are removed, and the separator columns and marker color remain unchanged.

The background and the square blocks of the secondary object color stay in place, while each rectangular block of the third color is turned by 90° in effect: its height and width are swapped while keeping the same center point. This means tall 7-by-3 bars become wide 3-by-7 bars, and wide 3-by-7 bars become tall 7-by-3 bars. If the rotated bar would extend beyond the grid or into one of the unchanged square blocks, those overlapping/out-of-bounds parts are simply omitted, so the fixed blocks keep their cells.

The input is split into several equal-width vertical panels placed side by side, and the output keeps only the leftmost panel. In that extracted panel, the large solid filler area is recolored from its original panel color to the alternate solid color used elsewhere in the grid, while background cells and the special rightmost column of marker values remain unchanged.

The tall grid is a stack of equal-height frames marked by the same header strip and bottom-right marker. Inside those frames, a single green shape appears in successive rotation states: the given frames show the first three states, where any dark "hole" cells inside the shape are turned back into plain background in the output.
The output repositions these cleaned shapes so they travel clockwise through the four corner regions of the frame, then adds the missing fourth rotated state in the remaining corner and finally repeats the first state to close the cycle.

The input contains several separated copies of the same nested corner motif: an outer border color, a middle border color, and an inner pattern color, with each copy anchored to a different corner of its own sub-block. From left to right, these copies progress through the corner positions around a square (for example top-left, bottom-left, bottom-right). The output extends the row by adding one more separated sub-block containing the same motif in the next corner orientation, completing the cycle with the missing corner while leaving the existing blocks unchanged.

The input contains one long vertical bar in a main color and several isolated single-cell markers in a second color. In the output, each marker grows into a 3×3 square centered on its original location, while the long vertical bar stays in place. When one of these new squares crosses the vertical bar, the bar’s cells are kept as the bar color, except for the original marker cell itself if it was on the bar.

The output widens the canvas to four times its original width and places repeated horizontal copies of the input objects, spaced one original-grid width apart. The irregular/larger shape is copied into all four horizontal slots, while the smaller more regular symmetric shape is copied into only three slots, being omitted from the second slot. Aside from this selective omission, each copied object keeps its original color, shape, and row position.

The input is split into several equal-width vertical panels by thin separator columns. Each panel has the same background/scaffold, but contains a small foreground pattern placed at a different vertical position. The output keeps exactly one panel: the one whose foreground pattern is positioned highest in the panel (closest to the top edge). Everything else, including the separators and the other panels, is discarded, while the chosen panel is copied unchanged.

Only the upper block made of background and one foreground color is transformed; the solid-colored rows at the bottom, including the row with the single odd cell, stay unchanged. In that upper block, find the row or rows whose first foreground cell appears farthest to the left. Those winning rows are turned into solid foreground rows across the full width, while every other row in the upper block is turned into solid background.

The picture contains a regular lattice of identical cross-shaped tiles, separated by blank rows and columns, plus a solid strip along the bottom. Some tiles are plain placeholder crosses, while a few are already shown in a two-color directional form with one arm marked by a special accent cell. In the output, the bottom strip is erased to background, and every cross in the lattice is repainted into the same standardized two-color version: the top arm becomes the accent color, and the center, left, right, and bottom cells become the main fill color.

The input contains two horizontally repeated copies of the same foreground shape, separated by background columns. The output keeps just one copy of that shape by cropping away the right-hand duplicate and its separating gap, leaving the left instance unchanged. Background cells and the internal structure of the kept shape stay exactly the same.

The input is a regular lattice: full horizontal divider rows in one color, and between them rows containing evenly spaced vertical bars of that same color separated by fixed-width background gaps. In the output, a background strip of one whole repeat-block is created at the far right, so the rightmost vertical bar/block disappears and all-solid divider rows are only changed by this new trailing blank strip. In the patterned rows, the bars in the left half are shifted one cell toward the center, while the bars in the right half stay in place, so the spacing tightens near the middle.

The output keeps the single large, solid rectangular block of one non-background color exactly where it is and leaves the background unchanged. Every other non-background cell—scattered specks, small groups, and differently colored marks outside that rectangle—is treated as noise and replaced with the background color. In effect, the task isolates the main filled rectangle and deletes all other foreground content.

The large block of one non-background color stays fixed and acts as a horizontal anchor. The other solid block is moved sideways, without changing its shape or row position, so that its left edge lines up with the center column of the anchor block’s bounding box; its old location is erased back to background. When this shifted block lands on existing cells, it overwrites anchor-colored cells, but cells where it lands on the small scattered marker color are turned into a distinct overlap color instead.

The input is made of several separate colored panels stacked vertically, with each panel divided from the next by a full blank row. The transformation keeps only the bottom-most nonblank panel and removes all panels above it, preserving that last panel’s contents, colors, and shape exactly. No objects inside the selected panel are altered; the task is just a crop to the final section.

The input is a strip of equal-sized panels separated by a single vertical divider color. Each panel shows a later stage of the same scene, with the small upper block shifting rightward across panels while the larger lower-left block and lower-right block settle into their final arrangement. The output is just the last (rightmost) panel copied out on its own, with the separators and all earlier panels discarded.

The input consists of one smaller pattern repeated several times side-by-side across the width. The transformation extracts a single repeated block, keeps its internal pixels unchanged, and rebuilds the image by stacking that same block vertically the same number of times instead of placing it horizontally. In other words, the tiling direction changes from horizontal repetition to vertical repetition.

Locate the non-background square/near-square pattern and identify its distinguished corner: the corner that breaks the local pattern (in the small examples it is the lone odd corner, and in the larger example it is the corner where the color sequence terminates). Remove the full row and full column that meet at that corner, so the figure shrinks by one cell in each dimension. Then place the remaining smaller sub-square back so that it stays anchored at that same distinguished corner position in the original grid.

The output is made by placing several full copies of the entire input grid side by side horizontally. The background and all scattered single-cell marker dots stay in the same relative positions in every copy, while the only change is in the main two-color object: its fixed body color remains unchanged, and its other object color is replaced by earlier colors from a fixed progression, with the final panel keeping the original color. Thus an object using a later-stage accent color produces more horizontal panels, showing each earlier variant before the original.

The grid is extended horizontally by placing a second copy of the entire input directly to the right of the first. Nothing is altered inside the original half: the background stays the same, and every colored motif reappears again in the same rows and with the same spacing in the new right half. In effect, the output is the input duplicated side-by-side, doubling the width while keeping the height unchanged.

Treat the two non-background colors separately, then place several same-sized copies of the whole canvas side by side. The right-hand color defines how many copies to make: take its bounding-box columns and, in each successive copy, rotate those columns cyclically by one step within that box while keeping the same rows and rowwise counts. The left-hand color is replaced in each copy by a packed solid rectangle at the left: start at the topmost row where that color appears, remove the gaps between its occupied rows so they become consecutive, and fill the first 1, 2, 3, ... columns (one more column in each successive copy) across that compressed height.

The input is divided into non-empty rectangular panels by full background separator lines, which may be entire blank rows or entire blank columns. Remove those separator lines, keep each panel unchanged, and repack the panels side by side from left to right in their original order. Thus vertically stacked panels become a single horizontal strip, while already-horizontal panels simply have the blank columns between them deleted.

The lone top and bottom cells mark a central vertical line, and the transformation acts only on the 7-column-wide band centered on that line. For each row between those two markers, the colored cells are not recolored but horizontally rearranged: the three columns on the left side of the band are reversed, and the four columns from the center column to the right edge of the band are also reversed. Everything outside this band, as well as the two endpoint marker cells, remains unchanged.

The wide input is made of several equal square panels placed side by side; each panel has the same height as the full grid. The output collapses these panels into one square of that same size by taking their overlap cell-by-cell: a cell stays in the drawing color only if that position is filled in every panel, otherwise it becomes background. In other words, the result is the pixelwise intersection of all the side-by-side squares.

The grid has two zones: an upper zone with a dark background, scattered small marker cells, and one solid rectangular block; and a lower zone with a different background containing a copy of that same block. In the upper zone, only the scattered marker cells move: each row shifts its markers by one cell horizontally, alternating by row (top row left, next row right, then left, then right), and any moved marker overwrites the block where it lands. In the lower zone, the copied solid block is replaced by a stylized version shifted up by one row: the top two rows become alternating filled/empty vertical stripes starting with a filled cell at the left edge, the middle rows stay solid, and the final bottom row becomes the complementary stripe pattern.

The input contains one composite figure on a uniform background: a top band with a small contrasting center, a solid middle block, and a bottom band. The output ignores the figure’s original location and redraws this same multicolor figure in a fixed canonical form inside a 10-row frame, with the upper part stepped diagonally down-right while the middle block and bottom band stay aligned below it. This standardized figure is then repeated four times across the width, with alternating copies shifted one row lower to create a high/low repeating pattern.

The input is a horizontal strip of several same-sized picture panels, separated by single blank columns. The transformation discards all panels except the one on the far right, and outputs that rightmost panel unchanged. All separator columns and everything to the left are removed, so the output is just a cropped copy of the last framed scene.

The input is an enlarged, checkerboard-encoded picture: two alternating scaffold colors fill the background, while the real image is embedded across that scaffold using a normal drawing color plus special marker colors. The transformation decodes/shrinks this encoding, collapsing each checkerboard-based section back to its smaller pixel grid, turning scaffold-only cells into blank output cells and preserving the ordinary filled cells and the special marked/accent cells. When the encoded picture is split into multiple adjacent sections, each section is decoded the same way and the results are reassembled in the same overall layout.

The input is a tall strip whose height is an exact multiple of its width, so it can be split into several square panels stacked vertically. These panels are symmetry-related versions of the same underlying picture (copies, flips, rotations, or transpose-like reflections), and the output rearranges them into one horizontal strip of square panels instead of a vertical stack. The left-to-right arrangement is chosen to show a consistent symmetry progression, reusing mirrored/rotated counterparts when a vertically stacked panel is just a redundant repeat of another view.

The large solid block and the small 2×2 marker in the upper-left stay fixed. The horizontal strip sitting just above the block, together with any scattered single colored cells above it, is rotated 90° clockwise around the strip’s leftmost cell: this turns the strip into a vertical column descending along the block, and moves the other colored cells into new positions inside or beside the block with the same rotated offsets. Their original locations are cleared back to background, and rotated cells overwrite the block where they land.

Each input contains a solid horizontal divider row and a vertical column made of a special marker color. In the output, the very top row is replaced by a copy of the divider row, while the rest of the grid stays in place except for added marker-color cells. Those added cells form a full marker-colored left border down the first column (below the top row) and a descending diagonal from the second row/second column down-right, overwriting whatever was there, including when it crosses the original divider row.

The grid is organized into horizontal zones: a plain top background, a middle band filled mostly with one dominant color, and a lower band made from another color with a right-side patch of the accent color. In the input, the accent color also forms a separate staircase/zigzag shape embedded inside the middle band. The transformation deletes that embedded staircase by repainting it with the surrounding middle-band color, while leaving the top background and the lower band, including its accent-colored right patch, unchanged.

The picture is split into equal-width vertical tiles: the two tiles in the input define a repeated motif, with the upper motif identical in both tiles and the lower motif differing only in how far its rightward arm extends. In the output, the whole scene is stretched horizontally into six same-width tiles, and the upper motif is simply copied unchanged into every tile. The lower motif becomes a 3-tile cycle repeated twice: first the shorter input version, then the longer version but with the leftmost cell of its arm recolored to the arm’s leading accent color, then a standardized one-step-shorter version of that longer form (which collapses back to the short form when the two inputs differ by only one cell).

Each object is a thin vertical marker line directly attached to a larger speckled rectangular panel beneath it. In the output, these two parts trade vertical order: the panel is moved upward to where the line was, and the line is placed directly below the panel, staying in the same column alignment and with no gap. While moving, the panel keeps its width and internal dot pattern but is flipped vertically, so its rows appear in reverse top-to-bottom order.

The output is a horizontal strip of animation frames: it places one copy of the whole input beside another, for as many frames as the input is wide. In each successive copy, the cells of the moving color shift one step to the right within their own rows, wrapping around from the right edge back to the left, while the other colored shape stays fixed. So the result shows the moving-color object sweeping cyclically across the unchanged figure over time.

Each input is a hollow rectangular frame around an empty interior, built from two non-background border colors that alternate along the top/bottom edges and alternate down the left/right sides. The output keeps this original framed rectangle unchanged, then stacks a second rectangle of the same size directly underneath it. In that lower copy, the two border colors are swapped everywhere, while the interior background remains unchanged.

The grid contains a repeating set of full-height vertical bars of a secondary color on a uniform background. In the output, every one of those vertical bars is moved exactly one column to the right, while the rest of the cells stay as background. The newly opened column on the left is filled with background color, and anything shifted beyond the right edge is simply lost rather than wrapped around.

The input contains a meaningful picture on the left, then a full-height vertical divider made of the empty color, with only irrelevant padding to the right. The transformation cuts the grid at the first such divider, removes that divider and everything beyond it, and keeps the left section unchanged. All internal shapes, including the central figure and any accent-colored border pieces, stay in the same positions within the retained crop.

The input is three horizontally separated copies of the same scene, each with the same top horizontal bar and the same long descending diagonal trail, but with a small two-color staircase motif placed at slightly different positions along that trail. The output collapses these three copies into a single panel of one-copy size by aligning them and keeping the stable shared structure. The staircase motif is merged by overlap: cells that agree can remain, conflicting parts are deleted, so only the exposed surviving fragment of the staircase is shown, sometimes leaving just its upper-right cell and a trailing cell near the lower-right end of the diagonal.

The grid contains a single large symmetric figure in one accent color on a uniform background, plus four isolated marker cells placed above, below, left, and right of that figure. In the output, the figure itself and the background stay unchanged, but only the top marker and the left marker are kept. The right marker and the bottom marker are erased back to the background color, so the surviving markers are the two on the upper-left side of the central figure.

Find the rectangular patch made of two alternating foreground colors on a plain background. Let its width be W; the output is formed by placing W copies of the entire input canvas side by side horizontally. In the first copy the patch is unchanged, and in each next copy the colored patch is circularly shifted one more step to the right within its own bounding box, while all background cells and the patch’s overall position stay the same.

The output keeps the same height but places four copies of the scene side by side. In every copy, the border-like structure and any unchanged interior pieces are repeated as-is, while the upper compact block may be widened by one cell toward the open space on its left and the lower compact block may be widened by one cell toward the open space on its right. The four panels enumerate the four combinations of these two optional widenings: lower-only expanded, both expanded, upper-only expanded, and neither expanded (the original form).

The outlined shape made of a main interior color plus a different border color is turned into a fully solid version: every border cell is recolored to the same color as the interior, so the whole diamond/blob becomes uniformly filled. Separately, each object in the third accent color is preserved and extended upward by one cell, adding a copy of its top edge one row above. All other background cells remain unchanged.

The empty background grid is turned into a pattern of four thin right-angle "corner" marks in a new foreground color, while all other cells stay as the original background color. Each corner arm has length equal to one quarter of the grid’s shorter side: two mirrored corners are drawn along the top edge, and two upward-facing corners are drawn lower down near the bottom. Horizontally, the top-left corner is inset by one arm-length from the left edge, the bottom-left corner touches the left edge, and the two right-side corners are aligned in the same columns near the right side.

The grid keeps its left border and the two large background regions unchanged, but two special patterns are updated. A diagonal chain made of one distinct “head” cell attached to several identical trail cells moves forward by one cell along its own diagonal direction: the head advances to the next diagonal position, each trail cell shifts into the previous cell’s place, and the trailing end is cleared to the upper-region background color. Separately, the lone movable marker in the lower region takes exactly one diagonal step toward the other lower marker, while that target marker stays where it is.

The layout is preserved exactly: the background stays empty, the special anchor color that forms the bars/spine remains unchanged, and every other colored cell stays in the same position and shape. The only transformation is a global recoloring of the non-anchor pattern by a fixed one-to-one substitution cipher, applied consistently to every occurrence of each content color across the whole figure. In other words, it is the same object after a consistent palette remap, not a movement or resizing.

The wide input is divided into equal square panels whose width matches the grid height; each panel is a separate frame of the same pattern progression. The output keeps all of these panels unchanged, then continues the sequence by appending the panels from the beginning again in the same order, but stops before repeating the final panel. In other words, the strip is extended horizontally to form one full sequence plus the first sequence minus its last frame, creating a seamless cyclic continuation.

The input contains two separate hollow frame-like shapes of different colors, one positioned above the other. Each shape is rotated 90 degrees clockwise, and then the lower shape is moved to the upper-left while the upper shape is moved to the lower-right, so the two rotated shapes end up diagonally adjacent with a small gap between them. The rest of the background stays empty.

The output is made by taking the entire input picture and stacking four same-sized versions of it vertically. The top section is the original image, the second section is the image rotated 90° counterclockwise, the third section is rotated 180°, and the bottom section is rotated 90° clockwise. All non-background cells keep their colors; only the orientation of the whole arrangement changes.

The grid is split into three vertical regions: a left field with scattered marker cells, a middle band (sometimes containing a small embedded shape), and a right field with another scattered marker color. In the output, the entire middle band and its embedded shape stay exactly unchanged, while every marker in the left field is moved straight upward by two rows, disappearing if it would move past the top edge. All markers in the right field are removed, leaving only that region’s background color.

The input is split into four equal-width vertical panels laid side by side on a common background. Sparse cue pixels in otherwise empty rows/areas act as labels for the panels: two panels share the same cue color, one panel has a different cue color, and one panel has no cue. The output is made by cropping out the entire panel associated with the repeated cue color, preserving that panel exactly (in these examples, this is the leftmost of the matching pair).

The input contains a single solid square of one non-background color. In the output, that square stays in place, and its center acts as a hub from which straight lines of the same color extend outward in all eight directions: horizontally, vertically, and along both diagonals, continuing until they reach the grid boundary. The result is the original square embedded in a large star/asterisk-like pattern centered on the square’s middle cell.

The whole grid is transposed: rows become columns and columns become rows. The solid header row of one uniform color at the top turns into a solid leftmost column, and the alternating full separator rows turn into alternating separator columns. The patterned rows made of cyclically shifted symbol sequences are preserved exactly, just reoriented into columns.

The input is divided into two equal square panels placed side by side. In the output, these panels are expanded into four horizontal panels: first the left panel unchanged, then a 180-degree rotation of the left panel, then a 180-degree rotation of the right panel, and finally the original left panel again. No recoloring occurs; only the spatial arrangement and rotations of the existing patterned squares change.

The input consists of several vertically stacked copies of the same shape pattern, each copy drawn in a different color and separated into equal-height bands. The output removes all repeated bands except the lowest one, keeping that shape exactly as it appears. In other words, the task crops out the bottom-most colored instance of the repeated figure and discards the rest.

Each non-background row contains a single solid horizontal segment of a fixed common width, but these segments appear at different horizontal offsets in the large canvas. The output removes the empty horizontal space: for every row, the non-background segment is cropped out and placed flush to the left in a new grid whose width is exactly that segment width. Vertical order is preserved exactly, and rows that were completely background stay as all-background rows.

The full-width horizontal strip stays fixed and acts as a divider. The small motif located just below this strip is reproduced directly above it in the same columns and in the same orientation, while the original motif below remains unchanged. The recreated upper version is extended by one extra top row consisting only of the motif’s central cell, so the above-strip figure is one row taller than the below-strip figure.

The grid has regularly spaced vertical divider columns that stay fixed, and only the pair of rows containing the colored horizontal bar changes. In those two rows, the input shows one finite stepped bar made of several cells of one color with a different-colored tip, shifting sideways from section to section to form a symmetric zigzag. The output widens the grid and continues this bar pattern horizontally by repeating the bar’s inner step sequence across more divider-separated sections, while all non-bar rows remain just background plus the divider columns.

The output keeps the same height but triples the width, turning the single wedge/triangle-like figure into three side-by-side horizontal placements of the same structure. The diagonal border and the alternating interior pattern are redistributed into these three offset copies, as if the original figure were repeated with different left/right horizontal shifts across the three panels. A small subset of border pixels at the exposed tips/leading ends of these shifted copies is recolored with a new highlight color, while the checker-like interior color stays the same.

Find the largest non-background connected shape and leave it unchanged. Every other foreground shape is turned 90 degrees in place by swapping its bounding box’s height and width while keeping the same upper-left anchor, and then the result is shifted downward by two cells. If part of a shifted/rotated shape would go outside the grid, that off-grid part is simply lost.

The input consists of several equal subgrids placed side by side, separated by single divider columns, and each subgrid contains the same basic scaffold plus its own small foreground pattern. The transformation collapses these repeated sections into one representative output panel: the divider columns are discarded, each section is converted into a narrower local-coordinate version, and the foreground marks from all sections are overlaid in the same place while the shared upper-left vertical segment is kept. Cells where contributions merge are recolored with new result colors, while untouched cells remain background.

The two non-background objects are a solid diamond-like shape and a matching hollow/outline diamond-like shape. The output widens the canvas into four side-by-side frames that show these same two shapes at successive horizontal positions, moving toward one another until they coincide in the middle frame. In the overlapped frame, the outline shape is drawn over the solid one, so its border remains visible while the solid shape shows through the interior gaps.

The output keeps the same height and reproduces the entire input picture as a horizontal strip of five identical copies placed side by side. Nothing inside the scene changes: the background bands, colored shapes, holes, and their relative positions within each copy are all preserved exactly, with only the canvas width expanding by a factor of five.

The input consists of several parallel descending diagonal traces, each trace having its own color and arranged in a fixed left-to-right order. The output keeps the same height but concatenates multiple equal-width copies of the grid side by side, with one copy for each diagonal trace/color. In the first copy nothing changes; in each following copy, the diagonal positions stay exactly the same but the colors are cyclically reassigned so that every trace takes the color of the trace immediately to its left, with wraparound from the leftmost trace to the rightmost.

The wide input is three equal 9-column snapshots placed side by side, and the output condenses them into a single 9-column scene. Parts that are unchanged across the snapshots are kept as they are, while the shape that shifts horizontally is merged into one composite path inside that single panel. Its earliest/shared cells stay in the original object color, and cells belonging to the later snapshots are marked with two trail/highlight colors to show the progression from one frame to the next.

The right-edge border column and the horizontal bar-shaped objects remain fixed. The other non-background colored cells near the right side are dropped downward within their own columns: each such cell moves to the nearest available background cell below it, so the group settles lower, stopping above blocking bars or reappearing just below them if the space immediately beneath is occupied. This preserves the number of cells in each affected column while only changing their vertical positions.

The full-width horizontal bands stay fixed, as does the single vertical column of path-colored cells that passes between and through them. All other small marker cells are removed, including the marker just below the top position, the marker between the first two bands, and the side-attached cell beside the lowest path segment. The only transferred information is the side-attached cell’s color: it is moved to the topmost marker position in the main column, replacing the original top cell there.

The input contains several copies of the same character-like shape in different internal states, spaced apart by empty columns. Each copy is cut out as its own fixed-width block, the empty gaps between blocks are removed, and the blocks are placed flush side by side in the output. If the new packed strip still has room for another whole block, the state sequence continues by reflecting back from the end (so after the last stage, the previous stage is repeated), while keeping the same row structure and colors within each block.

The tall input is split into three equal horizontal panels that show the same static scene: the border/background and the fixed colored shapes stay in the same arrangement, while a single bright trail is shifted between panels. The rule is to keep only the panel where that trail forms the correct complete zigzag/V-shaped diagonal through the scene—descending down-left, then turning and continuing down-right, with the turn occurring as low as possible while still fully visible. The output is that one selected panel by itself, discarding the other two candidate panels.

The grid is split into three horizontal color-coded sections: a left section, a middle section, and a right section, each topped by the same open rectangular frame shape. These three sections are merged into one composite by shifting the middle section left so it begins one column to the right of the left section, and shifting the right section left so it begins one column to the right of the middle section; overlapping cells are simply overlaid in that staggered order. The large top frames therefore collapse into one shared frame with three colored leading columns, and any smaller shapes below are combined using the same section-wise shifts, after which the result is cropped to its non-empty extent.

The unchanged background and the small corner marker stay as they are; only the mixed two-color line drawing is edited. In each figure, the two non-background colors form intertwined straight arms, and any pixel whose color disagrees with the clear continuation of a neighboring arm is recolored so that the arm becomes a cleaner, more continuous straight segment. In other words, the output resolves local color conflicts inside the pattern by extending the surrounding line color through mismatched cells, while leaving already consistent parts untouched.

The grid is divided into equal-width vertical panels, identifiable by the repeated column containing the same single upright marker and its nearby small motifs. The output performs a cyclic horizontal shift of these whole panels: each panel moves one slot to the right, and the rightmost panel wraps around to become the leftmost. Nothing inside a panel is edited independently—the paired top markers, the horizontal clusters around the center marker, and the lower block-with-interior pattern are all preserved exactly as part of the moved panel.

The input contains identical solid square tiles on a plain background, arranged like a cross: one tile above the center, a horizontal row through the center, and one tile below. Measure the horizontal spacing between neighboring tiles in the central row, then use the upper tile as the starting tile and repeat that same tile to the right at that spacing until the grid edge is reached (allowing the last copy to be clipped by the border). All other original tiles are removed.

The input consists of several small identical motif-panels placed side by side and separated by vertical divider lines.
