In each panel, the same framed pattern appears, but a single distinctive cell in the middle row shifts one step horizontally from panel to panel. The output removes the dividers and merges these panels into one panel of the same height, keeping the common frame unchanged while replacing the middle-row cells with a left-to-right sequence of different colors, one color for each panel’s shifted special-cell position.

The striped block on the left stays as a reference, while the scattered marker-color cells are reorganized into two right-side structures. First, the three isolated markers that appear on rows 2, 4, and 8 are consolidated so that the row-2 marker is removed and the row-4 and row-8 markers are placed together in the row-2 marker’s column, preserving their rows. Second, the separate vertical marker stack near the lower-right has its top pushed one row upward (so a short stack grows upward by one cell, and a 3-cell stack shifts upward).

The wide input is made of several equal-sized panels placed side by side, separated by single blank columns. The output keeps just one panel-sized view: it preserves the fixed structure from the first panel (the solid top band, the short bar near the top, and the constant bottom markers), then overlays onto that panel the extra small bottom-row markers that appear in the corresponding positions of the intermediate repeated panels. In effect, the repeated strip is compressed into one frame by superimposing the changing marker positions from the sequence, while the last panel is not used.

The whole input image is copied side-by-side three times, producing an output that is three times as wide while keeping the same height. Most objects are repeated unchanged in all three copies, but in the middle copy only, the large solid rectangular block in the lower area is edited: its central vertical third is recolored with a special highlight color, while the left and right thirds of that block stay the original block color. The left and right copies remain exact duplicates of the input.

The input contains two same-sized scenes placed side by side, and the output keeps only the left scene. In that kept scene, all objects stay in place except the narrow vertical stripe: it is extended downward by one cell into the top of the large block beneath it, replacing that block’s top-center cell with the stripe color. The scattered small marker cells and the rest of the background/base area are unchanged.

The entire input grid is copied once and placed directly to its right, doubling the grid’s width while keeping the height unchanged. Every cell value is preserved exactly, so the background stays background and all colored patterns, bands, and shapes reappear in the same rows and internal arrangement in the new right-hand half. The output is therefore two identical horizontal copies of the original grid side by side.

The output keeps the same width as the input but extends the canvas vertically to four times the original height. It is formed by stacking four full-size copies of the input pattern: the top two sections are exact repeats of the original grid, and the bottom two sections are repeats of the left-right mirror of that grid. When the input is horizontally symmetric, the mirrored sections look the same as the original.

The input contains a partially drawn set of nested, center-aligned rectangular layers: each layer is indicated by only one or a few sides or horizontal bars, with a small central motif already present. The transformation completes these hints into full concentric rectangular frames, mirroring and extending each layer so that every color becomes a closed ring at the correct distance from the center. The ordering of layers from outermost to innermost is preserved, and the original center cell/pattern remains unchanged inside the finished nested structure.

The input shows two horizontally separated copies of the same stacked motif; their spacing defines a repeat step. The output extends this motif sequence to the right so that there are five evenly spaced copies in total, keeping the upper solid block, the large middle mass, and the lower block unchanged in each repeated position. The only altered part is the thin horizontal marker attached near the top: instead of a full short bar, each copy keeps just the bar’s leading cell as a single marker.

The blue mound-like shapes with a single marker cell above them are the only patterns that survive; the solid auxiliary block and the marker cells themselves disappear. Each cell of the auxiliary block is treated as an offset instruction: make a same-width, same-height frame containing translated copy/copies of the blue marked shape(s) at that offset (clipped by the grid edges), then stack all of those frames vertically. So the output is a tall vertical list of stamp-placements of the blue objects, generated from the offset pattern encoded by the auxiliary block.

The input contains a fixed two-row header at the top and, below it, several horizontal-object bands: each band has a sparse pattern row and, two rows lower, a solid horizontal bar of the same color. The output extends the grid by four rows, copies the top two header rows into this new bottom section, and inserts into the copied first header row the sparse pattern of the lowest such band, recolored into the next/extra color for the sequence. In the third new row, a single cell of that same new color is placed one step to the right of the end of the lowest band's solid bar; the fourth new row stays blank.

Each input is a wide horizontal strip made of the same motif repeated at a constant spacing: a single marker cell in an upper row and a 3-cell bar in the lower rows. The output keeps only the leftmost three repetitions of this repeating pattern and crops away everything to the right. The height and vertical placement stay the same, so any extra repeats and the small attached block at the far right disappear because they lie outside the cropped region.

Each puzzle has a hollow rectangular outline in one non-background color and a separate irregular shape in another non-background color. The output preserves both original objects, then uses the irregular shape as a template to add a small/internal continuation of that pattern inside the rectangle’s interior, as if the rectangle is a display area containing a condensed copy of the shape. When the irregular shape already intrudes into the rectangle, only the missing interior cells are added, and any outline-colored cells needed to keep the frame coherent are also restored.

The picture is a horizontally periodic scene: a pair of small guide blocks repeats across the top, a special horizontal band runs through the middle, and patterned motifs made of another color appear every fourth guide position in the middle and lower parts. The output widens the canvas to the right by one full repeat cycle, continuing the top guide pattern and extending the central band. In that new space, the middle motif and the lower 2x2-block motif are copied with the next shape/placement in the same left-to-right progression already shown by the existing occurrences.

Ignore the scattered accent cells in the input and keep the outer background border unchanged. The inner nonzero area stays split at the same vertical boundary: the left block is recolored uniformly to one new base color, and the right block is recolored uniformly to a different new base color. Then a repeating pattern of accent-colored anti-diagonals is overlaid across the whole inner rectangle, running from upper-right to lower-left and appearing every sixth diagonal, cutting continuously across both blocks.

The grid keeps the same size, but the two non-background objects are relocated farther from the top-left while preserving their shapes and internal colors. The single horizontal bar at the top is shifted horizontally so its left offset is doubled, and the lower multicolored rectangular pattern is moved so both its row offset and column offset are doubled.

After the lower patterned block is moved, a new-color vertical strip is added immediately beside it on both the left and right for the block’s full height; if one side would fall outside the grid, that side is simply absent. The original locations are cleared back to background.

The input contains several framed shapes made of a common border color, with solid rectangular color blocks inside them, plus a separate vertical reference strip at the far right. In the output, each inner solid block is turned into a one-cell-thick border of a new companion color while keeping its original color only in the interior; if the block is only one cell thick, the whole block changes because there is no interior to preserve. This is applied independently to every filled block, and the far-right reference strip is also recolored to its corresponding companion color, while the structural frame itself stays unchanged.

The input is divided into three equal-height horizontal bands, each band being a same-sized subgrid. The output rearranges these three bands side-by-side from left to right, turning the vertical stack into a single horizontal strip. All cells inside each band are copied exactly, so the foreground blocks, empty/background areas, and any internal cutouts keep the same relative positions within their own subgrid.

The colored cells form a single structured pattern made from two non-background colors. In the output, the pattern’s shape and position are preserved exactly, but every cell of the secondary color is changed to the primary object color, making the whole figure monochrome. Nothing is added, removed, moved, or resized; only the color unification happens.

The input is a row of several identical large shapes placed side by side, separated only by empty background; what differs between copies is the small accent-colored pattern embedded inside each shape. The output keeps just one of these copies: the one whose accent-colored motif is the most mirror-symmetric and well-centered within its host shape, while the other variants are discarded. In effect, the wide strip is reduced to the single selected tile/object with its original outline and colors unchanged.

The output is a horizontal strip of consecutive frames rather than a single transformed scene: the first frame is the original grid, and additional frames are appended to its right. Across these frames, the blue structures stay fixed while the magenta pattern is advanced one diagonal step at a time through the scene, so detached magenta traces and magenta cells embedded in blue objects continue along the same diagonal path and overwrite blue where they land. The strip includes all such stages until the moving magenta pattern has been fully carried through, so the number of appended panels depends on how many steps are needed.

The input is a wide grid made of several separate 12×12 panels placed side by side, each panel containing its own small picture on the same background. The output does not alter any panel’s contents; it simply cuts the input into those equal-width vertical sections and stacks them vertically in the same left-to-right order. In other words, the layout changes from one horizontal strip of panels to one vertical column of panels, with all colors and internal spatial relations preserved inside each panel.

The output keeps the same width but becomes four times taller by stacking four same-sized snapshots of the scene one under another. Across these snapshots, the small structured motifs attached to the central divider are advanced through successive states: the upper hook is reduced/shifted, the central motif’s unique tip cell moves leftward step by step through its short bar while its old position becomes empty, and the lower attached motif is shown in corresponding later stages. The large solid region, the divider, and the isolated unrelated single cell stay otherwise unchanged.

Find the lone 3-row horizontal motif embedded in the background: the top and bottom rows are identical and act as a frame, while the middle row contains one or both of two interior colors. Leave the framing rows and the rest of the grid unchanged, but in the middle row swap those two interior colors everywhere. Thus every cell of the first interior color becomes the second, and every cell of the second becomes the first.

The grid contains a uniform background with a few isolated marker cells. In the output, each marker disappears from its original position and reappears one column to the right on the same row, with the moved marker recolored to a new highlight color while the old location returns to background. If a marker starts at the far right edge, it wraps around to the far left cell of that same row.

The scattered non-background pieces are not kept in place; they are reassembled into one compact two-color figure placed at the upper left, and the rest of the grid is cleared back to background. The darker pieces combine into an L-like shape: a small two-row block on the left with a long horizontal strip directly underneath, while the lighter pieces combine into a two-row horizontal block attached immediately to the right of the top part. In other words, the task compresses the dispersed fragments into a standard composite caption shape in the top-left corner.

The grid contains a background, one larger coherent figure in a primary foreground color, and a few stray cells in a second foreground color. The transformation preserves the main figure exactly and changes every cell of the stray secondary color back into the background color. In effect, the output is the same scene with the distracting marker/noise pixels removed.

Locate the repeated full-width separator rows; only the region from the top down through the lowest such separator is transformed, while any rows below it are left unchanged. Within that transformed region, all non-background marks are unified into one foreground color: both the separator rows and any scattered pattern cells become the same dark color. All remaining background cells in that region are recolored to a new fill color, preserving the original shapes and positions.

The full-width top band and the full-width horizontal divider remain unchanged. The symmetric diamond-like cluster centered on the divider is removed and replaced with a new-colored, one-sided half-diamond/kite of the same scale, drawn entirely above the divider and repeated symmetrically below it so each copy sits directly against the divider. In effect, the original figure is recolored and split into two separated upper/lower copies that keep only one lateral side of the original diamond.

The input is a tall stack of separate panels, with each panel boundary marked by a full-width horizontal divider row in a distinct separator color. The transformation keeps only the bottom-most panel: the 20-row region immediately below the last divider row. That extracted panel is copied exactly, while all upper panels and clue marks are discarded.

The output is made by rotating the entire input scene, not by editing individual objects. Identify the large contrasting region attached to one side of the grid and rotate the whole picture so that this region ends up along the top edge: if it starts on the bottom, turn the grid upside down; if it starts on the left, turn it clockwise. All smaller colored shapes and any holes keep their exact layout relative to that scene and simply move with the global rotation.

The grid contains a regular dotted scaffold, and each isolated non-scaffold cell on the far left acts as a seed. From every such seed, a fixed right-extending multicolor stencil is stamped onto the grid, aligned to the scaffold: it forms a tapered horizontal band across several neighboring rows, filled mostly with one color and punctuated at regular intervals by the other color, with the seed’s own color preserved at the front of the band. When several seeds are present, these stamped bands are superimposed, while scaffold dots outside the stamped regions stay unchanged.

The input is a blank square of a single background color, and its size determines the whole output. The output keeps the same height but becomes a horizontal strip of equally sized square panels, each panel as wide as the input, with centered hollow square outlines drawn in a second color. From left to right, these outlines grow through all odd side lengths: a single center cell, then a 3-by-3 ring, then 5-by-5, and so on until the final panel is a full border touching the panel edges.

The input is made of several side-by-side copies of a scene, and each copy contains the same small solid square near the top acting as a marker. The output ignores all the other lower shapes and keeps only this repeated top marker, but collapses it horizontally into a single-column trace. So the result is a 1-cell-wide grid with the same height as the input, filled with the marker color only in the rows where that top square appears.

The output turns the input into a 4-panel horizontal strip, where each panel has the same size as the original grid. These panels follow a repeating cycle: an empty background-only frame, then a centered plus-shaped figure in one accent color with four symmetric marker dots in the other accent color, then another empty frame, then the same figure with those two accent colors swapped. The given input is treated as one phase of that cycle, and the output lists the four consecutive phases from that starting point.

The entire input picture is duplicated horizontally: the output keeps the same height but expands the width to three times the original by placing three identical copies of the whole grid side by side. Every object is preserved exactly, including the top row of isolated marker cells, the lower paired rectangular blocks aligned beneath them, and all background gaps. Nothing is recolored or rearranged within a copy; the full pattern is simply tiled across the row three times.

The output keeps the same height but expands the grid to three equal-width panels placed side by side. The left panel is an unchanged copy of the input, while the middle and right panels repeat every non-background cell in the same row and column positions within their panel. Across these repeated panels, the three foreground colors are cycled: in the middle panel each color becomes the next one in the cycle, and in the right panel each becomes the remaining third color.

The grid is made of full-width horizontal color bands, and the output keeps those bands in the same top-to-bottom order with the same row counts. The only change is a horizontal enlargement: every column is duplicated four times, so the width becomes 4 times larger while the height stays the same. Equivalently, each solid row is stretched sideways by a factor of four without changing any colors.

The output is formed by taking the entire input grid and repeating it four times side by side in a single row. In each copy, the two background regions and the exact shape/placement of the non-background figure stay unchanged; only the figure’s color changes across the copies in the pattern: original figure color, first alternate color, second alternate color, original figure color again. All spatial structure is preserved exactly, with no resizing or movement—just horizontal duplication and recoloring of the main object in the middle two panels.

The foreground consists of several separate blobs of the same base color; the largest blob is kept as the base shape. The smaller blobs are then shifted together from left to right into that base region, preserving their vertical placement/order, so that they overlap each other and the base, and the picture is cropped to the occupied columns. Cells belonging only to the base stay in the original foreground color, cells additionally covered by one overlaid blob become one highlight color, and cells where overlaid blobs stack on top of each other become the second highlight color.

Each input contains a small patterned symbol in the middle plus one full-height vertical marker column on each side. The transformation discards those side marker columns and all empty background, then crops out only the central symbol using its tight bounding rectangle. The output preserves the symbol’s shape, row pattern, and color exactly, just in the smaller cropped frame.

The output takes the entire input grid and repeats it side-by-side four times across the horizontal direction. Every foreground mark keeps the same row and the same internal shape within each copy, while the blank background stays blank elsewhere. The height is unchanged; only the width becomes four times larger by concatenating identical copies of the original image.

The grid is compressed horizontally by identifying a repeating vertical slice width and folding all same-position columns from those slices onto each other, while keeping the row count unchanged. The background acts like empty space, so scattered marker cells from different slices combine into one narrow row pattern, and the long horizontal stripe color is preserved only where it survives this overlap. In effect, the output is a single representative vertical band made by superimposing the repeated bands of the input, with any incomplete leftover columns at the far right ignored.

Empty rows stay empty, and each non-empty row is turned into a compact left-side encoding instead of keeping its original long horizontal run. Every original horizontal object is shrunk to a tiny token of its role-color (usually a 2-cell bar, clipped to 1 cell at an edge) and these tokens are placed so that, across the preserved non-empty rows, each source object traces a down-right diagonal. The diagonals are overlaid in the output, and when a diagonal reaches the edge of the coding band it wraps back to the left.

The input is a wide canvas made of several identical horizontal repeats of the same smaller pattern, all on a uniform background. The output removes the repeated copies and keeps just one full repeat unit—the leftmost copy—while preserving the original height. Any colored marks at the top and bottom of that unit stay in the same relative positions inside the reduced frame.

The output keeps the original foreground shape unchanged in a top panel, then adds two more same-sized panels below it, making the canvas three times as tall while keeping the same width and background color. In the middle panel, the shape is reduced to its 8-neighbor interior core (one-cell erosion), leaving only cells surrounded on all eight sides by the original shape. In the bottom panel, the shape is expanded by one cell in every direction (8-neighbor dilation), producing a thicker, filled-out version of the original.

The input is a square scene with an X-shaped diagonal frame and a small colored motif at the center. The output places six same-sized copies of that square side by side, and in those copies the central motif is progressively thickened/spread into larger diamond-like interior patterns using a new fill color, while the original motif color remains as the core of the pattern. The diagonal frame is kept in place as the boundary for this expansion, except for the few frame cells nearest the center that can be absorbed into the new interior pattern.

The tall input is divided into several equal-sized square panels stacked vertically, each panel containing one foreground figure on a uniform background. The output rearranges these whole panels into a single horizontal strip: each panel is copied unchanged and placed side by side from left to right in the same top-to-bottom order they appeared in the input. No shapes are redrawn or recolored; only the large frame layout changes from vertical stacking to horizontal concatenation.

The input is made of several equal-width copies of the same small picture placed side by side. Some copies are corrupted: one has a single stray cell of a different color near the upper interior, and one is explicitly flagged by a 3-cell marker in the top border and matching marker-colored cells inserted into the copy. The output removes the repetition and keeps just one clean, unaltered copy of the repeated picture, including the matching slice of the top background row above it.

The input contains a solid rectangular block on the background and a single marker cell positioned directly above it. In the output, that marker is moved to the symmetric position directly below the rectangle, in the same column, and its original location is cleared back to background. Inside the rectangle, a vertical stripe three cells wide, centered on the marker’s column, is recolored from the block’s color to a new highlight color across the rectangle’s full height.

The input is a tall stack of four separated 7-row scenes, each containing the same main hollow square/ring with a distinct center cell and a fixed small marker near the lower-right. The transformation simply extracts the bottommost of these repeated scenes and discards all other copies and the blank spacer rows. Any extra accent cells attached to that last scene are kept exactly as they appear.

The input contains a dominant background color, plus several foreground marks: narrow vertical color bands that repeat down the grid and one small compact shape made of another color. In the output, all non-background content is removed entirely. The whole grid is reset to a uniform field of the original background color, with the size and frame unchanged.

The output keeps the grid size and all object positions exactly the same, but simplifies the color palette. Every non-background cell that is not the special dark anchor/bar color is recolored into one single common color, while the anchor/bar color itself stays unchanged. In other words, all ordinary shapes and line fragments are merged into one unified color without moving or reshaping them.

The marked cells depict a centered symbol with a clear horizontal bar and vertical bar, and in some cases additional diagonal spokes. The transformation completes the intended symmetric figure: every valid straight ray passing through the center is extended outward until it reaches the grid border, so partial arms become full edge-to-edge arms. Any scattered cells that do not belong to this completed centered pattern are removed, leaving a clean symmetric cross/star shape.

The repeating diagonal stripe pattern is cyclically shifted upward by one row: each row becomes the row below it, and the original top row wraps around to the bottom. After this row rotation, a fixed corner signature is added in the upper-left: a single distinct marker cell at the top-left, plus a 2-cell horizontal bar directly beneath it starting from the left edge. If that distinct marker color was already embedded in the top stripe row, it is removed from its old location and used only in the new corner position.

The middle of the grid is made of equal-width horizontal panels, each containing the same large solid block on the left and a small incomplete 5x5 symbol on the right. In the output, those small symbols are completed into their full canonical forms: a hollow square outline, a solid filled square, and a symmetric X-like mark. The panels are arranged as a repeating cycle that starts with the hollow-square panel, continues through the other two completed symbols, and then repeats the first panel once more, so the canvas becomes one panel wider while the header band and background simply extend across the new width.

The only changing object is the hollow foreground rectangle inside the left compartment; the outer border and the empty compartments stay unchanged. This rectangle is squeezed inward horizontally by one cell from both the left and right sides, so its height stays the same while its width decreases by two. Equivalently, the left and right edges move inward one step, removing the old corners and producing a narrower hollow frame (which becomes a single filled vertical line in the smallest case).

The grid shows a horizontal repeating pattern: a background field with the same multi-row motif reappearing across the width. The output keeps the height the same but extends the canvas by four columns, then copies the entire leftmost four-column slice of the input onto the new right edge. This adds one more repetition of the existing pattern without changing any other cells.

All non-background cells are translated horizontally to the left by a fixed amount equal to the grid’s height (the number of rows). The shift is cyclic, so anything that would move past the left edge wraps around to the right side, while shapes, colors, and vertical positions stay unchanged.

The grid contains a large solid block of one foreground color, with a top strip where those rows are only partially filled and the rest of each row is background. In the output, every row in that partial top strip is erased completely, turning the whole row into background from left edge to right edge. Rows that are already fully filled across the entire width with the foreground color are left unchanged.

The lone marker cell stays fixed and acts like a reference point. Each separate shape made of the main movable color is shifted outward away from that marker: its row relation to the marker determines up/down movement, its column relation determines left/right movement, and shapes offset on both axes slide diagonally until they reach the grid edge or corner. When outward-shifted shapes land on the same cells they simply merge, while the background is otherwise restored.

The input is an alternating checkerboard of one visible color and background; in the output, the background is replaced by a new second visible color so the whole result becomes a two-color alternating field. This field is then stretched far to the right by unrolling the checkerboard into a horizontal staircase/diagonal trace: each successive input row contributes an alternating segment shifted farther right, so overlaps create short doubled runs inside an otherwise regular alternation. The output keeps the same number of rows, but greatly increases the width to show this diagonalized, concatenated version of the original pattern.

The single foreground shape is reconstructed into a compact, right-anchored version of itself. Its rightmost vertical section stays fixed, while the broader parts extending to the left are collapsed/slid inward and packed against that right edge, turning the original wide block with gaps or protrusions into a narrower stepped shape. The background elsewhere is unchanged, and the transformed shape keeps the same general vertical placement but loses its large leftward span.

The grid is stretched horizontally by placing three identical copies of the entire input side by side. The background stays the same, and the non-background shape keeps its exact form, row positions, and internal structure within each copy. As a result, the output has the same height as the input but three times the width.

The input is made of three equal-width panels placed side by side on the same rows, each panel showing the same checkerboard-based scene with slight differences in the marked shape. The transformation discards the first two panels and keeps only the rightmost third of the grid. The output is therefore an exact crop of the far-right panel, with all colors and object placements unchanged.

The input consists of several equal-sized panels placed side by side, separated by vertical divider columns; the output removes the dividers and collapses everything into one panel of that same size. The panels are combined by superimposing them cell-by-cell: shared background stays unchanged, and any foreground parts from any panel are kept in the result. When different foreground colors land on the same cell, the more prominent detail color overrides the weaker/base one, so the output is the merged version of all panel contents.

The input’s geometry stays the same: the stacked frame structure, interior background cells, separator lines, and the special horizontal stripe are preserved. The four non-background colors are treated as an ordered cycle given by their positions around the figure: upper-left frame color, upper-right frame color, lower-right frame color, and lower-left frame color. The output is five copies of the whole grid placed side by side; copy 1 is the original, copies 2–4 recolor the same template by advancing one step around that four-color cycle each time, and copy 5 repeats the original. The internal stripe is recolored consistently with the same cycle so each panel matches its new adjacent-pair frame colors.

The input consists of repeated horizontal foreground blocks separated by background gaps, with some entire background rows splitting the grid into bands. The output keeps the same height but stretches the grid horizontally by repeating the whole input pattern once for each foreground block that appears across a filled row. In the 1st repeated copy, the 1st foreground block is recolored to a new highlight color; in the 2nd copy, the 2nd block is highlighted; and so on, while all other cells keep their original color and full background rows stay entirely background.

The input is partitioned into three horizontal panels separated by full-width divider rows. The transformation keeps only the lowest panel and its divider row, deleting the two upper panels. All colored shapes inside the retained bottom panel stay unchanged in position and form.

The output keeps the same width but makes the grid four times taller by stacking four vertical copies of the input one under another. In every copy, the full-height divider line and the larger hollow 3x3 block are preserved unchanged; only the small object immediately to the left of the divider is treated specially. That small object appears unchanged in the 1st and 3rd copies, is recolored in the 2nd copy, and is recolored plus shifted one cell farther left from the divider in the 4th copy.

The grid contains two separate figures: one irregular multicolor figure that stays exactly the same, and one compact block made mostly of a filler color with one or more contrasting marker cells embedded in it. In the output, that compact block is stripped down by deleting all of its filler-colored cells while leaving only the contrasting marker cells in their original positions. Nothing moves or is redrawn elsewhere; only the non-marker parts of that one block are erased.

The input is made of several same-sized panels stacked vertically, separated by full-width divider rows. Each panel has the same small marker near the top and the same main foreground shape, but different panels may contain extra protruding cells attached to that shape in different positions. The output removes the dividers and collapses the stack into a single panel by overlaying all panels and taking the union of the foreground-shape cells, so any shape cell present in any panel appears in the final combined panel while the background and top marker remain in place.

The input consists of several vertically stacked copies of the same scene, all with the same height. Some copies are complete while others are missing a few colored cells, so the output collapses these repeated bands into a single band by superimposing them and keeping every non-background cell that appears in any copy. In effect, it removes the vertical repetition and restores the one complete version of the picture without changing object shapes, colors, or relative positions inside the band.

A single filled 3×3 block acts as the template, while the thin length-3 bars of the other non-background color serve as alignment markers for where more such 3×3 blocks should appear. The output adds filled 3×3 copies to complete the larger rectangular/cross-like arrangement implied by the top, left, right, and bottom markers, centered on the same row/column bands as those markers. Any original thin marker that falls inside one of these completed filled areas is effectively absorbed, and nearby added blocks merge into one larger solid region or thick frame.

The scene contains outlined objects in one color and isolated single-cell markers in another. One marker indicates a direction relative to a nearby outlined frame; imagine duplicating that frame shifted outward in that direction until it lies mostly beyond the canvas, so only the boundary strip of the duplicate that touches the grid edge remains visible. Thus the output adds a new line of the frame color along the top, left, or right border, aligned with the chosen frame’s columns or rows, while all original objects and markers stay unchanged.

Each non-background shape is a broken rectangular border that sits on the perimeter of its own bounding box. In the output, each such border pattern is rotated/slid counterclockwise around that rectangle’s edge until the occupied cells on the top edge are pushed as far left as possible, touching the upper-left corner if they were offset. Colors, box sizes, and nesting stay the same; only the positions of the border cells along each frame perimeter are shifted.

The output stretches the canvas to three times the original width, creating three equal side-by-side panels while keeping the height unchanged. The left and right panels are exact copies of the input grid, including all background and object placement. In the middle panel, the same foreground shape is redrawn in the same area but rotated by 90 degrees, with the surrounding background left empty.

The input is divided into several equal vertical panels by full-height divider columns. Each panel contains background plus a small foreground shape positioned relative to the divider on its right edge.

The output extracts these panels one by one, keeping each panel’s full contents and its right-hand divider column, then stacks the panels vertically in the same left-to-right order they had in the input. Nothing inside a panel is redrawn or moved internally; only the overall layout changes from horizontal tiling to vertical concatenation.

The input shows identical small square blocks arranged on a coarse 3-by-3 lattice, with the middle position empty so the present blocks form a ring around a central gap. The output is made by stacking multiple full copies of the original grid vertically, one copy for each block in that ring. In each successive copy, exactly one original block is recolored with a highlight color, and the highlighted block moves around the ring in clockwise order starting from the left-side block next to the central gap.

The grid contains four separate horizontal bar-clusters of the same main color, arranged in a 2×2 layout, with small nearby marker cells and one extra single-cell accent color around each cluster. In the output, a single accent color is chosen and copied so that every cluster uses that same accent in the "above the bar" role, while the other accent colors disappear. The bar-clusters themselves stay in their same four general locations, but each one is locally repacked: the main bar is slightly shifted/trimmed and the marker cells are moved into standardized edge or adjacent positions around it.

The non-background pattern is organized into three equal-width vertical sections placed side by side. Each section contains the same sparse diagonal/zigzag shape, but the three foreground colors rotate roles from one section to the next. The output keeps the height and all existing cells unchanged, extends the grid by one more section on the right, and fills that new section with a copy of the leftmost section so the color-cycle pattern continues.

The wide input is made of several horizontal repeats of the same square-sized pattern on a uniform background, plus an extra altered segment at the far right that acts like leftover/marker material. The output shrinks the canvas to a square whose side length equals the input height and keeps just one representative copy of the repeated pattern. In practice, this is the leftmost square block, while all additional repeated copies and the special right-edge segment are removed.

The grid is partitioned into equal vertical compartments by full-height divider columns. Inside each compartment, the same small horizontal block appears at some vertical level above a fixed bottom marker, and the output keeps the dividers, background, and markers unchanged while reversing the compartment contents left-to-right. In other words, each compartment in the output takes the internal pattern that was in the symmetrically opposite compartment of the input.

The wide input is made of several smaller same-height panels laid out side by side. The transformation simply extracts the rightmost panel and discards all panels to its left. Nothing inside that final panel is changed: its colored cells and background are copied exactly into the output.

The grid is a horizontal sequence of same-sized glyph blocks, separated by single blank columns. Each glyph is a rectangular frame containing one extra internal stroke, and the output extends the sequence to the right by adding the next missing glyph(s) in the progression while keeping the original blocks unchanged.

That progression moves the internal stroke through a fixed series of positions/orientations inside the frame: from one vertical form, to a middle horizontal form, to the mirrored/opposite vertical form, and finally to a lower-right/bottom-edge corner-like form. If the input already contains the first three stages, only the last stage is appended; if it contains only the first two, the remaining two stages are appended.

The picture is split into equal-width vertical panels placed side by side, with each panel containing its own arrangement of small marker bars and a larger colored shape. The output keeps all existing panels unchanged and extends the canvas to the right by one more panel of the same width. That new rightmost panel is an exact copy of the leftmost panel, so the horizontal sequence wraps around and repeats from the start.

Use the first row as an ordered color key, look at the separate non-background pattern on the right, discard any key colors that do not appear in that pattern, and pick the second remaining key color as the target. The entire right-hand pattern is then homogenized into a solid block covering the same bounding box, filled only with that target color. The long horizontal strip on the second row keeps its color and left alignment but is shortened so its length becomes twice the number of rows in the original right-hand pattern that contained the target color.

Each input is split into two equal pictures by a single blank separator column. The output keeps only one picture-width and shows the cell-by-cell overlap of the two halves: a cell survives only where both halves have the same structural color in the same position, and all mismatches become background. The small auxiliary marker colors are ignored rather than preserved, so the result is the common part of the two larger patterns, including the shared bottom border and any shared top markers.

The input contains a single foreground shape near the top of a much taller background-filled grid. The output trims away all empty background-only rows and columns outside that shape, leaving only the minimal bounding box that exactly contains the colored figure. The figure itself is unchanged in color and pattern; only the surrounding canvas is cropped down to fit it.

The input is a horizontal sequence of repeated little framed motifs on a uniform background; what varies from copy to copy is the position of a small two-cell marker in the middle, as if it is moving sideways through the sequence. In the output, the copies where that marker has reached the later/rightward part of its motion are highlighted: their frame/outline color is changed to a new highlight color, and the left cell of the two-cell marker is absorbed into that highlight while the right cell stays. Also, along the upper marker row, a solid band of another new color is drawn from the far left across the traversed region up to the last highlighted copy, creating a visible trail.

The grid contains a pattern made from two non-background colors: a main object color and a secondary marker color, with empty background around it. In the output, every cell of the secondary color is changed into the main object color, while cells already in the main color and all background cells stay in place. Equivalently, the shape becomes the union of both colored parts, rendered entirely in one solid foreground color, without changing its position or the surrounding empty space.

The picture is built from many small equal-sized patches containing a single foreground color on a blank background. Each nonblank patch is a noisy or incomplete version of one quarter of the same rounded motif, and the output cleans each patch into the exact canonical quarter-shape while preserving its location and orientation. As a result, neighboring cleaned patches join into neat, symmetric larger rounded figures, while empty patches stay empty.

The grid contains a small solid 2x2 block and a larger, snaking marker shape approaching it from the upper left. The output deletes almost all of that larger shape and keeps only its terminal tip near the block, repositioned so it hugs the block’s left or lower-left side; if the tip meets the block, it can overwrite the touched corner cell, while the rest of the block stays in place.

The input is a tall comb-like path made from repeated horizontal bars connected by a right-side vertical spine; each bar begins with one contrasting marker cell at its left end. The output keeps the same width but stacks multiple copies of this whole structure, one copy for each marker/bar level in the input, creating a vertical animation strip. Across these copies, the contrasting marker is advanced through the shape from one bar to the next along the implied interior staircase/diagonal and right-edge route, while any place it leaves behind is converted into the ordinary path color.

The grids show two complementary phases of the same vertically and horizontally symmetric motif. When the input is the sparse/open phase, the output swaps the two roles of the colors to produce the dense/solid phase; when the input is already the dense phase, the empty channels inside it are widened so the solid mass is thinned while preserving symmetry, and in the small example that thinned dense form is stacked between two copies of the inverted sparse motif. Overall, the transformation is about exchanging filled vs empty structure and then carving the solid version inward around its internal voids.

The transformation keeps the same rows and preserves every non-background object, including the long horizontal marker bars and the scattered single accent cells, but it shrinks the grid horizontally. It does this by cutting away wide vertical stretches of pure background and stitching the remaining occupied column-bands together into a compact strip. When useful content exists on both sides of a removed empty gap, those surviving bands are concatenated in the new frame, so the former left-edge bar can end up shifted inward rather than staying on the border.

The input is split into three equal-sized horizontal panels stacked vertically. These panels are overlaid cell-by-cell: for each position, if any panel contains a non-background colored cell there, the output marks that position with a single unified filled color; positions that are background in all panels stay as the original background color. The result is therefore one panel tall, keeping only the combined silhouette of all foreground patterns while discarding their original color differences.

The grid is divided into equally spaced object-columns: each column contains one distinct colored symbol in the upper area and a small block of a common marker color in the lower area. The output keeps the original columns unchanged, then extends the grid to the right by copying all interior columns (everything except the leftmost and rightmost original columns) in reverse left-to-right order. Each copied column preserves both the exact upper symbol shape and its aligned lower marker block.

The input is a very wide strip made of horizontal bands: a large solid top band, two solid rows of a second color, one row containing a mixed pattern of the second color and a third color, and a solid bottom band. Split this wide strip into consecutive square-width slices, where each slice’s width equals the strip’s height.

Each slice becomes its own square panel in the output, keeping the same band structure and taking the matching segment of the patterned row. The output is formed by stacking all of these square panels vertically in their original left-to-right order.

Starting from a single marker cell on an otherwise empty grid, the output keeps the grid size the same and paints a horizontal band of non-background cells across every row. Each row contains the same fixed left-to-right multicolor motif, aligned so that the original marker’s column falls at a specific position inside that motif, while everything outside the band stays background. The only row-specific difference is at the marker’s exact location: that cell keeps the original marker color, overriding the motif there.

The single foreground pattern is expanded into a much wider image made of five equal-width vertical panels placed side by side. These panels form a left-right symmetric echo of the original row sequence: the middle panel shows the original pattern row-by-row, the adjacent panels use the neighboring rows, and the outer panels use rows two steps away, so each output row is a mirrored bundle of corresponding input rows. Where this row-offset pattern would run past the top or bottom of the source, the canvas is padded using the task’s border/filler rows, producing the extra rows at the extremes.

The wide input is a strip of equal-sized square panels placed side by side, and the strip is symmetric around its middle panel or middle pair. To make the output, align those panels on top of each other and treat both non-background input colors as simply "filled" cells. Each output cell is recolored according to how far outward in the symmetric panel sequence that filled position appears: one color for cells present only in the center layer, a second for cells that also appear in the next inner mirrored pair, and a third for cells that persist into farther outer pair(s).

The input contains a distinguished center cell and several colored corner/L-shaped fragments placed in different quadrants around it. Each fragment represents one layer of a set of concentric square rings centered on that special cell, ordered from the center outward. The output completes these partial clues by extending each fragment around all four sides, producing full nested square frames of those same colors, with the special center cell left unchanged.

Each colored shape above the fixed floor is turned from a solid block into a hollow, open-top outline of the same color. The output keeps only the cells one step outside the shape along its exposed left side, right side, and bottom edge (including the bottom corners), while the original filled interior disappears and the top edge is not drawn. If another object is adjacent, that side is treated as blocked, so no outline is added there; the bottom floor line remains unchanged.

The input consists of several copies of the same pixel pattern placed side by side, each copy using a different dominant color but keeping the same small accent colors in the same internal positions. The output extends the canvas to the right and appends one more copy of that pattern, shifted by the same horizontal spacing as the existing copies. The new copy preserves the shared shape and the accent-color details, but uses a new dominant color that continues the left-to-right sequence of dominant colors already present.

The input contains centered versions of the same symmetric figure in different forms: an upper large outline made from a border color around a main fill color, and lower smaller reference pieces that include the same main color plus an accent-colored cap/bar. The output keeps only the large upper figure’s bounding area, removes the border, and turns the outlined silhouette into a solid main-color shape. Where the lower reference shows an accent-colored cap aligned with the central stem/top of the figure, that accent pattern is copied into the corresponding top row(s) of the final shape; everything else is discarded to background.

The transformation deletes every completely empty horizontal row from the grid while keeping all non-empty rows unchanged. As a result, the colored shape fragments are vertically compressed together: their left-right positions, colors, and row order stay the same, but any blank gaps between them (including leading, internal, and trailing empty rows) disappear. The output is therefore a shorter grid made by stacking all occupied rows consecutively.

The non-background cells are propagated diagonally toward the upper-right: each marked cell or connected shape is copied again and again with a shift of one row up and one column right, and the output is the union of the original pattern with these shifted copies. As a result, isolated cells turn into northeast-rising diagonals, while the larger staircase-like cluster creates a broader repeated staircase/shadow in the same direction. The repeat distance is fixed within each puzzle and is implied by the prominent staircase motif present in the input.

Each input contains two separate objects: a small outlined/frame-like shape that includes a few interior marker cells, and a larger solid blob of another color. The output keeps only the larger blob, cropped to its bounding box, and preserves its shape and main fill color. The interior marker cells from the small framed shape are then transferred onto the vertical middle row of the large blob, keeping their left-to-right arrangement and approximately centered placement within the blob, while the small frame itself is discarded.

Each input is a same-sized grid built on a regular two-color background of alternating one-cell-wide vertical stripes, but parts of the interior have been corrupted by irregular patches that break this rhythm. The transformation removes those disrupted regions and reconstructs the entire grid as the clean repeating stripe pattern indicated by the intact surrounding cells. The output keeps the original size and uses only the two background colors in a perfect column-by-column alternation.

The output keeps every object exactly where it is: all diagonals, bars, small blocks, and cross-like center pieces retain the same shape, size, and position, and the background stays unchanged. The only transformation is a global recoloring of the four non-background colors, using the same 4-cycle everywhere in the grid: the color used by one set of motifs is replaced by the next motif’s color, that one is replaced by the next, and so on, with the fourth color wrapping back to the first.

The tall input is made of several equal-sized square panels stacked vertically, each panel having the same underlying pattern but possibly different special marker cells inside it. Cut the input into consecutive square blocks whose height equals the grid width, then rearrange those whole blocks from a single vertical column into a single horizontal row. Nothing inside a block changes: all colors, shapes, and marker positions are preserved relative to their own panel.

The key transformation isolates the one shaped object made of a color other than the bottom fill, the separator, and the scattered noise cells; that shape is flipped left-to-right and then placed flush in the upper-left corner. The large solid rectangle at the bottom is moved down by one row and loses a left strip, so its new left edge lines up with the original left edge of that extracted shape. Other small scattered cells mostly stay where they were, while the separator-colored vertical feature is cleared from its old column and recreated farther to the right; if a horizontal bar attached to it exists, that bar is also shifted down and right.

The input is a long horizontal strip made of several identical square panels placed side by side, with each panel separated by a single vertical divider line in a contrasting color. The output removes the dividers and repetition, keeping only one panel-sized square. That resulting square is then recolored uniformly with a new fill color, so all cells in the output become the same color.

The input contains a hollow rectangular frame in one border color on a plain background, with the frame’s top edge beginning with a short ordered sequence of distinct marker colors. In the output, that seed sequence is repeated cyclically to overwrite the entire frame border, continuing as one continuous pattern around the perimeter starting from the frame’s upper-left corner. Thus the top edge shows the sequence left-to-right, the right edge continues it downward, the bottom edge continues it right-to-left, and the left edge continues it upward, while everything outside the frame stays unchanged.

The input is divided into two equal vertical halves, and the output is a half-width grid formed by merging each left/right pair of corresponding columns. Cells that are empty on one side and filled on the other are simply copied, and matching shared structure is preserved; marker pixels from either half are also retained when they do not conflict. When the two halves contain alternative versions of the same object in the same place, the version associated with marker pixels is chosen and the unmarked version is dropped.

The grid is cleared completely: every cell that is not the main background color is replaced by the background color. This includes all interior shapes, colored patterns, rectangular patches, and even the solid contrasting strip along the bottom edge. The output keeps the same dimensions as the input, but becomes a uniform field of the original background color.

Keep the background and any pre-existing fixed structures unchanged, especially the solid horizontal band and the lone preserved special cell. Remove all scattered guide markers and the single extra marker of another color by turning them into background. Each right-edge seed cell is converted into a 2-cell horizontal block of a new color by keeping its position and filling the cell immediately to its right, so each resulting block reaches the grid’s right border.

Each input contains a single gate-like object: a horizontal top bar in one color, two vertical side posts in another color hanging from the bar’s ends, and one differently colored cell sitting inside the top bar as a marker. The output is formed by placing many full-width copies of the original scene side by side; in every copy, the marker is removed and the whole top bar is recolored uniformly with the bar color while the posts stay unchanged. Across these copies, cells of the bar color appear on the row immediately above the bar, starting from the marker’s column, spreading outward symmetrically until they vanish, and then contracting back, creating a horizontal sequence of animation frames.

There is one large compact blob of the non-background color on a uniform background, and it may contain a small background-colored hole/pattern inside it. The output clears the original blob and redraws that entire blob, with its internal hole preserved, shifted diagonally down and to the right by the same amounts as its original distances from the top edge and left edge. Any part of the shifted blob that would extend past the bottom or right border is simply clipped away.

The input is made of rows that are all views of the same horizontal band pattern, but with different horizontal phase offsets: some rows are aligned, some begin one cell later, and some begin partway through the first colored band. The output keeps the same height but stretches the picture far to the right by concatenating one row-width segment for every original row, effectively continuing the stripe pattern across each row using the sequence of row offsets seen from top to bottom. The right-edge background padding and any truncated left-edge band are preserved as the indicators of each segment’s phase.

The lone colored object on the plain background is turned into a much larger centered figure by projecting its occupied cells outward diagonally, so each lower row becomes a wider filled span of the same object color. A full horizontal band in a new color is added as a central baseline/seam. Below that band, the enlarged figure is reflected vertically, so the output is a tall top-and-bottom symmetric version of the original shape with the new-color stripe across its middle.

The input contains a single rectangular patch of alternating vertical stripes on a plain background. In the output, the height and vertical placement are kept, but the canvas is stretched horizontally and that striped row-pattern is repeated many times side-by-side to make one long striped band. The band’s left and right ends are slanted by shifting successive rows: moving from the top of the rectangle toward its middle, the repeated stripe run starts farther left and reaches farther across, then the shift reverses toward the bottom, creating a horizontally extended lozenge/parallelogram shape of the same alternating stripes.

The output keeps only the smallest rectangular region that contains all non-background cells, deleting the surrounding empty background rows and columns. Inside that cropped box, every colored cell stays in the same relative position and keeps its color, so the visible shape or combined pattern is unchanged except for the tighter frame.

The input is a tall grid made of three equal-height horizontal panels stacked vertically. Each panel contains the same central multicolored figure, while the small monochrome shape above it and the small monochrome shape below it vary from panel to panel. The output is simply the bottom (third) panel copied exactly, with the first two panels discarded.

The entire grid is rotated 90 degrees clockwise. All cells move with this rotation: the background stays background, the diagonal/zigzag shape made of the main object color turns accordingly, and the small marker cells rotate to their new corresponding positions as well. No colors are changed and no pieces are added or removed; only the orientation of the whole scene changes.

The input is an 8-spoked star-like pattern on a background, with one spoke (including the center) marked in a distinct highlight color while all other spokes use the main foreground color. The output is made by placing 8 same-sized copies of the grid side by side. Starting from the original highlighted spoke, each successive copy rotates that highlight one spoke farther around the star, so the special color visits all eight directions while the rest of the pattern stays unchanged.

The grid contains a single non-background drawing on a uniform background. Take the minimal rectangular bounding box around that drawing and flip the entire contents of that rectangle horizontally, so each occupied cell and each internal gap is mirrored left-to-right within the same frame. Everything outside the bounding box remains unchanged.

The scattered non-background cells are partial clues for a centered, axis-aligned square made of nested 1-cell-thick color layers. In the output, each clue color is expanded to complete its entire concentric ring (outer border, next border inward, and so on), producing a full symmetric target shape; if there is a special center cell, it is kept as its own color inside the innermost layer. Everything outside this reconstructed square remains background.

The grid contains one small hollow square-like block: a 5×5 object with a border in one color and a solid 3×3 interior in another color, sitting on a uniform background. In the output, only the interior of that framed block changes color, while the border, the background, and the separate horizontal bar near the bottom-right remain exactly where they are and unchanged. In effect, the transformation recolors the contents of the bordered square without moving or resizing any objects.

The input contains three separate foreground objects on a uniform background: two identical solid square blocks and one different cross/diamond-like pattern between them. The transformation identifies the shape that appears twice, removes the odd different shape, and outputs a tight crop containing just the repeated object. Thus the result is the duplicated filled 3×3 block by itself.

The input contains a single non-background cell on an otherwise uniform grid. The grid is treated as three equal-width vertical sections, and that cell’s horizontal offset within its section is repeated in the other two sections on the same row. As a result, the output shows three identical cells aligned horizontally—one in each third of the grid—while everything else stays unchanged.

The grid is split into an upper color field and a lower color field by a full horizontal row of gap-colored cells, and there is a gap-shaped motif that descends in the upper field and meets another gap motif just above the divider. The output places five same-size copies of the scene side by side. The first and last copies stay as the original, while the three middle copies show the gap/channel "bending" one cell to the left at the meeting area: the neighboring middle copies show the elbow/turn cells, and the center copy shows the full left-shifted continuation carried downward into the lower field, with all other background cells unchanged.

Identify the uppermost horizontal colored stripe and ignore the lower stripes and their colors. The output is built entirely from that top stripe’s color: every row becomes identical, repeating a row pattern that keeps the stripe’s original left colored run, inserts a background gap as wide as the original grid, and then adds a right colored run whose width matches the original top row’s remaining blank suffix. If the top stripe already spans the whole width, this reduces to filling the entire output grid with that top color.

Only the special structure in the upper part changes; the repeated solid 3×3 blocks lower in the grid stay unchanged. In the top region, each of the two foreground colors has a non-rectangular motif made from a block plus an attached trail, and the output completes/extends those motifs into nearby background cells: the left-side color grows an extra horizontal cap above its upper-left figure and continues its slanting trace through the upper-right mixed figure, while the right-side color gains a matching extension below/right of that area, including a continued down-right tail. The result is a more fully developed pair of complementary top patterns, with no changes to the lower repeated examples.

The input is a horizontal triptych: three equal-width vertical panels placed side by side on the same background, each panel containing a similar arrangement of a small top bar and a larger lower block with accent marks. The transformation crops away the first two panels and keeps only the rightmost third of the image. The kept panel is copied exactly, with its colors and internal pattern unchanged, so the output has the same height but only one-third the width.

Treat the input as a vertical list: identify the single row where the middle cell is marked, and count how many times the top row’s right-edge color appears in the rightmost column. The output is built by stacking that many full copies of the input’s height, where every row becomes a standard row with blank on the left, the marker color in the middle, and the counted right-edge color on the right. In each copy, the row aligned with the original middle-cell mark is changed to a highlighted middle color, and after all copies one extra bottom row is appended using a different middle color and the other right-edge color as a terminator.

The non-background pattern is preserved exactly, including any holes, but its color is changed to a new foreground color. The grid is then horizontally cropped so that all completely empty columns to the right of the pattern are removed, while the height and all empty rows above/below stay the same. In other words, keep the left-side drawing as-is, recolor it, and trim away the unused right margin.

Each input is divided into broad horizontal bands of two colors, where one color forms the larger background region and the other forms a smaller full-width stripe. The output keeps the same grid size but repaints every cell with the color of the smaller stripe. In effect, the minority horizontal band expands to cover the entire canvas.

The input is a row of several same-sized panels placed side by side, each panel beginning with the same vertical border color and containing its own interior pattern and small marker areas. The transformation simply crops out the final panel on the far right and copies it unchanged to become the output. Nothing inside that chosen panel is edited; all other panels are discarded.

The input is a 3×3 tiling of the same square motif, with blank strips separating the copies. The output keeps the same height but becomes much wider: for each row, it places several full-width copies of that input row side by side, using as a stencil the corresponding row of one motif’s padded frame. In that stencil, rows that are entirely separator/background stay empty, while within nonblank motif rows the motif’s filled cells become empty blocks and its internal/background cells become positions where a whole copy of the original row is inserted.

The output is made by placing five same-sized copies of the input side by side, so the height stays the same and the width becomes five times larger. Across these five panels, the connected region in the main "fill" color is animated: panel 1 shows it in its original place, and in each later panel that region is shifted one cell diagonally up and to the right.
As this moving region leaves its old position, those cells become background, while all other non-moving colored structures stay fixed in place within each panel unless the shifted fill region lands on top of them, in which case they are replaced by the moving color.

Identify the large filled rectangle and the separate short strip in a second color. The output surrounds the large rectangle with a one-cell-thick frame of the strip’s color, expanding the rectangle’s bounding box by one cell on all four sides while leaving the interior unchanged. Any existing cells of that frame color near the rectangle are treated as partial pieces of this border and are completed into the full rectangular outline.

The lone foreground figure is made of side-by-side vertical sections with different downward extents: a plain rectangular part and a deeper, stepped part. The transformation reorders these sections horizontally and flips the stepped/non-rectangular section left-to-right, so the figure’s asymmetry changes sides; when there is extra room, the two sections are also pulled apart to opposite sides of the canvas. The background stays unchanged and only the foreground silhouette is reassembled.

The input contains four isolated non-background cells arranged as the top, bottom, left, and right vertices of a diamond. The output enlarges the canvas and turns those four markers into a magnified diamond/rhombus outline, filling in the diagonal edges between corresponding neighboring vertices while leaving the rest of the background empty. In other words, the sparse four-point template is expanded into the full border of the shape it implies.

The output keeps the same height as the input but expands the width to make a horizontal strip of five 9-column panels. The first panel is the original foreground motif, and the remaining four panels are other members of the same motif family: they keep the same general backbone (a central vertical stroke with the left-side bar structure) while the extra foreground cells on the right/top/bottom are rearranged into the other allowed configurations. In other words, the task catalogs the input shape together with its related stroke variants, laid out side by side.

The input is split into three equal-width panels placed side by side, each showing a similar arrangement of colored objects. The output keeps only the rightmost panel, cropping away the other two panels so the height stays the same and the width becomes one third. Any scattered pixels of the small nuisance color inside that chosen panel are erased to the background, while all other object colors and shapes are preserved.

The image consists of a foreground pattern embedded in a uniform background, and the output makes the canvas wider by repeating that entire pattern horizontally. A second identical copy of the full input is placed immediately to the right of the first one, with no gap, no recoloring, and no change to the vertical arrangement. In other words, each row is continued by the same row again, so the whole picture becomes two copies side by side.

The input contains a single thin shape drawn in a contrasting color against a uniform background: one diagonal segment that approaches a central area, plus one horizontal segment and one vertical segment meeting around that same center. In the output, that entire shape is recolored to a new highlight color and copied through 90-degree rotations around the center, so the original motif appears in all four orientations. The background stays unchanged, and the result is a rotationally symmetric pattern built from the original path.

The input is a vertical stack of repeated copies of the same small pattern. The output compresses this stack down to one copy, preserving the unchanged structural cells and only reconsidering the positions that alternate between the two special non-background colors across the copies.

For each such varying position, count which of the two special colors appears in the stacked copies: if the darker special color is unanimous, it stays as-is; if the lighter special color is as common or more common, it stays as-is; if the darker special color is in a strict majority but not unanimous, replace that cell with one highlight color; and if the two special colors are tied, replace it with a different highlight color.

The full-width horizontal band acts as a reference line separating the active area above from empty space below. In the area above this band, each column is processed independently: count how many cells of the sparse foreground color appear in that column, then restack that many cells flush against the top edge, preserving only the columnwise totals and not the original row positions. Finally, on the horizontal band, every column that contains at least one such foreground cell above is marked with a different highlight color directly underneath it, while all other cells stay unchanged.

Identify the large solid rectangular area sitting inside the background. Recolor that entire area to the marker color used by the scattered accent cells, while keeping the internal paired vertical stripe pattern unchanged. Any other odd-colored single cells inside the rectangle are absorbed into the recolored field, so the result is a uniform rectangle with only the preserved stripe feature left in its original color.

The output keeps the same height but stretches the scene into a horizontal strip four times as wide, containing four side-by-side versions of the single non-background figure. The 1st and 3rd versions are the original figure, while the dominant block-colored mass is altered in the 2nd and 4th versions: first its outer right vertical slice is removed, then that slice is shown detached and shifted rightward so it sits just before the small side motif. The smaller patterned motif keeps the same row-by-row color arrangement, aside from the spacing change caused by that detached slice.

The input is split into several equal-width vertical panels arranged side by side. Across these panels, the cell layout stays the same while the participating colors are cyclically relabeled from panel to panel, so the last panel returns to the same coloring as the first. The output keeps just one canonical copy of this repeating structure: the leftmost panel, with all its rows and original colors unchanged.

The input consists of a background grid with several short horizontal colored bars near the right edge, plus a marker column on the far right made of a special filler color. First, that far-right marker color is removed by turning those cells into background, leaving the bar pattern unchanged. Then the entire cleaned grid is repeated vertically, stacked one copy under another, with the number of copies equal to the length of the longest horizontal bar in the input.

The input is a vertical stack of same-sized panels with three repeating solid background colors, each panel containing the same foreground shape in the same position. First identify one 3-panel cycle (the three background colors in order), then output four repetitions of that cycle stacked vertically.

Within each panel, keep the shape itself unchanged, but look at its tight bounding rectangle: every background cell inside that rectangle is recolored to the first panel’s background color. This makes the first-background panel look unchanged, while the other two background panels gain an inserted patch of the first background color around the shape, only inside the shape’s bounding box.

The transformation keeps the row structure the same but compresses the grid horizontally into a smaller, canonical version. The sparse foreground dots in the input are a horizontally expanded/shifted representation of a simpler dot pattern, so columns that belong to the same logical position are merged into one output column, collapsing duplicate or offset copies of the same feature. The result is a narrower grid that preserves the meaningful foreground-dot arrangement by row while removing the extra horizontal spacing and redundancy.

The grid contains two matching clusters built around the same trail of small marker cells. In the left/reference cluster, two larger objects (one upper object and one lower object, in different colors) have a particular placement relative to that marker trail; in the right cluster, those two objects are slightly misaligned. The output keeps all marker cells fixed and translates the right cluster’s larger objects so they match the reference cluster’s relative arrangement, turning their old positions back to background even when that leaves holes in the bottom border.

The multi-colored shape in the upper part of the grid is moved horizontally to the far right, so it sits against the fixed right-side vertical strip; any part of the shape that would overlap that strip is lost, while the strip itself stays unchanged. The left-side vertical bar also stays in place. A separate small marker near the bottom (a cell stacked above another different-colored cell) is preserved as a reference, and in some examples its upper cell is lifted straight upward by the same amount that the upper shape was shifted right.

The input is split into several equal-width panels by vertical separator columns. Each panel shows the same base figure on the same background, but each copy contains one small marker placed at a different position.

The output keeps just one panel-sized grid containing the shared base figure, with separators and duplicate panels removed.
