Every marker position from the separate panels is projected onto this single figure and changed into a new highlight color, replacing whatever was at those cells while all other parts of the figure stay the same.

The output keeps the same width but makes the canvas four times taller by stacking four identical copies of the entire input grid vertically. Every object, empty area, and background cell is preserved exactly in each copy, with no recoloring, movement, or reshaping—just a repeated vertical tiling of the full original scene.

The input shows several identical large rounded/diamond-like figures arranged in one horizontal row with fixed spacing, each made from a main fill color with a border/stem color and sometimes a small accent patch on one side. The output widens the canvas and continues this row to the right until there are five equally spaced copies total, preserving the same shape and spacing. As new copies are added, the accent patch keeps advancing around the figure’s perimeter in the same cyclic order seen in the examples (moving through the corner/side positions and then repeating).

The output keeps the entire input unchanged as its top section, but makes the canvas exactly four times taller. Below the original image, the bottom row of the input is repeated as a long vertical extension, then the remaining rows of the input are replayed in reverse vertical order (everything except that last row), and finally the original top row is repeated to fill the rest. In object terms, the lower small figure is stretched downward, the other motifs reappear below it in upside-down row order, and the very first row becomes the repeated bottom band.

The main change is applied only to the scattered foreground shapes on the background: any single background cell that sits exactly between two cells of the same foreground color in one row or one column is filled in with that foreground color. This bridges one-cell gaps and closes tiny holes, making broken bars and blocky shapes more solid and connected. The top border and the small marker near the upper left stay unchanged.

The input contains two similarly framed panels stacked vertically, separated by a blank divider and surrounded by constant border bands. Each panel has the same background and the same fixed central block, but each contains a separate small foreground shape of the same color in a different position.

The output keeps only one panel-sized frame: it overlays the two panels onto a single copy of the scene. The foreground shape from the upper panel is recolored to a new highlight color, while the foreground shape from the lower panel is copied in its original color; all shared background, border, and central block cells remain unchanged.

The grid keeps its height but is stretched horizontally into repeated row-tiles. For each row, build a second version where the background and the main drawing color are swapped everywhere, while the special accent color is left unchanged; then concatenate copies of that row as: some original copies, then a full block of inverted copies, then more original copies. The number of original copies shifts by row position from top to bottom: the top row has 1 original on the left and many on the right, each next row adds one more original copy to the left and removes one from the right, with the middle inverted block always having as many copies as the grid has rows.

Each input is mostly one background color with a single contrasting cell in every row, forming a diagonal path that moves one column per row and, when it reaches a side, reflects into a zigzag. The output keeps the same height but greatly extends the width by repeating this row-pattern horizontally as a periodic strip. In effect, the diagonal/zigzag motif is continued sideways so the same back-and-forth sweep across the columns repeats over a full cycle.

Find the repeated plus-shaped motif(s) on the plain background. The output is made by copying the entire input grid side-by-side into a long horizontal strip, as if showing repeated stages of the same scene shifting left across time. On top of those repeated copies, a second foreground color marks the intermediate diagonal/staircase positions of the plus motif, linking one vertical occurrence of the motif to the next while the original motif color stays unchanged.

The input contains a single non-background seed cell, and the output replaces it with a centered, mirror-symmetric figure in that same color. Around the seed, the immediate 7×7 neighborhood forms a thick cross/diamond-like motif: a solid middle row, broad filled rows above and below it, and three separated points on the top and bottom. On larger boards, this motif continues outward in the same self-similar recursive style, producing larger concentric layers of the same pattern, clipped where they hit the grid boundary.

The grid keeps the same shapes, positions, and background; only the non-background colors are reassigned. The color used by the small top cluster around the single black cell is applied to all former marker dots, the marker-dot color is applied to the large solid rectangle, and the rectangle’s color is applied to the small cluster. The black cell and the background remain unchanged.

The grid is transposed: every cell keeps its color, but its row and column positions are swapped. Because of this, the tall input made of several symbol-like foreground patterns stacked vertically becomes a short, wide output where those same patterns appear laid out side by side. Background cells stay background, and each vertical feature in the input turns into the corresponding horizontal feature in the output.

The grid contains several copies of the same large block-shaped object; earlier copies contain a special marker cell, while the last copy is unmarked and has a nearby pattern of guide cells. The output does not alter the repeated blocks themselves: instead, it adds new cells onto the guide/frame around the final copy so that the marker locations seen in the earlier copies are transferred there, preserving their relative row/column placement with respect to the repeated shape. When all source markers are of the same type they all use one new color, and when a marker comes from a different positional case (such as lying just outside the block) it is shown with a second new color.

The central multicolored figure is extracted from the otherwise uniform background, but its zero-colored interior/path is removed so that only the colored outer parts remain. The output canvas is made four times wider, and this cleaned figure is stamped four times side-by-side in separate width-sized panels. These four copies are vertically staggered according to the figure’s original row structure, creating a repeated stepped pattern rather than four perfectly level duplicates.

The input contains several equal-sized vertical sections separated by divider-colored columns, and some cells inside the sections are covered by a solid mask color. Treat the dividers and the mask as non-information: align the sections by their internal coordinates and keep any foreground mark that appears in any section at that position, with all other cells becoming background. The output is the recovered clean pattern with only background and foreground remaining, shown without the masked content and with the divider bands neutralized.

Identify the color that occurs in two separate solid rectangles: one small 2x3 block and one larger square block. In the output, the small block is copied repeatedly one cell up-left, for as many steps as the side length of the larger square, with all copies merged and clipped by the grid; if this diagonal trail reaches the larger block, they fuse into one shape. A separate fixed five-row marker in the accent color is also placed further up-left of that small block whenever that offset lands inside the canvas, while all existing objects otherwise remain unchanged.

The wide input is divided into three equal-width vertical panels. These three panels are then rearranged by stacking them vertically in the same left-to-right order: the left panel becomes the top section of the output, the middle panel becomes the middle section, and the right panel becomes the bottom section. All cell contents are preserved exactly, including background, solid color blocks, and any small internal patterns inside a panel.

The input is a wide image made of three equal square panels placed side by side, each panel being the same height as the whole input. The output cuts out these three square panels and stacks them vertically in the same left-to-right order, preserving every panel’s internal pattern exactly. Between the stacked panels, it inserts a single full-width horizontal separator row in a new highlight color.

All visible structures are ignored: the scattered markers, small patterned clusters, and the bottom-left block/row features are completely removed. The output keeps only the input’s height, collapses the width to a single column, and fills that entire column with the background color.

The large irregular foreground shape is preserved exactly but translated so that its bounding box is flush with the top edge and the left edge of the grid. The separate horizontal bar near the bottom, in a different non-background color, stays in its original position, and all remaining cells stay as background. In other words, only the main shape is slid up and left as far as possible without changing its pattern.

Each input is a diagonally repeating stripe/tile pattern, and the output only edits the outer L-shaped boundary while leaving the interior unchanged. The leftmost column is recomputed so the diagonal color progression continues smoothly into the grid from above/below, and the bottom row is likewise adjusted so the same repeating pattern extends cleanly across the lower edge. In other words, the transformation extrapolates the existing slanted periodic pattern onto the left edge and the bottom edge.

The grid size stays the same and the scattered single-cell markers plus the short 3-cell bar are left unchanged. The only edit is inside the compact multicolored cluster: all cells of the non-target colors are erased to background, while cells of the target color are kept in their original positions. In effect, the output isolates just the target-color shape from the mixed cluster.

A large outline made from one non-background color acts as a container, and a small plus-shaped object of a second color inside it is repositioned to a standard location within that container. The target location is the interior center of the container, with ties resolved toward the upper-left, so off-center pluses are shifted there while already centered ones stay put. After moving it, the old interior plus cells are cleared back to background/outline, and any extra solid outline strip inside the container is thinned back to just the side walls.

The grid keeps all existing objects unchanged, but adds a new horizontal bar in a previously unused color above the irregular multi-colored figure made of empty cells and accent cells. This bar is placed exactly two rows above that figure’s top edge, begins at the figure’s left edge, and extends across the figure’s full width plus two extra cells to the right, stopping at the grid boundary if necessary. The separate solid rectangular block elsewhere in the grid is not modified.

The output preserves all original non-background markers, but every cell of the special source color grows a square halo around itself. Using Chebyshev-distance bands, the source first expands to its full 3×3 neighborhood, and then the next four outward square rings are filled with four fixed new colors in order from inner to outer. These halos are clipped by the grid borders and can overlap each other, but the original scattered marker cells stay unchanged.

The output keeps the grid’s full height but removes the excess columns on the right, producing a square whose width equals the original number of rows. In other words, it is the leftmost square crop of the input. All colors and the small contrasting shape inside that left region stay unchanged; only the redundant right-side continuation of the background stripe pattern is discarded.

The entire input grid is copied unchanged and tiled into a 2-by-2 arrangement, doubling both the height and the width. Each quadrant of the output is an exact replica of the original, so the outer border, the inner rectangular frame, and the smaller enclosed shape all keep the same colors and relative positions within each copy. No internal object is altered; the only change is this full-grid repetition to the right and downward.

Each input contains a rectangular block of a main color, with a few cells inside it changed to a marker color. The output completes and propagates the marker-color pattern across the whole block: the sparse marker cells act as seeds for a horizontal stripe/fill pattern that is extended to cover the entire rectangle while the surrounding background stays unchanged. In some cases this completion becomes a full solid recoloring of the block, and in others it becomes repeated vertical stripes, but it always expands the internal marker arrangement to a regular full-block pattern.

The background and the diamond-like frame stay fixed. Inside that frame, the two colored diagonals exchange colors: every cell belonging to the down-right diagonal takes the other diagonal’s color, and every cell belonging to the down-left diagonal takes the first diagonal’s color. In addition, a centered cross is drawn through the interior of the frame, with a horizontal bar in the first diagonal’s color and a vertical bar in the second diagonal’s color, extending until just before the frame.

The shape(s) made of the movable accent color are translated straight upward by exactly two rows across the whole grid. Their old locations are erased back to background, anything shifted above the top edge disappears, and all other structures — including the solid marker block and the hollow/filled region in the other non-background color(s) — stay fixed. If the shifted accent cells would land on one of those fixed objects, the fixed object remains visible instead of being replaced.

The scene contains a left block, a right block, and a bent connector made of one line-color with a single different-colored tip sitting just below the connector’s vertical stem. In the output, the vertical stem above the junction is removed, the tip is lifted up into the main row and placed immediately to the right of the stem’s base, and the connector is straightened into a longer horizontal run. The new horizontal run is extended rightward by exactly the amount of height removed from the vertical part, even if this overwrites the top row of the right-hand block.

The grid shows a slanted wedge-like window bounded by two diagonals: a top/right border color and a left-side accent/border color, with various interior colored regions inside. In the output, the entire visible pattern is advanced upward by one row within this wedge, so each row is effectively replaced by the row below it and then clipped to the new slanted boundaries. Where the shifted content meets the new row edges, the left edge is redrawn with the accent border color and the right/top edge with the frame color, while cells that fall outside the wedge disappear and the lower vacated edge is filled by the frame color.

The three large colored anchor shapes and the bottom border remain fixed. Among the small pieces in the extra accent color near the top, only the rightmost piece or rightmost group of pieces is changed: all accent-color cells in that far-right region are translated horizontally together, preserving their rows and relative spacing, until their combined pattern is flush with the grid’s right edge. Everything else stays the same, even if this shifted group overlaps the upper part of the rightmost anchor shape.

A small set of detached motifs is chosen as movable pieces, while one top/central cluster acts as the focal pattern. The movable motifs keep their exact shapes and internal colors but are transplanted into empty positions around that focal pattern, as if filling its missing neighboring slots; their original copies are then erased. Larger unrelated structures mostly remain unchanged, and in some cases an old plain placeholder that the moved motif replaces is also removed.

The input contains several disconnected line-like fragments, and the output completes the pattern by translating those fragments to other aligned positions on the grid. Long vertical stems are extended through empty space to connect with other features, while short bars or marker pieces are copied upward or downward to matching rows so the separate motifs become repeated/continued versions of one another. Where an extended line meets another object, the contact cell can turn into a special junction color instead of keeping the original color.

The input contains several same-sized panels laid out horizontally on a common outer background. Inside each panel, a shape is drawn using a foreground color on a panel-colored field, and the shapes increase in filled extent from one panel to another. The output keeps only the single panel whose foreground shape is the largest/most complete (has the most foreground cells), preserving that panel exactly along with its surrounding outer-background margin, and discards the other panels.

Ignore the large blank area and the solid horizontal separator; only the patterned band above it matters. That band represents a square circulant pattern, where each row is the same repeating color sequence shifted by one position from the row above, but the very top row is faulty or misaligned (it may be truncated with background cells or redundantly repeated). The output is the corrected square of size equal to the input width, rebuilt so every row is a full, consistent continuation of the cycle and the row sequence flows smoothly without the top-row defect.

The grid contains a sparse upper row of seed cells and, lower down, a solid full-width horizontal bar of the same color. In the output, each seed is extended toward the bar as a three-part fan: a vertical line straight down from the seed, plus one diagonal line slanting down-left and one slanting down-right, so that at each intermediate row the diagonal branches sit at the corresponding offset from the seed. All such fans are overlaid together, clipped by the grid edges, while the original top row and the solid horizontal bar stay unchanged.

Each example contains one or more narrow vertical stacks of colored tiles/bars sitting above larger empty blocks, with some background-only rows left above the stacks. In the output, every such stack is extended upward until it touches the top edge by wrapping its own sequence cyclically: the bottommost colored segment is copied into the first empty row above, then the next-from-bottom if more rows must be filled. The stack keeps its width and column position, and everything else in the grid stays unchanged.

The grid contains several separated copies of the same multicolored motif on a uniform background. One copy is horizontally misaligned by exactly one cell compared with the others, and the output shifts that entire copy left or right so all motif instances have the same column alignment and identical internal layout. Nothing else changes: colors, shape, spacing between cells inside the motif, and the background remain unchanged.

The grid is split into equal square subpanels arranged side by side, and each subpanel contains a foreground shape on a uniform background. In the output, each subpanel is transposed independently: rows and columns are swapped, equivalently reflecting the shape across the panel’s main diagonal from upper-left to lower-right. The panel boundaries, panel order, and colors stay the same; only the internal orientation of each shape changes.

The wide input is split into two equal side-by-side square sections, each containing a single marker cell and some scattered other colored cells. The output keeps only the left section as a cropped square, preserving all cells there exactly and discarding the entire right section. No recoloring or shape editing happens; this is a left-half extraction centered on the left marker's panel.

The input contains four vertically separated copies of the same hollow rectangular pattern, each paired with one special colored marker placed in a different direction relative to the copy: above, right, below, and left. The output collapses these four clue-bearing copies into a single 7×7 composition that keeps one copy of the pattern and places the four markers around it in their corresponding sides: the top marker above, the right marker on the pattern’s middle-right, the left marker on the middle-left, and the bottom marker below. The repeated pattern itself is unchanged; only the layout is compressed from four stacked instances into one combined instance.

Each example has a large block of one dominant color with a lower central hollow/opening, and some accent-colored cells sitting in the top row of that opening. The transformation removes all of those accent cells from the opening, turning that whole strip into background so the hollow becomes one row taller. The removed accent cells are then redrawn higher up inside the large block as a small compact pattern, positioned roughly above the opening, while the rest of the grid stays the same.

Only the fourth row changes: it contains several same-sized slots of cells embedded in a solid frame-colored band, with the slots separated by frame-colored dividers. The contents of these slots are cyclically shifted one slot to the left, so each slot receives the pattern from the slot immediately to its right and the rightmost slot wraps around to the leftmost position. In the examples, these slot patterns are runs of object-colored cells followed by empty cells, but the top rows and the surrounding frame stay unchanged.

The output keeps the original width but expands the canvas to 5 stacked copies of the input, one above another. In the 1st and 5th copies the figure is unchanged; in the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th copies, the small horizontal protrusions attached to the right side of the main rectangle are removed from the outside and redrawn inside the rectangle, while the background and the inner marker cell(s) stay fixed. These three middle copies form a symmetric A-B-A pattern: one intermediate internal placement, then a further/rightward internal placement, then the intermediate placement again.

The input is made of several vertically stacked copies of the same kind of framed panel, with each panel separated by a blank row and a solid horizontal divider strip. The transformation discards the repeated upper panels and separator rows, keeping only the final (lowest) panel. The output is therefore a crop containing that one panel alone, preserving all of its internal colored objects and border exactly as they appear.

The input consists of several horizontal bands of the foreground color, separated by fully blank rows. Each non-blank band is a rectangular strip whose rows are identical, and the output removes the vertical stacking by taking these band patterns in top-to-bottom order and placing them side by side. The blank separator rows disappear, while each band keeps its exact internal row pattern and common height, so the output is a single horizontal sequence of the original strips.

Each input contains a fixed anchor cell, a block of same-colored cells extending to its right as a half-diamond, and one or two guide cells aligned vertically with the anchor. The output keeps the anchor and the right-side half-diamond, then adds a matching filled triangle of the same main color on the left side of the anchor: its tip is one row above or below the anchor, and it widens by one cell to both left and right as it extends outward. The triangle is drawn toward the guide cell that is farther from the anchor (breaking ties downward), so that guide may be overwritten while the guide on the opposite side remains unchanged.

The entire non-background drawing is copied three times side by side, so the output has the same height as the input but triple the width. Each copy preserves the exact shapes and positions within its own panel, but all foreground objects in a given panel are recolored to a single uniform color, ignoring their original different colors. The three panels use three different fixed colors in left-to-right order, while the background stays unchanged.

Each grid has a single special center cell and one partial diagonal arm (or two nested arms in different colors) extending away from it at fixed Manhattan distance(s). The output completes this into a full diamond-shaped pattern centered on the special cell by reflecting the given arm across the center into the missing quadrants. Existing cells stay in place, and each reflected arm keeps the same color and distance from the center as its source arm.

The output keeps the entire input unchanged on the left, then appends a second copy of the same picture to the right, doubling the grid’s width. In that new right-hand copy, the two non-background motif colors are exchanged with each other everywhere, while the background and the central vertical marker/bar color stay the same. Thus the shape layout is identical in both halves; only those two object colors are swapped in the added duplicate.

The colored pattern is kept exactly as it is, with no internal changes, movement, or recoloring. The only transformation is to trim away the empty background columns on the far right, stopping at the rightmost column that contains any part of the figure. Height stays the same, and any empty space on the left or inside the figure is preserved.

Take the non-background pattern, trim away the empty margins around it, and mirror that trimmed shape left-to-right. Place this mirrored shape at the upper-left corner of a much larger blank canvas. The new canvas is a horizontal strip of five square sections, each section having side length equal to the original input width, with single blank columns between sections; only the first section contains the shape and the rest stay empty.

The output places four side-by-side copies of the entire square input pattern on a wider canvas, keeping the background color unchanged. These four copies are the original figure and its successive quarter-turn rotations: first the original, then a 90° rotation, then the 180° rotation, then the 270° rotation. Because some input shapes are rotationally symmetric, some neighboring panels can look identical.

The output is made by compressing the picture: delete every row and every column that contains only background, while keeping the remaining rows and columns in their original order. This preserves the shape and relative arrangement of the foreground cells, but removes all empty margins and any completely blank gaps between separated parts, so disconnected pieces can become adjacent in the smaller frame.

The wide input is made of three equal-width vertical panels placed side by side. The output is produced by collapsing those three panels onto the same coordinates, so each output cell is the superposition of the corresponding cells from the left, middle, and right third. Background stays background, non-background pixels from any panel are kept, and when different colored pixels overlap, the result follows the same fixed color-dominance rule shown by the examples.

The grid is split into four consecutive 7-column panels, each containing a small multicolor motif on the same background. The output keeps those four panels unchanged on the left, then extends the canvas to the right by appending exact copies of the same panels in reverse order, making the panel sequence palindromic. Nothing inside a panel is flipped or altered: each motif and its small attached accent cells above or below are preserved exactly.

Inside the solid inner block, the secondary-color marks form an incomplete motif near the top. The output completes this motif by adding the horizontally mirrored counterpart of every existing secondary-color stroke across the motif’s implied vertical symmetry axis, so the top pattern becomes left-right balanced. The surrounding background and the main-color filled block stay the same; only new secondary-color cells are added in the previously empty mirrored positions.

The wide input is made of several equal square sections placed side by side, each section having the same height as the whole grid. The output is a single square formed by superimposing those sections cell-for-cell: for each position, the output keeps a foreground cell if that position is filled in any section, otherwise it stays background. In effect, the task collapses the horizontal strip of repeated-sized panels into one combined overlay.

The wide input is first split into several equal framed mini-grids using the full-height separator columns. Each mini-grid is then compressed into a single output column by ignoring horizontal detail and keeping only a vertical summary of its main interior trace: background remains background, empty corridor cells remain empty, and any special colored cells are preserved in their top-to-bottom order. Putting these one-column summaries next to each other forms the narrow output; mini-grids with no usable trace reduce to a blank/background column.

A vertical band of background cells separates a solid reference figure on the left from a sparse, incomplete counterpart on the right. The output uses the left figure as the template for the right-side figure’s overall footprint (as the counterpart across the divider), keeping the already present right-side cells and filling in the missing cells so the right object becomes a completed, more solid silhouette. Newly added cells alternate by row between the original object color and a second color, creating horizontal striping, while unchanged existing cells stay in the original color.

The output keeps the same height but stretches the image to six times the original width by placing six full-width copies side by side. Each horizontal color band is rewritten independently across these six panels: the top-band color follows a repeating 3-panel cycle of itself, then two newly introduced colors, then that cycle repeats once more; the middle-band color alternates between itself and one new color across the six panels; the bottom-band color stays unchanged in all six panels. Vertical order and band thicknesses are preserved exactly.

The input is a wide canvas made of three horizontally repeated panels separated by background columns. The output keeps only one panel—the leftmost copy—so the frame is narrowed to that single scene while preserving all other objects in their same relative positions.

Inside the retained panel, the only content change is that the small staircase-like diagonal trail is recolored from its original marker color to a new highlight color. The background, the top horizontal bars, the zero-filled cells, and any adjacent solid side blocks stay unchanged.

The input is divided into several horizontal panels by solid full-width separator rows. The rule is to discard every panel except the bottommost one, then crop that last panel out as the entire output. The foreground pattern inside that final panel is copied unchanged, with background preserved and all separator rows removed.

The output keeps the entire layout unchanged: every object stays in the same place with the same shape, size, and contacts, and the background also stays the same. The transformation is a pure recoloring by role: the scaffold/frame-like structures are recolored to one new color, the compact solid block clusters are recolored to another, the scattered single-cell marker color is recolored to a third, while the dotted/filled pattern color and the bright highlight color are left unchanged.

The grid contains several foreground cross/plus shapes of different sizes on a uniform background. In the output, the centers of these crosses stay in the same places, but their sizes are reassigned in reading order (top to bottom, left to right) so they form a symmetric sequence: smallest up to largest, then back down again. This means some crosses expand and some shrink, while the background and overall object layout remain unchanged.

The wide input is split into four equal vertical panels. The left panel contains a stepped triangular shape and various distractor pixels, while the two rightmost panels are identical clean templates that keep only two meaningful cells: one upper marker cell and one lower cell of another color in the same column. The output is that single clean panel, i.e. one quarter of the input width with all other objects and extra markings removed.

Ignore the solid full-width strip at the bottom, then make a new canvas that is five copies of the original width placed side by side. In the first section, redraw the main 3-row figure in its original place but remove its unique center cell; in the second and third sections, redraw that figure shifted diagonally up-right by 1 and then by 2 cells, with the two small top markers recolored differently at each shifted stage. The last two sections keep the figure at that shifted position and add a descending diagonal trail from its lower-right area: first a short trail in a new color, then a farther trail in another color whose endpoint is the figure’s original unique center cell.

Each grid is made of several equal-width monochrome panels placed side by side, with small background-colored holes cut out inside each panel. The output cyclically shifts these panels one place to the left: every panel moves left one slot and the leftmost panel is wrapped around to the far right. In addition, the hole pattern inside each panel is normalized/cleaned into a more regular version of the same motif, so the internal cutouts are adjusted rather than copied exactly from the noisy input.

The noisy, mostly-solid object on the right is cleaned up into a solid shape: the scattered contrasting pixels inside it are removed, while rows where this right object is most indented get a single special marker placed immediately to their left. A broad new filler-colored band is then added to the left of that right-hand shape, occupying the horizontal gap toward the middle of the grid but not overwriting other objects. The smaller separate objects on the left keep their shapes but are shifted downward by two rows, or by the largest amount possible before hitting the bottom edge.

Each input is split into two equal vertical halves. The two halves show the same scene at different moments: a connected shape made from the two standout colors appears in one position on the left half and in a later position on the right half, while the surrounding cells provide the background to reveal as it moves. The output turns this into a horizontal filmstrip: six successive copies of the left half, separated by one-column black dividers, with the special shape shifted step by step toward the arrangement implied by the right half and the cells it leaves behind updated accordingly; the unchanged right half is then appended as the final panel.

The input is divided into equal-width vertical tiles, each tile containing one small colored motif embedded in the same background. The output keeps all original tiles in place, then extends the grid to the right by repeating the earlier tiles in reverse order, making the tile sequence horizontally palindromic around the rightmost original tile. Each repeated tile is copied exactly, including its internal zeros, background cells, and motif shape; only the canvas width increases.

The dark separator color forms a fixed lattice of rectangular compartments, and the input contains one special colored cell inside one compartment that serves as a positional template. The output keeps the same height but extends the scene into a horizontal strip of repeated versions of that compartment layout; in each repeated section, extra separator-colored cells are added inside the compartments to show a different internal placement pattern derived from the special cell’s offset within its own compartment. The special cell keeps the same relative location in its home compartment in every section, while the outer lattice structure itself remains unchanged.

The filled cells in the input are interpreted as several separate shape-clusters that belong to distinct figures, even when the overall picture is crowded and some parts come close or touch. Each figure is extracted and cropped to its own bounding box, then the figures are laid out next to one another from left to right in the output, with their top edges aligned and background filling the remaining space. The shapes themselves are preserved; only their framing and placement change.

The color used by the lone top cell and the solid bottom row is expanded into a large outlined structure centered on that top cell’s column. A full-width rectangular frame is drawn from one row above the patterned horizontal strip down to the existing bottom row, with vertical sides at the left and right edges; on the patterned strip itself, the two endpoint cells are recolored to this frame color while the interior band and the special aligned cell stay unchanged. Above the frame’s top edge, a narrow connector is added from the original top cell straight downward, widening to a 3-cell cap just before it meets the frame.

Each grid has four large uniform corner regions meeting around a smaller central figure. In the output, the corner regions are pulled one step inward around that figure: the upper-left region extends one column to the right, the upper-right region extends one row downward, the lower-right region extends one column to the left, and the lower-left region extends one row upward. The central framed/multicolored object stays the same; only the thin background strips immediately adjacent to it are recolored to match the corresponding corner region.

The input is a long horizontal strip made of equal repeat-units on a plain background; each unit contains one 2-row horizontal bar, whose fill alternates between two colors, plus small marker clusters beside and below the bar. The output reduces the whole strip to a single square repeat-unit, choosing the unit at the center of the repeated sequence (taking the right-hand middle unit when there are two). In that extracted unit, the bar itself is kept, while the surrounding marker clusters are replaced by a highlighted decoration in a new color, with one small upper-right marker cell left in the original marker color.

The input contains two related motifs built from a dominant body color plus a contrasting tip color at the ends of their arms. The output stacks a sequence of frames vertically, starting with one input motif and ending with the other, while intermediate frames gradually shift the motif sideways and adjust its arm lengths/shape so it morphs step by step from the first object into the second. The originals are preserved as endpoints of this vertical animation strip.

The grid keeps the same height but is stretched horizontally to three times its original width by repeating each input column three times side by side. After this expansion, the center third of the new image (a vertical band as wide as the original grid) is highlighted: every cell belonging to the main solid pattern color in that middle band is changed to a new accent color, while the background/empty cells remain unchanged. The left and right thirds stay in the original colors.

Each input is made of several horizontal repeats of the same structural template: fixed colored marker columns stay in the same relative positions, while an extra accent color appears in different places within each repeat. The transformation folds those repeated sections together onto the leftmost retained section by superimposing the accent-color cells from all copies onto matching positions, but it does not replace the template’s fixed marker colors. After merging, the redundant repeated sections on the right are removed or blanked, leaving just the combined template area.

A small colored block near the right edge is moved straight upward to the top of the grid. The block keeps its internal pattern exactly: a horizontal strip of one accent color above two rows of another accent color, sitting immediately to the left of the unchanged vertical edge column. Everything else stays the same, with the main background filling the cells that were vacated.

The input contains several separate symbol-like patterns, each attached to a tall vertical bar of the same color; these groups are arranged from left to right across the canvas. The output isolates the rightmost such group by cropping to its bounding box, keeping the background and the symbol’s own colored pixels unchanged. Every pixel belonging to the bar-colored structure in that selected group—including any horizontal extension connected to it—is recolored to a new highlight color.

The input is a blank field with several evenly spaced, full-height vertical stripes of one foreground color. The output keeps the same height but extends the pattern far to the right by chaining overlapping copies of this striped scaffold, so the vertical stripes continue periodically across the whole result. Inside the gaps between stripes, extra foreground cells are added as right-pointing diagonal/triangular connectors: they are shortest near the top and bottom, grow toward the center rows, and in the middle can become long horizontal bridges where the diagonals meet.

The input contains a structural color that makes a left edge and sometimes full-width horizontal bars, a solid separator band in another color, and a small colored cluster lower in the grid. In the output, the separator band is recolored to a new uniform band color, the left edge is redrawn as a thin vertical line in the second column, and any full-width structural rows are reduced to right-side horizontal bars on those same rows. The small colored cluster is lifted upward to sit directly under the separator while keeping its original columns, with any cells covered by the reconstructed structural bars simply disappearing under them.

The input contains two aligned copies of the same pattern, separated by a vertical strip of blank cells. The output keeps just one copy (the left-sized frame) and discards the separator and the duplicate on the right. The blank holes marked in either copy are overlaid onto that single frame and turned into one filled shape: cells on the shape’s border become the motif’s accent color, while any fully enclosed interior cells become a different inner fill color; all other cells remain unchanged.

The grid is divided into stacked panels by full-width horizontal separator lines. The transformation discards every panel above the last separator and outputs only the bottom panel as its own smaller grid. All colored objects inside that final panel keep their exact arrangement; only the framing changes by cropping away the earlier stages and divider rows.

The upper part of the grid contains several horizontally repeated copies of the same two-color symbol, but each copy is only partially drawn. The missing cells are recovered by combining the information from the different copies to infer one complete template, then every copy is replaced by that full template in its own slot. Only the symbol area is completed; the empty background and the patterned strip at the bottom stay unchanged.

The input contains a single centered plus/cross on an otherwise empty square grid. The output keeps the same width but becomes a vertical stack of full-size frames: first the original cross, then centered copies of it that shrink step by step by shortening all four arms equally until only the center cell remains, and then grow again in the same sequence back to the original size. Each successive frame is recolored in a repeating 3-color cycle: the original foreground color first, then a second color, then a third color, and repeat as the size changes.

The input contains several separate, vertically centered motifs made from the same two non-background colors, arranged left-to-right in increasing size. In the output, the rightmost motif is treated as the center of symmetry: every motif to its left is copied to the right at the same horizontal distance, so the sequence of motifs becomes a mirror pattern around that rightmost figure. The original motifs are unchanged, and the grid is widened only to the right to hold the reflected copies.

The input is a tall image made of several identical square sections stacked vertically; each section has a uniform background with the same small contrasting cell in the same position. The output collapses these repeated sections into a single square section whose size matches the input width. The contrasting cell(s) stay in the same location, while the uniform background is recolored from the original fill color to a different fill color.

Each input contains repeated, highly regular foreground motifs arranged symmetrically, while any background and any plain separator line are irrelevant. The transformation throws away all spatial structure and reduces the whole scene to a 1x1 output colored with the motif’s foreground color.

The input contains a horizontal sequence of identical solid rectangular blocks near the bottom, each separated by a fixed gap, plus a matching 2-cell marker located above each block in a stair-step pattern that rises as you move right. The output widens the canvas and extends this sequence to the right by repeating the same block spacing and continuing the upward staircase of the small markers in the same progression. The original objects keep their shapes and relative spacing; only additional copies are appended on the right over the unchanged background.

The large input is a row of same-height framed subgrids separated by narrow gaps. The output keeps only the rightmost framed subgrid, preserving its border, empty cells, and any scattered marker-color dots.
Within that chosen subgrid, the small 3×3 multicolor pattern is finalized using the subgrid immediately to its left: marker-color dots indicate which positions of the rightmost 3×3 should be overwritten by the value from the same position in the neighboring 3×3. If those copied values already match, the 3×3 appears unchanged.

Only the one row that contains both irregularities is changed. In that row, the small horizontal bar in the plain right-hand field shifts one step to the right: the cells it previously occupied turn into the separator’s right color, and a single cell of the bar’s original color stays at the new rightmost tip. At the same time, in the left alternating-stripe field, the affected stripe segment has its dark stripe color and the special marker color exchanged cell-by-cell, while the light stripe color and all other rows remain unchanged.

The input is a horizontal strip made of several equal-sized square panels placed side by side, each panel sharing the same sparse corner markers and its own internal symbol pattern. The transformation extracts only the rightmost panel and discards all panels to its left. Inside that chosen panel, every colored cell keeps the same position and color-role; nothing is modified except the cropping to the final section.

Each example has a large untouched outer background and a rigid framed region made of separator/border lines. Inside that framed region, one common filler color acts as the local background around the meaningful colored blocks; in the output, only this filler color is replaced by black/empty. All other colors, including the outer background, the frame/separators, and the embedded colored patterns, stay in the same positions.

The input is a square made of concentric colored rings around a single unchanged center cell. The output stacks multiple copies of this same ring pattern vertically: first the original, then versions where the ring colors are cyclically rotated so the innermost ring color becomes the new outermost and every other ring shifts one level inward, continuing through all cyclic orders, and finally the original appears again at the bottom. The shape, size, and center cell stay fixed; only the assignment of colors to ring depths changes.

The output stacks three same-width panels vertically. The top and bottom panels are unchanged copies of the input, while the middle panel keeps the lone marker cell in the same relative position but replaces the wide horizontal block with a 90-degree-rotated vertical version whose center aligns with the marker and whose lower end reaches up to it. If that rotated block would not fit inside the middle panel, only the marker is shown there and the block is omitted.

The single large foreground figure stays in place, but its contour is annotated: different kinds of boundary features are marked with different colors. Upper outer corners/top caps are given one marker color, adjacent edge/transition cells another, lower endpoints a third, and inward notch or cavity corners a fourth. Matching marker cells are also placed in nearby empty background above, below, or beside the same vertical alignments, so the output becomes the original shape plus a color-coded map of its key corner and edge features.

The input is a long horizontal strip of repeated composite tiles separated by background; the output compresses this into a much narrower image that keeps only two tile positions, with the same vertical layout, marker row, and lower solid bands. The deciding information is the small cutout pattern inside the top block of each repeated tile: the output uses two summary versions of that top block and discards the extra repeated tiles to the right. In those kept summary tiles, cutout cells are normalized so that only the chosen hole pattern remains as holes, while other possible cutout positions are replaced by plain background.

The grid contains a lattice of wall-like lines and one special full horizontal line crossing one special full vertical line. In the output, that crossing becomes the center of an 8-direction star/diamond pattern: the special row and column are repainted along their length, and diagonal arms are extended outward through the surrounding compartments in all four diagonal directions. Cells touched by this overlay get one new color when they lie in open space and the other new color when they coincide with an original wall/intersection, while only the small central cross around the exact meeting point keeps the original special color.

The input is a uniform rectangle filled with a single background color, and that original color is discarded; only the grid’s height and width are preserved. The output repaints the whole rectangle with a 4-color repeating pattern: each row cycles through the same four colors, and each successive row is shifted by one position, creating diagonal stripes across the grid. The top-left cell always starts with the same first color of that 4-color cycle.

The input contains a compact triangular/wedge-shaped figure made from two non-background colors: one acts as the outline/edge color and the other as the interior color. In the output, this seed is expanded into a much larger self-similar triangular pattern, built from many offset copies of the same wedge so that the figure grows upward and outward while leaving background gaps between sub-parts. The edge-colored cells define the branching outer structure, and the interior-colored cells appear in the corresponding inner locations of the enlarged recursive pattern.

The only meaningful data in the input is the vertical list of non-background cells in the first column, beneath the all-background top row. The output keeps the same height, but stretches each row horizontally into blocks the width of the original grid, where only the first cell of each block can be non-background and the rest stay background. For each non-top row, take the first-column list, cyclically rotate it so that this row’s own value comes first, place that rotated list across the blocks, then continue with the same rotated list reflected backward (without repeating the turning-point item), making a symmetric sequence of length 2n-1. The top row becomes a full background row across the new width.

A full-height vertical stripe of a distinctive marker color acts as a divider. The output is made by deleting that divider and everything to its left, keeping only the part of the grid strictly to the right of the stripe. All remaining colored objects stay unchanged in shape and row position, and the output keeps the original height while shrinking to the right-side width.

The input is a staggered arrangement of short horizontal motif fragments, with populated rows separated by blank rows and alternate populated rows horizontally offset from each other. The transformation straightens this skewed layout into a smaller aligned rectangle by keeping only the central overlapping band, shifting the offset rows into alignment, and recombining neighboring fragments so they form compact motifs around the repeated middle color. The vertical spacing pattern is preserved, but much of the outer left/right material is discarded during this compression.

The grid keeps its size and the large background/main-shape structure stays in place, but the two embedded accent colors are normalized in different ways. Every patch of one accent color is erased to the global background color, while every patch of the other accent color is recolored into the dark outline/highlight color. All remaining cells, including any existing border or main body color, stay unchanged.

Treat the cells in the top row of the source color as column markers. For each such marker, if there is a target-colored cell somewhere below in the same column, the marker is converted into a new-colored cross centered on that target: the four orthogonal neighbors of the target are filled while the target itself stays unchanged. If a top-row marker has no target-colored cell beneath it in its column, it instead becomes a downward-opening 3-row V in the new color placed against the bottom of the grid, centered on that original column and clipped by the side edges.

Each input is a wide strip made by tiling the same square picture side-by-side several times, with the tile width equal to the grid height. Some repeated copies are intact, while alternating copies have selected pixels carved out into the background color. The output compresses the strip to a single square tile by keeping one full repeat, choosing the version that contains those carved-out/background holes wherever the repeats differ and otherwise preserving the unchanged parts.

The large divider structure stays fixed: the horizontal bar, vertical separators, and other border-like lines remain unchanged. Inside each small compartment, the only cells that matter are the specially colored marker cells; these are converted into the divider color, while all other interior non-background cells are erased to background. In effect, each output preserves the frame and shows only the former marker positions as solid cells.

The input is split into two equal-width vertical panels. In each panel, the fixed scaffold/base made from the frame color stays in place, while the other colored marks associated with the emblem are completed by reflecting the panel’s upper accent pattern downward across the emblem’s main horizontal band, making the accent pattern vertically symmetric and correcting mismatched cells below. The output then places three panels side by side: the processed left panel, the processed right panel, and a repeat of the processed left panel.

The main non-background object is a small hollow, frame-colored shape containing an accent-colored vertical spine, plus one sideways accent-colored protrusion in the middle and one dangling accent-colored cell below. In the output, the frame is expanded outward to surround those protrusions, creating an additional boxed lobe attached on the left of the upper part and another boxed lobe attached below the original shape. The accent-colored spine and lower dangling cell stay in place, but the single sideways protruding accent cell is absorbed into the new frame; any unrelated objects elsewhere in the grid are left unchanged.

The grid is extended horizontally to the right by one full repeat interval, while keeping the same height. Each non-background shape already appears in a horizontal progression with a fixed spacing, so the output adds the next copy of each shape at the same vertical position and with the same local form, continuing the pattern into the new columns. Existing cells stay unchanged; only the extra right-side area is filled as the next repeated segment of the scene.

The input contains several small rectangular islands of a secondary background color embedded in a dominant field, and each island holds exactly one special colored cell. In the output, those rectangular islands are erased completely and replaced by the dominant field color, while the special colored cells are left in their original absolute positions. The result is a clean grid showing only the marker cells that had been inside the islands.

The big sparse grid contains several separate multicolor motifs, each built around a vertical stem of one color with small side markers or short arms in the other two colors. Each motif is extracted and rewritten as a compact standard 3-column version that preserves its row-by-row structure while collapsing away the large horizontal gaps of the original layout. The output is then made by stacking these normalized motif strips vertically in a consistent positional order.

The input has a large upper rectangle made from two colors: a solid outer/background color, with several identical square patches of a second color repeated inside it. In the output, that whole patterned upper rectangle is erased and replaced by one centered diamond: the diamond is filled with the rectangle’s solid color, while the repeated-patch color appears as a one-cell outline at the left/right edges and at the top and bottom tips. The diamond’s size is determined by the side length of the repeated square patches, and the separate horizontal bar near the bottom is left unchanged.

The input is divided into several horizontal sections by full-width separator lines. In each section, there is an upper solid rectangular block in one foreground color and, lower in the section, a patterned block made from two non-background colors; across sections, these paired blocks increase in size. The output keeps only the largest such section: it removes all separators and empty spacing, then places that section’s solid rectangle directly above its corresponding patterned block, preserving both shapes and colors exactly.

The input is made of three equal-width vertical panels placed side by side. The transformation simply crops away the left two panels and keeps only the rightmost panel, preserving all colors and any marked shape inside it exactly as they appear. In other words, the output is the final third of the input grid.

The output keeps the original grid unchanged on the left, then adds one empty separator column and a new square panel on the right. That new panel is made by taking the rightmost square portion of the input whose side length equals the grid height, and transposing it: each colored cell at a row/column in that square is moved to the swapped column/row position, so horizontal runs become vertical runs and vice versa. In the square example, this means the whole input is transposed and appended.

The whole input grid is copied horizontally to make a second identical half on the right. Every colored object keeps its exact shape, colors, and row positions, including the block-like figure and the short separated marker patterns; only the canvas width doubles. The output is therefore two side-by-side copies of the original scene with no gap or other changes.

The input is three equal-width copies of the same picture placed side by side, but each copy has some cells knocked out to the background. The output collapses these three panels into a single panel one-third as wide by aligning corresponding positions and restoring missing cells. For each position, use the value from the left copy if it is not background; if that spot is background, take the middle copy’s value, and only if both are background take the right copy’s value.

Each input contains two same-sized scene panels placed side by side, separated by a narrow blank gap; these two panels act like consecutive frames. The output keeps those two panels and appends a third panel of the same size to the right, preserving the fixed background/layout while advancing every non-background colored object one more step according to how it changed from the first panel to the second. In other words, the rule is to continue the motion/state transition of the small colored marks and clusters into a next frame, with unchanged structures simply copied.

The multicolored stacked figure is redrawn with a leftward offset: in every row that contains part of the figure, the row’s colored pattern is shifted one cell left and also extended by one extra cell on its left edge, using the color that was already at that row’s left boundary. In addition, a new top row is created from the figure’s inner accent band, expanding that accent to the full width of its surrounding block and placing it at the very top of the grid. Finally, the two rightmost columns are turned into a solid strip of a new fill color.

The non-background cells form small polyomino pieces made of one main color plus a single contrasting tip cell. In the output, each piece keeps exactly the same internal shape and colors, but is nudged by one cell according to its orientation as indicated by that tip: left-ended pieces slide left, top-ended pieces slide right, upper-right-corner pieces slide down-right, and the bottom-right hook-shaped piece is already in its target placement so it stays fixed. The background remains unchanged.

The input is a vertical stack of four equal-sized square panels, each using the same palette and containing a small pattern inside a frame/background color. The output is formed by cutting the input into those four square panels and placing them side by side from left to right in the same top-to-bottom order. No panel contents are changed: every color arrangement inside each square is preserved exactly, only the overall layout changes from a tall column to a wide row.

The input contains a single closed outline drawn in one non-background color, and the output keeps that outline exactly in place. The empty interior of the outlined shape is filled with concentric inward bands centered on the shape’s middle: the innermost cell/region gets one fill color, the next surrounding ring gets a second fill color, the next ring gets a third fill color, and this three-color cycle repeats outward until the border is reached. The background outside the shape is unchanged.

The input is a tall grid filled with a regular two-color repeating wallpaper pattern, except for one small connected intruding shape in a third color that disrupts that pattern. In the output, that odd shape is removed and its cells are replaced so the surrounding periodic background is perfectly restored. After restoring the wallpaper, the grid is reduced to a square by keeping only the top section whose height equals the original grid width.

The top two rows are left unchanged, and the previously empty bottom row is filled with the set of all non-background colors that appear above, using one copy of each existing colored cell. Those colors are reordered into a consistent global palette order rather than preserving their original row or column positions, so the bottom row becomes a left-to-right sorted list of the colors present in the first two rows.

The grid contains a large background, a fixed central vertical spine, and some horizontal bar-shaped objects that stay unchanged. Each small marker pixel near the top acts as the seed of a vertical ray: it is copied straight downward in the same column through background cells only. The ray stops whenever it would run into an existing non-background object, so blocking shapes remain intact and are not overwritten.

The small patterned object above the large solid rectangle is the part that gets moved: it disappears from its original location and reappears at the far right, immediately next to the vertical border. When it is moved, its repeated blocks are rearranged from a horizontal run into a vertical stack with the same block sizes and gap pattern, top-aligned with the lower object and clipped if it would run past the bottom edge. The large central rectangle and the right border stay unchanged, while the lower object loses one of its disconnected branches so that only one branch remains in place.

The grid contains a large repeated scaffold plus a small set of evenly spaced marker slots colored with the scaffold color and one accent color. One row/part of these slots already shows the intended left- or right-leaning wedge pattern of accent cells, and the other corresponding row/part has one accent/base pair swapped; the output fixes this by exchanging those two misplaced cells so the accent cells form a consistent staircase/triangle. Everything else, including the big repeated structure, remains unchanged.

The input contains one large hollow figure drawn in a dominant outline color, plus a few cells in two marker colors placed on or near that figure. The output keeps the original figure unchanged and adds a smaller, similarly shaped copy of that outline inside the hollow center, aligned to match the outer contour. Most newly added cells use the dominant figure color, but where the copied inner contour corresponds to marked positions, the marker colors are preserved on the inner copy as well.

The main change is on the left side: each shape made of the distinctive object color is copied straight downward by a fixed vertical offset, while keeping the same columns and shape. The offset is indicated by the separate cue region on the right that contains holes and a single marker color; all original cells stay unchanged, and the shifted copy simply merges with anything already there. If the copied shape would go past the bottom edge, only the visible part is kept.

Each row contains one horizontal colored block against a uniform background. In the output, every colored block is slid horizontally to the far right until it touches the grid’s right edge, while keeping its row, color, and length unchanged. Any cells vacated by the shift become background.

The output is made by repeating the entire input grid side-by-side horizontally, keeping the same row structure and preserving every colored cell exactly. The number of horizontal copies equals the input grid’s height, so the output width becomes the input width multiplied by the number of rows. Background cells stay background, and any multicolor arrangement is duplicated unchanged in each repeated block.

The transformation crops away the two outer vertical border columns: the leftmost column and the rightmost column. These side columns are uniform background strips, so removing them leaves the internal repeated pattern unchanged. No colors are altered and no objects move relative to each other; only the grid becomes narrower by 2 columns while keeping the same height.

The input is a row of large horizontal color blocks; one block is special because its main color also appears as small accent cells inside the other blocks. In the output, that special full block is removed and turned into background, while the accent-color marks in the remaining blocks are propagated/adjusted so the outer patterned blocks become more paired and center-facing. The canvas is then widened to the right by appending an extra horizontal copy of the non-special structure around the removed block, with the removed block’s position shown as blank space.

The large inverted triangular canopy and the lower pole-like shapes remain structurally unchanged; the only active inputs are the isolated colored marker cells placed on the outer border. Their colors are copied into the open region associated with the upper middle horizontal block: when that 2-row block is the available target, it is split into equal vertical bands and recolored left-to-right using the border markers in the order upper-left, upper-right, then lower-left. If the triangle sits one row below the top and leaves empty side areas above it, those upper-left and upper-right gaps are filled instead with the available marker colors, while everything else stays the same.

Identify the small multirow figure embedded in the uniform background. Copy only the figure’s top two rows, keeping the light interior cells and turning the darker structural cells in those rows into background; then place these two rows at the bottom with their order reversed, so the figure’s second row becomes the upper output row and its first row becomes the lower output row. This 2-row strip is shifted to the right by the same amount as the original figure’s left offset, so it ends up in the lower-right corner and any part that would go past the right edge is clipped.

Treat the input as a row of equal-width vertical tiles, where each tile is 3 columns wide and keeps its full height and internal pattern. The output keeps the same height but becomes four times wider by concatenating four versions of this tiled row: first the original tile order, then the same tiles shifted left by one tile with wraparound, then shifted left by two, then shifted left by three. No tile contents are edited; only the horizontal ordering of the 3-column tiles changes.

The large outlined central frame and all of the small decorative markers around it stay fixed. Only the small two-color motif inside the frame is changed: it is reoriented within the interior (by a rotation or a mirror flip, as indicated by the surrounding cue markers) and then redrawn against the same background. The motif’s two colors are preserved, but their occupied cells move to the transformed orientation while all other cells remain unchanged.

Identify the full bounding box of the composite figure, including the outer scaffold/outline color and the interior colored pattern, and crop the grid to that rectangle. Then delete the scaffold color by turning all of its cells into background, while leaving every other colored cell exactly where it is inside the cropped area. The result is the same shape and internal picture, but without the surrounding border/structure.

The input consists of four equal-sized subgrids placed side by side, separated by single vertical divider columns. Each subgrid contains the same foreground pattern drawn in a different color on the common background. The output removes the divider columns, keeps the four subgrids in the same order, and then appends one more copy of the leftmost subgrid at the far right.

The grid is divided into horizontal bands by full-width separator rows that are already a single uniform color. In the output, each separator row is kept unchanged, while every non-separator band is overwritten into a solid rectangle using the color found in that band's top-left cell. Thus all internal variation inside each band disappears, but the original band heights, widths, and separator positions are preserved.

The non-background pattern is already drawn in the left part of the grid, while the rest of the input is just empty padding extending far to the right. The transformation removes that unnecessary right-side background and keeps only the leftmost square portion of the grid, with side length equal to the grid’s height. All colored cells stay in the same relative positions; only the canvas width is reduced by cropping off blank columns on the right.

The wide input is split into several equal horizontal panels (or repeated sections), each containing an upper sparse marker pattern, a lower dense shape, and a final row of panel-label colors. The transformation collapses these repeated panels into a single narrower frame: one clean copy of the lower dense shape is kept (dropping any intrusive cells from the upper marker color), while the upper sparse patterns from the repeated panels are folded together into one composite pattern in the reduced width. The bottom label row is also condensed by merging the panel-wide color bands into a single summary row for the reduced frame.

The input contains a solid square block of one color embedded in a plain background, with a single distinct marker cell placed in the square’s upper-left corner. The output repeats the entire input scene horizontally as many times as the square’s side length. In each repeated copy, the square stays the same size and position within its tile, but the marker shifts one step along the square’s main diagonal, so across the copies it moves from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner.

The input consists of several same-sized subgrids stacked vertically and separated by full-width divider rows. The output removes the dividers and compresses all subgrids into a single grid by overlaying them in the same position, copying every non-background cell from any panel into the result. When the two foreground colors would occupy the same cell, the color used for the thicker block/bar shapes takes precedence over the color used for the thinner line/point pattern.

The grid is split by a solid horizontal divider into an upper panel and a lower panel. The repeated small block patterns and all background areas stay exactly the same, but every isolated marker pixel in the upper panel changes from its original marker color to a new highlight color. No objects move, and nothing in the lower panel is altered.

The meaningful part of the input is the leftmost square block whose width equals the grid height; the extra columns on the right are just background. For each output row, take that row from the square block and place beside it the corresponding row from the same block read upside-down (top pairs with bottom, second with second-from-bottom, and so on), creating a double-width strip. Repeat this horizontal strip across the full output, so the result is a repeated tiling of each row paired with its vertically mirrored partner.

The grid is built from identical vertical background blocks placed side by side, with two example blocks containing the same foreground shape at two different vertical heights. The output extends the grid horizontally by repeating the whole background block pattern enough times so that the shape can appear in a step-by-step sequence: starting with the lower instance, then shifting upward by one row in each successive block, and ending with the higher instance. The bottom footer band is extended in the same repeated-block way, including the small boundary markers at the end of each block.

The input contains a single solid rectangular block of the non-background color inside a uniform background. The output places three panels side by side: the left and right panels are unchanged copies of the original input, while the middle panel replaces that rectangle with a centered diagonal/diamond-like version of the same block, as if the rectangle were rotated into a 45-degree isometric face. The rest of every cell remains background, and the canvas can be made taller if needed to fit that middle slanted shape.

The input is divided into horizontal bands of equal height. The upper band(s) are distractors: they have a main fill color with scattered stray cells of another color, while the bottom band is the clean pattern, consisting of one dominant color and a single contrasting cell near the right edge of each row. The output crops away all distractor bands and keeps only this lowest clean band, preserving its exact row shapes and any background padding.

The input contains one narrow capped strip near the top (a row of the fill color bracketed by the marker color at both ends) and several larger vertical bars lower down, where each bar is made of stacked fill-color rows sitting above a solid marker-color base row. The output keeps only the tallest of those lower bars, but increases its height by one row to account for the top capped strip. It then redraws a single compact figure: the enlarged fill-color rectangle, followed by one empty row, the full marker-color base row, and one more empty row.

The input is made of several vertically stacked copies of the same 6-row pattern: a uniform background band with the same small marked cells in the same positions in its middle two rows, but each copy uses a different background color. The output collapses these repeats into one single 6-row block, keeping the marked middle two rows from the top copy exactly as they are. The other four rows of that block are replaced by the plain background color from the lowest copy, and all extra repeated sections are discarded.

The input contains four small foreground bars of the same color: two horizontal pairs and two vertical pairs, arranged around one implied central cell in a pinwheel-like pattern. In the output, that foreground color expands to fill the entire grid, and the only cell left as background is the single center cell indicated by the arrangement of those four bars. In other words, the sparse markers are used only to locate the special central background cell; everything else becomes foreground.

The output is made by stacking four versions of the input vertically. The right-side separator column and trailing block stay unchanged in every copy, while the left main field keeps its original content in the first panel and is recolored with three different background fills in the next three panels.
Across those lower three panels, the tall object made of the same non-background color is shifted downward by 1, then 2, then 3 rows (wrapping to the top if it goes past the bottom), while the single distinct marker is shifted right by 1, then 2, then 3 columns. If that marker would move into the fixed separator area, it is no longer shown there.

The output is a 2× enlargement of the input in both width and height: the background, the bottom full-width stripe, and the interior horizontal bar are all expanded so each input cell becomes a 2×2 block. The small marker object near the upper-left is not enlarged in place; instead, its color is used to draw a filled isosceles triangle directly below the enlarged horizontal bar, centered on that bar. The triangle starts with a single-cell apex on the first row under the bar and grows by one cell to each side per row until it reaches the row just above the enlarged bottom stripe.

The input consists of several equal-sized subgrids arranged side by side, separated by single vertical divider columns. The transformation discards all divider columns and all earlier subgrids, and copies only the rightmost subgrid as the output. Everything inside that last panel is preserved exactly, including the upper area with scattered colored objects on a dark background and the lower area with marker cells on a lighter background.

The picture consists of full-width horizontal bands: a large background region on top and several solid-colored stripes at the bottom.
