The output keeps the same height and the same top-to-bottom order of bands, but stretches the grid horizontally by a factor of five. In effect, each input column is repeated five times, so every horizontal stripe becomes five times longer while nothing changes vertically.

The single framed rectangle is turned into a much wider banner by repeating its horizontal structure five times side by side, so the output width is five times the input width. A new empty/background-colored band two rows tall is added above, while the rectangle’s original top and bottom border rows become the top and bottom edges of the long strip below. In the middle of the strip, the central join is emphasized: the double border there is preserved, and the interior column immediately to its left and the interior column immediately to its right are changed to the new background color, forming two vertical slits.

The input is divided by the frame color into three separate small pictures placed side by side, all inside the same outer border. The output is a single one of these framed pictures: the version where the two non-background colored regions make the clean, consistent shape, while the other two panels are flawed variants with one colored piece shifted or malformed. In other words, crop out the correctly arranged panel and keep its frame unchanged.

The output is made by placing several full-width panels side by side, with one panel for each small marker cell scattered in the input. In every panel, the fixed scene (top strip, bottom strip, large solid block, and other unchanged cells) is repeated, but the small accent-colored motif is copied only once and moved so that its own reference point lands on one chosen marker location; when it overlaps other objects, it overwrites them. The panels are ordered by the marker positions in reading order, and the other marker cells are not kept as standalone dots.

The grid contains two similar large block-like structures near the bottom, each with a row of support marks above a solid rectangular body. In one structure, the support row contains a distinctive horizontal 3-cell support segment, while the rest of the supports are isolated single marks. The output copies the position of that distinctive 3-cell segment to the other structure at the same relative horizontal offset, but recolors it with a new highlight color; all other cells stay the same.

The bottom border/floor and the existing upper marker piece and lower multicolored cluster stay in place. The remaining isolated shape is removed from its original location and placed directly beneath the small upper marker, horizontally centered under that marker (using the leftward option when centering is uneven). It is lowered to occupy the space between the marker and the lower cluster, and if it is taller than the gap, it continues downward and overwrites the top part of the lower cluster; its old location is cleared to background.

The input is a wide canvas split into three equal vertical sections, each containing a small figure made from the non-background color on a uniform background. The output keeps only the rightmost third of the image and discards the left two thirds. Nothing inside that retained section is altered: the figure and surrounding background stay in the same relative positions within that cropped panel.

The grid contains two matching rectangular chambers outlined by the same border color, with one small colored figure inside each chamber. In the output, the chamber outlines and all background cells stay unchanged, but the two inner figures are exchanged between the left and right chambers. Each figure keeps its own shape and fill pattern while being relocated to the other chamber’s corresponding position.

The output places three versions of the same square scene side by side on one row, so the height stays the same while the width becomes three times larger. The left section is the original pattern, the middle section is the whole grid turned a quarter-turn clockwise, and the right section is the whole grid turned a half-turn. The background stays empty, and only the foreground shape is reoriented within each equal-sized section.

The non-background area consists of four separate rectangular motifs that are all rotated versions of the same pattern. In the output, these four motifs are not edited internally; instead, they are reordered so their orientations follow a consistent rotation sequence based on the first motif: original orientation first, then the 90° counterclockwise version, then the 180° version, then the 90° clockwise version. The surrounding background and spacing stay the same, and only whole motif positions are swapped.

The output is made by placing three copies of the input side by side, so the height stays the same and the width is tripled. The left and right copies stay unchanged, while in the middle copy the unique region marked by the special object color is replaced inside its same bounding box by a centered, filled diamond/lozenge-like version of that object, ignoring the original interior pattern. Everything outside that object's box keeps the same repeating background pattern.

The wide input is split into three equal framed panels placed side by side, and the output keeps just one panel-sized frame. Start from the rightmost panel, then align all three panels on top of each other: every cell that is already part of the rightmost object stays unchanged, while any extra occupied cells contributed only by the other panels are added in using the object's common connector/body color. In effect, the output is the rightmost variant completed by the union of the other two variants, with preserved special details from the rightmost panel and the same corner markers/frame.

The grid has a large left background region, a large right background region, and a narrow stepped separator between them. Every patch of the special accent color embedded in that separator is shifted exactly one row downward, keeping its shape. The cells it vacates are replaced by the left/background color, and any small blank cutout cells associated with those patches are also filled with that same background color; everything else stays fixed.

The changing part is the large composite object: a solid block of one color with a contrasting blob cut into its left side. In the output, that contrasting blob is kept at its original position, while the surrounding main-color cells are removed from around it. If there is a separate small solid block to the right that overlaps the composite object's row range, the remaining main-color cells are shifted right as a unit until they abut that block; otherwise those main-color cells disappear entirely. All other isolated solid rectangles stay unchanged.

Each input is a horizontal strip of three repeated large base symbols, where the first two have the same small side attachment and the third has a larger version of that attachment. In the output, the strip is duplicated side-by-side to make the grid twice as wide, and in each 3-symbol group the middle symbol is specially marked by recoloring the crucial cell(s) of its side attachment with a new highlight color, while the rest of the base symbol stays unchanged. This produces a repeating sequence of small, highlighted-transition, and large versions across the doubled strip.

The non-background cells are single points that are treated as an ordered chain from left to right. Starting from each point, add a 45-degree diagonal heading toward the next point to its right: slope upward-right if that next point is higher, or downward-right if it is lower; these diagonals can continue to the border when there is no later point to stop them. The original points stay in place, and the output is the union of those original points plus the added diagonal links/rays.

The input is split into several equal-width vertical panels placed side by side. Each panel shows a similar small foreground pattern near the top, but on different surrounding fills; the correct panel is the one where that pattern appears on the plain empty background rather than inside a colored block. The output is that entire panel copied out by itself, with all its rows kept exactly as they were in the input.

The wide input is divided into three equal 10-column panels placed side by side, and the output is just one of those panels copied unchanged while the other two are discarded. The selected panel is the one containing the extra anomalous marker segment in a fourth color; if no panel has that marker, the middle panel is taken instead.

The input is a horizontal strip made of several equal-sized square panels placed side by side. The transformation cuts the wide grid into these consecutive square panels, preserving every cell pattern exactly, and then stacks the panels vertically in the same left-to-right order. No colors or shapes are changed; only the overall arrangement shifts from one long row of panels to one tall column of panels.

The foreground consists of several separate copies of a similar shape placed far apart horizontally, sometimes with slight vertical offsets. In the output, these copies are packed into a compact left-to-right strip, and comparison blocks are added for neighboring copies: the cells that would coincide between the two compared shapes are recolored with a new highlight color (different neighbor-pairs use different highlights), while cells belonging to only one of the two shapes stay in the original foreground color. As a result, offsets show up as original-color protrusions above or below the highlighted overlap.

The input is split into two equal-width panels separated by a blank column, and the output stretches this into four such panels separated the same way. The occupied pattern is reused across the strip: the small accent-colored pieces progress through accent color, then body color, then marker color, then back to accent color, while the large body shows the marker color spreading through it. The two middle panels are the new ones: first the marker color partially/alternatingly propagates through the connected body (with accent cells absorbed into the body color), and then the entire non-background figure is converted to the marker color; the rightmost panel shows the original unfilled coloring again.

The marked cells form the left part of a larger repeating chevron/diamond-outline pattern: equal-width horizontal sections contain the same diagonal V-shaped structure, shifted so the peaks step upward to the right. The output keeps the height the same, extends the canvas to the right, and continues this sparse pattern section by section until the full chain is completed. The background color stays unchanged, and only new cells belonging to the ongoing zigzag pattern are added.

Each input is a full-height field of one color with two thin vertical stripes of another color cutting through it. In the output, the grid is expanded horizontally, the left region before the first stripe is kept unchanged, and that first stripe’s color is extended all the way to the new right edge. As a result, the second stripe and the entire area to its right disappear into one large solid block of the stripe color.

The input contains a hollow rectangular frame on a uniform background, with two single-cell markers placed inside it on different rows. The output horizontally unrolls the scene into many side-by-side copies of the same background and frame rows, effectively making a time-strip of the box. Across these repeated copies, the two interior markers are advanced one step at a time along their rows in opposite horizontal directions, reflecting off the frame’s vertical sides, so their successive positions form bouncing trails while the rest of the structure stays unchanged.

The input contains several separate solid rectangles of one foreground color; they all represent the same dimensions, but some copies are rotated vertically while others are horizontal. The output discards the original arrangement and keeps only one canonical copy of this repeated shape, reoriented into its wider-than-tall form and moved to the upper-left of a new blank grid. All other copies and the empty space between them are removed, and the frame is resized around this simplified result.

The input is made of several horizontally repeated panels that share the same overall layout: a reference strip at the bottom and a small colored motif near the lower right, while some marker-colored cells move systematically from panel to panel. The transformation collapses these repeated panels into one shared frame by aligning the repeated motif structure, so the drifting marker cells from successive panels pile up into vertical runs in the composite image. Finally, everything outside this merged aligned content is discarded and the result is tightly cropped to the smallest bounding rectangle.

The input is divided into three equal-width vertical panels placed side by side, each panel containing a similar local scene or object arrangement. The output is just the leftmost panel, cropped out at its original height and width, while the middle and right panels are discarded. Nothing inside the kept panel is altered; only the overall frame is reduced to that first repeated section.

The grid contains a repeating set of equally spaced anchor objects laid out from left to right, plus scattered marker pixels of another color placed around those repeated positions. Keep the repeated anchor objects unchanged, but treat each anchor as starting a vertical section that extends until the next repetition (or the right edge for the last one). Recolor only the scattered marker pixels that fall inside the final, rightmost section from the marker color to the highlight color; all other cells stay the same.

The sparse foreground cells act like hints for larger solid blocks: when several foreground cells form a tight local pattern, they are expanded into the filled axis-aligned square/rectangular region suggested by that cluster, and overlapping filled regions merge. Foreground cells that are isolated or only form small nonqualifying fragments are discarded instead of kept. In the third example no cluster qualifies, so the whole grid becomes background.

Each example has a clean repeated header at the top, a clean repeated footer at the bottom, and a noisy middle section. The top rows define a horizontal template with a central solid band surrounded by background; in the output, the entire noisy middle is replaced by a perfect rectangle using the opposite occupancy of that template on every row, so the former central band becomes a background window and the side areas become solid. All scattered holes/noise inside the middle are removed, while the top and bottom zones remain unchanged.

The large block of panel-colored cells on the right acts like a mirror area. In the output, cells from the ordinary area immediately to the left of that vertical border are reflected horizontally into the panel, so shapes/colors near the border reappear as a left-right mirror inside the panel. Only non-background reflected cells are painted there; background reflections do not erase existing cells, and everything outside this right-hand panel stays unchanged.

The input is a tall strip made of several consecutive square subgrids, each with the same width as the whole grid. The transformation cuts these square panels apart and places them side-by-side from left to right, so the output becomes a wide strip with the same panels preserved internally and in the same top-to-bottom order. In the shown examples the drawings inside each panel stay unchanged during this retiling, except that in the first example the bottommost cell of the final panel’s vertical stem is additionally recolored as a special endpoint marker.

The input contains three separate copies/variants of the same symbol, all drawn in one foreground color and spaced apart horizontally. In the output, these three symbols are horizontally collapsed onto the same position (the leftmost symbol’s column range), keeping their original row offsets, and their pixels are combined by odd-parity overlap: a cell is kept if it is occupied by an odd number of the overlaid symbols. The shared central vertical spine of the overlaid figure is recolored to a second highlight color, while the other surviving pixels stay in the original foreground color, and the rest of the wide canvas is cropped away.

The wide input grid is divided into three equal vertical panels. The output is simply the leftmost panel, copied exactly at full height, while the middle and right panels are discarded. This preserves the alternating two-color background, any solid separator-colored bands that fall inside that left third, and the small embedded object that appears in that panel.

The picture is a 3×3 array of small glyph-like objects, with large blank gaps between the nine local frames. Each object stays in its same local frame, but it is redrawn into a different standardized bitmap pattern determined by the object's original color (the input color is acting as a code/instruction rather than being preserved as paint). After that, every frame is recolored with a fixed output color based only on its position in the 3×3 layout, while the background and overall spacing remain unchanged.

The output keeps the same height but tiles the entire input scene horizontally five times, so the patterned background/frame simply repeats across five side-by-side panels. The only changing object is the solid contrasting block: it is copied into each panel at the same internal column position, but its vertical placement follows a symmetric stepped offset across the five panels—original row in the 1st and 5th copies, one row lower in the 2nd and 4th, and two rows lower in the middle copy. Wherever this copied block lands, it overwrites the repeated background.

Find the two largest groups of non-background cells, treating diagonally touching cells as connected, and ignore the smaller stray single-cell noise. Crop each of those two groups to its own bounding box, then place the cropped shapes into a new canvas with their left edges aligned to the same column while keeping their original vertical offset relative to each other. The output is the overlay of those left-aligned shapes on the background, sized just large enough to contain both.

The tall input is a vertical stack of equal-height panels, each showing one small motif on a background and ending with a full-width separator stripe; the panels are split from one another by single blank rows. The output removes those blank separator rows and arranges the panels side by side in the same top-to-bottom order, without changing any motif details. Finally, the first panel is repeated once at the far right, so the horizontal sequence ends with a duplicate of the starting frame.

The input is divided into several equal-sized subgrids placed side by side, separated by single vertical divider columns of the empty color. Each subgrid contains the same background with a small colored figure, possibly at a different vertical position, and these subgrids are kept unchanged. The output removes the divider columns and stacks the subgrids vertically in their original left-to-right order, forming one tall grid.

The non-background content is a horizontal strip made of several small 3-row patterned blocks, separated by single background columns. The output widens the grid and appends one more block at the far right, after one background-column gap, using an exact copy of the leftmost block as the template. Everything else stays in the same rows and positions relative to the left edge, with only the new repeated block added.

The striped/tiled background is discarded: the whole grid is repainted to a single uniform fill color. Cells of the small accent color are turned into black only when that accent appears elsewhere in the same row or the same column; isolated single occurrences are erased into the fill instead. The diagonal chain of the other special color is also usually erased, except in the case where the whole chain stays inside one uninterrupted light-colored block, where that diagonal is preserved.

The solid horizontal divider rows split the grid into stacked panels, with the top panel containing the source shape made from the non-background drawing color. In the output, that source shape is copied into each lower panel as a different orientation: one panel shows it rotated 90° one way, the next shows the opposite 90° rotation, and the last shows a left-right mirror image. The divider rows and the plain background are unchanged, and each transformed copy stays confined to its own panel.

The whole grid is repainted to a single new background color, so the long diagonal trace and the separate compact shape made from the other foreground color disappear into the background. Any black cells are preserved exactly where they are, including the black cells embedded in that compact shape and the two black cells flanking the diagonal’s lower endpoint. The bottom-left 3-cell horizontal bar remains in place but is recolored, and the lone isolated cell near the bottom is also kept in place with a different recolor.

The input contains a single foreground drawing on a blank background, and the output makes the canvas three times wider to place three identical copies of that drawing side by side. Each copy keeps exactly the same shape and row/column structure as the original, but the left copy is recolored to one new foreground color, the middle copy to a second new foreground color, and the right copy keeps the original foreground color. The background stays unchanged everywhere else.

The whole grid is transposed: every cell is moved so that rows become columns and columns become rows. As a result, repeated framed motifs that were arranged side-by-side in the input become stacked top-to-bottom in the output, while motifs that were already symmetric keep the same internal appearance. The background stays background, and all colors and local shapes are preserved exactly, only their global orientation/placement across the canvas changes.

The output keeps the same height but expands the picture to three equal-width panels placed side by side, each panel based on the full input scene. The large shared structure/background is copied unchanged in all three panels, but the three small distinctive inner pieces arranged from left to right are revealed progressively: the left panel keeps only the left piece, the middle panel keeps the left and middle pieces, and the right panel keeps all three as in the input. Any omitted piece is replaced by empty background cells.

The wide input is composed of three equal square panels placed side by side. To make the output, align those three panels on top of each other and merge them cell-by-cell into one square: whenever any panel has a non-background cell at a position, that colored cell is kept in the output, and background remains only where all three panels are blank. The result is a single combined picture that preserves both non-background colors while filling in missing parts from the other panels.

The input is a horizontal strip of several equal-sized copies of the same small panel, all sharing the same outer structure and main filled region. These copies are overlaid into one output panel: keep the shared frame/base pattern, preserve the meaningful accent marks that appear in some copies, use other copies to fill in places that are blank or missing in a given copy, and ignore the scattered distractor marks in the extra noise color. In short, the output is the single clean consensus panel obtained by merging the repeated panels while discarding noise.

The grid is split into equal rectangular sections by one or more full-height divider columns, and those divider columns stay fixed. The entire contents of each section—including all shapes, colors, and the single special marker cell—are cyclically rotated one section to the left: each section is replaced by the section immediately to its right, and the original leftmost section wraps around into the rightmost section. Internal object geometry is unchanged; only which section each pattern occupies changes.

The picture is split into three equal subgrids by two vertical divider columns. Across these three panels, the same small multicolored motif is evolving from left to right: a four-cell hooked cluster and a separate two-cell pair, with each panel meant to show the corresponding step of one consistent motion pattern. The input panels may be missing one square of the motif and/or have the whole motif shifted slightly, so the output restores the absent square and repositions each panel’s motif so the three panels form a clean, regular left-to-right sequence.

The transformation takes every non-background cell and rotates the whole colored pattern 90 degrees counterclockwise around the center of the grid, leaving the background unchanged. At the same time, the colors are advanced one step backward through the fixed seven-color sequence that the motifs use, so each rotated cell changes to the preceding color in that repeating order. The result preserves the same shaped fragments and relative color progression, just turned and recolored consistently.

The grids are built from one motif shown in directional variants, with a special marker color sitting on one side of the motif (left, bottom, right, or top) and separator columns of that same color between panels. The output reorganizes this into a full set of four side-by-side panels, one for each of the four marker positions; if the input already contains three directional panels, the missing fourth orientation is added, and if the input is a single composite figure, it is split into those four directional versions. Within each panel, the temporary/filler color is removed while the motif’s main structure and accent cells are preserved in the cleaned directional form.

The whole input grid is duplicated horizontally several times to make a much wider grid, while keeping the same height. Each row is copied side-by-side five times in the same order, so the frame/wall pattern, openings, and empty regions repeat as identical vertical slices across the output. Because each copy keeps its own border, adjacent copies create paired wall columns where one copy’s right edge touches the next copy’s left edge.

The colored pattern is preserved exactly, but the canvas is widened to the right. The new width equals the original width multiplied by the number of distinct non-background colors in the figure (equivalently, the number of differently colored spokes/arms), while the height stays the same. The original grid is placed flush on the left, and all newly added columns are filled with background.

The output makes the canvas four times taller by stacking four versions of the same arrangement of glyph-like objects underneath each other. First comes the original image, and below it are the same colored objects transformed within their own local frames to show the other symmetries: a left-right mirror, an upside-down/180°-turned version, and the remaining vertical-reflection counterpart. The separator columns and the relative placement of the object groups stay the same; only each shape’s orientation changes.

The grid is split horizontally into two equal halves, containing the same kinds of objects: sparse foreground marks, one or more special marker cells, and full-width divider bands. The upper half stays unchanged, while each row in the lower half is circularly shifted sideways, starting just below the midline with a 1-cell shift to the left, then 1 to the right on the next row, then 2 left, 2 right, and so on as you go downward. These shifts wrap around the row edges, so all colors in those rows move together, including the divider bands and special markers.

The input is split into several equal-width horizontal panels placed side by side, each panel containing a slightly different or incomplete copy of the same foreground shape on a blank background. The output keeps only one panel’s size and overlays all copies onto that single panel, marking a cell as foreground if any corresponding cell in the repeated panels is foreground. In other words, the repeated motifs are merged by position-wise union, producing one consolidated version of the shape.

The input is a single-color pattern made by overlapping several separate line-like shapes/strands into one composite drawing. The output untangles this overlap: it creates one full-size panel for each hidden strand, keeps that strand alone in its own panel, and concatenates those panels horizontally so the height stays the same while the width becomes a multiple of the original. The recovered strands are arranged in a consistent left-to-right order based on their placement in the original figure.

The output is made by stacking four versions of the same central figure vertically on one canvas. In every copy, the figure keeps its main body shape and top-center tip, but the two isolated outer marker pixels are lifted to the row above the body and then move one step farther outward in each successive copy. At the same time, the short bar at the bottom grows wider by one cell on both left and right per copy, and the interior vertical accent on the right side of the figure becomes longer, creating a step-by-step expansion from the first copy to the last.

The input contains several identical 2×2 colored blocks arranged in a horizontal repeating pattern above two full-width horizontal bands. The output removes the lowest full-width band, keeps everything above it unchanged vertically, and crops horizontally to just the final repeat-sized segment at the right edge. As a result, the output shows the rightmost occurrence of the 2×2 block with the same surrounding blank cells it has inside one repetition, plus the upper solid band still spanning the new width.

The grid contains a vertical sequence of small non-background motifs placed at evenly spaced row intervals. The output keeps the original sequence and then extends the canvas downward by continuing the sequence as a mirror image around the lowest existing motif: each earlier motif is copied below it at the same spacing, with the same shape and same columns. In other words, the ordered list of motifs becomes vertically palindromic, while the background remains unchanged elsewhere.

The output is made by placing four same-height copies of the slanted lattice side by side, so the width becomes four times larger. The lattice/connector color stays in place, but the colored symbol cells are split into two alternating parity groups: copies 1 and 3 show only one group, while copies 2 and 4 show the complementary group, with symbol locations from the hidden group turned back into connector-color cells. Across the four copies, the visible symbols pass through a fixed four-color rotation, advancing by 0, 1, 2, and 3 steps respectively.

The output is made by placing four horizontal copies of the entire input grid side by side, keeping the same height and repeating all background and shape positions exactly. The 1st and 4th copies stay unchanged, while in the 2nd and 3rd copies only the solid top cap/band of the main figure is recolored to a new accent color; the lower traced pattern and the background remain the same. In short, the row of copies follows an original–recolored–recolored–original pattern.

The input is a wide pattern of vertical stripes made from one solid color and narrow gap columns, where almost all rows share the same spacing but one row has its gaps shifted, creating a unique row. The output compresses this to a 3-column summary with the same height: the first column is entirely the gap color, the second column is entirely the solid stripe color, and the third column marks row type. In that third column, the odd shifted row keeps the solid color, while every normal repeated row is changed to a highlight color.

The transformation keeps every object exactly where it is and preserves all shapes, holes, and disconnected clusters; nothing is moved, resized, added, or removed. It simply remaps the two non-background foreground colors: the larger structural color used in blocks and patterns is changed to one new color, and the smaller marker/accent color is changed to a different new color, while the background and the dark empty/path color stay unchanged.

The grid contains several parallel vertical columns of a dark line color, with small same-colored marker pieces above and matching small blocks near the bottom, all on a uniform background. In the output, those existing structures stay in place, and a new horizontal bar of a new highlight color is drawn across the midpoint row of the vertical columns. This bar runs continuously from the leftmost vertical column to the rightmost one, overwriting whatever was on that row inside that span.

Each input has a small 3-by-2 block above a small 2-by-2 marker, with a long horizontal bar farther below. In the output, the upper block’s color takes over the lower marker and the space between them, growing into a larger hanging shape positioned above the bar: a 3-cell-wide vertical section that starts one row higher than before, plus a 5-cell-wide base in the two rows immediately above the horizontal bar. The long bar and the background stay unchanged.

The output triples the grid’s width by placing three same-sized panels side by side. The left and right panels are exact copies of the input, while the middle panel is the same pattern shifted downward by one row, so its top row becomes background and every other row shows the row that was directly above it in the input. All marked cells keep their shape and relative horizontal positions; only this panel duplication and vertical offset change.

Each input has several copies of the same main motif drawn in the dominant color: a plain reference copy near the top, a larger middle copy that contains one auxiliary color, and a lower copy that contains another auxiliary color. The output keeps the original picture as the first panel, then stacks more full-size panels underneath where the auxiliary-colored subpatterns are transferred onto the other matching motif copies, respecting their placement and orientation while leaving the dominant-color outlines unchanged. The result is a vertical catalogue of the original scene plus the different motif-variant combinations generated from those shared shapes.

Each input contains one large solid rectangular area in a dominant color, with smaller differently colored patches embedded inside it. The transformation removes all of those interior patches and restores the whole rectangle to a uniform fill of its surrounding dominant color. Everything outside that large rectangle stays unchanged.

The input is divided into several equal-sized vertical panels, separated by single blank delimiter columns. The transformation removes those blank separator columns and rearranges the panels by stacking them vertically in left-to-right order: the left panel first, then the next panel beneath it, and so on. Each panel’s internal pattern is copied exactly, including its background, main shape color, and any contrasting marked cells.

The non-background cells form a row of equal-width vertical tiles, each tile containing the same kind of figure made from a main body color plus accent-color details, and often marked by a single accent pixel near the bottom. The output widens the canvas to the right by adding more whole tiles of the same width. These added tiles continue the existing horizontal repetition/sequence of tile patterns exactly, preserving all internal shapes, colors, and spacing.

The non-empty part of the input is divided into several equal-sized panels placed side by side, separated by blank columns; the output keeps only a single panel-sized grid in the same vertical position. For each cell position, compare the corresponding cells across all panels: if every panel has the same color there, that color is copied to the output, and if they disagree, the cell is replaced by the task’s default/base color. Any blank area above the panels stays blank.

The output stretches the scene into four equal-width panels placed side by side. In every panel, the fixed structure—the vertical post, the horizontal bar near the bottom, and any other non-marker objects—is copied unchanged, but the sparse marker-colored cells are treated specially: they appear in the first panel exactly as in the input, disappear in the second and fourth panels, and in the third panel reappear as the same pattern rotated 180 degrees around the top cell of the vertical post.

The output turns the single input scene into a horizontal strip of five equal-size panels, each panel having the same height and width as the input. Across these panels, the simple fixed structure stays unchanged in place, while the distinctive asymmetric multicolored shape is shown in successive quarter-turn orientations, producing an animation-like sequence: original pose, rotated poses through a full turn, and then the original pose again at the end.

Treat the input as an ordered stack of colored horizontal strips with a staircase-shaped background indentation on the left, and first drop the first two background columns to make a base strip pattern. The output is a 3-by-4 tiling of this reduced pattern, preserving the same row order and colors in every tile. From tile to tile, each row pattern is cyclically shifted one step to the right (wrapping around), so the background gap in the strips drifts diagonally across the larger mosaic.

The grid is made of several identical blocks stacked vertically, with the blocks alternating which of two non-background colors is used for the side bars and small interior features; the full-width horizontal stripe stays in the same stripe color. The output keeps only one block (the top block’s shape and size), preserving all empty cells and the horizontal stripe position. Then every non-empty cell other than that horizontal stripe is recolored to the alternate color seen in the swapped copies below.

The grid is built from a diagonally repeating three-color cycle, interrupted by vertical blank separator columns. In the output, a new blank column is added at the far left, and every existing blank separator is widened from one column to two columns. The colored cells are then readjusted to keep the same underlying diagonal three-color repetition relative to their new positions, so each nonblank strip keeps its shape and size but its visible phase shifts because it has moved right.

The wide input is made of several equal-width horizontal panels placed side by side; the output compresses these repeated panels into a single panel of that width while keeping the full height. To do this, align the panels on top of each other and merge them cell-by-cell: background stays background unless any panel has a foreground color there, in which case those colored cells are copied into the single panel. So the result is one representative block containing the union/overlay of all repeated side-by-side copies.

Each input contains three foreground objects on a plain background: a single cell, a solid 2×2 block, and a 7-cell open 3×3 frame-like shape whose orientation may vary. The output ignores their original placement and normalizes them into a fixed horizontal layout in a larger grid: the single cell first, then the 2×2 block, then the open 3×3 shape rotated/reflected into one standard orientation. After that, the medium and small objects are repeated on the right, creating a symmetric size pattern centered on the standardized largest shape.

The non-background cells are clues on a diagonal checkerboard lattice for a larger 45-degree-rotated diamond/lozenge shape. In the output, that full symmetric diamond is reconstructed by extending and mirroring the given diagonal fragments, and all missing alternating positions inside it are filled with the main non-background color. The other non-background color marks the special internal spine/branch cells indicated by the input, so the result is a completed diamond with a highlighted inner structure.

The two matching vertical lines and the bottom horizontal bar define an open-topped rectangular interior. The cell above the bar is extended straight upward in its own color until the top of the grid, while the other interior seed cell is extended horizontally to the right in its own color until it reaches the opposite vertical border. At the crossing point of these two new lines, a distinct junction color is placed, and the original bottom bar is removed.

The output is formed by placing three copies of the whole input grid side by side. The left and right copies stay unchanged, while the center copy is the input flipped vertically (top-to-bottom), so every row order is reversed but the columns stay in the same order. This preserves all background, border/frame cells, and colored shape details exactly within each copy.

The input is a row of small candidate panels separated by vertical blank divider columns, each panel having a colored footer strip on its bottom row. Use the footer color of the far-right panel as the target class, then scan the panels from left to right and find the first panel whose main figure is a completed, intact version drawn in that same class color rather than an empty or partial version. The output is that whole panel alone, cropped out with its original height and width.

The grid contains a centered stack of concentric square rings on a uniform background, with a single central cell or tiny innermost region. The shape, size, and position of all rings stay the same, and the background outside the figure is unchanged. Only the ring colors rotate cyclically: each ring takes the color of the next layer closer to the center, and the original outermost ring color is moved into the center.

The non-background cells come in two foreground colors, and each color’s full pattern is flipped by 180 degrees inside its own tight bounding rectangle. The background stays unchanged, so the effect is that each colored figure is turned upside down and reversed in place rather than moved to a new region. When the rotated results would land on the same cells, the solid foreground shape remains visible and some cells of the other foreground color can be lost/hidden.

The background and the small corner marker stay unchanged. The two identical accent-colored side clusters keep their shapes, but the left one is moved down by one row while the right one is moved up by one row. The tall central rectangle of the third color is then reshaped into a short horizontal band, placed around the middle of its former position and stretched sideways to fill the gap between the left and right clusters, stopping just before they touch.

The input is a vertical stack of identical hollow square/rectangular panels: each panel has a solid border color around an empty interior, and adjacent panels touch through an extra full border-colored separator row. The transformation extracts one such panel and repeats it horizontally as many times as there were stacked panels in the input. The output is therefore a single row of the same framed panel copies placed side by side, preserving the original border and interior colors.

The input contains a single foreground bent line/polyline on an otherwise empty grid. The output keeps that shape and adds three more copies of it, rotated by 90°, 180°, and 270° around the center of the canvas, so the same line appears in all four cardinal orientations. The background stays unchanged, and the result is a rotationally symmetric arrangement of the original path.

The large grid is partitioned into three equal vertical panels, and the output is the final panel isolated from the rest. Its internal color regions and embedded shapes are preserved as the result, while the first two panels serve only as context and are discarded. In the example where the last panel has no real structure beyond a plain field, the output keeps just that plain background.

The grid is compressed horizontally by deleting every column where the second row contains the background color instead of the stripe color. Equivalently, the broken stripe in the second row is turned into one continuous strip by removing its gaps, and the top and bottom background rows shrink by the same column deletions. Any small symbols in the third row are carried along in order, so their shapes stay the same but their horizontal positions shift left as the gap-columns are removed.

Each input contains a cross-like figure: a vertical line in one non-background color, and on one row a short horizontal band that includes a contrasting central segment. In the output, that figure is completed to the grid borders: the vertical line is extended all the way to the top and bottom, and the horizontal row is extended all the way to the left and right edges. Along this full-width row, the center becomes a larger continuous block of the contrasting color, while the outer parts stay in the original line color; the lone isolated marker cell is left unchanged.

The input grid is split into three equal square sections placed side by side. The transformation extracts the rightmost square section and discards the left and middle sections. In these examples, that kept section is the one containing the larger open-top frame/U-shaped figure, and its contents stay in the same positions within the cropped square.

The input is a vertical stack of several 4-row scenes, separated by solid horizontal bands of one uniform separator color. Each scene contains scattered marker pixels plus a small multicolored motif; the rule is to select the first scene whose motif has a vertical spine (top special cell above bottom special cell) and, across its middle, a left special cell followed by two adjacent right-side special cells. The output is just that 4-row scene, cropped together with the separator band directly beneath it.

Each input is divided into several equal-sized pattern blocks placed side by side, and those blocks are then superimposed cell-by-cell to make one output grid of the shared block size. The output encodes overlap structure: background stays empty, positions where exactly three blocks contain a filled cell are highlighted with a special color, and other filled positions are shown as the ordinary occupied color; in the 3-block example, cells occupied by only one block keep that block’s own color while 2-way overlaps use the overlap color. In short, the task compresses multiple aligned shapes into one grid that summarizes which locations are unique and which are multi-way overlaps.

The input is split into several equal-width vertical panels, indicated by identical paired marker cells along the top; the output keeps the size of just one such panel. Within each panel, ignore both the top marker color and the bulky interior filler color, and align the remaining two meaningful colors from all panels on top of each other cell-by-cell. The result is the union of those surviving pixels: if any panel places the dominant accent color at a cell, that color is used there; otherwise, if any panel places the secondary accent color there, that one is used.

The output is formed by placing two equal-width panels side by side. The left panel is the original grid unchanged, and the right panel is a copy of the original in which the two non-background colors exchange roles while the background stays the same. Thus every stripe, dot, and embedded shape keeps the same geometry and row/column placement in the added right half, but its two foreground colors are swapped.

Each grid contains a single vertically symmetric composite figure made from two interlocking non-background layers: an outer enclosing shell and a more central/core pattern. The output keeps the figure in the same place and with the same overall silhouette, but redraws it using a standardized role-based coloring: cells belonging to the outer shell are changed to one output color, while cells belonging to the inner/core structure are changed to the other. When the two layers touch or merge, cells are reassigned by whether they function as outer boundary versus inner motif, not simply by their original color.

The wide input is divided into three equal vertical panels, each containing part of the foreground pattern on the background. The output is made by taking those panels from left to right and stacking them vertically from top to bottom, preserving each panel exactly. No cells change color; only the layout changes from a horizontal strip of panels into a vertical column of panels.

The input is split into several equal-width vertical panels arranged side by side; each panel contains the same central marker column, and the first panel may also contain extra colored shapes while later panels can be mostly blank. The transformation reorders these panels from a horizontal strip into a vertical stack, keeping each panel’s contents unchanged. In other words, the wide grid is cut into repeated blocks and those blocks are placed one under another in the same left-to-right order.

The output removes all stray marker colors and keeps only the background plus the two structured object colors: the horizontal band segments and the scattered diagonal/clustered trail segments. Any cell in a band that was occupied by some other color is turned into background, leaving a band with holes rather than restoring the band color. Likewise, any non-trail color mixed into or near the trail pattern is erased, so the result is a cleaned grid containing only the original band cells, the original trail cells, and background.

The input consists of several identical square picture panels placed side by side, with each copy separated by a single vertical divider line in a different color. The transformation removes the divider columns and all duplicate copies, keeping just one of the repeated panels as the output. The remaining panel preserves the foreground pattern exactly, with the background unchanged.

The input contains a large block-like object on the left in one dominant color and a small mixed-color patch on the right. In the output, the left object is replaced by a fixed multicolor motif that occupies the vertical mirror of the original left object’s footprint: the missing corner moves from bottom-left to top-left, and the cells inside this mirrored shape are recolored in a specific standard arrangement. The right patch is cleared away, except that the one cell in the same dominant color is preserved at its original position.

The input contains two aligned solid shapes of different colors, one above and one below, facing each other along the same vertical centerline. In the output, the occupied silhouette is preserved as the union of those two shapes, but it is recolored by a vertical split: every filled cell to the left side becomes the lower shape’s color, while the center column and everything to its right become the upper shape’s color. This turns the stacked pair into one single left/right two-colored figure.

The input is split into adjacent 7×7 panels laid out horizontally across the same 7 rows. Each panel shows the same central object in the same relative position, but only some of the border cells of that 7×7 picture are present in each panel. The output is formed by overlaying all panels onto one 7×7 grid, keeping every non-background cell at its aligned location so the scattered top, bottom, left, and right edge pieces combine into one complete image.

The top and bottom rows form an unchanged frame/template and stay exactly the same in the output. Only the middle row is modified: its sequence is shifted one cell to the right with wraparound, so the rightmost middle-row cell moves to the far left and all other middle-row cells move one step right. No colors are recolored; only the positions within the center strip change.

The grid contains several repeated outline-shaped symbols drawn in one foreground color on a uniform background, plus small marker blocks in a second color near the bottom. One of the repeated symbols is slightly damaged: a single background cell breaks its border where the other copies are continuous. The output repairs that defective symbol by filling in the missing foreground cell so it matches the intact copies, while leaving all other cells unchanged.

Each non-background object is copied one cell to the right while keeping its exact shape and internal pattern; the background stays unchanged, and any part pushed past the right edge disappears. At the same time, all non-background colors are relabeled by a fixed global substitution cycle shared by every example, so the same source color always becomes the same target color. Different objects do not merge or otherwise interact; they are all transformed independently by this same shift-and-recolor rule.

The grid is made of several one-cell-wide diagonals (parallel down-right stripes), with fixed gaps of background between them. In the output, every stripe keeps exactly the same cells and the whole layout stays unchanged, but the stripe colors are reassigned by following their left-to-right sequence through the shifting pattern: each stripe takes the color of the next stripe in that ordered list, and the last stripe wraps around to the first. So the transformation is a cyclic color shift across the diagonal stripes, not a movement of the stripes themselves.

Each grid contains repeated panels with a small motif centered on a vertical line of one color. Some panels already show the finished version of this motif, where the top and bottom horizontal strokes are a different surrounding color with the center cell left unchanged, while other panels show those same strokes incomplete, blank, or in the wrong color. The output copies the finished pattern to every occurrence: preserve the central line color, but fill/recolor the side cells of the top and bottom bars with the accent color so all panels contain the same completed symbol; all other objects remain unchanged.

The output is the input grid with its dimensions swapped: rows become columns and columns become rows. In other words, the whole monochrome rectangle is transposed across its main diagonal, so a tall narrow block becomes a short wide block while all cell colors stay unchanged.

The grid is mostly an alternating striped background of two main colors, with many isolated cells of other colors sprinkled into those striped rows. The transformation cleans the striped area by replacing every off-pattern cell with the correct background stripe color for its row, effectively restoring perfect alternating horizontal bands. The separate bottom row acts like a fixed footer/marker row and is left unchanged.

The tall input is composed of three vertically stacked, aligned copies of the same central figure. The output keeps only one copy-sized slice: it uses the lowest copy as the base pattern, preserving its normal figure cells and any special marked cells inside it. Then it compares the middle copy to that lowest copy, and any extra figure cells that appear in the middle copy but not in the lowest one are added as a new highlight color around the base figure.

The foreground pattern in the lower part of the input is really two same-sized square shapes placed side by side, overlapping in the middle column. The output combines these two shapes into a larger square of size 2n−1 by 2n−1 by using one shape as a stamp over the other across all foreground positions, marking the union of all translated placements. This turns the previously empty upper area into the offset-combination pattern of the two input shapes, rather than just moving or mirroring them.

The non-background cells appear in two separate horizontal bands, each band occupying exactly two adjacent rows. In each band, the sparse diagonal/staircase pattern is mirrored so that every small diagonal or zigzag reverses its slant within that same 2-row strip: what leaned one way in the input leans the opposite way in the output, with cells reassigned between the two rows accordingly. The bands stay in place and no new regions are created; only the orientation of the existing colored point patterns is flipped.

The input consists of two equal-sized rectangular pattern blocks stacked vertically: an upper block and a lower block. The output is built row-by-row by taking each row from the upper block, then appending the corresponding row from the lower block, then appending the same upper-block row again, so the height becomes that of one block and the width triples. All colors and internal row patterns stay unchanged; only the arrangement changes from vertical stacking to a horizontal left-center-right composition.

The input is divided into equal-width vertical panels, each panel containing a small pixel pattern made from a dominant background color and a secondary shape color. The output keeps all original panels unchanged and appends one more panel on the far right that is an exact copy of the leftmost panel. In other words, the whole image is extended horizontally by repeating the first tile at the end.

The whole input grid is copied unchanged and stacked vertically multiple times to make a taller output. Specifically, the output keeps the same width and consists of five identical copies of the entire original scene, one directly below another, preserving the background and the positions/shapes/colors of the horizontal top bar, the vertical stem, and the lower horizontal bar within each copy.

The input is a long horizontal strip made of several equal-width panels; the output collapses it to a single panel-sized view, keeping the upper-left 2x2 block, the empty space, and the bottom floor in the same relative places while discarding the far-right marker stripe. The only content that is summarized across panels is the small 2-column motif near the bottom: its special two-color row is placed at the selected/dominant vertical level seen among the repeated panels, while rows that are just plain filler are kept only if they are not contradicted by a competing special placement. In other words, the repeated lower motifs are merged into one representative lower motif inside a single-panel crop.

The input contains one or more shapes in a special solid color, plus scattered clue pixels from a hidden repeating background. Reconstruct that background across the entire grid as a 5-color diagonal pattern: each rising diagonal has one uniform color, and adjacent diagonals follow a fixed repeating cycle inferred from the clue pixels. The special solid-color shapes stay exactly where they are, while every blank cell is filled with the appropriate background color.

The output keeps the same height but stretches the picture to three times the width by placing three horizontal panels side by side. The left and right panels are direct copies of the input, including the full-width empty separator rows. In the middle panel, the same filled-row pattern is repeated, but the vertical empty stripes are shifted sideways by one cell on different row bands, creating a slight zigzag/step continuation while the empty rows remain unchanged.

The grid has a fixed checkerboard background, and the non-background cells form one or more colored horizontal/near-horizontal objects. Each such object is removed from its original place and translated diagonally down-right by an amount determined by its own top-left corner: move it down by its top row index and right by its leftmost column index. After moving, the uncovered cells revert to the checkerboard pattern, and any part of an object that would go past the grid edge is simply cut off or disappears.

The grids contain a large framed field with a neutral interior, a decorative striped/checker overlay in a second filler color, and a small central symbolic structure made of other special colors. The transformation removes that decorative overlay entirely by changing every cell of the overlay color into the ordinary interior color. All other colors and objects, including the outer frame and the small central pattern, stay fixed in place.

The output places four horizontal copies of the scene side by side, each with the same height and with the right-edge divider column repeated at the end of each copy. In every copy, the large solid rectangular blocks are removed, and each short vertical 2-cell marker that had been aligned with a block is shifted to the block’s center-left column while staying on the same rows. The small isolated accent cells on the top/bottom rows are preserved in the same positions in all four copies, but their color alternates by panel: the 1st and 3rd copies use a new highlight color, while the 2nd and 4th keep the original accent color.

The wide input consists of multiple horizontal repeats or partial repeats of the same motif: a top rectangular block, a diagonal trail of single cells, a lower rectangular block, and a fixed 2-column strip on the right. The output removes the repetition by consolidating the repeated sections into one compact, cleaned version, preserving the stable colored object parts while discarding inconsistent stray cells and redundant blank spacing. In other words, repeated copies are merged/aligned so only the essential structure remains in a smaller grid.

Each non-background connected object is replaced by a solid rectangle covering that object's full bounding box. The rectangle is filled with a single highlight color, so any holes or missing corner cells inside the box are completed. If the bounding box has a unique center cell (odd height and odd width), that one central cell keeps its original color while every other cell in the box becomes the highlight color.

A solid vertical divider stands near the left side, and the non-background structure on its left forms an incomplete bent/staircase outline. Take the colored cells in the column immediately to the left of the divider and copy that ordered strip onto the open end of the shape, turning it 90 degrees so it becomes the missing continuation along the lower outer edge. Everything else stays unchanged, including the divider and all other colored cells.

The input picture is kept unchanged and placed flush against the left side of a wider output canvas. The canvas keeps the same height but its width is expanded to four times the original, and all newly added columns on the right are filled entirely with the background color. The framed shape and its single opening in the top edge stay exactly where they were within the original left block.

The grid contains a large global checkerboard made from two alternating background colors, but some parts of that pattern have been obscured by a plain masking color near the outer regions. The transformation restores the missing background by replacing every masking-color cell with the correct checkerboard color, continuing the existing alternation with the proper phase across the whole grid. The framed rectangular structure, its interior, and any special marker pixels or short colored segments inside it are left unchanged.

The grid contains a single foreground shape on an otherwise empty background, and the output preserves that original shape in place. A second identical copy of the same connected shape is added in the upper-left corner, without rotation or reflection. The new copy is positioned so that its bounding box is flush with the top edge and left edge of the grid.

The grid is split into several equal-sized side-by-side panels, each with its own dominant fill color but representing the same underlying picture. The output cleans each panel by correcting mismatched interior cells: stray accent/noise pixels that do not fit the shared motif are repainted to that panel’s dominant color, while the accent cells that belong to the common pattern are kept. Nothing is moved or resized; the transformation is a consistency-based cleanup across corresponding positions of the repeated panels.

The wide input is split into four equal subgrids placed side by side, and the output has the size of just one of those subgrids. For each cell position, keep a colored cell only if all four subgrids contain the same color in that exact position; otherwise replace it with background. In effect, the output is the exact positional/color overlap shared by all four small scenes, while all differing, shifted, or extra parts disappear.

Each grid contains a small cross-shaped motif and a nearby larger structure made of another color, sometimes with a special core cell. The transformation relocates the cross to the opposite side of that larger structure, as if the structure were a mirror or docking surface, so the cross becomes attached to / wrapped onto the structure instead of staying in its original place. The moved cross may overwrite some outer cells of the structure, but the special core cell(s), background, blanks, and unrelated objects remain unchanged.

The output is made by placing four copies of the entire input side by side, so the height stays the same while the width becomes four times larger. In each copy, the hollow rectangular frame and the vertical strip just outside its right side remain in the same shape, but the single distinguished marker cell is relocated to a different corner position around that framed structure. Reading left to right, that marker appears at the lower-right end of the outside strip, then the lower-left corner of the frame, then the upper-left corner, then the upper-right end of the outside strip; its original top-right position is no longer marked.

The output turns the single input canvas into a horizontal strip of five same-sized panels placed side by side. In each panel, every non-background object keeps its original color and row positions, but its occupied cells are redrawn as a fixed sequence of horizontal variants: the first panel is the original object, the middle panels show row-wise squeezed/side-shifted versions of the same shape, and the later panels return to the original-style placement. In addition, the top row gains two small paired markers in two new colors above the central-right panels.

Each puzzle is a 2-row strip that should follow a repeating 4-column cycle of vertical color-pairs; equivalently, the top row follows one fixed 4-color loop and the bottom row follows its matched 4-color loop with the same phase. The input shows part of this cycle correctly, but some positions are corrupted: a special column with the same filler color in both cells appears, and some later columns repeat an earlier pair instead of continuing the sequence. The output repairs the strip by continuing the established 4-step cycle across the full width, replacing filler columns and wrong repeats with the missing pair(s).

The grid is a row of identical token-shaped templates on a striped background; the template positions and all background/frame pixels stay the same, and only the token/body colors are changed. Across the row, collect the distinct token colors and rewrite them so they follow one fixed canonical cyclic color order that is consistent across all examples. Because there is one more token slot than distinct colors, the sequence is closed into a loop by repeating the first color again in the last slot, so the leftmost and rightmost tokens end up with the same color.

Inside the contiguous non-background rectangle, each row is moved one cell to the right with wraparound, so the far-right cell of that row reappears at the far-left edge. The rectangle is mainly made of a left-colored region and a right-colored region, so this shift moves their vertical dividing line one step right and wraps the rightmost color to the left border. Any cells belonging to the special horizontal stripe color are then kept in their original positions, so these stripe segments act like fixed obstacles while the other colors shift around them.

Each input contains several separated copies or partial variants of the same multi-color motif on a uniform background. The transformation keeps just one motif: it reconstructs the fullest/combined version by comparing the repeated variants, places that single completed motif at the location of the leftmost copy, and removes all the other copies so the rest becomes background. The output uses a blank canvas whose height and width are swapped relative to the input.

The output is a tall vertical filmstrip built from copies of the whole input. A special 2-cell vertical marker is treated as the moving object: the first block is the original scene, and each lower block repeats the entire picture but shifts only that marker one column to the right each time, wrapping to the left edge after the last column; all other objects and patterned rows stay fixed. If no such movable vertical marker is present, the extra block(s) below remain blank, so the original picture just sits at the top of a taller canvas.

The input is split into equal vertical mini-boards by a repeated border column, with each mini-board showing a later stage of the same falling/changing shape. The output keeps just one mini-board’s frame size and merges those stages into a single image: take the cells of the earliest-stage shape color from the highest mini-board, then mark newly added cells from the next lower stage with a first intermediate color, and newly added cells from the next lower stage with a second intermediate color. Any remaining cells that appear only as the final-stage color are kept as that final color, while the background, left border column, and bottom border row stay unchanged.

The input is split into two equal side-by-side halves that contain the same set of objects, but some matching objects are shifted between the two halves. The output keeps only one half-width canvas and preserves the parts that coincide when the two halves are compared cell-for-cell, leaving shared objects in their original locations. If a matching object exists in both halves but does not fully line up, a single intact copy of that object is also retained and placed into an otherwise empty area of the output.

The output is formed by vertically cropping the input to keep only its left portion: exactly the left half of the columns are retained, while the entire right half is discarded. When the input has an odd width, the center column is also omitted, so the result contains only the columns strictly left of the midpoint. All colors and patterns within those kept columns stay unchanged, including the large uniform lower background region.

The non-background cells form a row of equal-sized panels, each containing the same centered motif at successive stages of growth from left to right: a compact core, then a more expanded version, then an even more expanded one. The output reverses the order of these existing panels, and if the rightmost input panel is not yet the final growth stage, it also adds one new panel at the far left showing the next larger expansion of that motif. If the rightmost panel is already the largest possible version, only the reversed earlier stages are shown.

The top compartment contains a 4-by-5 reference motif: a shape made in one foreground color, with a few cells in that window instead occupied by the compartment/frame color. Each lower compartment begins as an empty 4-by-5 window marked only by a solid top strip, and the output completes that window by copying the same motif layout there: the foreground cells match the reference shape, while the remaining cells take the compartment’s strip color. From top to bottom, the four lower compartments use a fixed color progression for that strip/background fill—first a new color, then another new color, then the original strip color, and finally the foreground color itself—so the last copied panel becomes a solid block.

The output keeps the original height but expands the canvas to four equal-width panels placed side by side. In each panel, the same foreground object(s) stay in the same overall positions, but they are redrawn using their horizontal/vertical span structure: some panels reproduce the filled shapes, while the others keep only the extreme cells from those row/column spans, making sparser outline-like versions of the same forms. The background remains unchanged.

A large mostly empty grid is divided into equal horizontal or vertical sections by single marker cells of a third color placed at regular intervals along one outer edge. The meaningful two-color shape appears in the first section, and the output crops the grid down to exactly one section size, taken from the top-left of the input. The shape is preserved unchanged, while the section-boundary marker cell is turned into background.

The output keeps the full height of the input grid but removes all columns that are entirely background. In other words, it horizontally crops the grid to the minimal column span containing the non-background pattern, while preserving the rows exactly as they were. Any empty padding to the left or right of the object disappears, but empty rows above or below remain.

The wide input is made of several equal-width horizontal repeats of the same scene, so the output compresses it down to just one repeat-width while keeping the full height. Static items from the first repeat are kept in place, and the one marker that changes position from repeat to repeat is overlaid into that single panel relative to its fixed nearby anchor. Those overlaid positions are recolored with a fixed progression of trail colors, turning the repeated frames into a single snapshot that shows the marker’s motion path/order around the anchor.

Each input has a uniform background, a hollow rectangular corridor made of a second color, and a few small marker patterns in other colors sitting on or next to that corridor. In the output, the corridor itself disappears into the background, the canvas becomes four times taller, and the marker patterns are copied downward through the stacked bands as if the corridor had been unfolded into a perimeter path: the motifs keep their internal color arrangement while shifting and turning around the ring’s sides and corners. All other cells are filled with the background color.

The figure is preserved row-by-row, but it is redrawn on a wider background canvas with each successive row horizontally offset to the right by a repeating triangular/stair-step pattern: the offset increases by 1 for several rows, then decreases again, and repeats as needed. This makes formerly vertical foreground lines turn into diagonal or zigzag bands, while horizontal foreground rows remain horizontal segments. Extra background space is added on the right to contain the furthest-shifted rows.

The input is a wide grid made by repeating the same smaller scene side-by-side across the row direction. The output removes this horizontal duplication and keeps exactly one complete repeat unit, preserving all colors, shapes, and their vertical positions. In effect, it crops the image to a single fundamental tile of the repeated pattern.

Each input contains a layered, vertically centered motif whose upper part is already left-right symmetric, plus an extra downward-slanting continuation attached only on the lower-left side. The transformation removes that lower-left continuation and redraws the same continuation as its mirror image on the lower-right side, reflected across the motif’s vertical centerline. All colors keep their relative layered order, and the already symmetric upper structure stays unchanged.

The tall input is made of several equal-height horizontal frames stacked vertically; each frame contains the same rectangular inset region of one color, with a small 2-column highlighted block inside it, while a separate marker color outside the inset traces how the frame shifts from one step to the next. The transformation collapses these stacked frames into a single image whose height is one frame tall and whose width expands to cover the full horizontal drift indicated by the marker trail. The repeated inset content is stitched into one panorama, the extra exposed area is filled with the main outer background color, and the marker color itself is omitted.

The input is a tall grid made by stacking multiple vertical repetitions of a basic pattern; the repeating period is the same as the grid’s width. The output keeps only the topmost full period, i.e. the first square block from the top, preserving the small corner marker and the first solid inner rectangle exactly as they appear. Everything below that first repeated unit, including later copies and larger hollow shapes, is discarded.

The entire input image is repeated horizontally three times to form the output. Height stays the same, while the full row pattern—including background, borders, and every interior shape or hole—is copied unchanged and placed side by side. In other words, the output is the original scene followed by two identical duplicates to its right.

The input contains two 3-row patterns stacked vertically with a single full-background row separating them. In the output, that separator row is removed and the patterns are restacked as: the original top pattern, then the original bottom pattern, then a repeat of the original top pattern, preserving all colors and internal layout exactly.

The non-background figure made of the second accent color stays fixed, while every object of the first accent color is an upright T-shape that is transformed in the same way. Each such T is moved down by one cell and rotated 90 degrees clockwise, turning its centered vertical stem-and-bottom-bar pattern into a left-column stem with a middle horizontal bar extending right. If this moved rotated shape lands on cells of the fixed central figure, the transformed T takes those positions.

The single non-background figure is copied unchanged in shape, orientation, and color, and translated diagonally toward the lower-right of the grid. Nothing is added or removed from the figure itself; only its position changes, with the shape relocated into the lower-right region, typically slid southeast until it is as far that way as the layout allows.

The wide input is divided into three equal vertical panels of the same height, and the output keeps only a single panel-sized grid. For each cell position, compare the three corresponding cells across the left, middle, and right panels: if any color appears in at least two of the panels, that repeated color is written to the output. If all three panels disagree at that position, the output keeps the color from the left panel, so the result is a cellwise majority/consensus version of the three panels.

The input is divided into three equal-width panels placed side by side on the same background. Two panels are identical copies of the same pattern, while the third is a slightly altered version with some cells changed, added, or removed. The output keeps the full height but extracts only that mismatching panel, preserving its colors and layout exactly.

The grid contains one compact rectangular patterned block made from two alternating colors on an otherwise empty background. In the output, the left half of that block is recolored into a different pair of colors while preserving the exact internal stripe/checker pattern; the right half stays exactly as it was. If the block has an odd width, the middle column is included in the recolored left portion.

The grid contains several vertically separated versions of the same motif in different source colors; the answer keeps only the top section and redraws it in a single new color. Use the lower copies as the reference form: if the top copy already matches the full reference motif, copy it unchanged, but if the top copy is the smaller compressed version of that motif, replace it with the reference motif’s centered X-shaped inner core in the same top position.

Identify the main solid rectangle in a non-background color and ignore the small horizontal marker strip. Build a new grid with the same height as the input, but with width equal to five copies of the main rectangle’s width (equivalently, one plus the marker length times that width). In the output, the main rectangle’s color becomes a full-height vertical band placed flush against the left edge, and everything else is filled with the background color.

The unique special marker at the left end of the top horizontal strip becomes the start of a new connector path. A new colored path is drawn downward through empty space; whenever continuing straight down would run into a lower horizontal strip, the path first goes right on the row just above that strip until it is just past the strip’s right edge, then continues downward. After passing all strips, the path goes right along the bottom row to the lower-right corner, and the original special marker is relocated there while its starting cell is recolored as part of the path.

The input is divided into several equal square panels stacked vertically, each panel containing the same border/frame pattern plus one interior symbol. The output rearranges those panels side-by-side from left to right in the same top-to-bottom order, turning a vertical strip of tiles into a horizontal strip. Within each panel, the border and background stay unchanged, while the interior symbol keeps its exact shape and placement but is recolored to a single common highlight color.

The grid keeps the left and middle regions essentially unchanged, but the uniform vertical band on the far right is rewritten: its plain background is recolored to a new fill color. Any non-background shapes that extend into that right band are not copied as solid blocks; they are simplified into a thinner remnant/trace, with only the part facing or continuing from the central special structure left visible while the rest of the band is converted to the new fill or back to the band’s old color. In particular, small square blocks in the right band are reduced to a single row, and long horizontal intrusions are thinned down inside that band rather than left thick.

The foreground cells form repeating diagonal or zigzag traces across the grid, sometimes as several parallel copies that can overlap. The output keeps the same width but expands the picture vertically to show a full unfolding of that repeating motion: it stacks all phase-offset versions of the row pattern, so the height becomes the square of the original height. Foreground positions are continued with the same relative shifts and periodic overlaps seen in the input, with coincident traces merging into single cells.
